title: The Puzzle Under Your Skates
text:
Every winter, millions of people slip on frozen pavements, and almost all of them blame the ice. Yet very few stop to ask a simple question: why is ice slippery at all? Most solid things are not. A dry wooden floor, a glass window or a smooth sheet of steel can be polished until it shines, but you can still walk across it without falling. Ice, on the other hand, seems almost anomalous. Remarkably, physicists have argued about the reason for nearly two hundred years, and even today the final answer is still being debated.

For much of the twentieth century, schoolbooks offered a neat explanation. When a skater stands on the ice, the books said, the thin blade presses down with enormous force on a tiny area. That pressure lowers the melting point of the ice, so a thin film of water forms under the blade, and the skater glides on water rather than on the solid. The theory was elegant, and it was based on real physics: pressure does lower the melting point of ice slightly. Unfortunately, when scientists finally did the calculations carefully, the numbers did not add up. The pressure from a skate can lower the melting point by only a degree or two, while people happily skate on ice at minus twenty or even minus thirty degrees. And the theory says nothing about why a person in flat shoes, whose weight is spread over a much larger area, also slips so easily.

A second idea replaced it, at least for a while. Perhaps, scientists suggested, the heat produced by friction melts the surface. When you rub your hands together they get warm, and a skate or a boot moving fast across the ice should warm it in the same way. This explanation has more support, and friction probably does play a part when a skater is moving quickly. However, it cannot be the whole story either, because ice is slippery even when you are standing perfectly still. Anyone who has stepped carefully out of a car onto a frozen car park knows this all too well.

The third idea is the oldest and, in hindsight, perhaps the most interesting. Around 1850, the great English scientist Michael Faraday noticed something odd. If he pressed two pieces of ice together, even in very cold air, they quickly froze into a single block. He suggested that the surface of ice is always covered by a very thin layer that behaves like a liquid, even well below zero. When two such surfaces touch, the layers join and then freeze. Many of his colleagues found this idea hard to accept, and it was largely ignored for more than a century.

Modern instruments, however, have lent credence to Faraday’s view. Using powerful microscopes and beams of light, researchers have found that the molecules at the very top of a piece of ice are not locked firmly in place as they are deeper inside. In the solid, each water molecule is held by its neighbours in a regular, crystalline pattern called a lattice. At the surface, the molecules have no neighbours above them, so they are held less tightly and can move around. This layer is extremely thin, only a few molecules deep in very cold conditions, and it becomes thicker as the temperature rises towards zero.

In 2018, a team in the Netherlands, led by the physicist Daniel Bonn, published experiments that added a further detail. They measured friction on ice at many different temperatures and concluded that the surface molecules seem to behave like tiny balls that roll around on the ice beneath them. These loose molecules, they argued, act rather like marbles scattered across a floor: they are not quite a liquid, but they make it very hard for a shoe to grip. Interestingly, the team also found that there is a temperature at which ice is ideal for skating. At around minus seven degrees, the surface is slippery enough for speed but still hard enough that the blade does not sink in. Ice rink managers, who had learned much the same thing by trial and error, were probably not surprised.

So which theory is correct? The honest answer is that several effects may work together, and their importance depends on the conditions. Friction heat matters for a fast skater, the loose surface layer matters for someone standing still, and pressure contributes a little. What is clear is that the simple story told in many classrooms does not stand up to scrutiny. It is a pleasing reminder that even the most familiar things around us can still hide unsolved puzzles. The next time you slip on an icy step, you may at least comfort yourself with the thought that you are taking part in one of physics’ longest-running experiments.

questions.q: Why is the pressure explanation no longer accepted as the main reason ice is slippery?
options: Faraday proved in the 1850s that pressure has no effect on ice
Skate blades are too wide to produce much pressure
Pressure lowers the melting point only slightly, yet people skate on much colder ice
Ice rink managers showed that pressure makes ice less slippery
questions.explain: Metne göre bir patenin basıncı erime noktasını yalnızca bir iki derece düşürür, oysa insanlar eksi yirmi otuz derecede de kayar. Doğru cevap ‘Pressure lowers the melting point only slightly, yet people skate on much colder ice’.

questions.q: What did the Dutch team suggest about the molecules on the surface of ice?
options: They roll around loosely, a bit like marbles, so shoes cannot grip well
They form a thick layer of real water at all temperatures
They become harder than the ice beneath them below minus seven degrees
They melt only when a skater moves very fast
questions.explain: Hollandalı ekip yüzeydeki moleküllerin altlarındaki buzun üzerinde bilyeler gibi yuvarlandığını ve ayakkabının tutunmasını zorlaştırdığını öne sürdü: ‘They roll around loosely, a bit like marbles, so shoes cannot grip well’.

title: The Boy Who Froze Hot Milk
text:
In 1963, a schoolboy in Tanzania named Erasto Mpemba was making ice cream with his classmates. The recipe was simple: boil milk, mix in sugar, let the mixture cool, and then put it in the freezer. Space in the freezer was limited, however, and Mpemba noticed that another boy was about to take the last place. Rather than wait for his hot mixture to cool, he hurriedly put it in while it was still hot. About an hour and a half later, he opened the door and found something that he could not explain. His mixture had turned into ice cream, while his classmate’s, which had gone in cold, was still a thick liquid.

When Mpemba asked his teacher why this had happened, he was told that he must have been confused. Hot water, everyone knew, could not freeze faster than cold water; it simply had further to go. A few years later, at secondary school, he raised the question again in a physics lesson and was laughed at by his classmates. His teacher reportedly joked that this was ‘Mpemba’s physics’, not the real thing. Many young people would have given up at that point, but Mpemba kept testing his idea with water in the school kitchen, and he kept getting the same result.

His chance came when a visiting physicist, Dr Denis Osborne from the university college in Dar es Salaam, gave a talk at the school. At the end, Mpemba asked him directly: if you take two containers with equal amounts of water, one at thirty-five degrees and one at a hundred, and put them in a freezer, why does the hot one freeze first? The physicist admitted that he did not know. Although he was doubtful, he promised to try the experiment himself. To his surprise, a technician in his laboratory found that the hot water did indeed freeze first under some conditions. In 1969, Osborne and Mpemba published a short paper together, and the strange result has been known as the Mpemba effect ever since.

Remarkably, the idea itself was far from new. More than two thousand years earlier, the Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote that some people warmed water before leaving it out to cool, because they believed it froze faster that way. In the seventeenth century, the English thinker Francis Bacon and the French philosopher René Descartes mentioned similar claims. Yet the observation had somehow been forgotten by modern science until a curious teenager brought it back to everyone’s attention.

Why might hot water freeze faster? Physicists have proposed a plethora of explanations, and each has some plausibility. Hot water loses some of its mass through evaporation, so there is simply less water left to freeze. Hot water also contains fewer dissolved gases, which may change the way ice forms. Inside a cooling container, warm water circulates more strongly, carrying heat to the surface, a process called convection. A hot container may even melt the frost underneath it and sit in better contact with the cold metal of the freezer. Finally, cold water sometimes ‘supercools’, staying liquid well below zero before it suddenly turns to ice, and this seems to happen more often to water that has never been heated.

The trouble is that the effect is very hard to reproduce. Tiny differences in the shape of the container, the position of the thermometer or even the definition of ‘frozen’ can change the outcome. In 2012, the Royal Society of Chemistry in London held a competition for the best explanation and received over twenty thousand entries, yet no single answer settled the matter. A careful study published in 2016 went further, casting doubt on whether the effect exists at all in the form that most people imagine. When the researchers controlled every factor they could think of, they found no conclusive evidence that hot water reliably wins the race.

Whatever the final verdict, Erasto Mpemba’s story remains an inspiring one. He went on to study wildlife management and spent many years working to protect Tanzania’s wildlife, and he lived to see his name appear in physics textbooks around the world. His real contribution was perhaps less a new law of nature than a lesson in attitude. He trusted what he had seen with his own eyes, kept asking questions when others laughed, and reminded scientists that an unexpected observation deserves a second look rather than a dismissive answer.

questions.q: How did Osborne first react to Mpemba’s question?
options: He laughed and said it was not real physics
He immediately explained it with the idea of convection
He refused to discuss it because he was only a visitor
He admitted he did not know and agreed to test it, though he had doubts
questions.explain: Osborne cevabı bilmediğini kabul etti ve kuşkulu olsa da deneyi kendisi yapmaya söz verdi: ‘He admitted he did not know and agreed to test it, though he had doubts’. Mpemba’ya gülen kişiler sınıf arkadaşları ve öğretmeniydi.

questions.q: What does the text say about the Mpemba effect today?
options: It has been fully explained by evaporation alone
Scientists still disagree, and one careful study even questioned whether it really exists
The Royal Society of Chemistry proved it was false in 2012
It only works with milk and sugar, not with water
questions.explain: Metne göre yarışma da tartışmayı bitirmedi ve 2016’daki dikkatli bir çalışma etkinin gerçekten var olup olmadığından şüphe duydu: ‘Scientists still disagree, and one careful study even questioned whether it really exists’.

title: The Spoon That Never Rusts
text:
Open any kitchen drawer and you will probably find a knife, a fork or a spoon made of stainless steel. It is so ordinary that we rarely think about it, yet it is a small miracle of chemistry. Ordinary steel, which is mostly iron with a little carbon, begins to rust as soon as it meets water and air. Leave an iron nail in a wet garden and within weeks it is covered in orange flakes. A stainless steel spoon, by contrast, can go through the dishwasher thousands of times and still shine. The story of how this metal came about is partly an accident and partly the work of a stubborn, practical man.

The man behind it, Harry Brearley, was born in 1871 in Sheffield, a city in the north of England that had been famous for its knives and tools for centuries. His father worked in a steel factory, and Harry left school young, eventually finding work as a bottle washer in a laboratory. He learned chemistry largely by himself, reading at night and watching the older workers closely. By the early 1900s, he had become a respected expert on steel, and in 1908 he was put in charge of a new research laboratory run by two of the city’s biggest steel companies.

In 1912, Brearley was given a practical problem to solve. The inside of rifle barrels wore away quickly because of the heat and the hot gases produced when a gun was fired. He began to experiment with steels containing chromium, a hard, silvery metal that was known to make steel tougher at high temperatures. In August 1913, he produced a steel with roughly thirteen per cent chromium. It did not turn out to be especially useful for guns, but it had another, unforeseen property that he soon noticed.

To examine steel under a microscope, metal scientists first polish a sample and then treat it with acid, which reveals its inner structure. He found that his new steel stubbornly resisted the acid. A popular version of the story adds that he had thrown some failed samples onto a heap of scrap metal outside the laboratory, and that months later, while everything else in the heap had rusted, these pieces were still bright. Historians are not sure whether this detail is true, but it captures the surprise. Familiar with Sheffield’s knife industry, Brearley immediately thought of cutlery. Kitchen knives at the time were made of carbon steel, which had to be dried and cleaned carefully after every meal and was easily stained by vinegar or fruit juice.

Why does chromium make such a difference? The answer lies in a layer that is far too thin to see. When iron rusts, it reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide, a weak, crumbly material that falls away and exposes fresh metal underneath, so the corrosion continues. Chromium also reacts with oxygen, a process known as oxidation, but the oxide it forms behaves quite differently. It creates a smooth, tight film only a few millionths of a millimetre thick that clings firmly to the surface. This film is chemically inert and almost impermeable to air and water, so they cannot reach the iron. Even more remarkably, the film repairs itself. If you scratch a stainless steel spoon, the chromium in the newly exposed metal reacts with the oxygen in the air and the protective layer forms again within moments.

He was not the only person working on such metals. In Germany and the United States, other researchers developed similar steels at around the same time, and there were later arguments about who deserved the credit. The inventor himself had a difficult relationship with his employers, who were at first unenthusiastic about his ‘rustless steel’, and he eventually left the laboratory. Yet within a decade, stainless cutlery from Sheffield was being sold around the world, and the new metal soon spread to surgical instruments, kitchen sinks, chemical factories and buildings. Many modern stainless steels also contain nickel, which makes them even tougher and easier to shape. The shining top of the Chrysler Building in New York, completed in 1930, is covered in it.

Stainless steel is not completely indestructible. In seawater, or in contact with strong cleaning products containing chlorine, the protective layer can break down and small spots of rust may appear. For most everyday purposes, however, it has stood the test of time remarkably well. The next time you stir your tea, you might give a brief thought to Harry Brearley, the bottle washer who taught himself chemistry and gave the world a spoon that never needs polishing.

questions.q: What was Brearley originally trying to improve when he made the new steel?
options: Rifle barrels that wore away because of heat and hot gases
Kitchen knives that were stained by vinegar
Surgical instruments for hospitals in Sheffield
The roof of a famous building in New York
questions.explain: Brearley’ye 1912’de verilen sorun, ısı ve sıcak gazlar yüzünden çabuk aşınan tüfek namlularıydı: ‘Rifle barrels that wore away because of heat and hot gases’. Çatal bıçak fikri ona sonradan geldi.

questions.q: According to the text, why does stainless steel stay shiny?
options: It contains no iron at all, only chromium and nickel
It is polished with acid in the factory before it is sold
Chromium forms a very thin oxide film that blocks air and water and repairs itself
Its rust is orange but too thin for people to notice
questions.explain: Metne göre krom, havayı ve suyu geçirmeyen, çizilince kendini onaran çok ince bir oksit tabakası oluşturur: ‘Chromium forms a very thin oxide film that blocks air and water and repairs itself’.

title: Colours Nobody Painted
text:
Few toys are as cheap or as magical as a soap bubble. Dip a plastic ring into soapy water, blow gently, and a shining ball floats away, its surface swirling with pink, green, blue and gold. Children chase bubbles across gardens, and adults often find themselves watching too. Yet if you look at the liquid in the bottle, it has no colour at all. There is no paint in a bubble and no dye. So where do those brilliant colours come from?

The answer begins with the wall of the bubble, which is astonishingly thin. A bubble is a layer of water held between two layers of soap molecules, rather like the filling in a sandwich. The whole wall is usually only a few hundred millionths of a millimetre thick, a microscopic distance that is roughly the same size as a wave of visible light. This coincidence is the key to everything. When something is about as thin as the light that strikes it, light begins to behave in surprising ways.

When sunlight hits a bubble, some of it bounces off the outer surface of the wall. The rest travels into the thin layer of water, and some of that bounces off the inner surface and comes back out. So two reflections reach your eye, one slightly behind the other. Light travels as waves, and when two waves meet they can either strengthen each other or cancel each other out, depending on how well their peaks line up. You may have seen the same thing with ripples on a pond: where two sets of ripples cross, some spots rise higher and others become almost flat. Physicists call this interference.

Sunlight, of course, is a mixture of all colours, each with its own wavelength. For a wall of a particular thickness, the two reflections of blue light might cancel each other, while the two reflections of red light might add together. In that case, the spot looks red or orange to us. A little further along, where the wall is slightly thicker or thinner, a different colour wins. Out of a myriad of possible colours, the ones you see are therefore a kind of map of the bubble’s thickness, drawn by light itself.

This also explains why the colours never stay still. Gravity slowly pulls the water in the wall downwards, so the top of a bubble becomes thinner while the bottom becomes thicker. At the same time, air currents push the liquid around and evaporation steadily removes water. As the thickness changes, so do the colours, and you can see bands of colour sliding and swirling across the surface. Watch a bubble resting on a wet table and you may see the bands move slowly downwards over many seconds, like a sunset in miniature.

Just before a bubble bursts, something curious often happens. Its top turns dark, almost black, as if a small hole had appeared. In fact, the wall there has become so thin that the two reflections cancel each other for every colour at once, so almost no light comes back to your eye. The great Isaac Newton noticed these dark spots more than three hundred years ago. He studied the colours of soap bubbles carefully and described them in his book Opticks, published in 1704, although the full wave explanation came about a century later. For a physicist, the black spot is a harbinger: the bubble is now so fragile that it will probably vanish almost instantaneously.

Once you understand bubbles, you start to notice the same effect elsewhere. A thin film of oil on a wet road after rain glows with rainbow colours for exactly the same reason. The special coatings on camera lenses and glasses use carefully controlled thin layers to cancel unwanted reflections, and some banknotes use similar layers to make them harder to copy. Even so, the humble soap bubble remains perhaps the most beautiful demonstration of all. Its beauty is ephemeral, but it carries a lasting lesson: colour is not always a property of things themselves. Sometimes it is created, for a few fleeting seconds, by the shape of the space that light passes through.

questions.q: Why does a soap bubble show colours although the liquid itself has none?
options: The soap contains tiny amounts of coloured dye
Gravity separates the soap into layers of different colours
The sun heats the bubble unevenly, so it glows
Light reflected from the two surfaces of the thin wall adds up for some colours and cancels for others
questions.explain: Renkler, ince duvarın iki yüzeyinden yansıyan ışığın bazı renklerde güçlenip bazılarında birbirini yok etmesinden doğar: ‘Light reflected from the two surfaces of the thin wall adds up for some colours and cancels for others’.

questions.q: What does a black spot at the top of a bubble usually mean?
options: The bubble has become thicker at the top
The wall there is so thin that the bubble is about to burst
Dirt from the air has collected on the bubble
The bubble is reflecting the dark sky above it
questions.explain: Siyah leke duvarın orada çok incelip bütün renklerin birbirini yok ettiğini gösterir; baloncuk birazdan patlayacaktır: ‘The wall there is so thin that the bubble is about to burst’.

title: The Ring Left by a Coffee Drop
text:
Spill a drop of coffee on a kitchen table, leave it for an hour, and you will find something odd. The stain is not an even brown circle. Instead, it is pale in the middle and dark at the edge, as if someone had carefully drawn a ring around it with a pen. Most of us simply wipe it away without a second thought. But in the 1990s, a group of physicists at the University of Chicago decided that this ordinary mark deserved a proper explanation, and what they found turned out to be useful far beyond the kitchen.

The scientists, including Sidney Nagel, Thomas Witten and a young researcher named Robert Deegan, began with a puzzle. Coffee is a mixture of water and countless microscopic solid particles. As the water disappears, one might expect the particles simply to settle where they are, leaving an even layer. Why should almost all of them gather at the edge? Several obvious suspects were quickly ruled out. The effect was not caused by the particular chemistry of coffee, because the same rings formed with tea, with salt water and even with tiny plastic balls in water. It did not depend on the type of surface either, as long as the edge of the drop stayed in place.

The key, it turned out, was that last condition. When a drop sits on a table, its outer edge often gets stuck on tiny bumps and dirt on the surface, so the drop cannot shrink inwards as it dries. Meanwhile, water evaporates faster near the thin edge than in the thick middle, because the edge is more exposed to the surrounding air. Since the edge cannot move, the water lost there must be replaced, and the only place it can come from is the centre. As a result, a slow, steady current develops inside the drop, flowing outwards from the middle to the rim. This current carries the coffee particles along with it, like leaves on a stream, and leaves them at the edge. By the time the water is gone, nearly all the particles are packed into a thin, dark ring.

The team published their explanation in the journal Nature in 1997, and it quickly attracted attention. Part of the appeal was its simplicity: an everyday mystery solved with clear experiments and a little mathematics. But the paper also mattered because the coffee ring effect is a real nuisance in industry. Many modern technologies involve placing tiny drops of liquid on a surface and letting them dry. Inkjet printers do this with ink, and manufacturers do it when they print electronic circuits or apply thin coatings of paint. In each case, they usually want uniformity, and the coffee ring effect pushes the material to the edges instead, leaving uneven, patchy results.

For years, researchers searched for ways to stop it. In 2011, a team at the University of Pennsylvania reported a surprisingly simple trick. Instead of round particles, they used particles that were slightly stretched, shaped more like grains of rice than like balls. These longer particles tended to lock together at the surface of the drop, forming a kind of loose skin that resisted the outward current. When the drop dried, they were spread far more evenly. Other groups found that adding certain chemicals, or gently heating the drop, could also disrupt the flow.

Scientists have since turned the effect from an enemy into a tool. Because the ring collects particles so efficiently in one place, it can make a faint substance more detectable. Researchers have explored using it in cheap medical tests, in which a drop of a patient’s blood or saliva dries into a ring that concentrates the signs of disease at the edge. Others study the patterns left by dried drops of blood at crime scenes, or by drops of paint in works of art.

There is something charming about the fact that serious science can begin with a dirty coffee cup. The researchers in Chicago did not need expensive equipment for many of their early experiments; they had drops of liquid, microscopes and a great deal of curiosity. Their work is a case in point for a broader idea. The world around us is full of small, unnoticed puzzles, and the person who drew the first coffee ring, an inadvertent artist at some breakfast table long ago, had no idea that a mystery was hidden in it. Paying close attention to such puzzles can occasionally lead to discoveries that matter far beyond the kitchen.

questions.q: What causes the particles in a coffee drop to collect at the edge?
options: The particles are heavier at the edge, so they sink there
A chemical in coffee makes the particles stick to the table
Water evaporates fastest at the fixed edge, so a current from the centre carries particles outwards
The drop shrinks towards the middle and leaves particles behind
questions.explain: Kenar yerinde sabit kalır ve su en hızlı orada buharlaşır; kaybedilen suyu merkezden gelen akıntı tamamlar ve parçacıkları kenara taşır: ‘Water evaporates fastest at the fixed edge, so a current from the centre carries particles outwards’.

questions.q: Why was the coffee ring effect a problem for industry?
options: Printing inks and coatings dried unevenly instead of forming an even layer
Coffee stains damaged electronic circuits in offices
Factories could not remove coffee rings from their machines
It made medical tests too expensive to produce
questions.explain: Mürekkep püskürtmeli yazıcılarda ve ince kaplamalarda üreticiler düzgün bir tabaka ister, ama etki malzemeyi kenarlara iterek düzensiz sonuç verir: ‘Printing inks and coatings dried unevenly instead of forming an even layer’.

title: Same Room, Different Touch
text:
Here is a simple experiment you can try at home. Find a metal tray and a wooden chopping board that have been lying in the same room all night. Touch each with your hand. The metal will almost certainly feel colder. Now ask yourself which one actually is colder. Most people, trusting their senses, would choose the metal without hesitation. Yet a thermometer would tell a different story: after a night in the same room, both objects are at exactly the same temperature, with no perceptible difference between them.

This is one of the classic puzzles of physics teaching, and it reveals something surprising about our own bodies. Our skin does not really measure temperature at all, at least not in the way a thermometer does. What it senses is the flow of heat into or out of the skin. When heat leaves your hand quickly, the nerves in your skin report ‘cold’. When heat flows in, they report ‘warm’. Under most conditions this is a perfectly good guide, but in some situations it can be misleading.

The surface of your hand is usually at about thirty-three degrees, while the room might be at twenty. So whenever you touch anything in the room, heat flows from your hand into the object. The question is how fast. Metals are highly conductive: tiny particles inside them called electrons move freely and carry energy away very quickly. Scientists describe this as high thermal conductivity. When you touch the tray, heat rushes out of your fingers and spreads through the metal, and your skin, losing heat rapidly, sends a strong ‘cold’ message to your brain. Wood, by contrast, is a poor conductor and in fact a fairly good insulator. Heat from your fingers enters the surface of the wood and stays there, warming a thin layer under your skin. Very soon that surface is almost as warm as your hand, so the flow of heat slows down and the wood feels pleasantly warm.

The same idea explains many familiar experiences. A stone bathroom floor feels freezing under bare feet on a winter morning, while a rug lying on the same floor feels comfortable, even though both are at the temperature of the room. Carpets, wool and feathers feel warm partly because they trap air, which carries heat very badly. Woollen clothes do not produce heat of their own; they simply slow down the loss of the heat that your body produces.

Interestingly, the effect works in reverse when an object is hotter than your body. In a sauna, the air might be at eighty degrees or more, and so might every surface in the room. People sit happily on wooden benches, yet the metal nails holding those benches together can be painful to touch. Again, the temperature is the same; the difference is how quickly each material can pour heat into your skin. That is why cooking pots often have wooden or plastic handles, and why oven gloves are made of thick cloth rather than anything shiny.

Teachers sometimes demonstrate this with ice cubes. They place one cube on a block of aluminium and another on a block of plastic, both at room temperature. Before the experiment, they ask the students to predict which cube will melt first. Because the aluminium feels colder to the touch, most students expect the cube on the plastic to melt faster. In fact, the cube on the aluminium melts dramatically quicker, often within a few minutes, while the other one sits almost unchanged. The aluminium carries heat from the room into the ice very efficiently, whereas the plastic keeps the heat away. The result leaves many students baffled, and it stays in their memory for years.

Engineers rely on the same principle every day. Computer chips sit on top of metal plates that help their heat dissipate, while houses are wrapped in layers of material that keep heat in. Polar animals, too, have developed thick fur and fat that slow the flow of heat out of their bodies. Perhaps the most valuable lesson, however, concerns our senses. They are wonderfully suited to survival, but they do not always report the world exactly as it is. Sometimes a simple apparatus, used carefully, is the only way to discover that the cold tray and the warm wooden board were, in fact, never different at all.

questions.q: According to the text, what does our skin actually sense when we touch something?
options: The exact temperature of the object
How quickly heat flows into or out of the skin
How heavy and hard the object is
Whether the object contains water
questions.explain: Metne göre deri sıcaklığı ölçmez; ısının deriye ne kadar hızlı girip çıktığını algılar: ‘How quickly heat flows into or out of the skin’.

questions.q: In the classroom experiment, why does the ice cube on aluminium melt faster?
options: The aluminium block is warmer than the plastic one
Aluminium produces its own heat when it touches ice
The plastic block is kept in a colder part of the room
Aluminium is a good conductor, so it carries heat from the room into the ice quickly
questions.explain: İki blok da oda sıcaklığındadır; alüminyum ısıyı iyi ilettiği için odanın ısısını buza hızla taşır: ‘Aluminium is a good conductor, so it carries heat from the room into the ice quickly’.

title: Light from a Snapped Stick
text:
At concerts, festivals and children’s birthday parties, you will often see them: thin plastic tubes glowing green, pink or blue in the dark. You bend one, hear a small crack, give it a shake and suddenly it shines. A glow stick needs no battery, no wire and no flame, and it does not get hot. To many people it seems almost like magic. In fact, it is a carefully designed chemical reaction, and the light it produces belongs to a family of natural events that scientists have studied for well over a century.

Most of the light we use every day comes from heat. The sun, a candle flame and the glowing filament of an old-fashioned light bulb all shine because they are extremely hot. When atoms are heated strongly, they give off energy as light; the hotter something is, the brighter and whiter it glows. A glow stick works in an entirely different way. There is no combustion inside it, and its light comes from a chemical reaction that releases energy directly as light rather than as heat. This is called chemiluminescence, which simply means ‘light from chemistry’, and the glow is sometimes described as cold light.

Inside the plastic tube there are two separate liquids. The outer tube contains one chemical mixed with a coloured dye, and floating in it is a thin glass container holding a second chemical, usually hydrogen peroxide, the same substance that is used to lighten hair. As long as the glass is unbroken, the two liquids cannot meet and nothing happens. When you bend the stick, the brittle glass breaks, and that is the crack you hear. Shaking the tube mixes the liquids, and the reaction begins.

What happens next takes place in several steps. The two chemicals react to form an unstable, energy-rich molecule that exists only for a very short time. As it breaks apart, it passes its energy to a nearby dye molecule. The dye molecule cannot hold on to the extra energy for long, and it releases it as a fleeting flash of light. Billions upon billions of these flashes, happening every second, produce the steady glow you see. The colour depends entirely on the dye: change the dye and you change the colour, while the rest of the chemistry stays the same.

Because it is a chemical reaction, the glow is sensitive to temperature. Drop a glow stick into hot water and it shines much more brightly, but it also fades sooner, because the molecules move faster and react more quickly. Put it in the freezer and the opposite happens: the reaction slows almost to a standstill, the light becomes faint, and the stick may still glow the next day when it warms up. Some people use this trick to make a glow stick last for a second evening, although it only works for a while, since the chemicals are inexorably used up. The liquids have fairly low toxicity, but they can irritate the skin and eyes, so a broken stick should be thrown away rather than played with.

The modern glow stick has a fairly short history. In the 1960s, Edwin Chandross, a chemist at Bell Laboratories in the United States, studied chemical reactions that produce light, and other chemists, notably Michael Rauhut at the American Cyanamid company, developed brighter and longer-lasting versions. Armies and emergency services were quick to adopt them, because, unlike torches or flares, they are light and waterproof, they keep working when batteries fail, and they cannot ignite flammable gas or fuel. Divers, miners and campers use them for similar reasons. Only later did they become a common toy.

Nature, of course, discovered cold light long before humans did. Fireflies flash on summer evenings, and many deep-sea fish and jellyfish shine in the dark ocean, all using chemical reactions related to the one inside a glow stick. When living things produce light in this way, scientists call it bioluminescence. Watching a child wave a glowing stick at a party, it is pleasing to remember that the same basic chemistry also lights up forests and seas, and that a simple crack of glass can set off a small, quiet firework of molecules.

questions.q: What happens when you bend a glow stick?
options: A thin glass container breaks, so two chemicals can mix and react
A small battery inside is switched on
The plastic tube warms up and begins to glow from the heat
Air enters the tube and the dye starts to burn
questions.explain: Çubuğu bükünce içteki ince cam kap kırılır, iki sıvı karışır ve tepkime başlar: ‘A thin glass container breaks, so two chemicals can mix and react’. Çubukta pil ya da yanma yoktur.

questions.q: Why might someone put a glowing stick in the freezer?
options: To make it shine more brightly for a short time
To change its colour from green to blue
To slow the reaction so that the stick lasts longer
To make the glass inside easier to break
questions.explain: Dondurucuda tepkime neredeyse durur; böylece çubuk ertesi gün yeniden ışık verebilir: ‘To slow the reaction so that the stick lasts longer’. Sıcak su ise ışığı parlatır ama ömrünü kısaltır.

title: Heat in Your Pocket
text:
On a freezing winter morning, few small comforts are as welcome as a hand warmer. Some come in paper packets that you tear open and shake; others are soft plastic bags with a little metal disc inside that you click with your fingers. Within seconds or minutes, both kinds become pleasantly hot and stay that way for a surprisingly long time. They look similar in your pocket, yet they work on two completely different chemical principles, and each one hides a small surprise.

The disposable packet relies on one of the most familiar chemical reactions on Earth: rusting. Inside the packet there is a fine iron powder mixed with salt, a little water, powdered charcoal and sometimes a material that holds moisture. When iron combines with oxygen from the air, it forms iron oxide, which we know as rust, and this reaction, a form of oxidation, gives off heat. Normally, rusting happens so slowly that we never feel it; an old bicycle left in the rain does not get warm. In a hand warmer, however, everything is arranged to speed the process up. The iron is ground into an extremely fine powder, which gives it an enormous surface area, and the salt and water help the reaction along. The charcoal spreads the heat evenly and holds air close to the iron.

Before use, the packet is sealed inside an airtight plastic wrapper, so no oxygen can reach the iron. Once you tear the wrapper open, air flows through the porous paper bag and the reaction starts. Shaking the packet mixes the ingredients and lets in more air. Depending on the design, it can stay warm for six hours or more, until most of the iron has turned to rust. Then it is finished and must be thrown away, because there is no practical way to turn rust back into fine iron powder at home.

The reusable kind is even more intriguing. It contains a clear liquid, a solution of a chemical called sodium acetate in water, and a small, flexible metal disc. At first glance, nothing about it looks ready to produce heat. The secret is that the liquid is in an unusual and unstable state. Sodium acetate dissolves very well in hot water, much better than in cold water. When the bag is boiled, a large amount of it dissolves, and as the liquid cools down again, it holds far more dissolved chemical than it normally could at room temperature. Chemists call such a liquid ‘supersaturated’. It is rather like a pencil balanced on its point: it can stay that way for weeks, but the slightest disturbance will make it fall.

Clicking the metal disc provides that disturbance. The tiny movement is thought to release a few microscopic crystals that were trapped in small cracks in the metal, although the exact mechanism has been debated. Once a single crystal appears, it acts as a seed, and the dissolved chemical begins to turn solid around it. You can watch a white, cloudy wave spread through the bag in a few seconds until the whole thing has become hard. As it crystallizes, it releases the energy that went into dissolving it, and the bag warms to around fifty degrees before the heat slowly dissipates.

Unlike the iron packet, this kind can be used again and again. To reset it, you simply put it in boiling water until all the crystals have melted and dissolved, and then let it cool slowly without disturbing it. Its heat lasts a much shorter time, usually under an hour, but it is ready instantly whenever you need it. The same chemical is also used as a food additive, and it stars in a popular classroom trick called ‘hot ice’, in which a teacher pours the liquid onto a single crystal and a tower of solid crystals seems to grow out of nowhere.

Both kinds of hand warmer show how chemistry can be put to work in clever, practical ways. One takes a reaction we normally regard as a slow, unwanted nuisance, the gradual rusting of iron, and makes it fast and useful. The other stores energy in a liquid that is quietly waiting to change its form. Next time you hold one at a cold bus stop, you might reflect that the warmth in your hand comes from atoms rearranging themselves, either by joining with oxygen or by locking into neat crystalline patterns.

questions.q: Why does a disposable hand warmer only start working after you open its plastic wrapper?
options: The wrapper keeps the iron powder too cold to react
Opening the wrapper breaks a small glass container of water
The salt inside needs light before it can dissolve
The wrapper is airtight, so oxygen cannot reach the iron until it is opened
questions.explain: Paket hava geçirmez bir ambalajda saklanır; ambalaj açılınca hava gözenekli kâğıttan geçer ve demir paslanmaya başlar: ‘The wrapper is airtight, so oxygen cannot reach the iron until it is opened’.

questions.q: What makes the reusable hand warmer produce heat?
options: The iron in the metal disc slowly turns into rust
Clicking the disc starts crystals forming, and the liquid releases energy as it becomes solid
Boiling water is stored inside the bag until it is needed
Shaking the bag mixes two liquids that burn together
questions.explain: Diske basınca küçük kristaller ortaya çıkar; aşırı doymuş sıvı bunların çevresinde katılaşırken enerji açığa çıkarır: ‘Clicking the disc starts crystals forming, and the liquid releases energy as it becomes solid’.

title: Bread That Hardens Without Drying
text:
Buy a fresh loaf in the morning and it is soft, fragrant and slightly springy. Leave it on the kitchen counter for two or three days and it becomes hard and crumbly, with a dull, cardboard-like taste. Most people would say, without thinking, that the bread has dried out. It seems the obvious explanation. Yet it is largely wrong, and the true reason is a small but fascinating piece of food chemistry.

The first clue came from France in the middle of the nineteenth century. In 1852, the chemist Jean-Baptiste Boussingault reported an experiment that seemed to defy common sense. He sealed bread inside a tightly closed container so that no moisture could escape, and found that it went stale anyway. Even more surprisingly, when he heated the stale bread again, it became soft anew, still without any change in the amount of water it contained. Something was happening inside the bread itself, something that had little to do with drying. His results helped to debunk the popular idea that staleness is simply a matter of losing water.

To understand what, we need to look at starch, the main ingredient of flour. Starch is a carbohydrate, and in raw flour it exists in the form of tiny, hard grains in which long chains of sugar molecules are packed together in tidy, crystalline patterns. When dough is baked, water and heat get into these grains. They swell up, burst and lose their orderly structure, and the starch chains spread out loosely among the water molecules. This change, which food scientists call gelatinization, is what turns a heavy, pale dough into a soft, moist crumb.

The problem is that this soft, disordered state is not stable. As the bread cools and then sits on the counter, the starch chains have a natural propensity to move back towards one another and line up again in neat, tightly packed crystals. As they do so, they push water out of their way and hold on to it less firmly. The crumb becomes firmer and more rigid, and because the water is now trapped in different places, the bread tastes dry even though it contains almost as much water as before. Food scientists call this process retrogradation, a word that simply means ‘going backwards’.

This explains one of the most surprising facts about bread. Many people put their loaves in the refrigerator, believing that cold will keep them fresh, as it does for milk or meat. In fact, the opposite is true. Starch crystals form fastest at temperatures just above freezing, so bread kept in a fridge goes stale considerably faster than bread kept at room temperature. The fridge does slow the growth of mould, which is why it may still make sense in very hot weather with high humidity, but for texture it is the worst choice. The freezer is a different matter: at very low temperatures the starch chains can barely move, and the process almost stops completely. That is why bakers advise freezing bread you will not eat within a day or two.

The French chemist’s second observation also makes sense now. Heating stale bread to above roughly sixty degrees melts the starch crystals again, so the chains spread out and the bread softens. This is why a slightly old roll can be brought back to life in a hot oven for a few minutes, or why toast made from yesterday’s bread tastes perfectly good. The revival is only temporary, though. Once the bread cools, the crystals begin to form again, and faster than the first time, so reheated bread should be eaten quickly.

Bakers and food companies have long tried to slow retrogradation. Bread rich in fat, sugar or eggs tends to stay soft longer, because these ingredients get in the way of the starch chains and make it harder for them to line up. Some factory bread also contains natural substances that cut starch chains into shorter pieces, which form crystals less easily. Still, many people would argue that nothing beats a loaf bought fresh that morning. If yours does turn hard, there is no need to throw it away. Old bread has its own place in kitchens around the world, from breadcrumbs to puddings and soups, and staleness, after all, is simply chemistry running its course.

questions.q: What did Boussingault’s experiment in 1852 show?
options: Bread kept in a sealed container never goes stale
Bread goes stale mainly because it loses water to the air
Bread can go stale even when no water escapes, and heating can make it soft again
Bread stays fresh longer in a cold place
questions.explain: Boussingault ekmeği nem kaçmayacak biçimde kapattı ama ekmek yine bayatladı; ısıtınca da su miktarı değişmeden yumuşadı: ‘Bread can go stale even when no water escapes, and heating can make it soft again’.

questions.q: Why does bread go stale faster in a refrigerator?
options: Starch crystals form fastest at temperatures just above freezing
The fridge removes water from the bread more quickly
Mould grows faster in cold, dark places
Cold air destroys the sugar in the bread
questions.explain: Nişasta kristalleri en hızlı donma noktasının hemen üstündeki sıcaklıklarda oluştuğu için ekmek buzdolabında daha çabuk bayatlar: ‘Starch crystals form fastest at temperatures just above freezing’.

title: The Curtain That Clings
text:
It happens in bathrooms all over the world. You step into the shower, turn on the water, and within moments the plastic curtain swells inwards and wraps itself around your legs, cold and damp. You push it away, and it drifts straight back. It is one of the small, irritating mysteries of daily life, and for a long time nobody could say with confidence why it happens. Surprisingly, the puzzle eventually attracted the attention of a serious engineer with a powerful computer.

Over the years, people proposed several explanations, each of them reasonable at first sight. The most popular was the chimney effect, a form of convection. Hot water heats the air inside the shower, the argument went, and hot air and water vapour rise, just as smoke does in a chimney. As warm air rises and escapes over the top of the curtain, cooler air from the bathroom rushes in underneath to replace it, pushing the bottom of the curtain inwards. This sounds convincing, but it has an obvious weakness: the curtain also moves inwards when the shower is cold. Anyone brave enough to try a cold shower can confirm it.

A second theory pointed to a principle described in the eighteenth century by the Swiss mathematician Daniel Bernoulli. Roughly speaking, Bernoulli showed that when a gas or liquid flows faster, its pressure drops. The falling water drags air along with it, so the air near the stream moves quickly, and according to this view its pressure falls, allowing the higher pressure in the bathroom to push the curtain towards the water. Others hypothesized that electric charge might be responsible: perhaps the falling water creates static electricity that attracts the light plastic. Each explanation had some plausibility, but none had faced proper scrutiny, and there was no conclusive test.

In 2001, David Schmidt, an engineer at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, decided to settle the matter. Schmidt studied the way liquids break up into sprays, which matters greatly for fuel in car engines, and he had access to powerful software for computer modelling of moving air and liquids. Partly as a light-hearted side project, he built a detailed computer model of a typical shower, with a bath, a curtain, a shower head and the water falling from it, divided into some fifty thousand tiny cells. He then let the computer calculate how the air in each cell would move. Running the calculation reportedly took around two weeks.

The results revealed something that earlier theories had missed. As the spray fell, it pulled air downwards and set it turning in a large, slow whirl, rather like a small tornado lying on its side, with its centre running horizontally across the shower. At the centre of any whirl like this, the pressure is lower than at its edges. That area of low pressure, sitting next to the curtain, was enough to pull the light plastic inwards. In effect, the shower creates its own small weather system inside the bath, and the curtain is caught in it. Humidity and temperature, it seemed, played only a minor role.

Schmidt was careful to say that his model did not rule out every other influence, and later researchers have suggested that more than one effect may be at work at once, with the importance of each depending on the shower. Still, his work attracted enormous public interest, and it even earned him an Ig Nobel Prize in physics that same year. These light-hearted awards, presented for many years at Harvard University, honour research that ‘first makes people laugh, and then makes them think’. Schmidt’s project fitted the description perfectly: it began almost as a joke, yet it used the same tools that engineers use for the aerodynamic design of aircraft and engines.

What can you actually do about the problem? Several practical solutions follow from the physics. A heavier curtain, or one with weights or magnets sewn into its lower edge, resists the pull better. Curtain rods that curve outwards give the whirl more room and keep the plastic away from your body. Opening a window or the bathroom door may help a little too. None of these will win a prize, but they may make your morning shower a little more peaceful, and give you a good story to tell the next time someone in your family complains about the curtain.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of the chimney-effect explanation?
options: Hot air does not rise in small rooms
The curtain also moves inwards when the water is cold
Bathrooms usually have no space above the curtain
It was rejected by Bernoulli in the eighteenth century
questions.explain: Baca etkisi sıcak havanın yükselmesine dayanır, oysa perde soğuk duşta da içeri doğru gelir: ‘The curtain also moves inwards when the water is cold’.

questions.q: According to Schmidt’s computer model, what pulls the curtain inwards?
options: Static electricity created by the falling water
Warm air escaping over the top of the curtain
The weight of the water drops hitting the curtain
An area of low pressure at the centre of a slow whirl of air made by the spray
questions.explain: Schmidt’in modelinde düşen su havayı yan yatmış bir kasırga gibi döndürür; bu girdabın ortasındaki alçak basınç perdeyi içeri çeker: ‘An area of low pressure at the centre of a slow whirl of air made by the spray’.

title: The Glowing Ball in the Storm
text:
Imagine a summer storm. Rain is hammering on the windows, thunder is rolling across the hills, and then something strange drifts into the room: a glowing sphere about the size of a grapefruit. It floats at waist height, moves slowly past the furniture, makes a faint hissing sound and, after a few seconds, either fades away quietly or vanishes with a sharp bang. People who have seen such a thing often struggle to describe it, and many of them are afraid that nobody will believe them.

This phenomenon is known as ball lightning, and for centuries it has been one of the most puzzling events in meteorology. Thousands of eyewitness reports have been collected from around the world, including some from pilots, scientists and police officers. The accounts differ in detail, but a common picture emerges. The balls usually appear during or just after a thunderstorm, often close to the place where an ordinary lightning bolt has struck. Most are no bigger than a football and glow in red, orange, yellow or white. Their lifetime is fleeting, usually under ten seconds, yet that is far longer than the split second of a normal flash.

One famous account comes from 1638, when a violent storm hit a church in the English village of Widecombe-in-the-Moor during a Sunday service. Witnesses described a great ball of fire that entered the building, damaged the roof and killed several people. Whether this was truly ball lightning is impossible to say today, but the story has been told and retold as one of the earliest detailed descriptions. Centuries later, in 1963, a physicist named Roger Jennison reported that a glowing ball had floated down the aisle of the passenger plane he was travelling in. Because the witness was a trained scientist, his short report attracted considerable attention.

For a long time, many researchers dismissed such stories as far-fetched. Laboratory scientists like evidence they can measure, and ball lightning refuses to appear on demand. Some argued that witnesses were simply baffled by the bright afterimage that a lightning flash leaves on the eye. Others suggested that strong magnetic fields near a lightning strike could stimulate the brain directly and create the illusion of a glowing object. These explanations may account for some sightings, but they struggle to explain anomalous cases in which the balls burned curtains, melted glass or were seen by several people at once from different angles.

A rare breakthrough came unexpectedly, almost by accident. In 2012, Chinese researchers were studying ordinary lightning on the Qinghai Plateau with cameras and spectrometers, instruments that split light into its colours. When a bolt struck the ground nearby, their equipment recorded a glowing ball that rose from the spot and lasted for about one and a half seconds. The spectrum of its light contained signs of silicon, iron and calcium, the same elements found in the local soil. The results, published in 2014, appeared to support an idea proposed by New Zealand scientists some years earlier.

According to this hypothesis, when lightning strikes the ground, its enormous heat turns minerals in the soil into vapour. The silicon in that vapour may then condense into tiny particles that join together in loose chains, forming a light, fluffy ball. As these particles slowly react with oxygen in the air, they release energy as light and heat, much like a very slow fire. The theory is attractive because it explains why the balls often appear near the ground, why they burn for several seconds and why they can drift with the wind.

Even so, the mystery is far from solved. The silicon theory does not easily explain reports of balls appearing inside closed rooms or inside aircraft. Other scientists have tested ideas involving microwaves, electrical charges and even tiny amounts of burning gas. Some laboratories have produced glowing balls by passing electric sparks into water or by heating silicon with microwaves. These artificial balls look similar in photographs, but nobody can yet be sure they are the same thing that people see in storms.

What makes ball lightning so fascinating is the gap between ordinary human experience and scientific certainty. The event is real enough that thousands of people describe it, yet rare and short enough that it almost never meets a camera. For now, anyone who sees a glowing sphere drifting across a room during a storm should do two things: keep a safe distance and write down exactly what happened. Their notes may one day help scientists finally understand it.

questions.q: What did the equipment of the Chinese researchers record in 2012?
options: A ball of light that was produced in a laboratory with microwaves
A ball that entered a building and damaged its roof
A strong magnetic field that created an illusion in the brain
A glowing ball whose light contained elements found in the local soil
questions.explain: Metne göre 2012'de Çinli araştırmacıların cihazları, ışığında yerel topraktaki silisyum, demir ve kalsiyum izleri bulunan parlayan bir top kaydetti. Doğru cevap: "A glowing ball whose light contained elements found in the local soil".

questions.q: According to the text, why has ball lightning been so hard for scientists to study?
options: It is rare, short-lived and cannot be produced on demand
Most witnesses refuse to describe what they have seen
It only appears in remote places such as high plateaus
It is too dangerous to observe from a safe distance
questions.explain: Metin, yıldırım topunun nadir ve çok kısa süreli olduğunu, laboratuvarda istenildiğinde ortaya çıkmadığını vurgular. Doğru cevap: "It is rare, short-lived and cannot be produced on demand".

title: The Day the Sky Caught Fire
text:
On the morning of 1 September 1859, an English astronomer named Richard Carrington was doing what he did on most clear days. In his private observatory near London, he projected an image of the Sun onto a screen and carefully drew the dark sunspots that appeared on its surface. Suddenly, two patches of intensely bright white light burst out among the spots. Carrington was so surprised that he rushed out of the room to find a witness, and when he returned a minute later the light was already fading. Within about five minutes, it had disappeared completely.

Carrington had seen a solar flare, a sudden release of energy in the Sun's atmosphere. Another observer, Richard Hodgson, happened to see the same event independently, which helped convince other scientists that it was real. Yet the most dramatic consequences were still to come. Roughly seventeen hours later, a huge cloud of charged particles thrown out by the Sun reached the Earth. Today such a cloud is called a coronal mass ejection. It normally takes several days to cross the space between the Sun and our planet, so this one travelled remarkably fast.

When the cloud struck the Earth's magnetic field, the result was the most powerful geomagnetic storm in recorded history. Over the following nights, auroras, the shimmering curtains of light usually seen only near the poles, appeared unexpectedly across much of the world. People reported them in Cuba, Hawaii and other places close to the tropics. In the north-eastern United States the sky was so bright after midnight that, according to newspaper reports, some people woke up believing it was dawn and began preparing breakfast. Others, baffled by the glow, were sure that a great city nearby was on fire.

The storm also affected the most advanced technology of the age: the telegraph. By 1859, telegraph wires connected cities across Europe and North America, carrying messages as electrical pulses. The magnetic disturbance created strong electric currents in these long wires. Operators reported sparks jumping from their equipment, and some received electric shocks. In a few offices, paper caught fire. Most surprisingly, several operators found they could disconnect their batteries entirely and still send messages, powered only by the current the storm was producing. A conversation between Boston and Portland, Maine, reportedly continued in this way for about two hours.

For the people of 1859, the event was a strange and beautiful spectacle with a few practical problems. For people today, it is a warning. Modern society depends on systems that are far more sensitive than the old telegraph. Power grids stretch across entire continents, and their long transmission lines can pick up the same kind of currents that ran through the telegraph wires. Large transformers could overheat and fail, and replacing them may take months. Satellites that provide navigation, weather data and communications could be damaged, and radio signals used by aircraft could be disrupted.

There is evidence that this is not just a theoretical worry. In March 1989, a much smaller geomagnetic storm caused the power grid of Quebec, Canada, to collapse within about ninety seconds, leaving millions of people without electricity for around nine hours. In July 2012, a coronal mass ejection thought to be comparable in strength to the Carrington event burst from the Sun. Fortunately, it was aimed away from the Earth. Had it erupted about a week earlier, our planet would have been in its path, and some scientists described it as a near miss.

Estimates of how often such extreme storms occur vary widely, but some studies suggest the chance of one hitting the Earth in any given decade may be roughly one in ten. For this reason, space weather is now taken seriously by governments and power companies. Spacecraft positioned between the Earth and the Sun watch for incoming clouds of particles and can provide a warning of perhaps fifteen to sixty minutes. With that warning, grid operators can reduce the load on vulnerable equipment, and satellite controllers can switch sensitive systems into a protective mode.

Carrington could not have imagined any of this when he hurried out of his observatory to find a witness. His careful drawing of a few minutes of white light became one of the first records of a solar flare, and his name is now attached to the type of extreme storm that engineers plan for. It is a reminder that the Sun, which seems so steady in our sky, is in fact a restless neighbour.

questions.q: What surprising thing did some telegraph operators discover during the 1859 storm?
options: They could send messages without their batteries
Their wires had been completely destroyed by fire
The auroras made it impossible to read messages
Messages travelled faster than ever before
questions.explain: Bazı telgraf operatörleri pillerini tamamen çıkarıp yalnızca fırtınanın ürettiği akımla mesaj gönderebildiklerini fark etti. Doğru cevap: "They could send messages without their batteries".

questions.q: Why does the writer describe the Carrington event as a warning for people today?
options: Because auroras are becoming harmful to human health
Because the Sun is expected to become much hotter soon
Because telegraph systems are still widely used around the world
Because a similar storm could seriously damage power grids and satellites
questions.explain: Yazar, günümüz toplumunun elektrik şebekeleri ve uydular gibi çok daha hassas sistemlere bağlı olduğunu, benzer bir fırtınanın bunlara ciddi zarar verebileceğini söyler. Doğru cevap: "Because a similar storm could seriously damage power grids and satellites".

title: The Land That Was Never There
text:
In 1913, a small American expedition sailed to northern Greenland to find a land that had appeared on maps for seven years. It was called Crocker Land, and an explorer had reported seeing its snowy peaks from a distance in 1906. In April 1914, after weeks of hard travel across the frozen sea, the team's leader, Donald MacMillan, and his companions finally saw it: hills, valleys and peaks covered with ice, stretching across the horizon. Yet as they moved forward, the land moved too. When the sun went down, it changed shape and finally disappeared. Crocker Land, MacMillan concluded, had never existed. What he and the earlier explorer had seen was a mirage.

Most people know mirages from films about the desert, where thirsty travellers see a lake that is not there. That common type, called an inferior mirage, appears below the real object. It happens when the ground is very hot and the air just above it is much warmer than the air higher up. Light travels slightly faster in warm air than in cold air, so when light from the blue sky passes down through these layers, it bends gradually upwards before reaching the eye. The brain assumes that light travels in straight lines, so it places the image of the sky on the ground, where it looks just like water. The same refraction produces the wet-looking patches that drivers see on hot roads in summer.

The polar mirage that fooled the explorers was of a different and rarer kind. Above cold seas and ice, the opposite arrangement often occurs: a layer of cold air lies close to the surface, with warmer air above it. Experts in meteorology call this a temperature inversion. Now light bends downwards, following the curve of the Earth, so objects that are actually below the horizon can appear in the sky, often stretched and lifted upwards. When the layers are complicated, the image can be broken into several parts, some upright and some upside down, which constantly change. This complex, shifting form is known as a Fata Morgana.

The name comes from Italian and refers to Morgan le Fay, a magical figure from the legends of King Arthur. In the Strait of Messina, between Sicily and the mainland of Italy, people sometimes saw cities, towers and castles floating above the water. According to local tradition, these were created by the fairy to lure sailors to their deaths. Today we know that the towers were probably distorted images of real buildings and cliffs on the far shore, and that the magic was entirely illusory.

Fata Morgana mirages have probably shaped many stories of the sea. Baffled sailors reported ships sailing in the sky, sometimes upside down, and it has been suggested that such sightings helped to inspire the legend of the Flying Dutchman, a ghost ship condemned to sail forever. Some historians have also argued that mirages influenced exploration in the past. Norse sailors in the North Atlantic, they suggest, could have glimpsed distant coasts lifted above the horizon long before they could see them directly, which may have encouraged them to set off towards Iceland and Greenland. Such ideas are difficult to prove, but they are not unreasonable.

Mirages are not only a source of legends. Because the shape of a mirage depends on the temperature of the air at different heights, scientists can use observations of them to learn about the atmospheric layers close to the ground. Mirages also have practical consequences. They can confuse sailors and pilots, and they can disturb measurements made with surveying equipment and telescopes. Ironically, the more carefully an observer looks through a powerful instrument, the more clearly a false image may appear.

Anyone can see a simple mirage. On a hot day, look along a long, straight road or across a flat beach, and you may see shimmering pools that vanish as you approach. Seeing a true Fata Morgana requires more luck, because the layers of warm and cold air must be arranged in just the right way, and the display is often fleeting. Cold lakes in spring, polar coasts and large bodies of water on calm days are good places to try. When it happens, distant islands may rise unexpectedly from the sea and turn into castles, and ships may sail upside down above the horizon.

MacMillan's expedition was, in one sense, a failure, because it found nothing. In another sense, it was a remarkably clear lesson in how easily our eyes can be deceived. The atmosphere does not simply let light pass through it. It bends it, stretches it and sometimes builds entire landscapes that are not there.

questions.q: What did MacMillan's team finally learn about Crocker Land?
options: It was much smaller than the maps had shown
It was a mirage and did not really exist
It was covered by the sea every summer
It had been confused with the coast of Iceland
questions.explain: MacMillan, ekibiyle ilerledikçe karanın da hareket ettiğini ve sonunda kaybolduğunu görerek Crocker Land'in hiç var olmadığına, bir serap olduğuna karar verdi. Doğru cevap: "It was a mirage and did not really exist".

questions.q: Which conditions produce a Fata Morgana, according to the text?

title: Clouds at the Edge of Space
text:
On a clear summer night in northern Europe, about an hour or two after sunset, observers sometimes notice something odd low in the northern sky. The ground is already dark and the first stars are shining, yet a group of thin, silvery-blue clouds glows brightly, with delicate waves and ripples like patterns in sand. These are noctilucent clouds, a name that comes from Latin and means night-shining. They are the highest clouds on Earth, and they have a surprising story.

Ordinary clouds form in the lowest layer of the atmosphere, mostly within about twelve kilometres of the ground. Noctilucent clouds float at around eighty-three kilometres, far above the stratosphere, in a layer called the mesosphere. At that height, the air is extremely thin, and there is far less water vapour than in the driest desert. That is part of what makes them so puzzling: how can clouds form in a place that is so dry?

The answer lies in temperature. Ironically, the mesosphere above the poles is coldest in summer, when temperatures can fall below minus 130 degrees Celsius, making it the coldest natural place in the Earth's atmosphere. At such temperatures, the few water molecules present can freeze onto tiny particles and form ice crystals. Many of these particles are thought to be dust from meteors, the small pieces of rock that burn up when they enter the atmosphere every day. In other words, noctilucent clouds may be made partly of space dust covered in ice.

They glow because of their height. After sunset, the ground and the lower atmosphere fall into the Earth's shadow, but clouds eighty kilometres up are still lit by the Sun shining from below the horizon. Against the dark sky, they shine with an electric blue colour. They are visible mainly between latitudes of about fifty and seventy degrees, and mostly in the weeks around the summer solstice, which means late May to August in the northern half of the world.

Interestingly, there seem to be no reliable reports of these clouds before 1885. In that year, observers in Germany, Russia and Britain began to describe them. Two years earlier, in 1883, the volcano Krakatoa in Indonesia had erupted with enormous force, throwing huge amounts of dust and gas into the atmosphere and producing colourful sunsets around the world. Because people were watching the sky closely after the eruption, some historians believe they may simply have noticed clouds that had always existed. Others suggest that the eruption itself added water and particles high in the atmosphere. Nobody can say for certain which explanation is correct.

What is clearer is that the clouds have changed since then. Over the past few decades, scientists have reported that they appear more often, shine more brightly and are seen at lower latitudes than before. In some recent summers, people have photographed them as far south as Paris and even southern California. Several factors may be involved. Methane, a gas released by farming and by fossil fuels, rises into the upper atmosphere, where it is broken down to produce water vapour. More water means more ice. At the same time, the gases that warm the lower atmosphere actually cool the upper atmosphere, making conditions there even more suitable for cloud formation.

There is also a curious link with spaceflight. Rocket engines release large amounts of water vapour, and the exhaust of a single launch can sometimes be followed by noctilucent clouds days later and thousands of kilometres away. In a study published in 2003, for example, researchers connected a sudden appearance of the clouds to the exhaust from a space shuttle launch. This shows how quickly winds in the upper atmosphere can carry water across the planet.

Because they form at the edge of space and respond to small changes in temperature and moisture, noctilucent clouds are sometimes described as a sensitive indicator of atmospheric conditions high above us. In 2007, NASA launched a satellite called AIM specifically to study them. Yet one does not need a satellite to enjoy them. On a clear midsummer night, look towards the north about an hour after sunset. If you see thin, shining waves glowing against a darkening sky, you are looking at ice crystals formed on dust from space, floating at the very top of our atmosphere.

title: The Pole That Will Not Stay Still
text:
Every compass needle in the world points towards a place that will not stay still. Most people imagine that a compass points north, and in a rough sense it does. But the needle actually lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, and the north magnetic pole, the point where that field points straight down into the ground, is not the same as the geographic North Pole around which the planet spins. Even more surprisingly, it is moving, and in recent decades it has been moving faster than at any time since people began to track it.

The pole was first reached in 1831 by a British naval expedition. On 1 June of that year, James Clark Ross stood on the Boothia Peninsula in what is now northern Canada and found that his dip needle, a compass that can tilt up and down, pointed almost vertically towards the ground. He raised a flag and declared the spot the position of the magnetic pole. Later expeditions found that it had moved. By 1904, when the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen measured it, it had shifted some distance to the north.

Why does the pole wander? The answer lies thousands of kilometres beneath our feet, far below the crust and the mantle. The Earth's magnetic field is generated in the outer core, a layer of liquid iron and nickel that surrounds the solid inner core. Heat escaping from the deep interior keeps this metal in constant motion, and the rotation of the planet twists the flows into complex patterns. Moving liquid metal produces electric currents, and these currents in turn produce magnetism, a self-sustaining system known as the geodynamo. Because the flows keep changing, the field they create changes too, and the magnetic poles drift as a result.

For most of the twentieth century, the north magnetic pole moved slowly, at around fifteen kilometres a year. Then, in the 1990s, it unexpectedly accelerated, reaching speeds of roughly fifty to sixty kilometres a year. It crossed the international date line in 2017 and has been heading across the Arctic Ocean from Canada towards Siberia. Some researchers have linked the change to a tug of war between two large patches of magnetic field deep under Canada and Siberia, with the Siberian patch gradually winning. More recently, the pole appears to have slowed down again, which shows how difficult its behaviour is to predict.

This might sound like a curiosity for scientists, but it has practical consequences. Smartphones, ships, aircraft and military systems rely on a mathematical description of the field called the World Magnetic Model, which is produced jointly by the United States and Britain and normally updated every five years. In early 2019, the model had become so inaccurate in the Arctic that its makers released an emergency update a year ahead of schedule. Without such corrections, a navigational app might point users in slightly the wrong direction, an error that matters greatly to a ship or a plane travelling long distances.

Airports feel the effect too. Runways are numbered according to their magnetic direction, rounded to the nearest ten degrees. A runway pointing roughly towards magnetic east is numbered 09, for example. As the magnetic field changes, some airports must repaint their runway numbers and update their charts. Several airports in the United States and elsewhere have done exactly this in recent years.

The wandering pole also raises a larger question. The geological record shows that the Earth's magnetic field has completely reversed many times, so that a compass would have pointed south rather than north. Scientists know this because volcanic rocks record the direction of the field as they cool. The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago. The field has also weakened by several per cent since the nineteenth century, which has led to occasional alarmist headlines claiming that a reversal is near. Most geophysicists, however, say there is no conclusive evidence that one is about to begin, and that if it did, it would probably take thousands of years.

For now, the pole continues its slow and unpredictable journey across the Arctic. The next time you open a map on your phone, it is worth remembering that the arrow on the screen depends on a molten ocean of metal deep inside the Earth, and on scientists who keep watching where it goes.

options: The heat of the Sun warming the Arctic Ocean
Volcanic rocks cooling near the surface
Changing flows of liquid metal in the Earth's outer core
The rotation of the Moon around the Earth
