title: Hunting for Space Rocks on the Ice
text:
Meteorites fall all over the Earth, roughly evenly, yet most of them are never found. Many land in the oceans, which cover most of the planet. Others fall into forests, fields or mountains, where they look much like ordinary stones and slowly break down in wind and rain. It may therefore seem surprising that the best place on Earth to collect meteorites is one of the coldest and emptiest: the ice sheet of Antarctica. Since the 1970s, expeditions there have recovered more meteorites than have been found everywhere else in the world combined.

The story began in 1969, when a team of Japanese scientists studying ice in the Yamato Mountains came across nine meteorites lying on the ice within a small area. At first this seemed a fortuitous accident, but researchers soon realised that it was not. In 1976, an American geologist named William Cassidy, working with Japanese colleagues, started a programme that is now called ANSMET, the Antarctic Search for Meteorites. Almost every southern summer since then, small teams have travelled to the ice to look for rocks from space.

Why does Antarctica work so well? The answer has two parts. The first is simple contrast. On a white or blue surface where there are almost no other stones, a dark rock is easy to see. The second part is more interesting, because it involves the slow movement of ice. Antarctica's ice sheet is not still. Under its own weight, it flows very slowly outwards from the centre of the continent towards the coast, carrying any meteorites that have fallen onto it and become buried in the snow. In some places, however, this flow is blocked by mountains. The ice is forced upwards, and at the same time, strong, dry winds remove the surface layer, not by melting but by turning the ice directly into vapour.

The result is a natural conveyor belt. Ice that may have travelled for thousands of years rises to the surface and disappears, leaving behind the heavier rocks it carried. In these areas, known as blue ice fields because the old, dense ice has a deep blue colour, meteorites collected from a large area and a long period gradually build up in one place. Some of the meteorites found there fell to Earth hundreds of thousands of years ago, and the cold, dry conditions have kept them remarkably well preserved.

Searching for them is hard work. Teams usually consist of eight or so people who live in tents for six weeks or more. When the weather allows, they ride snowmobiles in a line across the ice, about thirty metres apart, scanning the ground for dark spots. When someone finds a possible meteorite, the team stops, photographs it, records its position by GPS and gives it a number. Using clean tools, they place it in a sterile bag without touching it, so that it will not be contaminated by human skin or modern dust. The samples remain frozen until they reach a laboratory in the United States or Japan, where they are studied and made available to researchers around the world.

The rewards can be remarkable. Among the tens of thousands of Antarctic meteorites are pieces of the Moon and of Mars, thrown into space when large asteroids struck those worlds. The most famous is a Martian meteorite known as ALH84001, found in 1984. In 1996, a team of NASA scientists announced that it contained tiny structures that might be fossil traces of ancient bacteria. The claim caused a sensation and was even discussed by the American president. Most scientists today believe the evidence was not conclusive, but the debate encouraged a great deal of research into how life might be detected on other planets.

There is, however, a new worry. Recent research suggests that as the climate warms, some meteorites near the surface of the ice may absorb sunlight, heat up and slowly sink out of sight. Because dark rocks warm faster than the ice around them, even small changes in temperature could matter. A study published in 2022 estimated that around five thousand meteorites a year may be lost in this way, and argued that collecting them should become more urgent.

For the scientists who take part in these expeditions, the experience is unforgettable. Picking up a rock that has drifted through space for millions of years, fallen through the sky and waited in the ice for thousands more is a rare privilege. Antarctica, a continent with almost no people, has become an unexpected library of stones from across the solar system.

title: The Quiet Hum of the Planet
text:
Even on the calmest day, when no earthquake is shaking anything and the wind has died away, the ground beneath us is never completely still. Sensitive instruments called seismometers, which are designed to detect earthquakes, also record a constant background of tiny vibrations. For a long time, seismologists treated this as noise, something to be removed from their data. Today, it has become one of the most interesting signals in earth science, and it has a surprising source: the ocean.

The strongest part of this background is known as microseisms. They are tiny movements of the ground, usually far too small for people to feel, that repeat every few seconds. Scientists first noticed them in the nineteenth century, when early instruments showed small, regular movements even when nothing else was happening. In the first half of the twentieth century, researchers noticed that these vibrations grew stronger when storms were passing over the sea, even storms hundreds of kilometres away. The connection was explained by a theory published in 1950 by the British oceanographer Michael Longuet-Higgins. He showed that when ocean waves travelling in opposite directions meet, they create pressure changes that reach all the way down to the sea floor, pushing on the crust like a giant hand.

Smaller still is a phenomenon that some have called the hum of the Earth. In 1998, Japanese scientists analysing records from very sensitive instruments reported that the whole planet vibrates continuously at very low frequencies, with periods of several minutes, far too slow and too weak for any human to notice. At first, this was puzzling. Large earthquakes were known to make the Earth ring like a bell for days, but the hum was present even in long periods with no large earthquakes at all. Several explanations were proposed, including changes in the atmosphere. Studies in the following years, however, suggested that the main driver was again the ocean, in particular long, slow waves interacting with the sea floor near coasts and on shallow continental shelves.

Why should anyone care about such faint vibrations? One reason is that they turn out to be extremely useful. Because the background vibrations travel through the ground all the time, scientists can record them at two different stations and compare the signals. Using clever mathematics, they can then work out how quickly the vibrations travelled between the two points. This allows researchers to build images of the rock below without waiting for an earthquake, a technique sometimes called ambient noise imaging. It has been used to map the structure beneath mountain ranges, to watch changes inside volcanoes and even to detect changes in water stored underground.

The background noise is also a record of storms. Because microseisms grow stronger when large waves are produced at sea, old seismograms contain information about ocean storms going back more than a century, long before satellites existed. Researchers have used this archive to study whether ocean waves have become more powerful as the climate has changed. Some studies suggest that wave energy has increased in recent decades, though the results vary between regions.

Not all of the background comes from nature. Traffic, trains, factories and even crowds of people walking produce rapid vibrations that seismometers in cities can detect. This became strikingly clear in 2020, when many countries introduced a lockdown during the coronavirus pandemic. A study led by researchers at the Royal Observatory of Belgium, using data from hundreds of stations around the world, found that human-made seismic noise fell by up to about fifty per cent in some places, creating the longest and most widespread period of quiet ever recorded. For a while, scientists were able to detect small earthquakes that would normally have been hidden by the noise of daily life.

The idea that the planet constantly hums is a strangely poetic one. The sound is not one we could ever hear, and its notes are minutes long. Yet it tells a story of storms far out at sea, of waves pressing on the ocean floor, and of the busy lives of people in cities. What was once dismissed as useless noise has become, quite unexpectedly, a remarkably detailed way of listening to the whole Earth.

title: Lakes at the Bottom of the Sea
text:
Imagine diving to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico, about a kilometre below the surface. It is completely dark, the water is cold, and the pressure is enormous. Then the lights of your submarine reveal something that seems impossible: a lake, with its own shoreline and gentle waves, lying on the sea floor. The surface of the lake reflects your lights like a mirror, and when a heavy object falls into it, ripples spread slowly across its surface. Scientists call these features brine pools, and they are among the strangest places on our planet.

A brine pool is a body of extremely salty water that collects in a hollow on the sea floor. Because it contains far more salt than the surrounding seawater, often several times as much, it is much heavier. As a result, it does not mix easily with the water above it but sits beneath it, rather like oil and water in a glass, only the other way round. The boundary between the two layers can be so sharp that submarines sometimes appear to float on the surface of the pool.

Where does all this salt come from? In the Gulf of Mexico, the answer goes back roughly 150 million years, to a time when the region was a shallow sea that repeatedly dried up. As the water evaporated, it left behind thick layers of salt. Over millions of years, these layers were buried beneath mud and rock. Salt is lighter than the rock above it and slowly moves upwards, and where it comes close to the sea floor, it dissolves into the water, creating very salty brine. Similar pools are found in the Red Sea and the Mediterranean, where they are linked to other ancient salt deposits.

For most animals, brine pools are deadly. The water is not only salty but often contains almost no oxygen and high levels of methane and a gas called hydrogen sulphide. Fish, crabs and other creatures that swim into a pool by mistake can become shocked and die within minutes. Their bodies may remain well preserved for a long time, because the conditions are hostile even to the bacteria that normally break down dead animals. Researchers have sometimes found the bodies of fish and crabs lying around the edges, which has led to one pool being nicknamed the jacuzzi of despair.

Yet the edges of these pools are also full of life. Certain bacteria can use the methane and sulphur compounds rising from the brine as a source of energy, in the same way that plants use sunlight. These bacteria form the base of a food web. Large beds of mussels live along some shorelines, and the mussels carry bacteria inside their gills that turn methane into food. Shrimps, worms, crabs and fish gather around them. Some hunters seem to have learned to wait at the edge, catching animals that become confused after swimming into the toxic brine.

In 2023, a research team exploring the Gulf of Aqaba, part of the Red Sea, discovered several new brine pools at a depth of about 1,770 metres, surprisingly close to the coast. Because the pools are so isolated and so stable, the sediment at their bottoms builds up layer by layer without being disturbed. Scientists hope that these layers may contain a long record of past earthquakes, floods and changes in rainfall in the region, stretching back thousands of years.

Brine pools also interest scientists who study the possibility of life beyond Earth. The oceans thought to lie under the icy crust of some moons of Jupiter and Saturn may be salty, dark and lacking in oxygen. If microbes can thrive in the brine pools of our own oceans, this suggests that life may be more adaptable than we once assumed. Researchers test instruments and study these communities partly to prepare for future missions to such distant worlds.

Exploring these pools remains difficult and expensive. They lie at great depths, are often located first by sonar, and can be reached only with remotely operated vehicles or crewed submarines. Each visit often brings something new, such as an unknown species or an unexpected chemical process. For now, these lakes at the bottom of the sea remain a reminder of how much of our planet is still unexplored, and how many surprises may be waiting in the dark.

title: Mirrors on the Moon
text:
On 21 July 1969, before climbing back into their lunar module, the astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin placed a small, flat panel on the surface of the Moon. It was about half a metre wide and contained a hundred carefully shaped pieces of glass. Compared with the famous footprints and flag, it attracted little attention. Yet more than half a century later, this simple device is still in use, and it has helped scientists measure something remarkable: the Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth.

The panel is called a retroreflector. Each piece of glass inside it is a corner cube, shaped like the corner of a box, and it has a special property. Whatever direction light comes from, the cube sends it straight back towards its source. Later Apollo missions left two more of these panels, and two Soviet robotic rovers carried similar devices. Together, they turned the Moon into a giant target for an experiment known as lunar laser ranging.

The idea is simple, although the practice is extremely difficult. Observatories on Earth fire short, powerful pulses of laser light through a telescope towards one of the reflectors. The light travels about 384,000 kilometres, bounces back and returns to the telescope. By measuring the time this round trip takes, about two and a half seconds, scientists can calculate the distance to the Moon. The difficulty is that by the time a laser beam reaches the Moon, it has spread out to a circle several kilometres wide, and only a tiny fraction of the light hits the reflector. By the time the reflected light returns to Earth, it has spread out again. Of the enormous number of particles of light in each pulse, typically only one or a few come back to be detected, and sometimes none at all.

Despite these challenges, the measurements have reached astonishing precision. Early results were accurate to within about twenty centimetres. Modern observatories, such as the Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico, can measure the distance to within a few millimetres. That is a little like measuring the distance between two cities to within the width of a human hair.

These measurements show that the Moon is moving away from the Earth by about 3.8 centimetres every year, roughly the speed at which fingernails grow. The cause is the tides. The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth's oceans, creating two bulges of water. Because the Earth spins much faster than the Moon goes around it, the planet drags these bulges slightly ahead of the Moon. The gravity of the bulges then pulls the Moon forward, giving it extra energy and pushing it gradually into a higher orbit. At the same time, the friction of the tides is slowly slowing the Earth's rotation, so our days are becoming very slightly longer.

The effect is tiny on a human scale, but over geological time it adds up. Evidence from ancient sedimentary rocks suggests that hundreds of millions of years ago, a day lasted only around twenty-two hours, and the Moon was noticeably closer. Some scientists have pointed out a curious consequence for the future. Total solar eclipses happen because the Moon appears almost exactly the same size in the sky as the Sun. As the Moon continues to move away, it will eventually appear too small to cover the Sun completely, and total eclipses will no longer occur, though this will not happen for hundreds of millions of years.

Lunar laser ranging has also been used to test some of the most important ideas in physics. By following the Moon's orbital path so precisely, scientists have checked whether Einstein's theory of gravity holds true and whether gravitational strength has changed over time. So far, the theory has passed every test. The data have also suggested that the Moon probably has a liquid core.

The original reflectors are now old and covered in dust, and they return less light than they once did. Several new missions plan to place modern reflectors on the Moon to continue and improve the measurements. Still, there is something moving about the fact that a simple panel of glass, left behind by two astronauts more than fifty years ago, is still being used on clear nights. Every time a pulse of light returns from it, we receive a small message from the surface of the Moon, and a reminder that even our closest neighbour in space is slowly and inexorably drifting away.

options: The reflectors only work when the Moon is full

title: When the Ocean Turns to Milk
text:
For centuries, sailors told a strange story. Far out at sea, on a dark night with no moon, the water around their ship would begin to glow with a steady, pale white light. It did not flash or sparkle like the light sometimes seen in a ship's wake. Instead, the entire surface of the sea shone evenly, stretching to the horizon in every direction, as if the ship were sailing across a field of snow. Some crews said the glow was bright enough to read by. These events became known as milky seas, and for a long time scientists were not sure what to make of them.

Accounts of milky seas appear in ships' logs going back at least to the seventeenth century, and most come from the north-western Indian Ocean and the waters around Indonesia. Jules Verne included one in his novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, published in 1870, in which the submarine Nautilus passes through a sea that looks like milk. Yet real sightings were rare, unpredictable and impossible to check. A ship might sail through one, its crew would write a description, and by the time anyone else heard about it, the glow was long gone. Without samples or photographs, many scientists remained cautious, and some were openly puzzled.

One of the few direct samples came in 1985, when a research ship in the Arabian Sea passed through a glowing area and collected water. Scientists found that it contained large numbers of luminous bacteria, together with tiny algae. The leading suspect was a species of bacterium called Vibrio harveyi, which produces light through a chemical reaction. Unlike the brief flashes created by some plankton when the water is disturbed, these bacteria glow continuously. That fitted the sailors' descriptions of a calm, steady light.

There was, however, a puzzle. A single bacterium produces far too little light to see. To make the light visible, the bacteria must be present in enormous numbers. Many luminous bacteria only begin to glow when their population reaches a certain density, a process known as quorum sensing: each cell releases a chemical signal, and only when the signal is strong enough do they all switch on their lights together. For a milky sea to form, then, the bacteria must gather in vast concentrations, perhaps by growing on the remains of a large bloom of algae near the surface.

The next breakthrough came from space. In 2005, a team led by the scientist Steven Miller examined satellite images of the Indian Ocean at night and compared them with a report from a British merchant ship, the SS Lima, which had described sailing through a milky sea in 1995. Using a sensor designed to see faint light at night, they found the glow in the satellite data: a bright area of around 15,000 square kilometres off the coast of Somalia, roughly the size of a small country. It was the first time a milky sea had been seen from orbit, and the event was finally observable as more than a sailor's tale.

Newer satellites with better night-time sensors have since made it possible to search for these events more systematically. In 2021, Miller and his colleagues reported a huge milky sea south of Java in 2019 that covered more than 100,000 square kilometres and lasted for over a month. By chance, a private yacht called Ganesha had sailed through the area while it was glowing. Its crew described the water as looking like a snowfield and noted that the light seemed to come from beneath the surface. Their photographs and accounts, combined with the satellite images, gave researchers a valuable new source of evidence and an unforeseen chance to compare the two.

Many questions remain. Scientists still do not fully understand why milky seas form in some places and years but not others, or why they seem linked to certain ocean conditions, such as seasonal winds and rich nutrients rising from deeper water. There is also a deeper biological question. Why would bacteria glow at all? One idea is that the light attracts fish, which eat the bacteria and carry them inside their guts, a rich and comfortable place for microorganisms to live. If so, the glow would be a kind of invitation.

What makes milky seas so appealing is that they connect old sailors' tales with oceanography. For centuries, the stories sounded almost like legends, and the light itself was remarkably ephemeral. Now, with satellites watching from above, researchers hope to find milky seas as they happen, and perhaps one day send a ship to collect samples from the middle of a glowing ocean.

questions.q: Why was it difficult for scientists to study milky seas for so long?
options: Sailors refused to report what they had seen
Sightings were rare and the glow was gone before anyone could check
The bacteria could not survive outside the Indian Ocean
The light was too weak to be seen by the human eye
questions.explain: Görülmeler nadir ve öngörülemezdi; haber yayıldığında parıltı çoktan kaybolmuş olurdu, örnek ya da fotoğraf da yoktu. Doğru cevap: "Sightings were rare and the glow was gone before anyone could check".

questions.q: What was important about the 2005 study led by Steven Miller?
options: It proved that the glow was caused by plankton flashing
It collected the first water samples from a milky sea
It detected a milky sea from orbit for the first time
It showed that milky seas only form near Java
questions.explain: Miller'in ekibi uydu verilerinde Somali açıklarındaki parıltıyı buldu; bu, bir süt denizinin uzaydan ilk kez görülmesiydi. Doğru cevap: "It detected a milky sea from orbit for the first time".

title: The Doctor Who Rolled Up a Sheet of Paper
text:
In the autumn of 1816, a young French doctor named René Laennec faced a small but awkward problem at the Necker Hospital in Paris. A young woman had come to him with symptoms that suggested heart disease, and he needed to listen to her chest. The usual method at the time was simple: the doctor pressed his ear directly against the patient's body. But the patient was young, Laennec was a young man, and the rules of polite society made the method feel improper. In any case, she was rather plump, and he doubted that he would hear much through the extra layer.

What happened next has become one of the favourite stories of medical history. Laennec later wrote that he remembered a scene he had once watched in a courtyard: children playing with a long piece of wood, one scratching one end with a pin while another pressed an ear to the opposite end and heard the sound clearly. Sound, he reasoned, travels well through solid bodies. He took a few sheets of paper, rolled them into a tight tube, placed one end on the woman's chest and put his ear to the other. To his surprise and delight, he heard the beating of her heart far more clearly than he had ever heard it with his bare ear.

It is worth pausing on how strange this was. For centuries, doctors had judged illness mostly by what patients told them and by what could be seen from outside: the colour of the skin, the pulse at the wrist, the appearance of urine. The inside of a living body was largely hidden. Some doctors tapped on the chest and listened to the echo, a method that an Austrian physician had described decades earlier, but it was not widely used. Laennec's paper tube offered something new: a window, made of sound, into the workings of the heart and lungs.

Laennec did not stop at paper. He was a patient and methodical man, and he spent the next three years experimenting with different materials and shapes. He finally settled on a hollow wooden cylinder about 25 centimetres long, which could be taken apart for carrying. He named it the stethoscope, from Greek words meaning roughly 'to examine the chest'. More importantly, he did not treat it as a toy. He listened to hundreds of patients on the wards, wrote down exactly what he heard, and then, when patients died, compared his notes with what the autopsy revealed. In this way he learned to link particular sounds, such as crackles, whistles and rubbing noises, with particular diseases of the lungs and heart, including pneumonia and tuberculosis.

In 1819 he published his findings in a long book, which is often regarded as a seminal work in the history of diagnosis. Its influence spread swiftly across Europe and beyond, although not without resistance. Some older physicians ridiculed the wooden tube as a fashionable gadget, and a few argued that a good doctor should not need such a device. Others worried that it put a distance between doctor and patient. Yet the practical advantages were difficult to deny, and within a few decades the instrument had become a symbol of the medical profession itself.

There is a sad irony at the end of the story. Laennec himself suffered from tuberculosis, the very disease he had done so much to understand. He died in 1826, at only forty-five. According to some accounts, his illness was confirmed with the help of his own invention, although such details are hard to verify.

Today's stethoscope looks quite different. In the 1850s, designs with two earpieces and flexible tubes appeared, and modern versions use a flat disc to collect sound. Doctors now have ultrasound, scanners and many other tools that would have seemed like magic to Laennec. Still, the stethoscope remains around the necks of clinicians all over the world. It is cheap, it needs no electricity, and in skilled hands it can still reveal a great deal in a few seconds.

Perhaps the most charming part of the story is its modest beginning. One of the most familiar instruments in medicine was not born in a laboratory but out of embarrassment, a childhood memory and a roll of paper. It is a reminder that progress sometimes depends less on expensive equipment than on a curious mind willing to try a simple idea.

questions.q: Why did Laennec decide to use a rolled paper tube instead of his ear?
options: Pressing his ear to the young woman's chest felt improper and was unlikely to work well
He wanted to protect himself from catching tuberculosis
An Austrian physician had recommended the method to him
The patient refused to let him examine her at all
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Pressing his ear to the young woman's chest felt improper and was unlikely to work well’: metin, dönemin görgü kuralları nedeniyle kulağı göğse dayamanın uygunsuz göründüğünü ve hastanın tombul olduğu için iyi duyamayacağını düşündüğünü söyler.

questions.q: How did Laennec learn which sounds belonged to which diseases?
options: By asking patients to describe the noises inside them
By comparing his notes with what autopsies revealed after patients died
By testing the tube on children in a courtyard
By copying descriptions from older textbooks
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘By comparing his notes with what autopsies revealed after patients died’: Laennec duyduklarını not edip hastalar öldüğünde otopsi bulgularıyla karşılaştırarak sesleri belirli hastalıklara bağlamıştır.

title: The Surgeon Who Reached His Own Heart
text:
In 1929, a young German doctor named Werner Forssmann, then about twenty-five, had an idea that his superiors considered both dangerous and foolish. Working at a small hospital in Eberswalde, near Berlin, he had become fascinated by an old drawing of an experiment on a horse, in which a thin tube had been passed through a vein into the animal's heart. Why, he wondered, could the same not be done in a human being? If a doctor could guide a soft tube through a vein in the arm all the way to the heart, medicines could be delivered exactly where they were needed in an emergency, and doctors might even measure what was happening inside the living heart.

His chief listened politely and then refused permission. Most experts at the time believed that anything touching the inside of the heart would make it stop. Forssmann was not convinced, and he decided to test the idea on the one patient who could not complain: himself.

The story of what happened next has been told in slightly different versions, but the main events are well documented. Forssmann needed sterile instruments, which were kept under the control of an operating-room nurse, Gerda Ditzen. When he explained his plan, she was so impressed that she offered to be the subject instead. Forssmann appeared to agree. He asked her to lie on the operating table and strapped her down, but while she waited, he quietly numbed his own arm, made a small cut near the elbow and pushed a thin rubber tube, normally used for the bladder, into a vein. Only then did he release the nurse, who was reportedly furious.

With the tube already partly inside, Forssmann walked down to the X-ray department, possibly with the nurse beside him. There he pushed the tube further until it had travelled roughly 65 centimetres, and then he had an X-ray taken. The picture showed the tip of the tube lying inside the right side of his heart. He felt no pain in the heart itself, and he suffered no serious harm.

One might expect such a bold experiment to have made him a hero. In fact, it nearly ended his career. When he published a report, some newspapers treated it as a sensation, while senior surgeons ridiculed it as a stunt. He moved to the famous Charité hospital in Berlin, where the powerful surgeon Ferdinand Sauerbruch is said to have remarked that such tricks belonged in a circus rather than a clinic. Forssmann soon lost his position there. Discouraged, he gave up cardiac research and trained as a urologist. During the Second World War he served as an army doctor and was held for a time as a prisoner of war. Afterwards he worked quietly as a country doctor.

Meanwhile, his idea had not been forgotten. In the 1940s, two physicians in New York, André Cournand and Dickinson Richards, used and refined the method, now called cardiac catheterization, to measure pressure and blood flow inside the heart and lungs. Their work turned it into a reliable tool for diagnosing heart disease. In 1956, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Cournand, Richards and Forssmann together. The story goes that Forssmann, by then a little-known doctor in a small town, was astonished by the news.

Today, thin tubes guided through blood vessels are used every day in hospitals around the world. They allow doctors to open blocked arteries, place devices and examine the heart without opening the chest. Millions of patients have benefited from an invaluable procedure that began, remarkably, with one young man walking down a hospital staircase with a tube in his arm.

Forssmann's story raises uncomfortable questions too. Experimenting on oneself can look heroic, but it can also be reckless, and it bypasses the careful checks that protect both scientists and patients. Modern research rules would never allow what he did. Even so, it is hard not to admire his courage and his willingness to trust evidence over authority. In medicine, as elsewhere, the line between foolishness and genius is sometimes visible only in hindsight.

questions.q: What did Forssmann do when the nurse offered to be the subject of the experiment?
options: He let her go through the experiment first
He sent her to ask his chief for permission
He strapped her to the table but carried out the experiment on himself
He asked her to take the X-ray picture for him
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘He strapped her to the table but carried out the experiment on himself’: Forssmann hemşireyi masaya bağlamış, ama tüpü kendi koluna yerleştirmiştir.

questions.q: How was Forssmann's experiment received at first?
options: He was quickly given the Nobel Prize for it
Sauerbruch praised it and gave him a research post
American doctors invited him to New York to continue it
Senior surgeons mocked it, and he soon lost his position in Berlin
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Senior surgeons mocked it, and he soon lost his position in Berlin’: kıdemli cerrahlar deneyi bir gösteri numarası saymış, Forssmann da Charité'deki görevini kısa sürede kaybetmiştir; Nobel ancak 1956'da gelmiştir.

title: A Window Into the Stomach
text:
On 6 June 1822, at a fur-trading post on Mackinac Island, in what is now the American state of Michigan, a gun went off by accident in a crowded shop. The shot hit a young French-Canadian worker named Alexis St. Martin at very close range, tearing open his side and damaging his ribs, a lung and his stomach. The nearest doctor was William Beaumont, a surgeon in the United States Army who was stationed at a fort nearby. When he arrived and saw the wound, he reportedly thought the young man would not survive the day.

St. Martin did survive. Beaumont cleaned and dressed the wound over many months, and slowly the young man recovered. But the injury did not close completely. The edges of the hole in his stomach joined the edges of the hole in his skin, leaving a permanent opening, known in medicine as a fistula. A flap of tissue partly covered it, but when this was pushed aside, Beaumont could look straight into a living stomach.

At that time, nobody really knew how digestion worked. Some scholars believed that the stomach ground food like a mill; others thought that food simply rotted, or that some mysterious vital force broke it down. Beaumont, who had no university degree and had learned medicine as an apprentice, realised that he had an extraordinary opportunity. Around 1825 he began a long series of experiments.

His methods were simple, even crude. He tied small pieces of food, such as beef, bread and cabbage, to a silk string and lowered them through the opening. After an hour or two he pulled them out to see how much had been digested. He also drew out samples of stomach fluid, placed them in small glass containers with pieces of meat, and kept them warm, sometimes under his own arm. The meat broke down outside the body, though more slowly than inside. This was strong evidence that digestion was largely a chemical process, driven by an acidic juice, rather than a purely mechanical one. He also observed that the juice was a secretion of the stomach wall, produced mainly when food arrived, and that St. Martin's moods seemed to affect his digestive system: when the young man was angry or upset, digestion appeared to slow down.

In 1833 Beaumont published his results in a book describing more than two hundred experiments. It is still considered a classic of physiology, and it helped to lay the groundwork for the scientific study of digestion and of the gastrointestinal system as a whole.

Yet the story has a darker side, and modern writers rarely tell it without discomfort. St. Martin was poor and unable to read or write, and he depended on Beaumont for work and money. At one point he signed a contract that bound him to serve Beaumont and to submit to experiments in return for pay. He seems to have found the procedures tiresome and sometimes painful, and more than once he fled back to Canada, where he married and had children. Beaumont spent years trying to persuade him to return. Some historians see the relationship as a partnership that benefited both men; others regard it as the exploitation of a vulnerable person who had little real choice.

Today such questions would fall under the heading of informed consent. Could a man who owed his life and his living to his doctor ever freely say no? Beaumont never obtained the kind of agreement that a modern ethics committee would demand, and of course no such committee existed then.

The ending is striking. Beaumont died in 1853 after a fall on icy steps. St. Martin, despite the hole in his side, lived on for decades and died in Quebec in 1880. By several accounts, his family, determined that no doctor would take his body for study, delayed the burial until it had begun to decay, and then buried him in an unusually deep grave.

The window into St. Martin's stomach taught the world a great deal about digestion. It also left behind a lasting lesson: knowledge gained at the expense of another person's freedom comes at a price that science should not ignore.

questions.q: What did Beaumont's experiments mainly show about digestion?
options: That the stomach grinds food like a mill
That food rots slowly in the stomach
That a vital force breaks food down
That it is largely a chemical process driven by stomach juice
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘That it is largely a chemical process driven by stomach juice’: et, mide sıvısıyla vücut dışında da parçalanmış; bu da sindirimin büyük ölçüde asidik bir sıvının yürüttüğü kimyasal bir süreç olduğunu göstermiştir.

questions.q: Why do many modern readers feel uneasy about Beaumont's work?
options: St. Martin was poor and dependent on him, so he may not have been free to refuse
Beaumont copied his results from other scholars
The experiments caused St. Martin's death
Beaumont kept his findings secret for many years
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘St. Martin was poor and dependent on him, so he may not have been free to refuse’: metin, okuma yazma bilmeyen ve geçimi Beaumont'a bağlı olan St. Martin'in gerçekten hayır diyebilip diyemeyeceğini, yani bilgilendirilmiş onam sorununu tartışır.

title: Cold Enough to Save a Life
text:
On a bright afternoon in May 1999, a young doctor named Anna Bågenholm was skiing with two colleagues in the mountains near Narvik, in northern Norway. All three worked at the university hospital in Tromsø, and all three were experienced skiers. As Bågenholm came down a steep slope beside a frozen stream, she lost control, fell head first onto the ice and broke through it. Within seconds she was upside down in freezing water, with her head and body trapped beneath a thick layer of ice and only her skis and feet above the surface.

Her friends grabbed her feet and held on, but the current was strong and they could not pull her out. She was at the mercy of the water. She found a pocket of air under the ice and, according to later reports, kept breathing for around forty minutes while they struggled to reach her. Then her body went still. By the time a rescue team arrived with proper equipment and cut through the ice, she had been in the water for roughly eighty minutes. She showed no vital signs: she was not breathing, and her heart was not beating.

Under normal conditions, there would have been no hope. The human brain begins to suffer serious damage after only a few minutes without oxygen. But these conditions were not normal. The rescuers began chest compressions immediately, and a helicopter flew her to Tromsø. When she arrived, her body temperature was measured at 13.7 degrees Celsius, one of the lowest ever recorded in a person who survived. A healthy body is kept at about 37 degrees.

The doctors at Tromsø did not treat her as dead. In the cold regions of the world, emergency doctors often repeat a striking rule: no one is dead until they are warm and dead. A cold body can sometimes be revived long after the heart has stopped, because cold slows down the metabolic reactions inside cells. A brain that has been cooled needs much less oxygen, so it can survive far longer without damage.

The team connected Bågenholm to a heart-lung machine, which took the blood out of her body, warmed it, added oxygen and pumped it back in. Slowly, degree by degree, her temperature rose. After several hours, her heart began to beat again. A large team of doctors and nurses worked on her through the night, and it is said that more than a hundred people were involved in her care in one way or another.

Her convalescence was long. When she woke up in intensive care after about ten days, she could not move from the neck down, and she faced months of physiotherapy. Little by little, her strength returned. Some minor problems with her hands remained, but her mind was unharmed, and she went back to work at the same hospital, eventually as a radiologist. She has since spoken about her experience with modesty, often giving most of the credit to her friends and the hospital team.

What explains her survival? Doctors believe that the key was the order in which things happened. She was cooled very quickly by the icy water while she was still breathing and her heart was still pumping blood. Her brain therefore became cold before it was deprived of oxygen. In most people whose hearts stop, the brain is damaged before it has any chance to cool. In her case, the cold acted almost like a protective shield.

Her case has influenced medicine in other ways. It strengthened interest in cooling patients deliberately to protect the brain in some situations, such as after cardiac arrest or during certain operations, and doctors have studied such controlled cooling carefully since then, with mixed results. It has also reinforced the message to rescuers that they should not give up too early on victims of severe cold.

Anna Bågenholm's story is not a recipe for survival. Most people who fall through ice into fast-moving water do not live, and the conditions that saved her were extremely unusual. Even so, her case remains a powerful reminder that the human body can be remarkably resilient, and that the boundary between life and death is sometimes less fixed than it seems.

questions.q: According to doctors, what was the key to Bågenholm's survival?
options: She was rescued within a few minutes of falling
Her body cooled down before her brain was deprived of oxygen
She had trained her body to resist cold as a skier
Her heart never actually stopped beating
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Her body cooled down before her brain was deprived of oxygen’: metin, hâlâ nefes alırken buzlu suda hızla soğuduğu için beyninin oksijensiz kalmadan önce soğuduğunu ve bunun koruyucu bir kalkan gibi işlediğini söyler.

questions.q: What does the rule 'no one is dead until they are warm and dead' mean?
options: Cold patients should be kept cold for as long as possible
Doctors should wait until a patient is warm before starting treatment
A very cold person without a heartbeat may still be saved, so rescuers should not give up
Only patients with a normal temperature can be declared alive
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘A very cold person without a heartbeat may still be saved, so rescuers should not give up’: soğuk vücut, kalp durduktan çok sonra bile canlandırılabildiği için ısıtılmadan ölü kabul edilmemelidir.

title: The People Who Live on the Sea
text:
In the warm, clear waters between Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines live the Bajau, a nomadic people often described as sea nomads. For centuries, many Bajau families spent most of their lives on boats or in houses built on poles above the water, moving with the seasons and living largely from the sea. Today many have settled on land, but diving remains central to their way of life. Using simple wooden goggles and a spear, Bajau divers hunt fish and collect shellfish on the sea floor, sometimes at depths of forty metres or more.

What astonishes visitors is not only how deep they go but how long they spend underwater. A skilled diver may make dozens of short dives in a working day, and some estimates suggest that the total time spent beneath the surface can add up to several hours. Each dive usually lasts no more than a minute or two, but the effort is repeated again and again, and divers say they feel at home in the water in a way that people on land rarely do.

How does the human body cope with such a life? Part of the answer lies in a response that all of us share. When a person holds their breath and puts their face in cold water, the body reacts automatically. The heart slows down, the blood vessels in the arms and legs narrow, and blood is directed towards the most vital organs, such as the brain and heart. This is known as the diving reflex, and it is a mammalian response found in many animals, from seals to dolphins. It helps the body save oxygen while it cannot breathe.

Another part of this reflex involves a less famous organ: the spleen. The spleen, which sits in the upper left part of the abdominal area, stores a large supply of red blood cells, the cells that carry oxygen. During a dive it contracts and releases these cells into the bloodstream, a little like an emergency tank of oxygen. Seals that dive deeply have unusually large spleens, and scientists had long wondered whether something similar might be true of human divers.

In 2018, a team led by the geneticist Melissa Ilardo published a study that explored this question. The researchers travelled to Indonesia and used a portable ultrasound machine to measure the spleens of Bajau people and of the Saluan, a neighbouring people who live mainly on land and do not dive in the same way. The Bajau had spleens that were, on average, about fifty per cent larger. Importantly, this was true even of Bajau people who did not dive themselves, which suggested that the difference was not simply the result of training but was at least partly inherited.

The team then examined the DNA of both groups. They found signs of natural selection in several genes among the Bajau, including one called PDE10A, which in mice is linked to thyroid hormone levels and spleen size. The researchers proposed that, over many generations, Bajau people with larger spleens may have been more successful divers, gathered more food and raised more children, so that the trait slowly became more common.

Not every scientist was fully persuaded. Some pointed out that the sample size was small and that more work was needed to confirm exactly how the gene affects the body. The authors themselves were careful to describe their conclusions as a strong starting point rather than the final word. Still, the study attracted wide attention, because clear examples of recent human adaptation are rare and hard to prove.

The findings may matter beyond the Bajau. Doctors are interested in what happens when oxygen levels in the body fall dangerously low, for example during certain lung diseases or during surgery. Understanding how one population has adapted to repeated short periods without oxygen could, in principle, help researchers think about such conditions in new ways.

There is also a more human side to the story. The Bajau way of life is under pressure from overfishing, damaged reefs and policies that encourage them to settle on land. Some younger Bajau spend less time in the water than their grandparents did. If their traditions fade, the world may lose not only a remarkable culture but also a living record of how closely human bodies can be shaped by the places where people make their home.

questions.q: Why was it important that non-diving Bajau also had large spleens?
options: It suggested that the large spleens were at least partly inherited, not just the result of training
It proved that diving makes the spleen smaller
It showed that the Saluan were better divers than the Bajau
It meant that the ultrasound machine was not working properly
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘It suggested that the large spleens were at least partly inherited, not just the result of training’: dalış yapmayan Bajaular'da da büyük dalak görülmesi, farkın yalnızca antrenmandan değil kısmen kalıtımdan kaynaklandığını düşündürmüştür.

questions.q: How did some scientists react to the 2018 study?
options: They rejected it because the Bajau do not really dive
They claimed that the spleen plays no role in diving
They said it proved the gene's effect beyond any doubt
They wanted more evidence, partly because the sample size was small
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘They wanted more evidence, partly because the sample size was small’: bazı bilim insanları örneklemin küçük olduğunu ve genin vücudu nasıl etkilediğini doğrulamak için daha fazla çalışma gerektiğini belirtmiştir.

title: Thirty Years on a Scale
text:
Most of us step on a bathroom scale now and then, perhaps after a holiday or before a new diet. Santorio Santorio, an Italian physician who lived about four hundred years ago, did something far more extreme. For roughly thirty years, according to his own account, he weighed himself, everything he ate and drank, and everything that left his body. His aim was not to lose weight. He wanted to understand, in numbers, how the human body works.

Santorio was born in 1561 in Capodistria, a town on the Adriatic coast that is now Koper in Slovenia. He studied medicine at the University of Padua, one of the great centres of learning in Europe, and after practising as a doctor for some years he returned there as a professor. Padua was an exciting place. Galileo had taught mathematics at the same university until 1610, and the two men appear to have known each other. Both shared a belief that nature could be understood through careful measurement.

To carry out his study, Santorio built what has become known as the weighing chair. A chair was hung from a large steelyard, a type of balance with a long arm, so that he could sit in it and read his weight. He is said to have eaten his meals while sitting in it, watching how the scale moved as he ate. He compared his weight before and after meals, after sleep, after exercise and in different seasons, and he kept detailed, methodical records.

What he found surprised him. The weight of the food and drink he took in was considerably greater than the weight of everything he passed out of his body in the usual ways. Much of the difference, he concluded, must be leaving his body invisibly, through the skin and the breath. He called this 'insensible perspiration', meaning sweating that cannot be felt or seen. By his estimates, this invisible loss was larger than all the visible losses put together, although modern scientists consider his figures rather high.

In 1614 he published his conclusions in a short book called De Statica Medicina, written as a series of brief sayings. It became remarkably popular and was reprinted and translated many times over the following century. Readers enjoyed its practical tone, which mixed observations about weight with advice on eating, sleeping and moderation. Some of its claims now seem odd, but the method behind them was new.

Santorio is often described as a founder of the study of metabolic processes, the chemical changes by which the body uses food. That may be generous, since he had no idea of the chemistry involved. Still, his central insight was sound: the body is constantly exchanging matter with the world around it, and much of that exchange cannot be seen. Water is lost with every breath, and moisture leaves through the skin even on a cold day. Modern physiology confirms that this kind of water loss is real and significant.

Santorio was also an inventor of measuring devices. He is credited with adding a scale to an early instrument for measuring temperature, a forerunner of the clinical thermometer, and with designing a device that used a pendulum to compare the speed of a patient's pulse. Historians debate exactly how original some of these devices were, since ideas moved quickly between scholars in Padua, but Santorio clearly helped to bring measurement and precision into everyday medical practice.

It is easy to smile at the image of a serious professor eating his dinner while hanging from a beam. Yet the picture tells us something important. Before Santorio, much of medicine relied on ancient authorities and general theories about balance and temperament. He insisted on checking ideas against numbers, patiently, for decades. In that sense, the man in the weighing chair was an early example of what we would now call evidence-based medicine.

Today, laboratories use sealed rooms and sensitive instruments to measure exactly how much energy and water the body uses. These modern studies owe something to the stubborn curiosity of a man who refused to accept that the workings of the body were beyond measurement.

questions.q: What did Santorio conclude from his measurements?
options: That eating while seated helps people lose weight
That most food leaves the body in the usual visible ways
That a large amount of weight is lost invisibly through the skin and breath
That body weight never changes from season to season
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘That a large amount of weight is lost invisibly through the skin and breath’: aldığı yiyecek ve içeceğin ağırlığı görünür kayıplardan çok fazla olduğu için farkın deri ve nefes yoluyla görünmeden kaybolduğu sonucuna varmış, buna ‘hissedilmeyen terleme’ demiştir.

questions.q: Why does the writer call Santorio an early example of evidence-based medicine?
options: Because he followed the ancient authorities closely
Because he tested ideas against careful measurements over many years
Because he invented the modern bathroom scale
Because he worked in a sealed laboratory
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Because he tested ideas against careful measurements over many years’: yazar, Santorio'nun eski otoritelere dayanmak yerine fikirleri onlarca yıl sabırla sayılarla sınadığını vurgular.

title: The Students Who Breathed for Others
text:
In the late summer of 1952, Copenhagen was struck by one of the worst polio epidemics ever recorded in Europe. Polio is caused by a virus that usually produces only a mild illness, but in some people it attacks the nerves that control the muscles. In the most severe cases it leads to paralysis of the muscles used for breathing and swallowing. Patients in this condition slowly suffocate unless something breathes for them.

Most of the patients were sent to Blegdam Hospital, the city's hospital for infectious diseases. Within weeks it was overwhelmed. At the peak of the epidemic, dozens of new patients arrived every day, and many of them, often children and young adults, could not breathe on their own. The hospital had only a handful of machines to help them. The best known of these was the iron lung, a large metal cylinder in which the patient lay with only the head outside, while a pump changed the air pressure around the body to draw air into the lungs. Iron lungs were heavy, expensive and few in number. In the first weeks, the great majority of patients who developed breathing failure died.

The chief physician, H. C. A. Lassen, was desperate for new ideas. In late August he consulted an anaesthetist named Bjørn Ibsen. Anaesthesia was still a young specialty in Denmark, and Ibsen had recently trained in Boston, where he had seen how patients under deep anaesthesia could be kept alive by pushing air into their lungs through a tube. He suspected that the polio patients were dying not mainly from the virus itself but from a lack of oxygen and a build-up of carbon dioxide, and that the iron lung was not the only answer.

On 27 August, Ibsen tested his idea on a twelve-year-old girl named Vivi Ebert, who was close to death. A surgeon made an opening in the front of her neck, a procedure called a tracheostomy, and Ibsen placed a tube with a soft cuff into her windpipe. He then attached a rubber bag and began squeezing it by hand, pushing air into her lungs. At first the attempt seemed to be failing, and some onlookers began to leave. Then, after Ibsen gave her a drug to calm her, her colour improved and her breathing became steady. She survived.

The method worked, but it created an enormous practical problem. A patient treated in this way needed someone to squeeze the bag, day and night, without stopping, sometimes for weeks or months. There were not nearly enough nurses or doctors. The solution was to call on the city's medical students, and later dental students too. Around 1,500 of them took turns sitting beside patients' beds and squeezing bags in shifts of several hours. Estimates suggest that together they provided some 165,000 hours of breathing by hand during the epidemic.

The results were dramatic. Remarkably, the death rate among patients with breathing failure fell from around eighty per cent to roughly forty per cent, and later lower still. Many people who would almost certainly have died went home. The episode also showed something new about the organisation of care. Instead of scattering the sickest patients across many wards, the hospital gathered them in one place, with constant observation, trained staff and equipment for breathing support.

This idea did not disappear when the epidemic ended. In 1953, Ibsen set up what is often described as the world's first modern intensive care unit, at another Copenhagen hospital. Over the following decades, mechanical ventilators replaced the tired hands of students, and units like his spread around the world. Today intensive care is a normal part of every large hospital, and its importance became painfully clear to the whole world during the COVID-19 pandemic.

It is easy to remember medical history as a series of brilliant individuals and clever machines. The Copenhagen epidemic reminds us of another kind of hero. Ibsen's insight mattered, but so did the young people who, close to exhaustion, sat for hours in hot wards, squeezing rubber bags, talking to frightened patients and keeping them alive one breath at a time.

questions.q: Why did Ibsen think the polio patients were dying?
options: The virus was destroying their hearts
The iron lungs were spreading infection
They were given too many sedatives
They were not getting enough oxygen and carbon dioxide was building up
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘They were not getting enough oxygen and carbon dioxide was building up’: Ibsen, hastaların asıl olarak virüsten değil oksijen yetersizliği ve karbondioksit birikmesinden öldüğünden şüphelenmiştir.

questions.q: What practical problem did Ibsen's method create, and how was it solved?
options: Someone had to squeeze each bag nonstop, so hundreds of students took turns doing it
There were not enough rubber bags, so they were made by hand in the hospital
Patients refused the treatment, so the students persuaded them
The iron lungs broke down, so new ones were brought from Boston
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Someone had to squeeze each bag nonstop, so hundreds of students took turns doing it’: her hastanın torbası gece gündüz elle sıkılmalıydı; bu iş için yaklaşık 1.500 tıp ve diş hekimliği öğrencisi vardiyalarla çalışmıştır.

title: The Bark That Fought a Fever
text:
For most of human history, malaria was one of the deadliest diseases on earth. Its typical pattern of fever, chills and sweating, returning every few days, was known in ancient Rome, and it continued to kill vast numbers of people in Europe, Africa and Asia for centuries. Nobody knew that it was spread by mosquitoes or caused by a tiny parasite in the blood. What finally offered relief, for those lucky enough to get it, came not from a laboratory but from the bark of a tree growing high in the Andes mountains of South America.

The tree is known as cinchona, and it grows on the cool, wet slopes of what are now Peru, Ecuador and Bolivia. How Europeans first learned of its powers is not entirely clear. A famous story tells of a Spanish countess, the wife of the ruler of Peru, who was cured of a fever in the 1630s by a powder made from the bark and then carried it back to Spain. The story is charming, and the great Swedish scientist Linnaeus later gave the tree its botanical name in her honour, though he misspelled her title. Historians, however, have found little evidence that the story is true.

It seems more likely that Jesuit missionaries in Peru learned about the bark from local healers, who may have used it to stop shivering, and sent supplies to Europe. By the middle of the seventeenth century the powdered bark was being used in Rome, where malaria was common, and it soon became known as 'Jesuits' bark'. This religious connection caused problems. In Protestant England, many people distrusted a remedy linked with the Catholic Church, and the bark was regarded with suspicion.

One man found a clever way around this. Robert Talbor, an English healer with little formal training, became famous in the 1670s for a secret fever cure. He treated King Charles II successfully and then travelled to France, where he is said to have cured the son of King Louis XIV. Talbor grew rich and famous, and he kept his recipe hidden. Only after his death was it revealed that the main ingredient of his mysterious medicine was the very same Jesuits' bark, mixed with wine and other flavours to disguise it.

For almost two centuries, doctors used the powdered bark without knowing what made it work. Its quality varied greatly, and dishonest traders sometimes mixed it with useless material. Then, in 1820, two French chemists, Pierre Pelletier and Joseph Caventou, managed to isolate the active substance. They called it quinine. Now the drug could be measured with precision, and pharmaceutical factories began to produce it on a large scale.

Demand rose quickly, especially as European powers expanded into tropical regions of Africa and Asia, where malaria was a major threat to soldiers and settlers. This had a troubling side. Quinine became a tool of colonialism, helping to make European expansion possible, and the wild cinchona trees of the Andes were cut down so heavily that people feared they might disappear. South American governments tried to protect their valuable trade by banning the export of seeds.

In the 1860s, British and Dutch collectors smuggled seeds and young plants out of the Andes anyway. One of the most successful collections was made with the help of a Bolivian man, Manuel Incra Mamani, who gathered seeds for an English trader. According to several accounts, he was later arrested and beaten, and he died as a result. The seeds he collected ended up on Dutch plantations on the island of Java, which by the early twentieth century produced most of the world's quinine.

During the twentieth century, synthetic drugs largely replaced quinine as the first choice against malaria, although it is still used in some cases. Today most people meet it in a very different form: it gives tonic water its bitter taste. The story of the bark is a reminder that medicines have histories as complex as the diseases they treat, full of healing, profit, faith and the forgotten people whose knowledge made it all possible.

questions.q: Why did Robert Talbor keep his recipe secret?
options: Because the bark was too expensive to buy openly
Because people distrusted the Jesuits' bark, and his secret cure made him rich and famous
Because King Charles II ordered him to
Because he did not know what the main ingredient was
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Because people distrusted the Jesuits' bark, and his secret cure made him rich and famous’: Protestan İngiltere'de Katolik kilisesiyle bağlantılı ilaca güvenilmiyordu; Talbor tarifini gizleyerek zengin ve ünlü olmuş, ana bileşenin aynı kabuk olduğu ölümünden sonra ortaya çıkmıştır.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the role of Manuel Incra Mamani?
options: He isolated quinine together with two French chemists
He protected the wild trees from foreign collectors
He collected seeds that ended up on Dutch plantations, and he reportedly died after being beaten
He discovered that malaria is spread by mosquitoes
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘He collected seeds that ended up on Dutch plantations, and he reportedly died after being beaten’: metin, Mamani'nin bir İngiliz tüccar için tohum topladığını, bu tohumların Java'daki Hollanda plantasyonlarına gittiğini ve onun dövülerek öldüğünün aktarıldığını söyler.

title: The Men Who Walked Into an Oven
text:
In the mid-1770s, a group of gentlemen in London carried out one of the strangest experiments of the eighteenth century. Their aim was to find out how much heat the human body could bear, and they decided to answer the question in the most direct way possible: by walking into a room heated far beyond the boiling point of water and staying there for as long as they could.

The leader of the experiments was the physician George Fordyce, and the person who wrote the best-known account of them was Charles Blagden, a young doctor and member of the Royal Society. Other visitors joined them, including, it is said, the explorer and naturalist Joseph Banks. Fordyce had a set of rooms with a stove that could heat the air to extreme temperatures. The men entered fully dressed, wearing clothes to protect their skin, and observed what happened to themselves and to various objects around them.

According to Blagden's report, the air temperature in one session rose to more than 100 degrees Celsius, and on some occasions it was reportedly higher still. The men stayed inside for several minutes at a time. They found that the air felt intensely hot, especially when they breathed out or moved, and their metal watch chains became too hot to touch. Yet, to their astonishment, their bodies did not cook. When they placed a thermometer under the tongue or held it in the hand, their own temperature remained close to normal, rising only slightly.

To make the point vividly, they brought food into the room. Eggs placed on a metal frame were soon cooked hard. A piece of raw steak was cooked through in a little more than half an hour, and even faster when the air was moved around it with a pair of bellows. Meanwhile, the living men standing beside the steak remained more or less comfortable. A dog was also reportedly taken into the room in a basket, and it too came out unharmed, though its feet had been protected from the hot floor.

What protected them? Blagden and his colleagues noticed that they were sweating heavily. They concluded that the body has a power of 'destroying heat', and that sweating played an important part in it. We now understand the process more clearly. When sweat evaporates from the skin, it takes heat away with it, cooling the body. Evaporation uses a great deal of energy, which is why a wet towel on the neck feels so refreshing on a summer day. In very dry air, sweat evaporates quickly, so the cooling effect is powerful. This is one reason why people can sit for a short time in a dry sauna at temperatures that would be deadly in water.

The experiments therefore showed something fundamental about human physiology: the body is not a passive object that simply heats up like a piece of meat, but an active system that works constantly to keep its internal temperature stable. This balance is now called homeostasis, and temperature control is one of its most important examples.

The same knowledge carries a warning. Evaporation depends on the air being dry enough to absorb more water. When the air is both hot and very humid, sweat cannot evaporate easily, and the body loses its main way of cooling itself. In such conditions even healthy people can develop heatstroke, a dangerous condition in which body temperature rises out of control. Scientists who study climate change are increasingly concerned about regions where the combination of heat and humidity may approach the limits that the human body can tolerate. Dehydration makes matters worse, because a body without enough water cannot produce enough sweat.

Today, no ethics committee would allow researchers to walk into an oven to test their own limits. The gentlemen of the 1770s were brave, perhaps foolishly so. Still, their strange afternoons in a superheated room left a lasting lesson, and it is one worth remembering on the hottest days of summer: our bodies are remarkably good at handling heat, but only as long as the air allows our sweat to do its work.

questions.q: What did the men discover about their own bodies in the hot room?
options: Their body temperature stayed close to normal while food around them cooked
Their body temperature rose as fast as the air temperature
They could not stay in the room for more than a few seconds
Their skin was badly burned despite their clothes
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Their body temperature stayed close to normal while food around them cooked’: yumurtalar ve biftek pişerken adamların termometreyle ölçülen vücut sıcaklığı normale yakın kalmış, ancak hafifçe yükselmiştir.

questions.q: Why is very humid heat more dangerous than dry heat, according to the text?
options: Humid air contains less oxygen
Humid air makes people drink too much water
Humid air heats the body faster than an oven
Sweat cannot evaporate easily, so the body loses its main way of cooling
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Sweat cannot evaporate easily, so the body loses its main way of cooling’: metin, hava hem sıcak hem nemliyken terin buharlaşamadığını ve vücudun başlıca serinleme yolunu yitirdiğini açıklar.

title: The Little Clip on Your Finger
text:
If you have ever been in hospital, you have probably worn one: a small plastic clip on the end of a finger, glowing faintly red, connected to a screen that shows two numbers. One is the pulse. The other is the oxygen saturation, a measure of how much of the oxygen-carrying protein in the blood is actually carrying oxygen. In a healthy person it is usually somewhere between 95 and 100 per cent. The device is called a pulse oximeter, and it has become so familiar, like the other vital signs on a hospital screen, that few people stop to wonder where it came from.

Its story begins in Tokyo in the early 1970s, with an engineer named Takuo Aoyagi, who worked for a company that made medical equipment. Aoyagi was not trying to measure oxygen at all. He was working on a method to measure how much blood the heart pumps, by injecting a dye into a vein and then detecting the dye with light shone through the ear. The problem was that the pulse kept getting in the way. Every heartbeat sent a wave of fresh blood through the ear, and this made the light signal rise and fall, spoiling his measurements.

Most engineers would have treated this pulsing signal as noise and looked for a way to remove it. Aoyagi, however, had an insight. The pulsing part of the signal came from arterial blood, the fresh blood pushed in by each heartbeat, while the steady part came from everything else: skin, bone, tissue and the blood in the veins. If he compared the pulsing signal at two different colours of light, he reasoned, he could calculate the oxygen level in the arterial blood alone, without the rest getting in the way.

The science behind this is elegant. Blood rich in oxygen and blood poor in oxygen absorb red and infrared light differently. Oxygen-rich blood is bright red and lets more red light through; oxygen-poor blood is darker. By shining both kinds of light through a finger or ear and watching how much is absorbed with each pulse, a device can estimate the proportion of oxygen-rich blood in the arteries, continuously, with surprising precision and without a single needle.

Aoyagi and his company applied for a patent in 1974, and an early device was produced. At first, though, it attracted limited interest. The technology was not yet reliable, and much of the later development took place elsewhere. In the late 1970s and 1980s, companies in the United States produced smaller, more accurate versions, and anaesthetists quickly saw their value. During an operation, a patient's oxygen level can drop dangerously without obvious signs, and a continuous measure allowed doctors to notice problems within seconds. By the late 1980s, pulse oximeters had become a standard part of anaesthesia in many countries, and they soon spread to intensive care, emergency rooms and ambulances.

For years, Aoyagi received relatively little recognition outside his field. That began to change later in his life, when he was honoured by several professional bodies. He continued to work on improving the technology into old age, and he died in 2020, at the age of 84, just as his invention was taking on new importance. During the COVID-19 pandemic, millions of people used small oximeters at home to check whether their oxygen levels were falling, sometimes before they felt short of breath.

The pandemic also drew attention to a serious weakness. Several studies, including a widely discussed one published in 2020, found that pulse oximeters were more likely to overestimate oxygen levels in patients with darker skin. Because skin pigment also absorbs light, the readings can be misleading if devices are not carefully designed and tested on a wide range of people. Patients whose true oxygen levels were dangerously low could therefore appear to be safe. The finding was not entirely new, as some researchers had raised similar concerns decades earlier, but it had received little attention.

Regulators and manufacturers have since begun to look again at how these devices are tested. The episode is a useful reminder that a medical tool is only as fair as the research behind it. Aoyagi's idea, turning a nuisance in his data into a clever measurement, has helped to save countless lives. Making sure that it works equally well for everyone is the work of the generations that follow.

questions.q: What was Aoyagi originally trying to do when he got his idea?
options: Build a device to measure skin colour
Find a way to measure oxygen in the veins
Measure how much blood the heart pumps by detecting a dye in the ear
Design a cheaper machine for anaesthetists
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘Measure how much blood the heart pumps by detecting a dye in the ear’: Aoyagi aslında damara boya verip kulaktan ışıkla saptayarak kalbin pompaladığı kan miktarını ölçmeye çalışıyordu; nabız sinyali bu ölçümü bozuyordu.

questions.q: What weakness of pulse oximeters did the pandemic bring to wider attention?
options: They stop working when patients are short of breath
They can overestimate oxygen levels in people with darker skin
They give false readings for the pulse
They cannot be used outside hospitals
questions.explain: Doğru cevap ‘They can overestimate oxygen levels in people with darker skin’: pandemi sırasında yapılan çalışmalar, deri pigmenti de ışığı emdiği için cihazların koyu tenli hastalarda oksijen düzeyini olduğundan yüksek gösterebildiğini ortaya koymuştur.

title: Have I Been Here Before?
text:
You walk into a café you have never visited before, in a city you are seeing for the first time. A waiter puts down a cup, someone laughs at the next table, and suddenly you are certain that you have lived this exact moment before. The feeling is strong, strange and fleeting. A few seconds later it is gone, leaving you slightly puzzled. The French have given the experience its name: déjà vu, which means ‘already seen’.

The term is usually credited to the French researcher Émile Boirac, who wrote about it in the late nineteenth century, but the sensation itself is far older and appears in the writing of many cultures. It is also remarkably common. In reviews of dozens of surveys, the American psychologist Alan Brown concluded that roughly two out of three people report having had déjà vu at least once. It seems to be most frequent in young adults and to become rarer as people grow older. People who travel a lot, those with more years of education and those who are tired or stressed also tend to report it more often, although the reasons for these patterns are not fully clear.

For a long time, déjà vu was difficult to study because it cannot be ordered on demand. It arrives without warning and disappears before anyone can attach a scanner to the person's head. Scientists therefore had to rely on people's reports after the event, which are open to the usual errors of memory. Some of the most useful clues came from medicine. Patients with a certain kind of epilepsy, which affects the temporal lobes of the brain, sometimes experience an intense feeling of déjà vu just before a seizure. In the middle of the twentieth century, the Canadian neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield found that gently stimulating parts of the temporal lobe during surgery could trigger similar feelings of familiarity. These observations pointed to brain regions involved in memory, including the hippocampus, as part of the story.

In healthy people, however, déjà vu is not a sign of illness, and researchers have looked for explanations in the ordinary workings of memory. One influential idea is that we can feel that something is familiar without being able to remember why. Imagine meeting someone in the street whose face seems known, but you cannot recall where you met them. Déjà vu may be a special version of this: a sense of familiarity switches on, but because there is no matching memory to explain it, the feeling seems mysterious. The psychologist Anne Cleary and her colleagues tested this idea using virtual reality. Volunteers explored a series of computer-generated scenes. Later, they were shown new scenes whose objects were completely different but whose layout matched an earlier one, for instance with furniture arranged in the same positions. People were more likely to report déjà vu in these new scenes, even when they could not remember the original. The similarity in layout, it seems, was enough to produce a feeling of familiarity without a clear memory behind it.

Another group, led by Akira O'Connor at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, created déjà vu in the laboratory by using lists of related words. Volunteers heard words such as ‘bed’, ‘pillow’, ‘night’ and ‘dream’, but never the word ‘sleep’ itself. When later asked whether they had heard any words beginning with the letter s, they said no. Yet when asked whether they had heard ‘sleep’, many felt strangely that they had, while knowing that they could not have. When the researchers scanned their brains, the areas that became most active were not mainly memory areas but frontal regions often linked to decision-making and checking. One plausible interpretation is that déjà vu is a sign of the brain checking its own memory and noticing a mismatch, a kind of error message showing that the system is working as it should.

If that interpretation is correct, it might also explain why déjà vu becomes less common with age. Older people do not necessarily have fewer memory errors, but their brains may be slightly less active in catching and flagging them. The theory is still debated, and some researchers think there may be several different causes of the same feeling.

What scientists do agree on is that déjà vu does not let us see the future. Many people describe a sense that they know what will happen next, but when researchers have tested this, the predictions have not been reliably correct.
