The feeling of knowing is real; the knowledge is not. So the next time déjà vu visits you in a café, enjoy the strange little shiver. It is not a message from another life, but a brief glimpse of your own memory checking its work.

glosses.déjà vu: déjà vu (daha önce yaşamış gibi olma hissi)

questions.q: What did Anne Cleary's virtual reality experiments suggest?
options: Déjà vu happens only to people with epilepsy
A similar layout can create a feeling of familiarity without a clear memory
People can predict the future during déjà vu
Déjà vu is caused by tiredness alone
questions.explain: Cleary'nin deneyinde nesneleri farklı ama yerleşimi önceki bir sahneyle aynı olan yeni sahneler déjà vu hissini artırdı; yani benzer düzen, net bir anı olmadan tanıdıklık duygusu yaratabiliyor: “A similar layout can create a feeling of familiarity without a clear memory”.

questions.q: According to the O'Connor study, what might déjà vu be a sign of?
options: Serious damage to the hippocampus
A memory from a previous life
The brain checking its memory and noticing a mismatch
A lack of activity in the frontal regions
questions.explain: Taramalarda en çok karar verme ve denetimle ilişkili ön bölgeler etkinleşti; araştırmacılara göre déjà vu, beynin belleğini kontrol edip bir uyumsuzluk fark etmesinin işareti olabilir: “The brain checking its memory and noticing a mismatch”.

title: The Song That Will Not Leave
text:
You wake up, make coffee, and there it is: the chorus of a pop song you heard once in a supermarket, playing in your head again and again. You did not choose it, you may not even like it, and it refuses to leave. Psychologists call this experience involuntary musical imagery, but most people know it by a friendlier name borrowed from German: the earworm.

Earworms are remarkably common. In surveys carried out by the marketing professor James Kellaris in the early 2000s, almost every participant reported having had one, and a later Finnish study suggested that close to nine in ten people experience them at least once a week. They tend to appear when the mind is lightly occupied rather than fully busy, for instance while walking, showering or doing the washing-up. Stress, tiredness and recent exposure to a tune all seem to heighten the chance of an attack, and people who listen to music every day or play an instrument report them more often. For most people the visit is fleeting, but for some it is incessant.

Why do some songs stick while others vanish? In 2016 a team led by the music psychologist Kelly Jakubowski compared thousands of tunes that people named as earworms with similar songs that were never mentioned. The sticky songs were usually fairly fast, and their melodies followed a common, easy shape, rising and then falling like many nursery rhymes, while also containing a few unusual jumps or repetitions that made them stand out. In other words, the ideal earworm is simple enough to remember but slightly surprising. Lady Gaga's ‘Bad Romance’ topped the list in that study, which will not shock anyone who has tried to forget it.

Scientists still debate what is happening in the brain. One explanation links earworms to the way memory stores music. Songs are learned as sequences, and once the first few notes are triggered, the rest tends to unfold automatically, like a chain of falling dominoes. Another idea draws on an observation associated with the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik: people remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones. If you hear only a fragment of a song, your brain may keep playing it in an attempt to complete it. This would explain why the part that gets stuck is so often a short loop of the chorus rather than the whole piece.

Most earworms are harmless and fade within minutes, but a persistent one can be truly annoying, so researchers have tested ways to get rid of them. Some advice sounds strange at first. Listening to the song all the way through, for example, sometimes helps, perhaps because it closes the unfinished task. In 2015 psychologists at the University of Reading reported that chewing gum reduced the number of times people heard an unwanted tune in their heads, possibly because the jaw movements interfere with the silent singing that the brain uses to replay music. Other studies suggest that a task of moderate difficulty, such as a word puzzle, can divert attention. A task that is too easy leaves room for the music, while one that is too hard makes the mind wander back to it.

Not everyone sees earworms as a problem, though. Some musicians say that tunes repeating in their heads help them compose, and for many people a familiar melody on a dull morning is pleasant company. Advertisers, of course, have long tried to leverage the effect, building short, catchy jingles that will follow customers into the shop. Whether that counts as clever marketing or a small invasion of privacy is a matter of opinion.

What is clear is that earworms reveal how powerful musical memory is. People with severe memory loss can sometimes still sing songs from their youth, and music is often among the last things such patients lose. The tune that bothers you in the shower is a byproduct of the same remarkable ability. Next time one gets stuck, you might try a stick of gum, a crossword or simply patience. Sooner or later it will run its course, probably just in time for another one to take its place.

questions.q: According to the 2016 study, what did sticky songs usually have?
options: A fairly fast tempo and a simple melody with a few surprises
A slow tempo and long, complex lyrics
A melody that changes key many times
A completely unpredictable structure
questions.explain: Jakubowski'nin çalışmasında akılda takılan şarkılar genellikle hızlıydı, kolay bir ezgi kalıbı izliyor ama birkaç şaşırtıcı sıçrama içeriyordu: “A fairly fast tempo and a simple melody with a few surprises”.

questions.q: Why might chewing gum reduce earworms, according to the text?
options: It makes people feel sleepy
It releases chemicals that block memory
Its flavour distracts people from music
Jaw movements may interfere with the brain's silent singing
questions.explain: Reading Üniversitesi araştırmacılarına göre çene hareketleri, beynin müziği tekrar çalmak için kullandığı sessiz şarkı söylemeyi engelliyor olabilir: “Jaw movements may interfere with the brain's silent singing”.

title: Why Your Phone Ignores Your Gloves
text:
Every winter, millions of people perform the same small ritual. They stand at a cold bus stop, pull a phone from their pocket, tap the screen with a gloved finger, and nothing happens. Off comes the glove, and the frozen finger does the job at once. The phone is not being difficult. It is simply doing what it was designed to do, and the reason reveals how most modern touchscreens work.

The idea is older than many people assume. In 1965 an engineer named E. A. Johnson, working at the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, England, described a screen that could sense the touch of a finger. He imagined it helping air traffic controllers, who needed a quicker way to select aircraft on their displays than typing codes. His design used what is now called capacitive sensing, and versions of it were used in British air traffic control in the following decades. It took roughly forty more years, and the arrival of smartphones, for the technology to reach ordinary pockets.

To understand capacitive sensing, it helps to know that the human body conducts electricity. It is not a particularly good conductor, but it is far better than air, plastic or dry wool. Beneath the glass of a phone screen lies a fine grid of transparent electrodes, usually made of a material called indium tin oxide, which conducts electricity yet lets light pass through. A small voltage is applied across this grid, creating a weak electric field above the surface. When a conductive object such as a fingertip comes close, it draws away a tiny amount of charge and changes the electrical properties, the capacitance, at that spot. The phone's chip measures these changes many times every second and works out exactly where the finger is.

This explains the glove problem. Wool, leather and most other fabrics act as insulators, so a gloved finger hardly disturbs the electric field, and the screen does not notice it at all. Manufacturers have responded by sewing conductive thread into the fingertips of special touchscreen gloves. People have also improvised. In South Korea, during an unusually cold winter around 2010, news reports claimed that sales of a sausage-shaped snack rose because people were using the sausages to operate their phones outdoors. The story may be somewhat exaggerated, but the physics behind it is sound: a sausage, being salty and moist, conducts electricity well enough to fool the sensor.

Not all touchscreens work this way. An older and cheaper design, the resistive screen, uses two flexible layers separated by a thin gap. When you press, the layers touch, and the device calculates the position from the change in current. Resistive screens respond to any pressure, whether from a fingernail, a pen or a glove, which is why they were long popular in cash machines, factory equipment and early handheld computers that came with a plastic pen, or stylus. Their drawback is that they need a firm press and usually register only one point at a time.

Capacitive screens, by contrast, can track several fingers at once, which made gestures such as pinching to zoom possible. That ability helped revolutionize how people interact with computers: instead of pointing with a mouse, we now push, swipe and stretch images directly. Yet the technology has its own weaknesses. Drops of water conduct electricity too, so a screen can become confused in the rain, registering touches that nobody made. Engineers constantly tweak the software to tell the difference between a finger and a raindrop, with mixed success.

Researchers are now experimenting with screens that respond to a finger hovering just above the glass, or that can sense how hard you press. Some devices even emulate the feel of real buttons by making the glass vibrate slightly under your fingertip. The humble touch, it seems, still has room to evolve.

So the next time your phone ignores a gloved hand, do not take it personally. It is listening for the faint electrical signature of your skin and, as it turns out, that of a sausage.

questions.q: Why does a gloved finger usually fail to work a capacitive screen?
options: The glove is too thick to press the glass firmly
The screen is programmed to ignore cold fingers
Most fabrics are insulators and hardly disturb the electric field
Gloves block the light coming from the screen
questions.explain: Yün, deri ve çoğu kumaş yalıtkan olduğu için eldivenli parmak ekranın üstündeki elektrik alanını neredeyse hiç bozmuyor: “Most fabrics are insulators and hardly disturb the electric field”. Sorun bastırma gücü değil, elektriksel.

questions.q: What is one advantage of resistive screens mentioned in the text?
options: They respond to any kind of pressure, including a pen or a glove
They can track many fingers at once
They are never confused by water
They react to a finger hovering above the glass
questions.explain: Dirençli ekranlar tırnak, kalem ya da eldiven fark etmeksizin her türlü basınca tepki verir: “They respond to any kind of pressure, including a pen or a glove”. Birden çok parmağı izlemek ise kapasitif ekranların özelliğidir.

title: The Parachute Full of Holes
text:
Blow on a dandelion clock and you set off one of nature's most efficient flying machines. Each seed hangs beneath a tiny umbrella of white bristles, and together they drift away on the slightest breeze, sometimes travelling a long way before they land. Children have played this game for centuries. Yet until quite recently, scientists could not fully explain how such a light, open structure manages to stay in the air for so long.

The puzzle lies in the design. A normal parachute is a solid sheet of material that traps air beneath it and slows the fall. The dandelion's version, called a pappus, is nothing like that. It consists of roughly a hundred thin filaments spreading out from a central stalk, like the spokes of a bicycle wheel, and around ninety per cent of it is empty space. By common sense, air should simply flow through the gaps, and the seed should drop like a stone. It does not.

In 2018 a team at the University of Edinburgh, including the engineer Cathal Cummins and the biologist Naomi Nakayama, published an explanation in the journal Nature. They placed dandelion seeds in a vertical wind tunnel, a tube in which air is blown upwards so that the seed floats in place, and used lasers and high-speed cameras to make the movement of the air visible. What they saw surprised them. Just above the bristles, a ring of swirling air formed, and, unlike similar rings observed behind other objects, it stayed detached from the seed, hovering at a steady distance above it. The researchers called it a separated vortex ring, and they believed it was the first time such a stable, free-floating ring had been seen in nature.

This ring is the secret of the dandelion's success. The swirling air creates an area of low pressure above the seed, which increases drag and slows its descent. The exact spacing of the bristles matters enormously. The team found that if the gaps were much wider or narrower, the ring became unstable and broke apart. The pappus is therefore not a messy bundle of hairs but a finely balanced aerodynamic structure, in which the amount of air allowed to pass through is carefully controlled. According to the researchers' calculations, for the amount of material it uses, it is several times more efficient than a conventional parachute, a reminder that natural selection has had millions of years to refine its designs.

There are other tricks too. Later work by the same group suggested that the pappus can open or close depending on the humidity of the air. In damp weather the bristles fold in, which tends to keep seeds on the plant or bring them down sooner. In dry conditions they spread out, ready for a long journey. Since dry, windy weather is good for travel, the seed in effect waits for the right moment to leave. Most dandelion seeds land within a few metres of their parent, but a small proportion are lifted by rising air currents and carried much farther, which helps explain why the plant is found in so many parts of the world.

Engineers have taken note. Tiny flying devices, such as sensors that could drift through the air to monitor pollution or weather, face the same problem as the dandelion: they need to stay up for a long time without using energy. Copying the bristly design might allow such devices to float with very little material and no motor at all. Unlike a drone, they would need no battery to stay in the air. Researchers have already built small fliers inspired by the dandelion, and engineering that borrows from biology continues to find ideas in the most ordinary places.

There is something pleasing in the thought that a weed most gardeners try to remove hides a piece of physics that experts overlooked for so long. The dandelion did not need equations; it solved the problem through trial and error over countless generations. The next time you see a child scatter its seeds across a lawn, you might watch them a little more carefully. Each one is riding an invisible ring of air.

questions.q: What did the Edinburgh team discover above the dandelion's bristles?
options: A solid sheet of air that carries the seed
A thin layer of water that makes the seed lighter
A tiny electric charge that lifts the seed
A ring of swirling air that stays separate from the seed
questions.explain: Edinburgh ekibi kılların hemen üstünde, tohuma bağlı kalmadan sabit mesafede duran dönen bir hava halkası gördü: “A ring of swirling air that stays separate from the seed”. Buna ayrık girdap halkası dendi.

questions.q: What happens to the pappus in damp weather?
options: It spreads wider to catch more wind
Its bristles fold in, so the seed tends to stay or land sooner
It falls off the seed completely
It becomes heavier and breaks apart
questions.explain: Nemli havada kıllar içe kapanır ve tohum ya bitkide kalır ya da daha erken iner: “Its bristles fold in, so the seed tends to stay or land sooner”. Kuru havada ise açılarak uzun yolculuğa hazırlanır.

title: Five Thousand Years of Chewing
text:
Humans, it seems, have always liked to chew on something that is not quite food. Archaeologists working in Scandinavia have found lumps of birch-bark tar, thousands of years old, still marked with the prints of human teeth. In 2019 researchers in Denmark went further. From a piece of such tar about 5,700 years old, found on the island of Lolland, they extracted enough DNA to reconstruct the complete genome of the person who had chewed it: a woman with dark skin, dark hair and blue eyes. The same piece even preserved traces of the bacteria in her mouth and of a recent meal, which seems to have included duck and hazelnuts. A prehistoric piece of gum, in other words, turned out to be a remarkable archive.

Why chew tar? Birch-bark tar was used as a glue for fixing stone tools to handles, and warming it in the mouth made it soft enough to work. But people may also have chewed it to ease toothache, since the tar contains substances with mild antiseptic properties, or simply for pleasure. On the other side of the world, the ancient Maya and Aztecs chewed chicle, a natural gum collected from the sapodilla tree in Central America. Historians report that among the Aztecs, chewing in public was subject to social rules: it was acceptable for children and some women but thought impolite for adult men, an early example of gum etiquette.

The modern industry began in the nineteenth century with a story that sounds almost too good to be true. According to the usual account, the exiled Mexican general Antonio López de Santa Anna, living in New York in the 1860s, had a supply of chicle and hoped it could be sold as a cheap substitute for rubber. He met an inventor named Thomas Adams, who experimented with the material for some time. The rubber plan failed, but Adams noticed that chicle was pleasant to chew. In the early 1870s he began selling chicle gum, and within a few decades chewing gum had become a huge business, with flavoured brands sold across the United States and later the world. Some details of the tale may be exaggerated, but the link between Santa Anna, Adams and chicle is widely reported.

Today very little gum is made from chicle. Most of it is based on a synthetic polymer, a material made of long, chain-like molecules similar to those used in some plastics and rubbers, mixed with softeners, sweeteners and flavours. This is why gum can be chewed for hours without dissolving, and also why a piece dropped on the pavement can stick there for a very long time. Cleaning gum off streets costs many cities a great deal of money each year, and some have tried fines or special bins to tackle the problem. Singapore took the most famous step: in 1992 it banned the import and sale of chewing gum, and although the rules were later relaxed for certain therapeutic gums, the country is still associated with the ban.

Does chewing do anything for us? The clearest benefits concern teeth. Chewing increases the flow of saliva, which helps to neutralize acids produced by bacteria after meals and to wash away bits of food. For this reason, many dentists say that chewing sugar-free gum for a short time after eating can lower the risk of tooth decay, though it is an addition to brushing, not a replacement. Some gums contain a sweetener called xylitol, which mouth bacteria cannot easily use, and there is some evidence that it is helpful. Other claims are less certain. Several studies have suggested that chewing gum makes people feel slightly more alert or less stressed, but the results show some inconsistency, and the effects, where they exist, are small.

There are also a few odd findings. Surgeons have tested whether chewing gum after abdominal operations helps the gut start working again sooner, and some trials have found modest benefits, perhaps because chewing tricks the digestive system into expecting food. Researchers continue to study the question.

From a Stone Age woman on a Danish island to a commuter in a modern city, the habit links us across thousands of years. The material has changed from tree tar to chicle to plastic-like polymers, but the impulse remains the same: to keep the jaw busy, the breath fresh and, perhaps, the mind a little calmer.

questions.q: What did researchers obtain from the 5,700-year-old tar found in Denmark?
options: Enough DNA to reconstruct the genome of the woman who chewed it
The recipe for an ancient kind of glue
Proof that the tar was used as money
Evidence that it was made from chicle
questions.explain: Lolland adasında bulunan 5.700 yıllık katrandan, onu çiğneyen kadının tüm genomunu yeniden kurmaya yetecek DNA elde edildi: “Enough DNA to reconstruct the genome of the woman who chewed it”.

questions.q: Which benefit of chewing gum does the text describe as the clearest?
options: It makes people much more intelligent
It permanently reduces stress
It increases saliva, which helps protect the teeth
It removes the need to brush
questions.explain: Metne göre en net fayda dişlerle ilgili: çiğnemek tükürüğü artırır, bu da asitleri nötrleştirip yemek artıklarını temizler: “It increases saliva, which helps protect the teeth”. Fırçalamanın yerini tutmadığı da özellikle belirtiliyor.

title: The Most Human Expression
text:
Charles Darwin, who spent much of his life comparing humans with other animals, found one human habit particularly puzzling. In his 1872 book on the expression of emotions, he described blushing as the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions. Monkeys may go red with anger, he noted, but no other animal seems to redden because it feels embarrassed. More than 150 years later, scientists are still trying to understand why we do it.

The physical process is reasonably well understood. When we feel embarrassed, ashamed or suddenly the centre of attention, the body releases adrenaline, the same hormone involved in the fight-or-flight response. In most parts of the body, adrenaline causes small blood vessels to tighten. In the face, however, some of the vessels respond by widening, so that more blood flows close to the skin. The result is the familiar warm flush across the cheeks, which may spread to the ears, the neck and the upper chest. Because the process is controlled by the nervous system rather than by conscious thought, it works almost like a reflex, and we cannot simply decide to stop it. In fact, trying hard not to blush is often counterproductive and makes things worse.

Blushing happens in people of every skin colour, even when it is difficult to see. Darwin himself collected reports from travellers and doctors around the world and concluded that dark-skinned people blush in the same way as everyone else, with the change sometimes visible as a slight darkening and always felt as warmth. This suggests that blushing is a basic part of human physiology, not a cultural habit.

But what is it for? A red face seems an odd thing for evolution to favour, since it reveals feelings that we might prefer to hide. One popular explanation turns this disadvantage into the answer. Because a blush cannot be faked, it may serve as an honest signal. When someone breaks a social rule, for example by forgetting a name, spilling a drink or making an awkward remark, a blush shows that they are aware of the mistake and care about what others think. In a well-known set of experiments around 2009, the Dutch psychologist Corine Dijk and her colleagues showed volunteers pictures of people in embarrassing situations. Those who appeared to be blushing were judged more positively and seemed more trustworthy than those who did not. In other words, the blush works rather like an apology that needs no words, and it may help to assuage anger and repair relationships.

Researchers have also looked at what happens in the brain. In a 2019 study from the University of Amsterdam, girls and young women in their late teens were asked to sing karaoke songs. Later, while lying in a brain scanner, they watched videos of their own singing as well as of other people's. Their cheeks grew warmer when they saw themselves, a sign of blushing. Interestingly, the brain areas that became most active were those linked to emotional arousal and attention, rather than those used when we think carefully about what other people believe. The authors suggested that blushing may be a fairly automatic reaction to being looked at, rather than the result of complex reasoning about how others judge us.

For most people, blushing is a minor nuisance. For some, however, the fear of turning red becomes so strong that they start avoiding meetings, presentations or parties. This condition, sometimes called erythrophobia, can severely restrict a person's life. Psychological treatments that help people pay less attention to the blush and accept it often work better than attempts to stop it, since the fear itself tends to trigger the very reaction it is worried about. In rare and severe cases, surgery on the nerves involved has been used, but doctors are cautious because of unintended side effects.

Perhaps the most comforting message from the research is that blushing is rarely as damaging as the person blushing imagines. Observers usually notice it less than we think, and when they do, they tend to read it kindly. A sudden red face may feel like a betrayal, but it often tells the world something rather good: that we care. Darwin was right to call it deeply human.

questions.q: What did Darwin conclude about blushing in dark-skinned people?
options: They do not blush at all
They blush in the same way as everyone else
They blush only when they are angry
They learned to blush from travellers
questions.explain: Darwin topladığı raporlara dayanarak koyu tenli insanların da herkes gibi kızardığı sonucuna vardı; değişim bazen hafif bir koyulaşma olarak görülür, her zaman sıcaklık olarak hissedilir: “They blush in the same way as everyone else”.

questions.q: According to Dijk's experiments, how did people view someone who appeared to blush after a mistake?
options: As dishonest
As physically ill
As angry and defensive
More positively and as more trustworthy
questions.explain: Dijk ve meslektaşlarının deneylerinde utandırıcı bir durumda kızarmış görünen kişiler daha olumlu ve daha güvenilir bulundu: “More positively and as more trustworthy”. Kızarmak sözsüz bir özür gibi işliyor.

title: The Insects That Count to Seventeen
text:
Imagine spending seventeen years in the dark, quietly drinking from the roots of a tree, and then climbing into the sunlight for a few weeks of noise, romance and death. That is the life of the periodical cicada, an insect found only in eastern North America and one of the strangest timekeepers in the natural world.

There are several species of periodical cicada. Some emerge from the ground every thirteen years, others every seventeen. Across the region they are divided into groups called broods, each of which appears in a particular year in a particular area. When a brood emerges, the numbers can be astonishing: in some places scientists have estimated more than a million insects per acre, an area a little smaller than a football pitch. For a few weeks in late spring the foliage is covered in red-eyed insects, empty skins cling to fences and tree trunks, and the air is filled with the loud, buzzing songs of males trying to attract mates. In some spots the noise reportedly reaches levels comparable to a lawnmower.

The young cicadas, called nymphs, spend almost their whole lifespan underground, feeding on the watery sap that flows through tree roots. This sap is deficient in nutrients, which may partly explain why they grow so slowly. Then, after their long wait, they all leave the soil within a few days of each other, usually on a warm evening when the soil about twenty centimetres down reaches roughly 18 °C. They climb the nearest vertical surface, split their skins and come out as winged adults. The adults live only a few weeks. They mate, the females lay eggs in thin branches, and the newly hatched nymphs drop to the ground, dig in and begin the life cycle again.

Why such long and precise cycles? One of the leading explanations focuses on predation. A myriad of hunters, from birds, squirrels and snakes to dogs, eat cicadas eagerly, but when millions of them appear at once, the hunters simply cannot eat them all. Scientists call this strategy predator satiation: by flooding the area, the insects make sure that enough of them survive to reproduce. A cicada that emerged a year early or late, alone, would almost certainly be eaten.

The numbers thirteen and seventeen have attracted particular interest because both are prime numbers, which means they can be divided only by one and by themselves. Some researchers postulate that this is no coincidence. If a predatory animal had, say, a population cycle of four or six years, a cicada with a twelve-year cycle would meet it at its peak very often, whereas one with a seventeen-year cycle would meet it only rarely. Another version of the theory suggests that prime cycles help different broods avoid emerging together and mixing. These ideas are elegant, but they are difficult to test, and they remain hypotheses rather than settled fact.

An equally intriguing question is how the cicadas keep count. They have no calendar, and conditions underground change little from year to year. The best evidence suggests that they track the seasons through the trees themselves. In a clever experiment published in 2000, the biologist Richard Karban and his colleagues placed young seventeen-year cicadas on trees that had been made to go through two growing seasons in a single year. Many of the insects emerged a year early, as if they had counted the extra season. It seems that they register the yearly rise and fall in the flow of sap, rather like counting the rings of a tree.

In 2024 people in parts of the American Midwest witnessed a rare event: a thirteen-year brood and a seventeen-year brood emerged in the same spring, something that, according to experts, had not happened for those two broods since 1803. Newspapers had fun with the story. Yet for all the noise, cicadas are mostly harmless to people. They do not bite or sting, and although they can damage young trees, mature forests have lived alongside them for thousands of years. When the cicadas die, their bodies rot into the ground and return nutrients to the soil, which may even benefit the trees on which the next generation will feed.

The periodical cicada reminds us that nature does not always run on a yearly calendar. Somewhere beneath an ordinary garden in Illinois or Virginia, a young insect is counting slowly towards a day in the sunlight that may still be many years away.

questions.q: What is predator satiation?
options: Predators learning to avoid cicadas
Cicadas hiding deeper underground when birds are near
Appearing in such huge numbers that predators cannot eat them all
Cicadas eating the food that predators need
questions.explain: Milyonlarca böcek aynı anda ortaya çıkınca avcılar hepsini yiyemez ve yeterli sayıda ağustosböceği hayatta kalır: “Appearing in such huge numbers that predators cannot eat them all”.

questions.q: What did Karban's experiment in 2000 suggest?
options: Cicadas count years by tracking seasonal changes in their trees
Cicadas count only by measuring soil temperature
Cicadas leave the ground at random times
Cicadas can see sunlight from underground
questions.explain: Bir yılda iki büyüme mevsimi geçiren ağaçlara konan böceklerin çoğu bir yıl erken çıktı; yani ağaçtaki özsu akışının mevsimsel değişimini sayıyor gibiler: “Cicadas count years by tracking seasonal changes in their trees”.

title: A Thousand Birds and No Leader
titleTr: Binlerce kuş, tek bir lider yok
text:
On winter evenings in parts of Europe, people gather on bridges, piers and fields to watch a show that costs nothing and can never be repeated exactly. As the light fades, flocks of starlings arrive from the surrounding countryside and join together in the sky above the place where they will spend the night. Soon a myriad of birds, thousands and sometimes hundreds of thousands, of them, are flying as one, twisting into shapes that stretch, fold and pour across the sky like smoke or liquid. In English the display is called a murmuration, after the soft rushing sound of so many wings.

Famous sites include the city of Rome, where enormous flocks gather over the parks and riverbanks in winter, the seaside town of Brighton in England, and the marshes of south-western Denmark, where the gathering is so dense that local people call it the black sun. Wherever it happens, the experience raises the same question: how can so many birds move together so quickly without crashing into one another, and without anyone in charge?

For a long time the question was almost impossible to answer, because a murmuration is extremely hard to measure. In the mid-2000s a team of Italian physicists, led by Andrea Cavagna and Irene Giardina, took on the challenge as part of a European project called STARFLAG. From the roof of a building in Rome they filmed flocks with several cameras working together and then used computer software to reconstruct the three-dimensional position of each bird. It was slow, careful work, but it produced the first detailed maps of real flocks containing thousands of individuals.

The results, published in 2008, helped to overturn an assumption many scientists had held. Earlier computer models had usually assumed that each bird responds to all its neighbours within a fixed distance. The Rome data suggested something different: each starling seems to pay attention to a fixed number of neighbours, about six or seven, regardless of how near or far they are. This matters because it helps the flock stay together. When the birds spread out, each one still tracks the same number of companions, so the group does not easily break apart. Simple rules, followed by every individual, are enough to create the complex patterns we see from the ground.

Later studies by the same group found something even more striking. When one bird changes direction, the change travels through the flock almost instantaneously, like a ripple across a pond, so that birds far apart still respond to each other. The researchers compared this to certain physical systems in which a small disturbance can cascade through the whole system. For the starlings, such sensitivity has an obvious advantage: news of danger spreads swiftly from one edge of the flock to the other.

And danger is often present. Peregrine falcons and other birds of prey regularly hunt near the places where starlings sleep. A predatory bird usually tries to pick off a single starling at the edge of a group, and a dense, rapidly shifting mass of wings makes that very difficult. A study of thousands of murmurations in Britain, based partly on observations sent in by members of the public, found that flocks tended to be larger and to perform longer when predators were present. This supports the idea that the display is, at least in part, a form of protection against predation. Other benefits have been proposed too. Gathering in large numbers may help birds share information about good feeding areas, or keep warm on cold nights once they have settled into the reeds and trees. These explanations do not exclude one another.

Unfortunately, starling numbers have fallen sharply in some countries, including Britain, over recent decades, possibly because of changes in farming that reduce the insects and grassland the birds depend on. Some starlings are migratory, travelling to Britain from colder countries for the winter. In other places, such as North America, where starlings were introduced in the nineteenth century, they are so numerous that they are considered a pest. The same bird can be a cause for concern on one continent and a nuisance on another.

Still, few people who have stood beneath a murmuration think about any of this at the moment. They simply watch, as the dark cloud swells and shrinks, splits and joins again, and finally pours down into the trees in a rush of sound. Then, quite suddenly, the sky is empty, and the show is over until the next evening.

questions.q: What did the STARFLAG study find about how starlings follow each other?
options: Each bird follows a leader at the front of the flock
Each bird reacts to all birds within one metre
Birds watch only the bird directly in front of them
Each bird tracks about six or seven neighbours, whatever the distance
questions.explain: Roma'daki ölçümler her sığırcığın, ne kadar yakın ya da uzak olursa olsun, yaklaşık altı ya da yedi komşuyu izlediğini gösterdi: “Each bird tracks about six or seven neighbours, whatever the distance”. Sürünün bir lideri yok.

questions.q: What did the British study of murmurations find?
options: Murmurations happen only in summer
Flocks were larger and performed longer when predators were present
Predators never appeared near the sleeping places
Smaller flocks were safer than larger ones
questions.explain: Halkın gönderdiği gözlemlere de dayanan İngiliz çalışmasında, avcı kuşlar varken sürüler daha büyük oluyor ve gösteri daha uzun sürüyordu: “Flocks were larger and performed longer when predators were present”.

title: The Film Star and the Jumping Signal
text:
In the 1940s Hedy Lamarr was often described by film studios as one of the most beautiful women in the world. Audiences knew her face from Hollywood films, but very few knew that, in her spare time, she was an inventor. One of her ideas, patented during the Second World War, turned out to be a forerunner of technology that many of us now carry in our pockets.

Lamarr was born Hedwig Kiesler in Vienna in 1914. She became famous as a young actress in Europe and married a wealthy Austrian arms manufacturer, Fritz Mandl. According to her own later accounts, she sat through many dinners at which her husband discussed weapons with military officials and engineers, and she listened more carefully than anyone suspected. Unhappy in the marriage, she left Austria in 1937 and eventually reached the United States, where she signed a contract with the MGM film studio and changed her name.

Lamarr had always enjoyed taking things apart to see how they worked. During the war, she became interested in a specific military problem. A torpedo could be guided by radio signals, but an enemy who discovered the radio frequency could easily jam it, that is, send a strong signal of their own to block or confuse the guidance. Lamarr wanted to foil such attempts. Lamarr's idea was to make the signal jump constantly from one frequency to another in a pattern known only to the sender and the receiver. An enemy listening on any single frequency would hear only a tiny, meaningless fragment, and blocking every possible channel at once would be very difficult. It was, in a sense, an early form of encryption.

The problem was timing: how could the torpedo and the ship that controlled it change frequency at exactly the same moments? Here Lamarr worked with an unexpected partner, the composer George Antheil, who had experimented with making several mechanical pianos play together for one of his pieces. Their solution borrowed from that world. Both sender and receiver would use identical rolls of paper with holes punched in them, like those that operate a player piano, to switch between 88 frequencies, the same as the number of keys on a piano. In 1942 they were granted a US patent for a secret communication system.

The US Navy, however, did not adopt the system. Officials apparently thought the mechanism too bulky to fit inside a torpedo, and some accounts suggest they did not take a film star's invention seriously. Lamarr was encouraged to support the war effort in a more traditional way, by selling war bonds, which she did with great success. The patent expired before it ever earned her any money.

The underlying idea, now known as frequency hopping, did not disappear. In the following decades, as electronics became smaller and faster, engineers developed related techniques for military telecommunications, and versions of the approach were reportedly used by the US Navy in the 1960s. Later, similar principles helped shape everyday wireless connectivity. Bluetooth, for example, hops rapidly among dozens of frequencies, around 1,600 times per second, which reduces interference with other gadgets sharing the same airwaves. It would be an exaggeration to say that Lamarr invented Bluetooth or Wi-Fi; many engineers worked independently on these ideas, and the technology owes much to later developments. But her patent is widely recognised as an early and ingenious contribution.

Recognition came late. In 1997 Lamarr and Antheil, who had died decades earlier, received an award from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital rights organisation. Lamarr, by then in her eighties and living quietly in Florida, reportedly responded with a dry remark that it was about time. She died in 2000, and in 2014 she and Antheil were added to the National Inventors Hall of Fame in the United States.

Her story is a reminder that talent does not always appear where we expect it. For decades the public saw Lamarr only as a glamorous face on a cinema screen, and she later complained that people judged her by her looks rather than her mind. Today, when your wireless headphones or other wearable gadgets connect to your phone without fuss, it is worth remembering the actress who, between films, sat at a table and worked out how to keep a signal one step ahead of the enemy.

questions.q: What problem was Lamarr's invention meant to solve?
options: Enemies jamming the radio signals that guided torpedoes
Ships running out of fuel during long voyages
Mechanical pianos falling out of time
Films being copied without permission

title: When Your Foot Falls Asleep
text:
You have been sitting cross-legged on the floor for too long, watching a film or playing with a child. When you finally stand up, one foot feels strangely heavy and distant, as if it belonged to someone else. A moment later comes the tingling, a swarm of tiny, prickling sensations that can be almost unbearable to touch. In English we say the foot has fallen asleep, or that we have pins and needles. Doctors call the sensation paresthesia, and although it is usually harmless, it says something interesting about how our nerves work.

A common belief is that the foot goes numb because its blood supply has been cut off. That is only part of the story. The main cause is pressure on a nerve. Nerves are bundles of long, thin fibres that carry electrical signals between the body and the brain, a bit like cables carrying messages. When you sit on your leg, you compress one of these bundles, as well as the small blood vessels that feed it. Short of oxygen and physically squeezed, the nerve fibres stop passing messages properly. Signals from the foot do not reach the brain, so the foot feels numb, and commands from the brain may not reach the muscles, so the foot can feel weak and clumsy.

Interestingly, not all fibres are affected equally. The thicker fibres, which carry information about light touch and about where your limbs are in space, tend to be the most sensitive to pressure and are often the first to stop working. That is why a sleeping foot can feel so strange: your brain temporarily loses track of where it is, which explains why people sometimes stumble when they try to walk on it. Some thinner fibres, including those that carry certain kinds of pain and temperature signals, keep working longer.

The famous tingling comes not when the pressure starts but when it ends. Once you move and the pressure is released, blood rushes back and the nerves begin to recover. During this recovery they become unusually excitable and fire off signals in a disorganised way, even though nothing is touching the skin. The brain receives this burst of random messages and interprets it as prickling, buzzing or burning. Different types of fibre wake up at different speeds, so the feeling changes over a minute or two before normal sensation returns. Moving the limb gently and changing position usually speeds things up.

Arms are just as vulnerable. Many people wake in the night with a numb hand after sleeping with an arm bent under the pillow or the head. The so-called funny bone offers another familiar example. It is not a bone at all but the ulnar nerve, which runs close to the surface at the elbow, protected by little more than skin. A knock in exactly the wrong place presses the nerve against the bone and sends a shock of tingling down towards the little finger.

Occasional pins and needles after an awkward position are no cause for concern. The body is well designed to cope with them, and the uncomfortable sensation itself acts as a warning: it encourages us to move before any real damage is done. Indeed, our habit of shifting position every few minutes, often without noticing, is one of the ways the body protects its nerves. People who cannot feel or move normally, such as some patients under anaesthesia, must be turned regularly by a caregiver for exactly this reason.

Tingling that appears without obvious pressure, lasts a long time or is recurrent is a different matter, and it is worth discussing with a doctor. Persistent paresthesia can be a symptom of a range of conditions. Diabetes, for example, can damage nerves over time, particularly in the feet. People who are deficient in vitamin B12 can also develop problems, as can people with a trapped nerve in the wrist, known as carpal tunnel syndrome, which often produces tingling in the fingers at night. In such cases a neurologist may test how well the nerves carry signals, and the tingling turns out to be a useful early warning of an impairment that needs attention.

For most of us, though, pins and needles is simply a small, temporary reminder that our sense of touch depends on a delicate network of living wires. Stand up, shake your foot, wait a minute, and the network quietly switches itself back on.

questions.q: According to the text, what is the main cause of a foot falling asleep?
options: Cold temperatures in the room
Too much blood flowing into the foot
A lack of sleep the night before
Pressure on a nerve
questions.explain: Metin, yaygın inancın aksine asıl nedenin kan akışının kesilmesi değil sinirin sıkışması olduğunu söylüyor: “Pressure on a nerve”. Kan damarlarının da sıkışması işin yalnızca bir parçası.

questions.q: When does the tingling usually begin?
options: As soon as pressure is put on the leg
When the pressure is released and the nerves recover
Only after several hours of sitting
When the person falls asleep at night
questions.explain: Karıncalanma baskı başladığında değil bittiğinde ortaya çıkar; kan geri gelir ve toparlanan sinirler düzensiz sinyaller gönderir: “When the pressure is released and the nerves recover”.

title: The Number on Your Door
text:
Imagine trying to send a letter in London around 1700. There would be no number on the door, and often no sign with the name of the street either. Instead, people gave directions the way a friend might today: the house opposite the church, the third door past the baker's, the shop with the golden lion hanging over the entrance. Painted signs were the real addresses of the city. A merchant might tell customers to find him 'at the sign of the Blue Boar', and letters were delivered, slowly and with a good deal of guesswork, to whoever happened to live nearby.

The system worked surprisingly well in small towns, where everyone knew everyone. In growing cities it fell apart. Signs multiplied until whole streets were crowded with swinging boards, some so heavy that they occasionally fell on people walking below. Two neighbours might choose the same picture, and a newcomer had no way of telling them apart. In hindsight, it is remarkable that such a makeshift arrangement lasted as long as it did.

Historians generally agree that house numbers did not spread because citizens asked for them. They spread because governments wanted to find people. A state that wishes to collect taxes, register young men for the army or count its population needs to know exactly who lives where. In the Habsburg lands, for example, a large campaign under Empress Maria Theresa in about 1770 gave numbers to houses largely so that officials could record men who might be called up as soldiers. In Paris, several attempts were made during the eighteenth century, and the system that most visitors would recognise today, with even numbers on one side of the street and odd numbers on the other, is usually dated to a decree of 1805, in Napoleon's time.

Unsurprisingly, many people distrusted the new numbers. A number painted on your wall by a stranger from the government did not feel like a convenience; it felt like being watched. In some places residents rubbed the numbers off or painted over them, and there are stories of wealthy families who considered it beneath them to live in a numbered house, as if it turned their home into an entry in a bureaucratic list. Their mistrust was not entirely misplaced: the numbers really did make it easier for the state to tax, count and recruit.

Yet once the system took root, its everyday benefits became hard to ignore. Doctors could find patients at night. Postal services, which grew rapidly in the nineteenth century, could deliver letters swiftly instead of relying on the memories of local people. Shops could advertise an address rather than an image, and visitors could find their way in a strange city with nothing more than a piece of paper. A tool designed for control turned out to be a tool of freedom too, a double-edged sword that cut in a helpful direction more often than not.

Numbering methods still differ greatly from place to place. In much of Europe and in Turkey, numbers rise along a street from one end to the other. In many North American cities, by contrast, the number tells you roughly how far a building stands from a fixed starting point, so that 1520 might be found in the fifteenth block. Japan offers perhaps the most surprising case: in many Japanese cities most streets have no names at all. Addresses are given by district, then by block, then by building, and buildings have often been numbered in the order in which they were built rather than by their position. Visitors can find this baffling, yet local people manage perfectly well, often with the help of small maps placed at street corners.

Even today, not everyone has a proper address. Researchers and aid organisations have estimated that hundreds of millions of people, many of them living in fast-growing informal settlements, lack one. Without an address it can be hard to open a bank account, receive a delivery or call an ambulance to the right door. Some cities have begun projects to name streets and number houses in such neighbourhoods, and new digital systems divide the whole surface of the earth into small squares, each with a code of its own.

So the next time you write your address on a form, it may be worth remembering that those few numbers carry a long history. They began as a way for rulers to keep track of their subjects. They have stood the test of time because they also help the rest of us find a friend, a doctor or a pizza on a dark evening.

questions.q: According to the text, why did governments first introduce house numbers?
options: Because citizens demanded a better postal service
Because painted signs were too expensive to make
Because they wanted to tax, count and recruit people more easily
Because doctors needed to find patients at night
questions.explain: Metin numaraların vatandaşlar istediği için değil, devletin insanları bulmak istediği için yayıldığını söyler; doğru cevap 'Because they wanted to tax, count and recruit people more easily'. Posta ve doktorlar sonradan gelen faydalardır.

questions.q: What does the writer say about addresses in many Japanese cities?
options: Most streets have no names, and addresses are based on districts and blocks
Every street is named after a famous person

title: Left or Right?
text:
On the morning of 3 September 1967, something strange happened in Sweden. At ten to five, drivers across the country were asked to stop their vehicles. They carefully moved from the left side of the road to the right, waited, and at five o'clock started again. Overnight, millions of people had to unlearn a habit they had practised all their lives. The day became known as Dagen H, the 'H' standing for högertrafik, Swedish for right-hand traffic.

Why should a country go to such trouble? And why does the world drive on two different sides in the first place? The answers say a great deal about how customs begin, how they spread and why they are so hard to change once they become entrenched.

For most of history, there was no rule at all. People walking, riding or leading animals simply avoided one another as best they could. Some historians suggest that riders in medieval Europe tended to keep to the left. Since most people are right-handed, a rider on the left side of the road kept his sword hand toward any stranger coming the other way, and it was also easier to climb onto a horse from that side. The evidence for this is patchy, and the explanation may be partly a pleasant story, but in Britain keeping left does seem to have been common long before it became law.

In other places, different habits took root. In parts of France and the United States, large farm wagons were pulled by several pairs of horses, and the driver often sat on the left-hand horse at the back so that he could use his whip with his right hand. From that position it was easier to judge the distance to an oncoming wagon if it passed on his left, which meant keeping to the right. Whatever the true origins, by the nineteenth century the two systems were clearly established, and they spread with trade and empire. Countries influenced by Britain, from India to Australia, mostly kept left, while much of continental Europe kept right, partly because of Napoleon's conquests, according to some accounts. Japan, which was never a British colony, adopted left-hand traffic too, probably because of early railway and engineering links with Britain.

For a long time this did not matter very much. Then cars arrived, and with them borders that could be crossed in an afternoon. Sweden was a case in point. Its neighbours, Norway and Finland, drove on the right, and many Swedish cars already had the steering wheel on the left, which made overtaking on narrow roads risky. Change had been discussed for decades. In a referendum in 1955, however, more than eighty per cent of voters rejected it. A few years later, parliament decided to override the result, judging that the long-term safety benefits outweighed public opinion.

The preparations were enormous. Thousands of road signs had to be replaced, many of them covered up in advance and then revealed at the last moment. Junctions were redesigned, and buses had to be rebuilt or replaced because their doors were on the wrong side. A national campaign used radio, television, posters and even a popular song to prepare drivers. On the day itself, most private traffic was banned from the roads for several hours. Remarkably, the number of accidents in the following weeks actually fell, perhaps because everyone drove with unusual care. After a while, as drivers relaxed, it returned to its usual level.

Iceland made the same switch the following year. Other countries have changed too, but fewer than one might expect, and the reason is cost. Once roads, vehicles, signs and the habits of millions of people are all built around one system, changing it becomes a nationwide project. Economists sometimes call this 'path dependence': an early choice, perhaps made for reasons nobody remembers, shapes everything that follows.

Today roughly a third of the world's people live in countries that drive on the left, including the United Kingdom, Japan, India, South Africa and Australia. Most travellers adjust within a few days, although the first roundabout can be a frightening experience. The two systems are a reminder that many rules we treat as natural are, in hindsight, accidents of history that simply stood the test of time.

questions.q: What happened in the Swedish referendum of 1955?
options: Most voters supported moving to the right
Voters asked for new road signs
The result was accepted and nothing ever changed
More than eighty per cent of voters rejected the change

title: Why Seven Days?
text:
Of all the ways we divide time, the week is the strangest. A day follows the turning of the earth, a month roughly follows the moon, and a year follows the earth's journey around the sun. The week follows nothing in nature at all. Seven days do not fit neatly into a month or a year, and no animal or plant keeps to them. Yet almost everyone alive today organises work, school, worship and rest around a seven-day cycle. How did such an arbitrary unit gain so firm a hold?

Scholars usually point to two ancient sources. One is the Jewish tradition, in which the seventh day, the Sabbath, is a day of rest. This practice is described in the Hebrew Bible and was later carried into Christianity and, in a different form, into Islam, with Friday as the day of communal prayer. The other source is the astronomy of the ancient Near East and the Greek world, where scholars watched seven moving lights in the sky: the sun, the moon and the five planets visible without a telescope. By Roman times, a week in which each day belonged to one of these seven heavenly bodies had become popular, and the names survive in many languages. Saturday still carries the name of Saturn, Sunday the sun and Monday the moon, while French and Spanish keep Mars, Mercury, Jupiter and Venus in their weekday names.

The two traditions came together over several centuries. In the year 321 the Roman emperor Constantine declared the 'day of the sun' a day of rest for city workers and courts, an early example of a state making the week official. From then on the seven-day cycle spread across Europe, the Middle East and beyond, carried by religion, trade and empire, until by the twentieth century it had become almost universal.

Not everyone has been content with it. Reformers have repeatedly tried to replace the week with something more rational, and their attempts make a fascinating story of failure. During the French Revolution, the new government introduced a calendar in 1793 in which each month was divided into three periods of ten days. The tenth day was a day of rest, which meant that workers now rested one day in ten instead of one in seven. Unsurprisingly, the idea never gained traction. Many people quietly continued to observe Sunday, and the ten-day week was largely ignored in daily life well before Napoleon restored the old calendar at the start of 1806.

The Soviet Union made an even bolder attempt. In 1929 it introduced a 'continuous working week' of five days. Workers were divided into groups, each with a different day off, so that factories could run without ever stopping. In theory, this would raise production. In practice, it backfired. Husbands and wives often had different days off, friends could not meet, and family life was badly disrupted. Machines broke down more often because they were never switched off. The system was replaced by a six-day week in the early 1930s, and the seven-day week returned in 1940.

Why did these schemes fail when they looked so sensible on paper? Part of the answer is religion: for millions of people the weekly day of rest was a sacred observance, not a convenience to be redesigned. But another part is social. The week works because everyone shares it. A day off is valuable largely because your family and friends have the same day off. When planners gave different people different days, they destroyed the very thing that made the week useful. Sociologists sometimes describe the week as a shared rhythm that coordinates the lives of strangers, much as a common language does.

Turkey offers its own interesting example. For centuries, Friday was the traditional day of rest in the Ottoman lands, linked to Friday prayers. In 1935, as part of a wider set of reforms that brought the country closer to European practice, the weekly holiday was moved to Sunday, at first beginning on Saturday afternoon. Business and government could now work on the same days as their trading partners abroad, a practical concern that mattered as much as any symbolic one.

The week, then, has stood the test of time not because it is logical, but because it is shared. It is a reminder that some of the most powerful institutions in our lives rest on nothing more than agreement. Seven days is simply the number that, over thousands of years, most of humanity happened to agree on.

questions.q: Why did the Soviet 'continuous working week' fail, according to the text?
options: Workers refused to work five days in a row
It reduced production in the factories immediately
Families and friends no longer had the same days off
The government could not print new calendars
questions.explain: Metne göre sistem ters tepti çünkü eşlerin ve arkadaşların izin günleri farklıydı, aile hayatı bozuldu; doğru cevap 'Families and friends no longer had the same days off'. Üretim fikri teoride vardı ama metin üretimin hemen düştüğünü söylemez.

questions.q: What is the writer's main point about the week?
options: It lasts because it is shared, not because it is logical
It was invented by Napoleon after the French Revolution
It follows the movements of the moon very closely

questions.explain: Son paragraf haftanın mantıklı olduğu için değil, paylaşıldığı için ayakta kaldığını söyler; doğru cevap 'It lasts because it is shared, not because it is logical'. Metin haftanın doğadaki hiçbir şeyi izlemediğini de vurgular.

title: A Small Card with a Long History
text:
Every year, printers around the world produce billions of small rectangles of card, each about the size of a credit card, carrying a name, a job title and a few ways of making contact. In an age when almost every adult carries a phone that can store thousands of contacts, the business card ought to be outmoded. Yet it has survived, and in some countries the way it is handed over is still treated almost as a ceremony. Its history helps to explain why.

The card's ancestors were not about business at all. In seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Europe, members of the upper classes began to use small printed or handwritten cards when they paid social visits. A caller who arrived at a house would hand a card to the servant at the door, who carried it in to the family. If the family wished to receive the visitor, he or she was invited in; if not, the card was kept as a polite record that the visit had been made. The custom seems to have spread from France and the royal courts to wealthy households across the continent.

By the nineteenth century, especially in Victorian Britain, these 'calling cards' had developed a remarkably detailed code. Etiquette books explained how many cards a married woman should leave, when a visit had to be returned and how soon after a dinner party a guest should call again. According to some accounts, folding down a particular corner of a card could signal that it had been delivered in person or that the visitor was saying goodbye before a long journey. Wealthy homes kept a silver tray in the hall to receive them, sometimes arranged so that the most impressive names lay on top. A card, in other words, was a tool for managing a hierarchical social world: who visited whom, and who chose not to.

Alongside these social cards, a more practical relative was developing. In seventeenth-century London, where streets were crowded and house numbers were not yet in use, traders printed 'trade cards' to advertise their goods. These often included directions to the shop, along with an elaborate picture of what was sold there. As printing became cheaper, trade cards turned into an everyday form of publicity, and the line between the social card and the commercial card gradually blurred. By the twentieth century, the modern business card had taken its familiar shape: plain, small and focused on a person's work rather than on their family.

Nowhere is the card taken more seriously than in Japan, where it is known as meishi. A first business meeting usually begins with an exchange of cards, and the rules are widely known. The card is offered with both hands, turned so that the receiver can read it, often with a slight bow. The receiver accepts it with both hands too, takes a moment to read it carefully, and does not immediately put it in a pocket, still less write on it. During a meeting, cards are often placed on the table in front of the receiver, arranged in the order in which the guests are seated, so that names can be checked discreetly. To treat someone's card carelessly is to treat the person carelessly. Similar, though usually less strict, customs exist in China and Korea, where cards are often printed in two languages, with one side for foreign partners.

For a visitor, the safest rule of thumb is to watch and follow. A card dropped into a back pocket and sat on later may seem a trivial matter, but in a culture that values respect for status and relationships, it can leave a poor first impression that is hard to repair. Many companies that send staff abroad now include card etiquette in their training, a modest but telling example of how globalization has made small customs matter more, not less.

Digital alternatives have been predicted to bring about the demise of the paper card for decades. Electronic address books, online networks for professionals and phone apps that swap details with a single tap all promise the same function with less waste. Some of these have gained traction, especially among younger workers, and the pandemic, when face-to-face meetings became rare, reduced demand further. Yet printers report that cards are still ordered in very large numbers.

The reason may be that a card was never only about information. Handing someone a physical object is a small act of trust and attention, a gesture that a quick scan of a phone cannot quite replace. Like its ancestor on the silver tray, the business card says: I was here, and I would like you to remember me. That simple message, it seems, has stood the test of time.

questions.q: What happened when a family did not wish to receive a visitor?
options: The visitor had to wait outside until evening
The card was kept as a polite record that the visit had been made
The servant returned the card with a message
The visitor was asked to leave a gift instead

title: Three Golden Balls
text:
Walk down certain streets in London, Chicago or Sydney and you may notice an odd symbol hanging above a shop door: three golden balls suspended from a bar. It marks a pawnbroker, a business that lends money in exchange for goods left as security. The customer leaves a watch, a ring or a guitar, receives a sum of cash and is given a ticket. If she returns within an agreed period and makes the repayment along with a fee, the object is hers again. If she does not, the pawnbroker may sell it.

Pawnbroking is often called one of the oldest forms of lending, and it is easy to see why. It requires no knowledge of the borrower at all. The pawnbroker does not need to know whether you have a job, a good reputation or a history of paying your debts. The object itself is the guarantee, or, in financial language, the collateral. Records of similar arrangements are said to survive from ancient China, and loans against goods were common in the ancient Mediterranean world.

The trade has also attracted suspicion for most of its history. Because many of its customers were poor and desperate, pawnbrokers were frequently accused of charging excessive interest. In medieval Europe, where religious teaching was hostile to lending money at interest, the business was pushed to the edges of society and often left to groups shut out of other occupations. The stigma that surrounded it lasted for centuries.

One of the most interesting responses came from Italy in the fifteenth century. Franciscan friars, troubled by the high rates charged by private lenders, began setting up charitable pawn banks known as monti di pietà, roughly 'mountains of mercy'. One of the earliest was founded in Perugia in 1462. These institutions lent small sums to the poor against pledged goods at low rates, enough only to cover their costs. The idea spread across Italy and later to other parts of Europe, and some of these charitable banks eventually grew into ordinary banks, a few of which still exist in some form today. Ironically, an institution created to protect people from lenders became one of the roots of modern banking.

As for the three balls, their origin is uncertain. A popular explanation links them to the Medici family of Florence, the famous bankers, whose coat of arms showed several balls. Another connects them with Saint Nicholas, who, according to legend, gave three bags of gold to three poor girls so that they could marry. Both stories are told with confidence in many places, but neither can be proved, and the symbol may simply have been borrowed from earlier Italian merchants and moneylenders.

In the nineteenth century, pawnshops became a familiar part of working-class life in industrial cities. Many families lived from week to week, often indebted to their landlords, and pawning was a regular way of getting through until payday. In some British cities, according to historians, a family's best clothes were habitually pawned on Monday and taken back on Saturday so that they could be worn to church on Sunday. Researchers have used the records of pawnbrokers to study what ordinary people owned and how close they lived to poverty.

Pawnshops have not disappeared. Indeed, they tend to do well during an economic downturn, when banks become cautious and more people need small, quick loans. Critics point out that the fees can add up to very high interest rates over a year. Supporters reply that pawnbroking has one advantage over many other forms of credit: if a borrower cannot repay, she loses the object but is not chased for further debt, and her credit record is not harmed. The risk, in other words, is limited to the thing she brought through the door.

In the end, the pawnshop reveals something basic about money. Lending always depends on trust, and when trust in a person is missing, it can be replaced by trust in a thing. The three golden balls have stood the test of time because that simple bargain is one that people in difficulty will probably always need.

glosses.monti di pietà: merhamet dağları (İtalyanca, hayır amaçlı rehin bankaları)

questions.q: Why does the writer call the story of the monti di pietà ironic?
options: They were founded by bankers who wanted high profits
They charged more interest than private lenders
They were created to protect the poor from lenders but helped give rise to banking
They were closed by the Medici family
questions.explain: Metin, borç verenlere karşı insanları korumak için kurulan bir kurumun modern bankacılığın köklerinden biri olmasını ironik bulur; doğru cevap 'They were created to protect the poor from lenders but helped give rise to banking'. Bu bankalar düşük faizle borç vermiştir.

questions.q: What advantage of pawnbroking do its supporters mention?
