title: Hands, Bows and Kisses
text:
Few things feel as automatic as greeting another person. A stranger offers a hand, and we take it without thinking. A relative leans forward, and we know whether to expect one kiss, two or three. Yet these small rituals are among the most carefully learned customs we have, and they vary so much from place to place that travellers regularly get them wrong.

Consider the handshake. In much of the world today it is the standard greeting for business and for first meetings. A popular story claims that it began as a way of showing that neither person held a weapon, and that the shaking was meant to make any hidden knife fall from a sleeve. This explanation is often repeated, but there is little firm evidence for it. Images of two people holding hands in this way appear in ancient Greek art, often on gravestones, where they seem to express a bond, an agreement or a farewell rather than a weapons check.

Some historians argue that the handshake as an everyday greeting owes a lot to the Quakers, a Christian movement that arose in England in the seventeenth century. Quakers refused to bow or remove their hats before people of higher rank, gestures they saw as marks of a hierarchical society that treated some people as superior to others. The handshake, by contrast, was the same for everyone. Whether or not the Quakers deserve all the credit, the handshake did come to be associated with equality, and it spread with the growth of commerce and of more egalitarian ideas.

Bowing reflects a different logic. In Japan, the depth and length of a bow can communicate respect, apology, gratitude or the relative status of the people involved. A slight nod might do between colleagues, while a deep bow expresses serious apology or great respect. Learning these differences is part of growing up, and companies sometimes train new employees in them. For a visitor, a sensible rule of thumb is simply to return a bow politely, and local people are usually forgiving of foreigners' mistakes.

In Turkey, as in many parts of the Middle East and the Balkans, greetings carry a strong sense of age and family. During religious holidays, children and young people take the hand of an older relative, kiss it and touch it to their forehead. This gesture of deference is usually answered with blessings and, for children, sweets or a little money. Between friends and relatives of the same generation, two kisses on the cheeks are common. The number of cheek kisses is one of Europe's small puzzles: it may be one, two, three or even four, depending on the country, the region and sometimes the family.

Why do such customs matter so much? Anthropologists point out that greetings do more than say hello. They tell each person where they stand: whether they are strangers, equals or kin, and whether the meeting is formal or relaxed. A greeting that is too cold can seem like an insult; one that is too warm can feel like an intrusion. Getting it right signals that you understand the unwritten rules of a community, and getting it wrong can make a foreigner seem rude even when no offence is intended.

Customs can also change quickly when circumstances demand it. During the COVID-19 pandemic, health authorities in many countries advised people to avoid handshakes and kisses, and a variety of substitutes appeared: elbow bumps, small waves, hands placed on the heart. Some commentators predicted that the handshake would never recover. In most places, it seems, they were wrong; once the danger passed, many people returned to their old habits with something close to relief.

That return may be the most revealing detail of all. A greeting is a tiny ritual, lasting only a second or two, but it carries a long history of ideas about respect, equality and belonging. People will give up a great deal in a crisis. The familiar touch of another human hand, it seems, is not among the things they abandon lightly.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the story that the handshake began as a weapons check?
options: It is proved by ancient Greek gravestones
It was invented by the Quakers
It is the only explanation historians accept
It is often repeated but has little firm evidence
questions.explain: Metin bu hikâyenin sık tekrarlandığını ama sağlam kanıtı olmadığını söyler; doğru cevap 'It is often repeated but has little firm evidence'. Yunan mezar taşlarındaki el tutma bir bağı ya da vedayı ifade ediyor gibidir, silah kontrolünü değil.

questions.q: What happened to the handshake after the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the text?
options: It disappeared completely in most countries
Many people went back to it with relief
It was replaced everywhere by elbow bumps
Governments made it illegal
questions.explain: Metne göre tehlike geçince birçok insan rahatlamaya yakın bir duyguyla eski alışkanlıklarına döndü; doğru cevap 'Many people went back to it with relief'. Tokalaşmanın asla geri gelmeyeceğini söyleyen yorumcular yanılmıştır.

title: The Neighbourhood's Own Official
text:
In almost every neighbourhood in Turkey, there is a small office, often on the ground floor of an ordinary building, with a sign that reads 'Muhtarlık'. Inside, there is usually a desk, a few chairs, a kettle and a person who seems to know everyone. This is the muhtar, an elected local official who represents a single neighbourhood, or mahalle, in a town or city, or an entire village in the countryside. Many people visit the office only a few times in their lives, but for others it is a familiar part of daily life.

The institution has a surprisingly precise beginning. Historians generally date its inception to 1829, during the reign of Sultan Mahmud II, when muhtars were appointed in Istanbul neighbourhoods. Before that, neighbourhoods were largely organised around their places of worship, and the local imam often acted as a link between residents and the state, keeping track of births, marriages and newcomers. The new office was part of a wider attempt by the Ottoman government to modernise its administration and to know more precisely who lived in the capital. In time, the system spread to other cities and to villages throughout the empire, and it survived the transition to the Turkish Republic.

What does a muhtar actually do? Much of the work is administrative. The office keeps records of who lives in the neighbourhood and issues documents that confirm a person's address, which may be required for jobs, schools or official applications. In the past, before many services moved online, such papers were needed for a long list of everyday matters, and a visit to the muhtar was the first step in many bureaucratic procedures. The muhtar also informs residents about official matters and passes the neighbourhood's concerns on to the city council.

Yet the role has always been about more than paperwork. Because the muhtar is elected by neighbours and usually lives among them, he or she often becomes a kind of informal social worker. People come to ask for help finding a job, to report a broken street lamp, to settle small disputes between neighbours or simply to talk. During emergencies such as earthquakes or floods, muhtars may know which elderly residents live alone or which families need help. In a large city where people barely know the family next door, this local knowledge can be invaluable.

The position is unusual in one respect: candidates for muhtar may not run as members of a political party. They stand as individuals, and their campaigns tend to be personal, built on reputation, family networks and years of being seen around the neighbourhood. Some critics regard the office as antiquated, a relic of a time before databases and digital services. Others argue that, precisely because so much of official life has become distant and impersonal, a familiar face at the end of the street is more valuable than ever. In their view, the muhtar is democracy at its most grassroots level.

The debate has a long history. Over the years, as more services have moved online, the muhtar's administrative duties have been reduced. Documents that once required a visit can now often be obtained through government websites. Some observers predicted the demise of the office as a result. Instead, many muhtars have shifted their energy toward the social side of the job, organising aid during hard winters, helping elderly people with online forms they find confusing, or bringing neighbours together for local events.

Similar figures exist in other countries. Many societies have some form of village head or neighbourhood representative standing between residents and a larger state. What makes the Turkish version distinctive is how close it remains to people's daily lives and how firmly it has taken root in both villages and big cities. In a sense, the muhtar is a reminder of something that rapid urbanization tends to wear away: the idea that a neighbourhood is a community with its own voice, not just a set of addresses.

Next time you pass a muhtarlık and see people drinking tea inside, it may be worth remembering that you are looking at an institution almost two hundred years old. It began as a way for the state to count its people. It has lasted because, in the end, people want someone nearby who will listen.

questions.q: Why was the office of muhtar created in 1829?
options: To replace the Sultan's ministers
To help the Ottoman government know who lived in the capital
To organise religious holidays in the neighbourhood
To collect rubbish from the streets
questions.explain: Metne göre yeni makam, Osmanlı yönetimini modernleştirme ve başkentte kimin yaşadığını daha kesin bilme çabasının parçasıydı; doğru cevap 'To help the Ottoman government know who lived in the capital'.

questions.q: How have many muhtars responded as more services moved online?
options: They have closed their offices
They have joined political parties
They have focused more on the social side of the job
They have started selling documents online
questions.explain: Metin, idari görevler azalınca birçok muhtarın enerjisini işin sosyal yönüne kaydırdığını söyler; doğru cevap 'They have focused more on the social side of the job'. Muhtar adayları bir partiden aday olamaz.

title: The Price on the Label
text:
In many parts of the world, buying something still begins a conversation. In a traditional market, the seller names a figure, the buyer laughs or looks shocked, and the two of them settle, after some theatre, on a price somewhere in between. For most of human history, this was simply how buying worked. The idea that every customer should pay the same price, written on a label for everyone to see, is surprisingly recent.

Bargaining makes a lot of sense in certain conditions. When goods are handmade and no two items are exactly alike, there is no obvious 'correct' price. When the seller is also the owner, he can judge each customer and decide how low he is willing to go. A rich-looking visitor may pay more, a regular customer less. Bargaining allows the price to adjust to the person, the moment and the seller's need for cash. It can also be enjoyable: in many markets, a good bargaining session is a social event as much as a commercial one, a longstanding custom with its own rules and jokes.

But bargaining has costs. It takes time, it rewards confidence and experience, and it leaves shy or inexperienced buyers at a disadvantage. It also depends on the owner doing the negotiating himself, which becomes difficult once a business grows large enough to employ many assistants. An owner who lets every assistant bargain freely must trust them not to give goods away or to keep part of the payment for themselves.

One of the earliest groups often credited with promoting fixed prices is the Quakers, a religious movement that emerged in seventeenth-century England. Quakers believed strongly in honesty in every part of life, and some Quaker shop owners concluded that asking one customer for more than another was a kind of lie. They began setting a single price for each item and refusing to bargain. According to accounts from the time, customers were suspicious at first, and some Quaker businesses suffered. Over time, however, the idea gained traction, and these shops earned a reputation for fairness: people learned that even a child could be sent to a Quaker shop and would not be cheated. Whether Quakers were truly the first is hard to prove, but their example is often cited.

Unsurprisingly, the practice took root slowly, and a case in point is how long many ordinary markets kept bargaining. The decisive change came in the nineteenth century with the growth of large shops in industrial cities. As businesses expanded and hired many workers, fixed prices became a practical necessity. A clearly marked price allowed even a new assistant to serve customers quickly, reduced arguments and made it possible to keep accurate accounts. Price labels, printed catalogues and newspaper advertisements all depended on prices that did not change from customer to customer. In hindsight, the fixed price was as much a management tool as a moral principle.

The shift also changed the experience of shopping. Without the need to negotiate, people could look around at leisure, compare goods in different shops and walk away without any awkwardness. Shopping became less of a contest and more of a pastime. Some historians argue that this helped create a modern consumer culture, in which looking is almost as important as buying.

Yet bargaining has never fully disappeared. It survives in markets in many countries, in the buying and selling of houses and cars, and in salary negotiations. And in recent years, a new form of changing prices has quietly returned. Airlines and hotels change their prices constantly according to demand, and online sellers can adjust prices many times a day using software. Critics worry that, with enough data, companies might eventually charge different customers different prices based on what each is likely to pay. That would bring back the logic of the old market, but without the human conversation. Ironically, it would be a machine doing the bargaining, and the buyer might not even know it was happening.

The price on the label, then, is not as natural as it seems. It is a social agreement that took centuries to develop, built on ideas about fairness, trust and efficiency. Whether it will stand the test of time in a world of clever software remains to be seen.

questions.q: Why did some Quaker shopkeepers refuse to bargain?
options: They believed charging different customers different prices was dishonest
They wanted to sell goods more cheaply than their rivals
The law did not allow them to bargain
They did not have enough time to talk to customers
questions.explain: Metne göre bazı Quaker esnaf, bir müşteriden diğerinden fazla istemenin bir tür yalan olduğunu düşündü; doğru cevap 'They believed charging different customers different prices was dishonest'.

questions.q: What worry do critics have about modern online pricing?
options: Prices online will always be higher than in shops
Customers will have to bargain with every seller
Software may charge each customer according to what they are likely to pay
Price labels will disappear from markets
questions.explain: Eleştirmenler, yeterli veriyle şirketlerin her müşteriden ödemeye yatkın olduğu fiyatı isteyebileceğinden endişe eder; doğru cevap 'Software may charge each customer according to what they are likely to pay'. Metin bunun pazarlığı insansız biçimde geri getireceğini söyler.

title: The Art of Waiting in Line
text:
Nobody writes the rules of a queue down, yet almost everyone knows them. You join at the back. You do not save places for large numbers of friends. You keep a polite distance from the person in front. And if someone pushes in ahead of you, you feel a flash of anger remarkably out of all proportion to the few seconds you have lost. The queue is one of the most ordinary social institutions there is, and one of the most revealing.

Its basic principle, 'first come, first served', seems almost natural, but it is only one of several ways to decide who gets something first. In many societies and situations, priority has gone instead to the strongest, the richest, the oldest or the best connected. A queue replaces all of these with a single rule that treats everyone alike. Social scientists have described it as a small model of equality: the wealthy businessman and the student wait in the same line, and neither can claim to deserve more.

This may explain why people react so strongly when the rule is broken. In many places, pushing in is close to a taboo, because what is at stake is not just time but fairness. Psychologists who have studied queues report that people are often more upset by unfairness than by waiting itself. In one well-known study in the 1980s, researchers asked volunteers to push into queues in New York and watched what happened. Those already waiting often objected, but, interestingly, the protests usually came from the people directly behind the intruder, who were the ones actually losing time. People further back tended to stay quiet, perhaps unwilling to make a scene.

The British are often described as the world's most devoted queuers. Some historians link the habit to the Second World War, when food was strictly limited and orderly waiting became a patriotic duty praised in newspapers as a national virtue. Others think the reputation was established earlier, during the growth of industrial cities in the nineteenth century, when crowds gathering for buses, tickets and public services needed some way of organising themselves. Either way, the image of patient solidarity in the queue has become part of national identity, even if visitors may notice that British queues are not always as patient as the legend suggests.

Managers of banks, airports and theme parks have learned a great deal about the psychology of waiting. One rule of thumb is that waiting feels longer when you have nothing to do, which is why mirrors are often placed near lifts and screens near check-in desks. Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones, so many places now display estimated times. A single line feeding several counters, rather than a separate line for each, is widely seen as fairer, because nobody has to watch a neighbouring line move faster. The numbered ticket, now common in banks, post offices and hospitals, solves another problem: customers can sit down while their place is kept for them, without anyone standing guard.

Queues also raise difficult questions about money. In some cities, people are paid to stand in line for others, for concert tickets, new phones or even seats at public hearings. Theme parks sell passes that let paying customers skip the line. To some economists this is efficient: those who value their time most can pay to save it. To critics, it undermines the very thing that makes the queue fair. If time can be bought, then the egalitarian promise of the line, that everyone waits the same, disappears, and the queue becomes one more place where wealth takes precedence over patience.

Technology is changing queues in other ways too. Online booking systems and apps can now hold a place in a virtual queue, so that diners or patients can wait at home instead of in a corridor. Yet the basic logic remains the same, and so does the anger when someone jumps ahead. A virtual queue may be invisible, but people still care deeply about whether it is fair.

Waiting in line can be boring, and unsurprisingly few people enjoy it, but it tells us something important. Every orderly queue is a small act of cooperation among strangers, built on nothing more than shared expectations. It works only because most people, most of the time, agree to keep to the rules, and quietly trust that others will do the same.

questions.q: In the New York study, who usually protested when someone pushed into a queue?
options: Everyone in the queue equally
Only the staff working at the counter
The people at the very back of the queue
The people standing directly behind the intruder
questions.explain: Metne göre itirazlar genellikle araya girenin hemen arkasındaki, yani gerçekten zaman kaybeden kişilerden geldi; doğru cevap 'The people standing directly behind the intruder'. Daha arkadakiler çoğunlukla sessiz kaldı.

questions.q: Why do critics object to paying someone to stand in line or buying a pass to skip it?
options: It makes the queue move too slowly
It destroys the idea that everyone waits the same
It is against the law in most cities
It makes theme parks less profitable
questions.explain: Eleştirmenlere göre zaman satın alınabilirse sıranın eşitlikçi vaadi, yani herkesin aynı şekilde beklemesi ortadan kalkar; doğru cevap 'It destroys the idea that everyone waits the same'.

title: Lost and Found
text:
Every day, in every large city, thousands of things go missing. Umbrellas are habitually left on trains, phones slip down the sides of taxi seats, and keys, gloves, wallets and children's toys are forgotten on buses and park benches. Most of these objects are never seen again by their owners. But a surprising number find their way to one of the quieter institutions of modern life: the lost property office.

The problem of lost things is, of course, ancient. Many old legal systems contained rules about what a person should do on finding something that belonged to someone else. Some required the finder to announce the discovery publicly, for example in a market or a place of worship, so that the owner could come forward. Others set out how long the finder had to wait before the object became his, and whether the owner had to pay a reward. These rules expressed an idea that still underpins the modern system: finding something does not make it yours.

What changed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries was scale. Railways, buses and underground trains carried millions of passengers, and millions of passengers forget millions of things. Transport companies needed a way to collect, store and return them. London's transport authorities, for instance, have run a central lost property office since the 1930s, and over the decades it has received an extraordinary variety of items: not only bags and books but, according to its staff, false teeth, wedding dresses, a stuffed animal and, reportedly, a human skull from a medical student's collection.

The work is more complicated than it sounds. Each object must be recorded, described and stored in a way that allows it to be found again. Valuable items need to be kept safe, food has to be thrown away, and some objects raise awkward legal questions. An office must also check that a person claiming a phone or wallet is truly its owner, usually by asking for a detailed description of the contents. After a fixed period, unclaimed items are typically sold, given to charitable organisations or destroyed, and the money may help pay for the service.

How often lost things are returned depends a great deal on the behaviour of finders, and here countries seem to differ. Japan is frequently cited as a case in point. Its lost property system, supported by a dense network of small police posts, receives millions of items a year, and a large share of the lost cash handed in is eventually returned to its owners. Researchers have suggested several reasons: a long legal duty to hand in found property, a small reward for finders, strong social expectations about honesty and the sheer convenience of the system.

A large international experiment published in 2019 added a twist. Researchers 'lost' more than seventeen thousand wallets in 355 cities across forty countries, handing them in at banks, hotels and offices as if they had found them on the street. Some wallets contained no money and some contained a modest sum. Contrary to what many economists had predicted, people in most countries were more likely to report a wallet when it held money than when it was empty. The researchers concluded that many people simply do not want to see themselves as thieves, and that more money makes keeping a wallet feel more clearly like stealing. Unsurprisingly, the finding attracted wide attention, because it cast doubt on the simple idea that people always act in their own narrow interest.

Today, technology is changing the old system. Some offices now use online databases where owners can search for missing items, and small electronic tags allow people to follow their keys or bags on their phones. Yet the basic process still depends on someone, somewhere, deciding to pick up an object that is not theirs and hand it in rather than walk away.

For owners who have lost something precious, the service can be invaluable. In that sense, every lost property office is a small monument to ordinary honesty. Behind the shelves of forgotten umbrellas lies a quiet agreement among strangers that what belongs to someone else should, if possible, find its way home.

questions.q: What surprising result did the 2019 wallet experiment produce?
options: People were more likely to report a wallet that contained money
Most wallets were never reported at all
Wallets with money were usually kept by the finders
Results were exactly the same in every country
questions.explain: Deneyde, birçok ekonomistin beklentisinin aksine insanlar çoğu ülkede içinde para olan cüzdanı boş olana göre daha sık bildirdi; doğru cevap 'People were more likely to report a wallet that contained money'.

questions.q: Which idea, according to the text, lies behind both old and modern rules about lost things?
options: The finder should always receive the object
Finding something does not make it yours
Lost objects belong to the state
Owners must pay a large reward
questions.explain: Metin eski kuralların modern sistemi de destekleyen bir fikri ifade ettiğini söyler: bir şeyi bulmak onu sizin yapmaz; doğru cevap 'Finding something does not make it yours'.

title: Elephants in the Snow
text:
In the spring of 218 BC, a young general named Hannibal left the city of New Carthage, on the south-eastern coast of Spain, with one of the strangest armies the ancient world had ever seen. Tens of thousands of foot soldiers marched beside horsemen from North Africa, slingers from the Balearic Islands and, most famously, around thirty-seven war elephants. Carthage, his home city in what is now Tunisia, was at war with Rome, and Hannibal had chosen a plan that most people would have called ludicrous. Instead of fighting the Romans by sea, where they were growing stronger, he would march to Italy and attack them from the north.

The route was long and fraught with danger. The army first crossed the Pyrenees and then reached the wide River Rhône, where the elephants refused to step into boats. According to the Greek historian Polybius, Hannibal's engineers built huge rafts, covered them with earth so that they looked like solid ground, and led two female elephants on first. The others followed. When the rafts moved away from the bank, some of the frightened animals jumped into the water, but they kept their trunks above the surface and walked across the riverbed. Remarkably, none of them was lost.

The real test, however, was the Alps. Hannibal reached the mountains in autumn, when the first snow was already falling on the high passes. Local tribes, who saw the army as an invader, rolled rocks down on the soldiers from the slopes and attacked the slow baggage animals at the back. On the narrow paths, horses and mules slipped on the ice and fell hundreds of metres. Men who had grown up under the warm Mediterranean sun had never seen anything like it. Some writers claim that near the top, Hannibal stood on a rock and pointed to the plains of Italy below, telling his tired men that the worst was over.

It was not quite over. On the way down, the army found the path blocked by a landslide. The Roman writer Livy, who lived almost two centuries later, tells a famous story about how the obstacle was removed: the soldiers cut down trees, lit huge fires against the rock and then poured sour wine over the hot stone until it cracked. Historians have long treated this account with scrutiny. Heating rock and then cooling it quickly can break it, as ancient miners knew, but whether an army really had enough wine and enough time for this remains a point of debate. Most agree, though, that the descent took several more days of hard work in freezing conditions.

When Hannibal finally reached northern Italy, roughly fifteen days after starting the crossing, his army had paid a terrible price. Polybius, who said he had talked to people who were there and had walked part of the route himself, reports that only about twenty thousand foot soldiers and six thousand horsemen remained. Exhaustion, cold, hunger and constant attacks had taken their toll on the rest. Surprisingly, most of the elephants seem to have survived the mountains. It was the following winter, after a battle near the River Trebia, that nearly all of them died. Ancient sources suggest that by the next year only one was left, which Hannibal himself may have ridden through flooded marshes.

The bold march set the stage for some of the worst Roman defeats in history, including the battle of Cannae in 216 BC. Yet one question has never been answered with certainty: which pass did Hannibal actually use? Scholars have proposed at least a dozen, and the ancient descriptions are too vague to be conclusive. In 2016, a team of scientists offered a new kind of evidence. Digging in a bog below the Col de la Traversette, a high pass between France and Italy, they found a layer of soil that appeared to be full of churned-up animal dung. It contained large numbers of a type of microbe found mainly in the stomachs of horses, and it was dated to roughly the right period.

The researchers argued that this could be the mark left by thousands of animals that had stopped near the water. Other experts were more cautious, pointing out that armies and traders had used the Alps for centuries, and that a single layer of soil cannot name the army that left it. The finding lends credence to one route, but it does not end the debate.

Perhaps that is part of the appeal of the story. More than two thousand years later, people still try to picture the scene: the frozen soldiers, the tribesmen on the cliffs, and the great grey animals moving slowly through the snow, far from the warm lands where they were born.

questions.q: What did the 2016 study find below the Col de la Traversette?
options: Bones of an elephant buried in the ice
A layer of soil with signs of a large number of horses
Pieces of rock that had been cracked by fire
Roman weapons left after a battle
questions.explain: Bilim insanları bataklıkta, atların midesinde yaşayan bir mikroptan bolca içeren bir toprak tabakası buldular; bu yüzden doğru cevap 'A layer of soil with signs of a large number of horses'.

questions.q: According to the text, when did most of Hannibal's elephants die?
options: While crossing the River Rhône
During the climb to the top of the Alps
In the winter after a battle near the River Trebia
At the battle of Cannae in 216 BC
questions.explain: Metne göre fillerin çoğu dağları geçmeyi başardı; neredeyse hepsi ertesi kış Trebia yakınındaki savaştan sonra öldü. Doğru cevap 'In the winter after a battle near the River Trebia'.

title: The King Who Made Gold Cheap
text:
In July 1324, the people of Cairo watched an extraordinary procession arrive at the edge of their city. It belonged to Mansa Musa, the ruler of the Mali Empire, a vast West African state that stretched from the Atlantic coast deep into the Sahara. Musa was a devout Muslim, and he was on his way to Mecca to perform the pilgrimage. But he did not travel lightly. According to the accounts that survive, his caravan included thousands of people, among them soldiers, officials, doctors and servants, as well as a long line of camels carrying gold.

The numbers in these accounts vary, and some are almost certainly exaggerated. One later writer spoke of sixty thousand people; another described eighty to a hundred camels, each loaded with gold dust. Historians treat such figures as rough impressions rather than precise counts. What is not in doubt is that Mali was extremely rich. Much of the gold used in the Mediterranean world at that time came from mines in or near Musa's lands, and it was carried north across the desert by traders in exchange for salt, cloth and other goods.

The fullest description of the visit comes from al-Umari, a scholar who worked for the Egyptian government and arrived in Cairo about twelve years after the king had passed through. He talked to officials and merchants who remembered the event clearly. They told him that Musa had been astonishingly generous. He gave gold to the sultan's court, to religious scholars, to the poor and to almost everyone who did him a service. His followers spent freely in the markets, buying a plethora of goods, from fine cloth to horses, often without bargaining over the price.

This generosity had an unforeseen result. With so much gold suddenly moving around the city, its value dropped. Al-Umari reports that the price of gold in Cairo had still not fully recovered when he was writing. In other words, a single visitor seems to have devalued one of the world's most important metals in one of its busiest markets. For merchants, money changers and speculators who held their wealth in gold, the fallout was real. Modern economists sometimes use the episode as a vivid case in point of what can happen when the supply of money grows faster than the goods it can buy.

There is a curious twist to the story. On his way home, Musa appears to have run short of funds, and he borrowed money from Cairo merchants at very high interest. Some writers have suggested that this was a deliberate attempt to take gold out of circulation and repair the damage he had done. That interpretation is attractive, but it is not supported by firm evidence; it is equally possible that the king had simply given away more than he had planned.

The journey had effects far beyond Egypt. News of the golden king spread across the Mediterranean, and in 1375 a mapmaker on the island of Majorca drew him on what is now called the Catalan Atlas. He sits on a throne, wearing a crown and holding a large golden ball, while a rider on a camel approaches him. For many Europeans, this was one of the first images of West Africa they had ever seen, and it presented the region as a place of enormous affluence.

Musa also brought people and ideas back with him. He is said to have returned with scholars and with an architect, often named as Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, who is linked to the design of the great mud-brick mosque of Djinguereber in Timbuktu. Over the following decades, Timbuktu grew into a famous centre of learning, with libraries and teachers who attracted students from across the region. Not every detail of this story can be confirmed, but the general picture, of a city that gained a foothold in the wider Islamic world of scholarship, is widely accepted.

In hindsight, it is easy to reduce Mansa Musa to a single label: the richest man who ever lived. Popular lists repeat this claim often, but it is impossible to compare his wealth with that of modern billionaires in any meaningful way. Perhaps a better way to remember him is as a ruler who used one long journey to put his empire on the map, quite literally, and whose gifts were so prodigious that a whole city felt them for years.

questions.q: Why did the price of gold fall in Cairo?
options: Mines near Cairo suddenly produced much more gold
The sultan ordered merchants to sell their gold

title: The Summer the City Danced
text:
One hot day in July 1518, a woman known in the records as Frau Troffea stepped into a narrow street in Strasbourg, then a free city of the Holy Roman Empire, and began to dance. There was no music and no celebration. She simply moved her arms and legs, hour after hour, as if she could not stop. According to later chronicles, she continued for days, collapsing from exhaustion at night and starting again in the morning.

Within a week, other people had joined her. By the end of the month, the number of dancers may have reached several dozen, and some accounts give much higher figures, up to four hundred, although these may be exaggerated. Men and women danced in the streets and squares, their faces blank or full of distress, their feet bleeding. Witnesses described them as being unable to rest, as though some outside force had taken control of their bodies.

The city council was alarmed, and its first response looks strange to us today. After consulting local doctors, who said that the problem was caused by 'hot blood', the councillors decided that the cure was to let the victims dance it out. They cleared two halls, built a wooden stage in the horse market and even hired musicians and strong young men to keep the dancers moving and hold them up. The plan backfired. The music and the public spectacle seem to have drawn even more people into the dance. Some sources claim that people were dying from heart attacks and strokes, perhaps several a day, though historians note that this detail is poorly supported by documents from the time.

Eventually the authorities changed their minds. They decided that the dancing was not a medical problem but a punishment from Saint Vitus, a Christian saint who, according to popular belief, could send a dancing curse on those who angered him. Music and dancing in public were banned, and the sufferers were taken to a shrine dedicated to the saint in the hills near the town of Saverne. There they were given red shoes, led around an altar and prayed over. Over the following weeks, the outbreak seems to have faded away.

What really happened? For a long time, the most popular explanation was poisoning. Ergot is a fungus that grows on damp rye, the grain used to make bread in much of Europe. It contains toxins related to the drug LSD, and eating contaminated bread can cause hallucinations and seizures. The theory sounds neat, but it does not stand up to scrutiny. Ergot poisoning also reduces the flow of blood to the arms and legs, which makes coordinated movement for days on end very unlikely. It is also hard to explain why only some people, rather than whole families eating the same bread, would have been affected.

The historian John Waller, who has written a detailed study of the event, offers a different explanation. He argues that the people of Strasbourg had suffered a series of terrible years, with failed harvests, rising bread prices, severe winters and outbreaks of disease. Many of them were hungry, poor and frightened. At the same time, the belief in Saint Vitus and his dancing curse was deeply rooted in the region. In such conditions, Waller suggests, an extreme form of what is now called mass psychogenic illness could spread: people under great stress fall into a trance-like state, and they behave in the way their culture tells them a cursed person should behave.

This theory has its own critics, and of course we cannot interview the dancers of 1518. Yet it has the advantage of explaining why similar outbreaks happened in the same part of Europe, along the Rhine and Moselle rivers, but almost nowhere else. The dancing seems to have needed both a desperate population and a shared story about what dancing could mean. Rather than naming a single culprit, such as a poison, it treats the event as the product of a whole society under pressure.

The episode is sometimes told as an amusing curiosity from the past, but for those involved it was a frightening predicament. It also serves as a reminder that minds and bodies are deeply connected, and that fear, belief and hardship can work together in ways that are still not fully understood.

questions.q: What happened when the city council hired musicians and built a stage?
options: The dancers soon became calm and went home
The doctors were dismissed from the city
Even more people seem to have joined the dancing
The dancers were sent to the shrine at once

questions.q: Why does the writer think ergot poisoning is a weak explanation?
options: Rye was not grown anywhere near Strasbourg
Ergot only affects animals, not people

Ergot reduces blood flow, making days of dancing unlikely

title: The Night the Moon Turned Red
text:
In June 1503, Christopher Columbus was in serious trouble. He was on his fourth and final voyage to the Americas, and his two remaining ships had been eaten through by shipworms, small creatures that bore holes in wooden hulls. Water poured in faster than his sailors could pump it out. With no other choice, he ran the ships aground in a bay on the northern coast of Jamaica, where they became a kind of fixed, leaking fort. More than a hundred men were now stranded on an island far from any Spanish settlement, with no way to sail home.

At first, the local Taíno people were willing to help. They brought cassava bread, fish and fruit, and in return the Spaniards gave them small bells, beads and other trade goods. But weeks turned into months. One of Columbus's officers, Diego Méndez, set out with a few companions in canoes to cross the open sea to the island of Hispaniola and ask for help, a dangerous journey that took several days. Meanwhile, the stranded crew grew restless. Some of the men rebelled against Columbus, left the camp and treated the Taíno badly, robbing them and causing anger and mistrust. The Taíno, who saw little reason to keep feeding a large group of demanding strangers, began to bring less and less food.

By early 1504, the Spaniards were at the mercy of their hosts, and hunger was becoming a real threat. It was then that Columbus remembered a book he had carried with him: an almanac of tables prepared by the German astronomer Regiomontanus. Such tables predicted the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets with impressive precision, and sailors used them to help work out where they were at sea. According to the almanac, a total lunar eclipse would take place on the night of 29 February 1504.

Columbus called the local leaders to a meeting. Through an interpreter, he told them that his God was displeased with them for withholding food and would soon show his anger in the sky. The Moon, he said, would rise red and inflamed, as a warning of the punishment to come. Some of the leaders are said to have laughed at the threat. That evening, however, the Moon rose already darkened, and as the night went on, it turned a deep, dull red.

According to Columbus's son Ferdinand, who was on the voyage and later wrote an account of it, the Taíno were terrified. They hurried to the ships with food and begged Columbus to ask his God for forgiveness. Columbus went into his cabin, telling them he would pray. In reality, he seems to have been timing the eclipse with an hourglass. Shortly before it was due to end, he came out and announced that God had pardoned them, and that the Moon would soon return to normal. When it did, the supply of food was restored.

The story has been retold many times, and it has even inspired scenes in later novels. It is often presented as an example of ingenuity, and in a narrow sense it was: Columbus used scientific knowledge to escape a dangerous predicament. It was certainly an astute move. But it is also worth looking at it from the other side. The trick depended on deceiving people who had been generous to a group of uninvited visitors. It belongs to a much larger history in which Europeans used their advantages, in weapons, writing and knowledge, to exploit the peoples of the Americas, often with devastating results.

Historians also add a note of caution about the details. Most of what we know comes from Ferdinand's account and from Columbus himself, both of whom had reasons to present the admiral as clever and in control. We have no record of the event from the Taíno point of view, and we cannot know exactly what they believed about the eclipse. It is possible that the famous scene was more complicated, or less dramatic, than the Spanish version suggests.

Help finally arrived in June 1504, a full year after the ships had been run aground. Columbus returned to Spain that autumn, ill and disappointed, and died less than two years later. Of all the moments of his long and controversial career, few are retold as often as the night he borrowed the power of the Moon.

questions.q: How did Columbus know that the Moon would turn dark and red?
options: He had a book of astronomical tables
Taíno leaders had warned him about it
Diego Méndez sent him a message
He had seen the same event a year earlier
questions.explain: Columbus, Regiomontanus'un hazırladığı ve tutulmayı önceden bildiren bir almanak taşıyordu; doğru cevap 'He had a book of astronomical tables'.

questions.q: Why do historians advise caution about the details of the story?
options: The eclipse did not really happen in 1504
The main sources had reasons to make Columbus look clever
The Taíno wrote a very different account
Ferdinand was not on the voyage
questions.explain: Bilgilerin çoğu Ferdinand'dan ve Columbus'un kendisinden geliyor ve ikisinin de amirali zeki göstermek için nedenleri vardı; doğru cevap 'The main sources had reasons to make Columbus look clever'.

title: Secrets in a Hollow Stick
text:
For many centuries, silk was one of the most valuable goods in the world, and only one country knew how to make it. In China, people had learned thousands of years earlier that a certain moth caterpillar, fed on the leaves of the white mulberry tree, spins a cocoon from a single thread that can be more than a kilometre long. If the cocoon is boiled before the moth comes out, the thread can be unwound and woven into a cloth that is light, strong and beautifully shiny. The Chinese guarded this knowledge carefully, and for a long time the rest of the world could only buy the finished product.

By the sixth century AD, one of the biggest customers was the Byzantine Empire, the eastern half of the old Roman world, with its capital at Constantinople. Its emperors, officials and churches used enormous amounts of silk for robes, curtains and ceremonies. The problem was that the trade routes from China passed through the lands of the Sasanian Persians, Byzantium's great rival. Persian merchants controlled much of the flow of raw silk to the west and took the lion's share of the profits. Wars between the two empires could cut off supplies completely, and the Emperor Justinian, who ruled from 527 to 565, went to great lengths to find another way.

He tried several solutions. He fixed prices for silk, tried to bring the industry under state control, and looked for a route that would bypass Persia, either by sea through the Red Sea or across the steppes to the north. None of these attempts worked well. Then, according to the historian Procopius, who lived at Justinian's court, an unexpected offer arrived around the year 552.

Some monks, Procopius writes, came to the emperor from a land beyond India where they had lived for a long time. They told him that they knew how silk was made, and that it was not, as many Romans believed, collected from trees. It came from worms. The worms themselves could not be transported alive over such a distance, but their eggs could. The monks promised that, if the emperor rewarded them well, they would go back and bring the eggs to Byzantium. Justinian agreed. The monks made the long journey and returned with the eggs. A later writer adds a detail that has become the most famous part of the story: they hid them inside hollow walking sticks in order to smuggle them past the border guards.

Back in Byzantine territory, the eggs were kept warm, perhaps buried in manure as a simple form of incubation, until they hatched. The young caterpillars were fed on mulberry leaves, and the whole process of raising them, collecting cocoons and unwinding the thread slowly took root. Within a few generations, the region around Constantinople, and later Greece, had a silk industry of its own. The state kept strict control over the finest cloth, especially the purple silk reserved for the imperial family, and silk would remain an important part of the Byzantine economy for centuries.

Historians argue about many parts of this story. Procopius does not say exactly where the monks came from; modern scholars have suggested places in Central Asia, such as Sogdiana or the kingdom of Khotan, where silk production had already spread. This points to something important: by Justinian's time, China's secret had already escaped. A well-known legend from Khotan tells of a Chinese princess who was sent to marry the local king and hid silkworm eggs in her headdress, because she did not want to live without silk. Whether or not that tale is true, it shows that the knowledge travelled west in stages, carried by individuals who were willing to break the rules.

The episode is sometimes described as one of the earliest examples of industrial spying. That label may be a little modern, but it captures what happened. A tiny cargo, carried by a handful of tenacious travellers, helped to change an industry and weakened a near monopoly that had lasted for a very long time. It is a reminder that the most valuable things to move across borders are not always heavy or expensive. Sometimes they fit inside a walking stick.

questions.q: Why was Justinian eager to find a new source of silk?
options: Chinese silk had become poor in quality
The church had banned imported silk
Silk was needed to pay the army
Persia controlled much of the trade and its profits
questions.explain: İpek yolları Pers topraklarından geçiyordu ve Pers tüccarlar kârın büyük kısmını alıyordu; doğru cevap 'Persia controlled much of the trade and its profits'.

questions.q: What does the legend from Khotan suggest?
options: Silk was first invented in Khotan
Chinese princesses often worked as spies
Knowledge of silk had already spread west before Justinian
Monks were not allowed to travel to China
questions.explain: Hotan efsanesi, ipek bilgisinin Justinianus'tan önce aşama aşama batıya yayıldığını gösterir; doğru cevap 'Knowledge of silk had already spread west before Justinian'.

title: A Giraffe for the Emperor
text:
In the autumn of 1414, a very unusual guest arrived at the court of the Yongle Emperor in Nanjing, then the capital of Ming China. It was tall, gentle and spotted, with a long neck, large dark eyes and two small horns covered in skin. No one at court had ever seen anything like it. It was a giraffe, and it had travelled thousands of kilometres by sea to get there.

Its journey was connected to one of the most impressive projects of the age. Between 1405 and 1433, the Ming court sent seven great fleets into the Indian Ocean under the command of Zheng He, a Muslim official from the south-western province of Yunnan who had served the emperor since his youth. These fleets were prodigious. The largest voyages are said to have included more than two hundred and fifty ships and over twenty-five thousand men. The biggest vessels, known as treasure ships, are described in Chinese records as well over a hundred metres long, although many modern historians doubt that wooden ships of that size could have sailed, and suggest that they were smaller. Even so, they were far larger than any European ships of the time, and they reflected great navigational skill.

The purpose of the voyages was not conquest in the usual sense. The fleets visited ports in Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf and East Africa, carrying silk, porcelain and other gifts. In return, local rulers were encouraged to send envoys and gifts to China and to recognise the emperor's authority. It was a way of displaying Ming power and wealth, and of drawing the wider world into a system in which China stood at the centre.

The giraffe came by way of Bengal. A ship from Zheng He's fleet was in Bengal when envoys from Malindi, on the coast of what is now Kenya, arrived with a giraffe as a gift for the Bengali sultan. The sultan, in turn, sent the animal on to China. When it reached the court, officials saw at once that it resembled the qilin, a creature from Chinese legend that was said to appear only during the reign of a wise and benevolent ruler. Like the qilin, the giraffe seemed to have the body of a deer, the tail of an ox and soft horns, and it was peaceful, eating only plants. To the courtiers, it was a perfect sign from heaven, a harbinger of a golden age.

The emperor responded with careful modesty. He is reported to have said that good government, not strange animals, was what mattered, and that the officials should not make too much of the event. Yet he also made sure that the giraffe was received in an impressive ceremony. A court painter, Shen Du, produced a picture of the animal with its keeper and wrote a poem in its praise. Copies of the painting are still extant, and they show a remarkably accurate giraffe, with its long neck and patterned coat, standing calmly while a man holds its rope. A year later, envoys from Malindi brought another giraffe directly, along with zebras and other animals.

These dramatic expeditions did not last. After the Yongle Emperor died in 1424, many officials argued that the voyages were too expensive, and that the empire's real dangers lay on its northern borders, where the Mongols remained a threat. One more voyage took place in the early 1430s, during or soon after which Zheng He probably died. After that, the great fleets were discontinued, and that moment is often seen as the zenith of Ming power at sea. Stories are told that some records of the voyages were later destroyed by officials who wanted to prevent them from ever being repeated, though the evidence for this is uncertain.

In hindsight, some writers have called the decision to stop the voyages myopic, arguing that China turned its back on the sea just as European sailors were beginning to explore it. Others say this view is unfair: the Ming state had good reasons to focus its resources on defence and the economy at home, and Chinese merchants continued to trade privately across Asia for centuries.

Whatever the verdict, the giraffe remains one of the most charming images from that brief period. For a moment, an animal from the African coast walked through the palaces of Nanjing, and a whole court chose to see in it a message about their emperor, a mixture of real curiosity and careful political theatre.

questions.q: Why were the courtiers so excited about the giraffe?
options: It was the first animal ever brought from Bengal
It looked like the qilin, a sign of a wise ruler
It could be used to carry goods on the ships
It had been captured by Zheng He himself
questions.explain: Saraylılar zürafayı yalnızca bilge ve iyiliksever bir hükümdar döneminde görünen efsanevi qilin'e benzettiler; doğru cevap 'It looked like the qilin, a sign of a wise ruler'.

questions.q: What reason is given for ending the voyages?
options: They were costly, and the main threat was in the north
Zheng He refused to sail again
The treasure ships had all sunk
Foreign rulers stopped sending envoys
questions.explain: Pek çok yetkili seferlerin çok pahalı olduğunu ve asıl tehlikenin kuzey sınırlarında olduğunu savundu; doğru cevap 'They were costly, and the main threat was in the north'.

title: The Queen's Voyage to Punt
text:
About three and a half thousand years ago, in the fifteenth century BC, Egypt was ruled by a woman who called herself king. Her name was Hatshepsut. She had first acted as regent for her young stepson, Thutmose III, but within a few years she had taken the full titles of a pharaoh, and in many statues she was shown with the traditional false beard of an Egyptian king. Her reign lasted around twenty years and is usually remembered as a time of peace, building and trade. Its most famous adventure was a voyage to a distant land called Punt.

The Egyptians had known about Punt for centuries. It was a source of luxury goods: gold, ebony, ivory, animal skins and, above all, the sweet-smelling resins myrrh and frankincense, which were burned in temples every day. Trips there were rare, however, and in the period before Hatshepsut's reign they seem to have stopped altogether. The queen decided to revive them, and according to the inscriptions on her temple, she presented the expedition as a command from the god Amun himself.

Five ships set out, probably from a harbour on the Red Sea coast. They may have been built in pieces along the Nile, carried across the desert and put together on the shore, a method for which archaeologists have found evidence at other Egyptian ports. The ships then sailed south, using both oars and a large sail, until they reached Punt.

We know about the voyage because Hatshepsut had it recorded in a series of detailed carved and painted scenes on the walls of her great temple at Deir el-Bahari, near modern Luxor. They are among the most charming images in Egyptian art. The people of Punt live in round houses raised on poles, with ladders leading up to the doors. Their ruler, a man named Parahu, comes to meet the Egyptians with his wife, Ati, who is shown with a large, heavy body that has puzzled modern viewers. The Egyptians offer jewellery, weapons and tools, and in return they load their ships with goods: bags of resin, ebony logs, gold, leopard skins and live animals, including baboons, a type of large primate, that climb about on the ropes.

Most remarkable of all, the expedition brought back living incense trees, their roots wrapped in baskets of soil, so that they could be planted in Egypt. This may be one of the earliest recorded attempts to move plants from one country to another, and later botanical writers have pointed to it as a forerunner of the great plant-collecting journeys of much later times. Some scholars believe that the trees were planted in front of the temple, where the remains of old tree pits have been found, although this is not conclusive.

But where exactly was Punt? This has been one of the great puzzles of Egyptian history. Suggestions have ranged from Somalia to Yemen, and even to places much further away. A study published in 2020 brought new evidence. Researchers examined the teeth of mummified baboons that the ancient Egyptians had kept in temples. By measuring the isotopes of certain elements, which reflect the local rocks, water and food where an animal grew up, they could estimate where the baboons had come from. Some of the animals appeared to have been born in a region that includes modern Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia. This does not settle the question once and for all, but it lends credence to the idea that Punt lay somewhere in the Horn of Africa.

Hatshepsut's own story had a strange ending. After her death, Thutmose III became sole ruler, and in the later part of his reign many of her statues were broken, and her name and images were cut out of monuments. For a long time, scholars assumed that this was an act of revenge by a bitter stepson who wanted to tarnish her memory. Today, many suggest a less personal motive: Thutmose may have wanted to secure the throne for his own son as his successor and to restore the traditional idea that only men should be king. Whatever the reason, the attempt to erase her largely failed. The Punt scenes survived, and in retrospect they are some of the clearest evidence of her reign, telling the story of a queen who sent her ships into the unknown and brought back trees.

questions.q: What was especially remarkable about the goods brought back from Punt?
options: Living incense trees were carried back in baskets
The ships returned with the ruler of Punt on board
Gold was found there for the first time
The Egyptians brought back a new type of ship
questions.explain: Metin en dikkat çekici şeyin, kökleri toprak dolu sepetlere sarılmış canlı tütsü ağaçlarının getirilmesi olduğunu söylüyor; doğru cevap 'Living incense trees were carried back in baskets'.

questions.q: How did the 2020 study try to locate Punt?
options: By reading new inscriptions at Deir el-Bahari
By finding the remains of the five ships
By comparing ancient maps of the Red Sea
By studying chemical signals in baboon teeth
questions.explain: Araştırmacılar mumyalanmış babunların dişlerindeki izotopları ölçerek hayvanların nereden geldiğini tahmin ettiler; doğru cevap 'By studying chemical signals in baboon teeth'.

title: A Small Island with a Big Window
text:
In the harbour of Nagasaki, in south-western Japan, there once stood a tiny artificial island shaped like an open fan. It measured only about 120 metres along its longest side and some 75 metres across, and it was connected to the city by a single short bridge, watched day and night by guards. For more than two hundred years, this little piece of land, called Dejima, was almost the only place where Japan and Europe met.

The island was built in the 1630s, at a time when Japan's rulers were growing deeply suspicious of foreigners. Portuguese traders and missionaries had arrived in the previous century, and Christianity had spread quickly in parts of the country. The shogun's government, based in Edo, now Tokyo, came to see the new religion as a threat to its authority. A series of edicts restricted contact with the outside world, banned Christianity and forbade Japanese people from travelling abroad. Dejima was originally constructed to keep the Portuguese merchants in one place where they could be watched. But in 1639, after a rebellion in which many of the rebels were Christians, the Portuguese were expelled altogether.

That left a gap, and the Dutch East India Company filled it. The Dutch were Protestants who had shown that they cared more about trade than about spreading their faith, which reduced the government's mistrust. In 1641 they were ordered to move their trading post from the town of Hirado to Dejima, and there they stayed until the middle of the nineteenth century. The rules were strict. Usually only a dozen or so Dutch employees lived on the island at any one time. They could not leave without permission, could not bring their wives, and were under constant scrutiny from Japanese officials and interpreters. Each year, the head of the trading post had to travel to Edo to present gifts to the shogun and answer his questions about events in the world. The journey took several weeks, and the Dutch visitors were sometimes asked to sing, dance or speak a few words of their language for the amusement of the court.

Life on Dejima could be dull and lonely, a kind of comfortable detention. Yet this small, insular community became a remarkable channel for ideas. Dutch ships brought sugar, cloth, glass, clocks and books, and took back copper, porcelain and other Japanese goods. Among the most valuable cargo were the books. Japanese scholars, working at first quietly and later more openly, began to study Western science through Dutch texts, a movement that came to be known as rangaku, or Dutch learning.

One famous moment came in 1771. A group of doctors in Edo watched the dissection of the body of an executed criminal and compared what they saw with the pictures in a Dutch anatomy book. The book was far more accurate than the Chinese medical texts they had been trained with. Without a proper dictionary, and knowing very little Dutch, they spent about three years translating it, word by word, and published the result in 1774 as Kaitai Shinsho, often called the New Book of Anatomy. It had a lasting influence on Japanese medicine.

The exchange went in both directions. Several European doctors who worked on Dejima became pioneers in the study of Japan. The German physician Engelbert Kaempfer, who served there in the 1690s, wrote a history of Japan that was widely read in Europe. In the 1820s, another German doctor, Philipp Franz von Siebold, taught Western medicine to Japanese students and collected thousands of plant and animal specimens, contributing greatly to European botany and taxonomy. His story ended badly, however: in 1828 he was found with detailed maps of Japan, which foreigners were forbidden to own, and he was eventually expelled from the country.

When Japan opened its ports to foreign trade in the 1850s, Dejima lost its special role. Over the following decades, the water around it was filled in, and the island disappeared into the growing city. Since the 1990s, Nagasaki has been reconstructing parts of it, rebuilding warehouses and houses as they appear in old drawings. Visitors can now walk across the fan-shaped site and imagine how such a small place once served as a window through which two very different worlds watched each other.

questions.q: Why were the Dutch allowed to stay in Japan when the Portuguese were not?
options: They agreed to teach Japanese officials their language
They paid the shogun much more money
They seemed more interested in trade than in spreading their religion
They had built Dejima at their own cost
questions.explain: Hollandalılar dinlerini yaymaktan çok ticaretle ilgilendiklerini göstermişlerdi; doğru cevap 'They seemed more interested in trade than in spreading their religion'.

questions.q: What did the doctors in Edo discover in 1771?
options: Their Chinese texts were more reliable than Dutch ones
A Dutch anatomy book matched what they saw much better
Siebold had hidden maps inside the book
Dissection was forbidden everywhere in Japan
questions.explain: Doktorlar gördüklerini Hollandaca anatomi kitabıyla karşılaştırdılar ve kitabın Çin metinlerinden çok daha doğru olduğunu fark ettiler; doğru cevap 'A Dutch anatomy book matched what they saw much better'.

title: The Emperor Who Regretted a War
text:
Around 261 BC, the armies of the Mauryan Empire marched into Kalinga, a kingdom on the eastern coast of India, roughly where the state of Odisha lies today. The Mauryas already ruled most of the Indian subcontinent, from Afghanistan in the north-west to the south, and Kalinga was one of the few independent regions left. The war was won, but at a terrible cost. Years later, the emperor who had ordered it described the result in his own words: a hundred and fifty thousand people had been carried away, a hundred thousand had been killed, and many times that number had died.

That emperor was Ashoka, the grandson of the dynasty's founder, Chandragupta. Some later stories describe the young Ashoka as a cruel despot, although these tales were written to make his later change look more dramatic. What makes his story unusual is not the war itself, since rulers of every age have fought wars of conquest, but what he did afterwards. In a message carved in stone, Ashoka declared that he felt deep sorrow and regret for the suffering caused by such a devastating war. From then on, he claimed, he would seek conquest by dhamma, a word that can be translated as moral law, duty or right conduct, rather than by the sword.

We know about this change largely because Ashoka was determined to disseminate his ideas. He ordered his messages, now usually called edicts, to be carved on rock faces and on tall polished stone pillars across his empire. More than thirty of these inscriptions have been found, from Nepal to southern India and from Bengal to Afghanistan. Most are written in Prakrit, the everyday languages of the time, using the Brahmi script; but near Kandahar, in Afghanistan, versions were also carved in Greek and Aramaic so that the local communities could read them. Officials were instructed to read the edicts aloud to people who could not read.

The content is remarkable for its period. Ashoka asked his subjects to respect their parents and teachers, to treat servants and slaves kindly, and to show tolerance towards all religious groups, not only their own. He spoke out against the killing of animals for sacrifice and reduced the number killed in the royal kitchens. He also described practical, almost humanitarian measures. Wells were dug, rest houses were built and shade trees were planted along the roads; herbal remedies were grown, and care was provided for both humans and animals. He appointed special officers to spread the message of dhamma and to check that local officials were acting fairly.

Ashoka became a strong supporter of Buddhism, and later Buddhist traditions describe him as an ideal, benevolent king. They claim that he built tens of thousands of stupas, or shrines, and sent missionaries to Sri Lanka and other lands. Historians question the veracity of some of these accounts, because they were written long after his death by people who wanted to celebrate him. It is also worth noting that the edicts do not show a ruler who gave up power. He kept his army, and one edict warns the forest tribes on the borders that the emperor, while merciful, also has the strength to punish them. His regret may have been sincere, but it was the regret of an emperor who remained firmly in control.

After Ashoka's death around 232 BC, the empire declined, and within about fifty years the Maurya dynasty had come to an end. Over the centuries, the Brahmi script was forgotten, and the meaning of the inscriptions was lost. It was only in 1837 that James Prinsep, a British scholar working in Calcutta, succeeded in deciphering the script, and the voice of the emperor could be heard again. At first, scholars did not even know who the king called Beloved of the Gods in the inscriptions was; the link with Ashoka was confirmed later.

Today, one of the most famous traces of his reign is the sculpture of four lions standing back to back that once topped a pillar at Sarnath, where the Buddha is said to have given his first sermon. India adopted it as its national emblem, and the wheel carved beneath the lions appears in the centre of the national flag. In this way, a king who regretted his greatest victory became a symbol for a modern nation.

options: Ashoka himself spoke only those languages
Prakrit had not yet been written down

Local communities near Kandahar could read them

title: Out of the Window
text:
On the morning of 23 May 1618, a group of angry noblemen climbed the stairs of Prague Castle and pushed their way into a room in the Bohemian Chancellery. They were Protestants, and they had come to confront two senior officials, Vilém Slavata and Jaroslav Martinic, who governed the Kingdom of Bohemia on behalf of the Catholic Habsburg ruler. After a heated argument, in which the Protestants accused the two men of violating their religious rights, the visitors seized them, dragged them to a window and threw them out. Their secretary, Philip Fabricius, soon followed.

The window was high above the ground, with a drop usually estimated at around sixteen to twenty metres. Anyone watching would have expected the three men to die. Instead, all of them survived. Martinic and Slavata were injured, Slavata seriously, but they managed to escape with the help of servants and supporters, and Fabricius ran off and soon left the city to report what had happened to the emperor in Vienna.

How was this possible? Almost immediately, the event became a battle of stories. Catholic writers declared that it was a miracle: the Virgin Mary, or angels sent by God, had caught the men and lowered them gently to the ground. Protestant writers preferred a less dignified explanation. According to their version, the officials had landed in a large pile of rubbish and manure in the castle ditch, which broke their fall. This account has been repeated so often that many people treat it as fact, but historians point out that it does not appear in the earliest reports and may have been invented later to ridicule the Catholic side. More likely explanations are simple: the men wore thick cloaks, they slid down a sloping wall on the way, and the ground below may have been soft.

The event was not an isolated act of madness. Bohemia had a long tradition of religious tension, and two centuries earlier, in 1419, a crowd of followers of the reformer Jan Hus had thrown several town councillors out of the windows of Prague's New Town Hall, killing them. In 1609, the Emperor Rudolf II had granted Bohemia's Protestants a document called the Letter of Majesty, which promised them freedom of worship. By 1618, however, many Protestants believed that the Habsburgs were slowly taking these rights away. The closing of Protestant churches on land controlled by Catholics had caused particular anger. Throwing the officials out of the window was a dramatic way of announcing that the nobility would no longer accept such treatment. It was also, in a sense, a way to avoid a formal trial: the instigators could later claim that the men had simply been punished as traitors to the kingdom.

The fallout was enormous. The Bohemian nobles set up their own government and, the following year, offered the crown to a Protestant prince, Frederick of the Palatinate. The event galvanized the Habsburgs, who responded with force, and in 1620 the Bohemian army was defeated at the Battle of White Mountain, just outside Prague. Many of the rebel leaders were executed, and Protestant worship in Bohemia was suppressed. But the upheaval had already spread beyond Bohemia, drawing in other German states and, in time, Denmark, Sweden and France. It grew into the Thirty Years' War, one of the most destructive wars in European history, which devastated large parts of central Europe before it ended in 1648.

There is a final, slightly comic twist. Philip Fabricius, the secretary who had been thrown out after his masters, was later given a noble title by the emperor. He chose the name von Hohenfall, which means something like 'of the high fall'. It seems he decided that, if he was going to be remembered for one thing, he might as well make the most of it.

Today, visitors to Prague Castle can see the window, and guides often tell the story with a smile. Yet in hindsight, behind the comedy lies a serious lesson. A single act of anger, aimed at two unpopular men, became the tipping point that turned a long, slow conflict into a disaster for millions of people.

It may have been invented later to mock the Catholic side

It was confirmed by Fabricius himself

title: Schools Built by Their Students
text:
In the spring of 1940, the Turkish parliament passed a law that would shape the lives of thousands of village children. At the time, most of the country's people lived in villages, a large share of them were illiterate, and many villages had no school at all. Teachers trained in the cities rarely wanted to move to remote places without roads, electricity or a doctor, and those who went often left as soon as they could. The new law tried a different approach. Instead of sending city teachers to the villages, it would take bright children from the villages, educate them, and send them back home as teachers.

The idea is usually linked to two men. Hasan Âli Yücel, the minister of education, gave the project political support, while İsmail Hakkı Tonguç, an educator who had studied teaching methods in Europe, shaped its daily practice. Tonguç believed that a village teacher had to be much more than a person who taught reading and writing. He or she should also be able to build a classroom, grow better crops, keep bees, repair tools and give basic health advice. Education, in his view, had to improve the livelihood of the whole community, not only the marks of the pupils sitting at desks.

The institutes were therefore unusual places. Most of them were set up on empty land far from towns, and the first students quite literally built their own schools. Teenagers who had just arrived from their villages made bricks, dug foundations, laid water pipes and planted fruit trees. Lessons followed a simple rule: learn by doing. In the morning a group might study mathematics or Turkish literature; in the afternoon the same group might be working in the fields or in a woodwork shop. Girls attended too, which was a bold step at a time when many rural families did not send their daughters to school at all.

Daily life combined hard physical work with a surprising amount of culture. Students read classics of world literature, many of which were being translated into Turkish by the ministry in those same years. Most of them learned to play a musical instrument, often the mandolin or the bağlama, and folk dances and theatre were part of the timetable. Every student was expected to read a set number of books each year. For children who had grown up in houses without a single book, this was a sea change.

By the late 1940s there were around twenty institutes across the country, and thousands of graduates had gone back to villages to open schools. Some of them later became well-known writers. Mahmut Makal's Bizim Köy, a short and honest account of village life written by a young teacher, caused a stir when it appeared in 1950, because it showed city readers a poverty they had preferred to ignore. Fakir Baykurt and Talip Apaydın, among others, also came from the institutes and went on to write novels about village life.

Yet the project soon came under fire. Some critics argued that the institutes were too political, or that boys and girls should not study together in boarding schools. Others, including some powerful landowners, may simply have been uneasy about educated villagers who knew their rights and asked awkward questions. As the political climate changed after the Second World War, the original spirit was gradually watered down. Tonguç lost his post in 1946, the curriculum became more conventional, and in 1954 the institutes were turned into ordinary teacher-training schools. The experiment had lasted only fourteen years.

Historians still debate how successful the Village Institutes really were. Admirers see them as one of the most original educational experiments of the twentieth century, a rare attempt to empower underprivileged rural people through practical skills and culture at the same time. More cautious observers point out that the schools ran on very small budgets, that students sometimes worked far too hard, and that the results varied from one institute to another. In retrospect, though, few would deny their lasting influence. Many graduates spent their whole working lives in places that nobody else wanted to go, and for a generation of village children, the first teacher they ever met was someone who had grown up just like them.

questions.q: What was the main idea behind the Village Institutes?
options: Sending experienced city teachers to remote villages for a few years
Training village children to return to their own villages as teachers
Moving poor village families into towns with good schools
Building schools in villages with money from rich landowners
