title: The Shop on Toad Lane
text:
On a cold evening shortly before Christmas in 1844, a small shop opened its doors in Rochdale, a mill town in the north of England. It did not look like the start of anything important. The shelves held only a few basic goods: flour, butter, sugar, oatmeal and some candles. The owners were so worried about being laughed at that, according to a well-known story, they hesitated before taking down the shutters. Yet this modest shop on Toad Lane is often described as the birthplace of the modern co-operative movement, which today has hundreds of millions of members around the world.

To understand why the shop mattered, it helps to picture life in an industrial town at that time. The weavers of Rochdale worked long hours for low wages, and the 1840s were a period of economic downturn and hardship across Britain. Workers often had little choice about where to buy their food. Some shopkeepers sold flour mixed with chalk, or tea mixed with leaves that had already been used, and weights and measures could not always be trusted. Families who were already struggling to pay the rent were being cheated on the very things they needed to survive.

A group of local men, many of them weavers, decided to stop complaining and build a grassroots alternative. Over many months they saved up enough to put about one pound each into a common fund, which was a serious sum for people on their wages. With this money they rented the ground floor of an old warehouse and bought their first stock. Because they had paid for it themselves, the shop belonged to them. They called their society the Rochdale Equitable Pioneers, and they would later become known simply as the Rochdale Pioneers.

What made the Pioneers different from earlier attempts was not the shop itself but the rules behind it. Membership was open to anyone who could buy a share. Each member had one vote, however many shares he or she owned, which was a strikingly egalitarian idea in an age when most working people could not vote in national elections. Women could join on the same terms as men. Goods had to be pure and honestly weighed. Prices were set at normal market levels, and the profit was shared out among members according to how much they had spent, a payment that became known as the "divi", short for dividend. Part of the money was also set aside for education, and the society soon had its own reading room and library.

These principles, set down in plain language, proved remarkably practical. The shop grew slowly at first, but within a few years it had added more goods, more opening hours and more members. Other towns copied the model, and by the end of the century co-operative shops, wholesale societies and even factories had spread across Britain. In time the movement gained momentum far beyond the country's borders, where it grew alongside other forms of mutual help, such as farmers' co-operatives in Denmark and credit unions in Germany.

It would be naive to present the story as a simple fairy tale. The Pioneers were not the first people to try co-operation; there had been earlier experiments, several of which collapsed through poor management or debt. Some historians also note that the movement later grew into large, bureaucratic organisations that ordinary members found hard to influence. The founders themselves held differing views about how far co-operation should go: some wanted only a better shop, while others dreamed of whole communities owned by their members.

Still, the core of their idea has stood the test of time. The International Co-operative Alliance, the global body for co-operatives, bases its principles largely on the rules written in Rochdale. Democratic control, open membership, solidarity and a concern for education still appear in its statements today. The original building on Toad Lane has been turned into a small museum, where visitors can see a reconstruction of the shop as it may have looked on that first winter evening. It is a reminder that some of the most far-reaching changes in social history began not with a revolution, but with a few ordinary people pooling their savings to buy a sack of flour.

options: They wanted to sell their own cloth directly to customers
The government offered them money to start a business
The town had no food shops at all in the 1840s
Local shops often sold poor or dishonest goods at unfair weights

title: Japan Opens Its Doors
text:
For more than two centuries, Japan had kept most of the world at arm's length. Under the Tokugawa shoguns, the military rulers who held real power while the emperor lived quietly in Kyoto, foreign trade was strictly limited and most Japanese people were forbidden to travel abroad. Then, in 1853, American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry sailed into the bay near Edo, today's Tokyo, and demanded that Japan open its ports. The ships, belching black smoke, made a deep impression. Many Japanese leaders realised that their country was far weaker than the Western powers, and they feared, in an age of aggressive imperialism, that it might share the fate of China, which had already been forced into unequal treaties.

The years that followed were full of upheaval. Some groups wanted to drive the foreigners out; others argued that Japan had to learn from them in order to survive. In 1868 a coalition of powerful domains toppled the shogunate and restored formal authority to the young Emperor Meiji, who was only fifteen at the time. This event, known as the Meiji Restoration, was in some ways oddly named. It claimed to restore an ancient order, yet it opened one of the most rapid periods of change that any society has experienced.

The new leaders, most of them young men from the samurai class, set about dismantling the old order and reshaping the country from top to bottom. The old feudal domains were abolished in 1871 and replaced by prefectures run from the capital. A national army based on conscription was created, which ended the samurai's monopoly on carrying weapons. Within a few years, the samurai lost their special income and, eventually, the right to wear swords in public. A national school system was announced in 1872, with the aim of bringing basic education to every child, and the first railway, linking Tokyo with the port of Yokohama, opened the same year.

One of the most remarkable episodes of the period was the Iwakura Mission. In 1871 around fifty senior officials, accompanied by dozens of students, set off on a journey that lasted almost two years and took them across the United States and much of Europe. They visited factories, parliaments, schools, prisons and shipyards, asking endless questions and taking careful notes. Their original hope of renegotiating the unequal treaties came to nothing, but what they saw convinced them that Japan needed patient, sweeping reform at home rather than hasty military adventures. The mission also included a few young girls who were left in America to study, one of whom, Tsuda Umeko, later founded a well-known college for women in Japan.

The pace of change could be dizzying. Western clothes, calendars, banks and newspapers arrived within a single generation. Foreign experts were hired to build lighthouses, design schools and advise ministries, though the government was careful to replace them with trained Japanese as soon as it could. A written constitution followed in 1889, creating a parliament with limited powers. By the early twentieth century, Japan had become an industrial power and had won wars against both China and Russia, a result that astonished observers in Europe.

Not everyone welcomed this transformation. Some former samurai, who felt betrayed by a state they had helped to create, rose in rebellion; the largest uprising, in 1877, was crushed by the new conscript army. Many peasants found that the land tax weighed heavily on them, and the rapid growth of factories brought harsh working conditions, especially for young women in the silk mills. Later historians have also pointed out that the military strength built in this period helped set the stage for the aggressive expansion of the following decades.

Even so, the Meiji era remains a striking case of a society deciding, quite deliberately, to reinvent itself. Its leaders did not simply copy the West; they chose carefully, adapting foreign ideas to local traditions and keeping a strong sense of national identity. Whether one admires or criticises the results, it is hard not to be impressed by the speed and ambition of a country that, in less than fifty years, went from sailing ships and swords to railways, factories and a modern state.

questions.q: What was the main purpose and result of the Iwakura Mission?
options: It signed new, fair trade treaties with Western countries
It brought foreign soldiers to train the new Japanese army
It studied Western institutions and convinced leaders to favour patient reform at home
It tried to persuade Japanese students living abroad to return home

Doğru cevap 'It studied Western institutions and convinced leaders to favour patient reform at home'.

title: The Matchgirls Walk Out
text:
In the summer of 1888, a few hundred young women walked out of a match factory in Bow, in the East End of London, and refused to go back. Within a day or two, nearly all of the factory's workforce, around fourteen hundred women and girls, had joined them. Most of them were teenagers or in their early twenties, many were the daughters of Irish immigrants, and few had any experience of organised protest. Yet within about three weeks they had won most of their demands, and their action is often remembered as a turning point in British labour history.

The factory belonged to Bryant and May, a successful company whose matches were sold all over the country. Its owners presented themselves as respectable and even charitable employers, but conditions inside told a different story. The women worked long days, often standing for hours, for wages that were barely enough to live on. A complicated system of fines could reduce their pay still further: they might lose money for talking, for having dirty feet, for dropping matches or for being a few minutes late. Some workers claimed that they had been made to contribute part of their wages to a statue of a politician that the company wished to put up.

Worse still was the danger from white phosphorus, the chemical used to make the match heads. Over time, the fumes could cause a terrible illness known as "phossy jaw", in which the bone of the jaw slowly rotted. The disease was painful, disfiguring and sometimes deadly. Victims were often dismissed quietly, and the company was accused of trying to keep the problem out of sight.

The spark for the strike came from outside the factory. In June 1888, the social reformer and journalist Annie Besant published an article about Bryant and May in her weekly paper. After speaking with a group of workers, she described their low pay, the fines and the poor treatment in angry, vivid language, calling the factory a kind of prison. The company was furious and reportedly tried to make its workers sign a statement denying the story. When they refused, and one woman was dismissed, the walkout began.

What followed surprised many observers. The strikers marched through London, visited Parliament and told their stories to anyone who would listen. Besant and her colleagues helped them raise money and win public sympathy, and several newspapers took their side. In the past, unskilled workers, and particularly women, had been seen as almost impossible to organise. The matchgirls proved otherwise. Faced with growing pressure, the company agreed to abolish the fines, improve some conditions and take back the dismissed workers. Soon afterwards, the women formed their own union, which was at the time one of the largest unions of women in the country.

Historians continue to argue about how the strike should be told. Older accounts tended to give most of the credit to Besant, presenting the workers as passive victims who were rescued by a brave middle-class woman. More recent research has challenged this picture. It suggests that the women themselves took the decisive step of walking out, and that Besant, at least at first, was surprised by their action. This shift reflects a wider trend in social history: a growing interest in ordinary people as actors in their own stories, rather than as background figures.

The strike did not end the use of white phosphorus overnight. The company introduced some safety measures, but it took years of campaigning, and an international agreement signed in 1906, before a British ban on the chemical in match making finally came into force in 1910. Even so, the events of 1888 set a precedent. In the following year, dock workers in London staged a much larger strike, and a new wave of unions for unskilled workers began to take root. Many of them looked back to the matchgirls as proof that people with little money and no formal power could still make their voices heard.

options: A punishment used by managers for talking at work
A song sung by the strikers during their march
A nickname for the factory owners
A disease caused by the fumes of the chemical used in matches

title: A Train from Sirkeci
text:
In the early 1960s, a particular scene became familiar at Sirkeci station in Istanbul. Young men, and later many women, stood on the platform with cardboard suitcases, saying goodbye to tearful relatives before boarding trains that would carry them across the Balkans to Munich. Most of these migrants expected to be away for a year or two. They planned to work hard, save money and come home to build a house, buy a tractor or open a small shop. Few of them imagined that they were taking part in one of the largest movements of people in modern European history.

The story began with an agreement signed on 30 October 1961 between Türkiye and West Germany. After the destruction of the Second World War, the West German economy had grown so quickly that factories, mines and building sites were desperately short of workers, and the domestic workforce could not keep up. The building of the Berlin Wall in August 1961 also cut off the flow of workers from East Germany. The government had already signed similar agreements with Italy, Spain and Greece. For Türkiye, the deal promised to ease unemployment at home and bring in valuable foreign currency through the money workers sent back to their families.

Getting a place was not simple. Applicants went through careful selection at a recruitment office in Istanbul, where German doctors checked their health, examined their teeth and tested their strength. Some later remembered the examinations as humiliating. Those who passed were given a contract, a train ticket and often a job in a factory they had never heard of, in a town whose name they could hardly pronounce. On arrival, many lived in crowded hostels near their workplaces, sharing rooms with strangers and cooking on small stoves.

At first, both governments imagined a system of rotation: workers would stay for a limited period and then be replaced by new arrivals. In practice, this made little sense for employers, who did not want to keep training new people. The time limits were soon relaxed, and many workers stayed on. They called themselves, half jokingly, "Almancı", and the Germans called them Gastarbeiter, or guest workers, a term which assumed that they would one day leave. In 1973, when an oil crisis hit the European economy, West Germany stopped recruiting workers from outside the European Community. Rather than going home, however, many of those already there brought their families to join them, and the temporary arrangement quietly turned into permanent settlement.

The second generation grew up between two worlds. Children born in Germany often spoke German better than Turkish, while their parents still dreamed of returning. Summer holidays meant long, exhausting car journeys across Yugoslavia and Bulgaria, with cars loaded high with presents for relatives. In the villages, where many households now depended on a breadwinner abroad, the "Germans" were admired for their success but sometimes teased for their strange new habits. In Germany, meanwhile, they faced suspicion, xenophobia, discriminatory treatment and, in the worst moments, violent attacks. The arson attacks in Mölln in 1992 and in Solingen in 1993, in which members of Turkish families were killed, shocked both countries.

Over the decades, however, the picture has become far richer and more complex. Today, around three million people of Turkish origin are thought to live in Germany, forming one of the largest diasporas in Europe. They include factory workers and shop owners, but also doctors, footballers, film directors, writers and members of parliament. The döner kebab, in the form now found all over Europe, is widely said to have been popularised in Berlin in the early 1970s. Debates about citizenship, language and assimilation in an increasingly multicultural society have continued for decades, and German law has changed several times to make it easier for long-term residents and their children to become citizens.

Looking back, the agreement of 1961 had unforeseen consequences for both governments. It was designed as a short-term solution to a labour shortage, yet it reshaped families, towns and identities in both countries. For many families, the story is still being written. Intergenerational ties now stretch across two countries, and children and grandchildren move easily between two languages; for many of them, both Istanbul and Cologne, in different ways, feel like home.

questions.q: Why did the rotation system fail in practice?
options: Workers refused to sign contracts with time limits
Employers did not want to keep training new workers
The Turkish government asked workers to stay longer
The trains from Istanbul stopped running in 1973

questions.q: What happened after West Germany stopped recruiting workers in 1973?
options: Most Turkish workers returned home within a year

title: A City Fed from the Sky
text:
In June 1948, the people of West Berlin woke up to find themselves cut off from the outside world. After the Second World War, defeated Germany had been divided into four zones, run by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. Berlin, the old capital, was divided in the same way, but the whole city lay deep inside the Soviet zone. When the Western powers introduced a new currency in their zones, the Soviet authorities responded by closing the roads, railways and canals that linked West Berlin to the West. More than two million people suddenly faced the prospect of running out of food and fuel within weeks.

The blockade was a test of will between two emerging superpowers at the very start of the Cold War. The Soviet leadership seems to have hoped that the Western powers would decide that holding on to their part of Berlin was not worth the trouble and simply withdraw. Sending armed convoys along the roads risked bringing Europe to the brink of another war, which nobody wanted. Leaving the city to its fate, on the other hand, would have been a huge political defeat. The answer that American and British planners came up with sounded almost impossible: they would supply an entire city by air.

At first, the operation was improvised and chaotic. The planes available were small, the airfields were too few and the weather was often terrible. Experts calculated that the city needed several thousand tons of supplies every day, a figure that seemed far beyond what aircraft could deliver. Yet the organisers soon brought order to the logistics. Planes flew along fixed corridors at carefully separated heights, landing and taking off according to a strict timetable. If a pilot missed his landing, he was not allowed to try again but had to return to his base with his cargo, so that the whole system would not come to a standstill.

The most surprising thing about the airlift was perhaps what the planes carried. Flour, dried milk and dried potatoes were essential, but the largest single cargo was coal, which was needed to heat homes and run the power stations. Planes became so covered in coal dust that crews joked about it. The demand for runways was so great that a new airport was built at Tegel in about three months, largely by Berliners, many of them women, working in shifts with shovels and simple machines. In April 1949, during a special effort that became known as the Easter Parade, crews delivered nearly thirteen thousand tons in a single day, with planes landing roughly every minute.

Life in the city remained hard. Electricity was available only a few hours a day, families went cold during the winter of 1948, and many people survived on a monotonous diet. But morale held up remarkably well. One reason was a series of small gestures that captured the public imagination. An American pilot named Gail Halvorsen began dropping sweets tied to tiny handkerchief parachutes to children waiting near the airport. Other crews joined in, and he became known as the "Candy Bomber". The story spread widely and did much to change the way many Germans, who only a few years earlier had been the enemy, viewed the Western Allies.

By the spring of 1949 the relentless flow of aircraft had turned the tide, and it was clear that the airlift could continue indefinitely. On 12 May, the Soviet Union lifted the blockade, and the first trucks drove into West Berlin to cheering crowds. Flights went on for several more months to build up reserves. In total, aircraft had made well over two hundred thousand flights and carried more than two million tons of supplies. The cost had also been human: dozens of airmen and several German civilians lost their lives in accidents during the operation.

Historians see the airlift as a turning point in post-war Europe. It hardened the division of Germany, which was formally split into two states later in 1949, and it helped set the stage for the founding of NATO. It was also a major propaganda victory for the West, changing the image of the Western powers in the eyes of many Germans from occupiers to protectors. For Berliners of that generation, the steady roar of engines overhead remained one of the defining memories of their lives. Today a memorial near the old Tempelhof airport, with three arms reaching towards the west, honours those who kept the city alive.

questions.q: Why did the Western powers choose to supply Berlin by air?
options: Because flying was cheaper than using trucks and trains
Because sending armed convoys by road risked starting a war
Because the Soviet Union had asked them to do so
Because the canals around Berlin were frozen

title: A Petition on a Broom Handle
text:
In July 1893, a long roll of paper was carried into the parliament building in Wellington, New Zealand. It had been made by gluing together hundreds of sheets, each covered with signatures, and it had been wound around a broom handle so that it could be moved. When it was unrolled across the floor of the debating chamber, it stretched for well over two hundred metres. Together with several smaller petitions, it carried the names of nearly thirty-two thousand women, a large share of the country's adult female population. Their demand was simple: the right to vote.

The woman most closely linked with that petition was Kate Sheppard. Born in Liverpool in 1847, she had moved to New Zealand with her family as a young woman, settling in the city of Christchurch. Like many campaigners of her time, she became involved in politics through the temperance movement, which fought against the harm caused by heavy drinking. Members of the Women's Christian Temperance Union soon realised that, without the vote, they could do little to change the laws they cared about. Sheppard became the head of the union's campaign for suffrage, and she proved to be a gifted organiser and a sharp, witty feminist writer.

The campaign was neither quick nor easy. Petitions were sent to parliament in 1891 and 1892, and each time the reform failed. Opponents offered a familiar list of objections. Some claimed that women were too emotional or too poorly informed to take part in politics. Others warned that voting would distract them from their duties at home or damage family life. Such arguments reflected the patriarchal attitudes of the age. The alcohol industry, which feared that women voters would support stricter controls on drinking, also worked behind the scenes against the bill. Sheppard and her colleagues answered these arguments in leaflets, letters and public meetings, often using humour to show how weak they were.

The third petition, in 1893, was the largest. It was a truly grassroots effort: volunteers travelled from town to town and farm to farm to collect signatures, and the sheer length of the final roll was a powerful piece of political theatre. Even so, the outcome remained uncertain until the very end. The bill passed the lower house, but its fate in the upper house was in doubt. The premier, Richard Seddon, was known to oppose it, and according to one well-known account he tried to persuade a member to change his vote. The plan seems to have backfired: two members who had been expected to vote against the bill switched sides in protest, and it passed by a narrow margin. On 19 September 1893, the governor signed it into law.

New Zealand thus became the first self-governing country in the world in which all adult women had the right to vote in national elections. Māori women gained the vote at the same time. The first election under the new law was held only about ten weeks later, and the women's turnout was impressive: around two-thirds of adult women are thought to have cast a ballot. Many observers had predicted chaos at the polling stations; instead, newspapers reported that the day passed calmly, with women dressed in their best clothes and some voting for the first time with their daughters beside them.

The victory was important, but it was not complete. Women could vote, but they could not stand for parliament until 1919, and the first woman was not elected until 1933. Sheppard, a lifelong activist, continued to campaign for wider changes, including equal pay, fairer divorce laws and better rights for married women. She also helped to found a national women's council and later spent time in Britain, where the struggle for suffrage was much longer and more bitter.

Today Kate Sheppard's face appears on New Zealand's ten-dollar note, and the day the law was signed is marked every year as a celebration of the right to vote. Her story is a reminder that major political change often hinges not on one dramatic moment, but on years of patient, unglamorous work: writing letters, holding meetings and knocking on doors, one signature at a time.

questions.q: Why did the alcohol industry oppose the women's suffrage bill?
options: It feared that women voters would support stricter controls on drinking
It believed that women were not interested in politics
It wanted women to work in its factories instead of voting
It had a contract with the government that the bill would end

title: Professors in Exile
text:
In the spring of 1933, thousands of university teachers in Germany received letters that ended their careers overnight. A new law introduced by the Nazi government removed Jewish academics, along with political dissidents and others considered unreliable, from public service. Distinguished doctors, lawyers, chemists and economists suddenly found themselves without work, without income and, in many cases, in danger. As persecution grew, an exodus of scholars began. Some went to Britain or the United States. A surprising number, however, went somewhere that few of them had ever imagined: Türkiye.

The timing was a remarkable coincidence. The young Turkish republic had been planning to reform higher education for some time. The country's main university, the Darülfünun in Istanbul, was widely criticised as old-fashioned, and the government had invited a Swiss professor, Albert Malche, to study it and write a report. His recommendations were sweeping. In the summer of 1933, the old institution was closed and Istanbul University was founded in its place. The new university needed a large number of experienced professors very quickly, and the government was prepared to look abroad to find them.

The link between these two needs was made by a doctor named Philipp Schwartz. A pathologist who had himself been forced to leave Germany, he set up an organisation in Switzerland to help dismissed scholars find work abroad. In July 1933 he travelled to Ankara for talks with Turkish officials. According to his own later account, the negotiations went so well that around thirty professors were offered contracts in a single day. Over the following years, the number of German-speaking academics, assistants and specialists who worked in Türkiye grew considerably; estimates usually put the total well above a hundred.

For the newcomers, the move was both a rescue and a challenge. Most of them knew nothing about the country, and almost none spoke Turkish. At first they lectured in German, with assistants translating sentence by sentence for the students. Their contracts generally required them to learn Turkish within a few years, and several became fluent enough to teach and write in the language. They also wrote textbooks, founded laboratories and institutes, and trained a generation of Turkish scholars who would later lead those institutions themselves.

The list of names is impressive. The economist Fritz Neumark helped to shape the teaching of public finance. The legal scholar Ernst Hirsch contributed to Turkish commercial law and wrote widely used textbooks. The architect Bruno Taut designed school buildings before his death in Istanbul in 1938. Ernst Reuter, who taught urban planning in Ankara, later returned to Germany and became mayor of West Berlin. Perhaps the most famous work produced in this period was Mimesis, a classic study of how reality is represented in European literature. Its author, Erich Auerbach, wrote it in Istanbul during the Second World War, and he later suggested that the lack of a large specialist library had, ironically, forced him to write a bolder and more personal book.

The story is not a simple one, and historians have been careful not to romanticise it. The Turkish government invited the exiles mainly because it needed their skills, not out of pure humanitarian feeling, and it was selective about whom it accepted. Some exiles felt isolated and uncertain, as their contracts were renewed only for a few years at a time. Turkish colleagues sometimes resented the high salaries and status of the foreign professors. Most of the exiles eventually left, either emigrating to the United States or, after the war, returning to Germany, though a few stayed for the rest of their lives.

Even so, the episode left a lasting mark on both sides. For many scholars it meant safety at a time when staying in Germany could have cost them their lives. For Turkish universities it meant a sudden injection of expertise that helped lay the groundwork for modern research in medicine, law, economics and the sciences. In retrospect, it is one of the more unusual chapters of twentieth-century history: a young republic building its future with the help of people whom their own country had rejected.

options: He wrote the report that led to the closure of the Darülfünun
He was the Turkish minister who signed the professors' contracts
He organised help for dismissed scholars and negotiated jobs for them in Türkiye
He was the first rector of Istanbul University

title: The Year They Walked
text:
On the evening of 1 December 1955, a forty-two-year-old woman named Rosa Parks got on a city bus in Montgomery, Alabama, after a long day at work as a seamstress. At that time, buses in the city, like much of public life in the American South, were segregated under discriminatory laws. Black passengers had to sit at the back, and if the front seats filled up, they could be ordered to give up their places to white passengers. When the driver told Parks and three other Black passengers to move, the others obeyed. Parks stayed where she was. She was arrested and taken to the police station.

Parks is often remembered as a tired woman who simply did not want to stand up, but that picture is misleading. She was an experienced activist who had worked for years as secretary of the local branch of a national civil rights organisation. She later explained that she was not physically tired, but tired of giving in. Nor was she the first to resist. Earlier that year, a fifteen-year-old schoolgirl named Claudette Colvin had also refused to give up her seat and had been arrested. Local leaders, however, had decided at the time that her case was not the right one with which to challenge the law.

The grassroots response to Parks's arrest was remarkably quick. Jo Ann Robinson, a college teacher and leader of a local women's political group, stayed up through the night with a few colleagues to produce tens of thousands of leaflets calling on Black residents to stay off the buses on Monday, 5 December, the day of Parks's trial. Ministers spread the message from their pulpits on Sunday. On Monday morning, the buses ran almost empty. That evening, at a packed church meeting, local leaders decided to continue the boycott, and they chose a young, newly arrived minister as their spokesman. His name was Martin Luther King Jr., and he was just twenty-six years old.

What began as a one-day protest lasted for more than a year. Black residents, who made up a large majority of the bus company's passengers, walked to work, shared cars or used a carefully organised system of volunteer drivers. Some walked many kilometres each day, in heat and in rain. One elderly woman, asked whether she was tired, is said to have replied that her feet were tired but her soul was at rest. Churches raised money to buy station wagons, and supporters from other cities sent donations.

The authorities and many white residents responded with hostility. Drivers in the car pool were stopped and fined for minor offences, and King himself was arrested for driving slightly over the speed limit. In January 1956 his house was bombed while his wife and baby daughter were inside; fortunately, no one was hurt. Dozens of boycott leaders were later indicted under an old law against boycotts. Yet these efforts to crush the protest seemed only to strengthen the solidarity of the community, and national newspapers began to pay close attention.

In the end, the decisive battle was fought in the courts. Lawyers filed a case on behalf of several Black women, including Colvin, arguing that segregation on the city's buses violated the constitution. A federal court agreed, and in November 1956 the Supreme Court upheld that decision. When the order finally reached Montgomery in December, the boycott was called off after 381 days. The next morning, King and other leaders boarded a bus and sat at the front.

The Montgomery bus boycott did not end segregation across the South; that struggle would continue for another decade and beyond. But it set a precedent in several ways. It showed that ordinary people acting together, with discipline and patience, could put real economic pressure on a powerful system. It brought King to national attention and helped make non-violent protest the central strategy of the civil rights movement. And it turned Rosa Parks into a symbol whose quiet refusal still strikes a chord around the world.

questions.q: Why does the writer say the common picture of Rosa Parks is misleading?
options: Because she was actually much younger than people think
Because she was an experienced activist, not just a tired passenger
Because she had planned the boycott with Martin Luther King Jr.
Because she was never arrested by the police

title: Rails Across the Desert
text:
For centuries, the journey from Damascus to the holy city of Medina was one of the great ordeals of the Muslim world. Pilgrims travelled in huge caravans across some thirteen hundred kilometres of desert, a trip that could take more than a month. They faced fierce heat by day, cold nights, a shortage of water and, at times, attacks by raiders. Many fell ill on the way, and some never returned. At the end of the nineteenth century, the Ottoman sultan Abdülhamid II decided to replace this ancient route with something entirely modern: a railway.

The Hejaz Railway, named after the region of Arabia in which Mecca and Medina lie, was announced in 1900. It was an ambitious project for an empire that was short of money and under constant pressure from European powers. The sultan presented it not only as a service to pilgrims but also as a symbol of unity among Muslims everywhere. A campaign for donations was launched across the Islamic world, and money arrived from places as far apart as India, Egypt and Morocco. Inside the empire, civil servants gave part of their salaries, special stamps were sold, and fees were collected on various transactions. Historians usually estimate that a large share of the cost, perhaps around a third, came from voluntary donations.

The construction itself was a formidable task. The line ran through rocky hills and empty desert where water was scarce and temperatures could be extreme. Thousands of soldiers did much of the heavy labour, working alongside skilled workers and engineers. The chief engineer for much of the project was a German, Heinrich Meissner, but as the tracks approached the holy cities, non-Muslims were not allowed to work there, so the final sections were planned and built by Muslim engineers. Bridges, stations, water towers and small forts were built along the route, some of which still stand in the desert today.

On 1 September 1908, the first official train arrived in Medina. The date was symbolic, as it had been chosen to mark the anniversary of the sultan's accession to the throne. A journey that had once taken weeks could now be completed in a few days. In the years that followed, the line carried many thousands of pilgrims, along with traders, soldiers and goods. It also had geopolitical value, strengthening the Ottoman state's control over a distant and often restless province, which was one of the reasons why some local leaders viewed it with suspicion. The planned extension to Mecca was never completed.

The railway's peaceful years were short. During the First World War, it became a vital supply line for the Ottoman garrison in Medina. It also became a target. During the Arab Revolt, which began in 1916 with British support, fighters repeatedly sabotaged the line, blowing up tracks and bridges and derailing trains. The British officer T. E. Lawrence, who took part in many of these raids, later wrote about them in his famous memoir. Ottoman troops worked relentlessly to repair the damage, often with makeshift materials, and remarkably, the garrison in Medina under Fahreddin Pasha held out until early 1919, months after the war had officially ended.

After the war, the Ottoman Empire collapsed and the territories through which the railway passed were divided among new states. With no single authority responsible for it, and with much of the southern section badly damaged, the line through the Hejaz was gradually abandoned. Plans to restore it have been discussed several times over the past century, but none has come to fruition. Today, short sections in Jordan and Syria have been used for local or tourist trains, and the elegant old station in Damascus remains a well-known landmark.

The Hejaz Railway can be read in different ways. To some, it is a story of faith and generosity, built with the savings of ordinary believers. To others, it is an example of late Ottoman modernisation, an attempt to use new technology to hold a vast imperial state together. Either way, the rusting rails and empty stations in the desert are a quiet reminder of a moment when steam and steel seemed about to transform one of the oldest journeys in the world.

questions.q: Why were the final sections near the holy cities built by Muslim engineers?
options: Because the German engineers had all gone home by then
Because non-Muslims were not allowed to work in that area
Because the sultan wanted to save money on salaries
Because the British had banned foreign engineers from Arabia

title: One Small Bag and Seventy-Two Days
titleTr: Bir Küçük Çanta ve Yetmiş İki Gün
text:
In November 1889 a young American reporter stepped onto a steamship in New Jersey carrying a single small bag. Inside it were a coat, some underwear, a cup, a few writing materials, a jar of face cream and very little else. Her name was Nellie Bly, and she had promised her newspaper, the New York World, that she would travel around the globe faster than Phileas Fogg, the hero of Jules Verne's popular novel Around the World in Eighty Days. Many readers thought the idea was ridiculous. A woman, they said, would need trunks full of dresses and a male protector. Bly needed neither.

Her real name was Elizabeth Cochran, and she was born in Pennsylvania in 1864. Her father, a mill owner and local judge, died when she was six, and her upbringing was shaped by money worries and a mother who struggled to keep the family together. As a young woman she read a column in a Pittsburgh newspaper which argued that women belonged at home and that working women were almost unnatural. She wrote an angry reply. The editor, impressed by her passionate tone rather than her spelling, offered her a job. Women reporters usually wrote about fashion, gardens and parties, but she wanted to write about factories, divorce and poverty. Her pen name came, with a small spelling mistake, from a popular song.

Her first great success came in New York in 1887. Pretending to be mentally ill, she got herself sent to the women's asylum on Blackwell's Island, where she spent ten days observing how patients were treated. She described rotten food, freezing baths, cruel nurses and women who seemed perfectly sane but could not make anyone listen to them. Her reports, later published as a book, caused a public outcry, and the city soon increased the money it spent on caring for the mentally ill. This kind of undercover journalism was risky, and some critics called it sensational, but it set a precedent for reporters who wanted to expose hidden abuses.

The trip around the world was a different kind of story, less about injustice and more about speed and nerve. Bly crossed the Atlantic, took trains through England and France, and made a detour to the French town of Amiens, where Jules Verne himself and his wife received her warmly. Verne reportedly told her that if she finished in seventy-nine days he would applaud with both hands. From there she continued by ship through the Suez Canal to Ceylon, Singapore, Hong Kong and Japan. Storms delayed her, and in Hong Kong she learned that a rival had appeared: a monthly magazine had sent another young writer, Elizabeth Bisland, around the world in the opposite direction, hoping to beat her.

Bly had not known about the competition until then, and she later admitted that the news shook her. But she pressed on. While she crossed the Pacific, the World kept its readers excited with maps, updates and a guessing contest about the exact length of her journey, which reportedly attracted hundreds of thousands of entries. When she reached San Francisco, the paper arranged a special train to carry her across the continent, and crowds gathered at stations to cheer as she passed.

On 25 January 1890 she arrived back in New Jersey, seventy-two days, six hours and eleven minutes after she had left. For a short time it was the fastest journey around the world ever made. Bisland, delayed by a missed ship, arrived several days later. Bly became one of the most famous women in America; there were board games, songs and even products named after her. In hindsight, her race was partly a clever piece of publicity for a newspaper eager to increase its readership, and she herself complained that she was paid little for all the fame she brought it.

Her later life was full of unforeseen turns. She married a wealthy manufacturer much older than herself and, after his death, tried to run his iron company, where her name appeared on designs for new kinds of steel containers, though the business eventually failed. During the First World War she reported from Austria, and in her final years she wrote a newspaper column that helped orphans and poor mothers find homes and work. She died in New York in 1922.

What remains of Nellie Bly is not only a record that others soon broke. It is the picture of a young woman with one small bag who refused to accept what she was told she could not do, and who believed that a reporter's job was to go and see things for herself.

questions.q: What did Bly do in New York in 1887?
options: She travelled to Amiens to interview a famous novelist.
She pretended to be ill in order to report on conditions inside an asylum.
She started a column that helped orphans find homes.
She took over a company that made steel containers.

questions.q: How does the writer view the round-the-world race?
options: As a purely scientific test of the fastest routes.
As a failure, since Bisland arrived first.
As an adventure that was also partly a marketing idea for the newspaper.

title: The Explorer Who Let the Ice Decide
text:
Most explorers try to fight the ice. Fridtjof Nansen had the strange idea of letting the ice carry him.

Born near Oslo in 1861, Nansen grew up skiing and hunting in the Norwegian forests, and he was a champion skier before he was twenty. He trained as a zoologist and studied the nervous system of small sea creatures, but laboratory life never fully held him. In 1888, at the age of twenty-six, he led a small team on skis across the inland ice of Greenland, from the empty east coast to the inhabited west. Earlier attempts had started from the west, so that explorers could always turn back to safety. Nansen deliberately chose the opposite route: once his group had landed, the only way home was forward. Many people called the plan madness. It worked, and it made him a national hero.

His next idea was even bolder. Pieces of an American ship that had sunk north of Siberia had been found years later on the coast of Greenland, on the other side of the frozen sea. To Nansen this suggested that a slow current crossed the top of the world. If a ship could survive being frozen into the ice, he reasoned, it might simply drift with it, perhaps close to the North Pole itself. Most experts were dismissive. Ships caught in such ice were normally crushed like eggshells.

Nansen's answer was the Fram, a ship built with ingenuity rather than brute force. Her hull was rounded and extremely strong, so that when the ice pressed against her from both sides, she would be squeezed upwards and sit on top of it instead of breaking. In 1893 she sailed with thirteen men and was deliberately frozen in north of Siberia. The design worked perfectly. For month after month the ship drifted, while the crew took measurements of the sea, the weather and the ice, played cards, read and celebrated birthdays in the endless dark.

But the drift was too slow, and its path passed too far south. In March 1895 Nansen and one companion, Hjalmar Johansen, left the ship with dogs, sledges and two light boats and set off on skis towards the north. The ice was a formidable chaos of ridges and open water, and it kept moving backwards under their feet. After about three weeks they had reached a point farther north than anyone before them, but they realised that going on would kill them. They turned south towards land.

What followed was one of the great survival stories of the far north. The two men reached the islands of Franz Josef Land too late in the year to go farther, so they built a makeshift hut of stones, earth and animal skins and spent the winter inside it, living mainly on bear and walrus meat. In spring they continued south. Then, in June 1896, in an astonishing piece of luck, Nansen heard a dog barking and met an English explorer, Frederick Jackson, whose team happened to be camped on the same island. The two Norwegians reached home in August, and within days the Fram, which had drifted free of the ice exactly as planned, arrived as well.

Nansen could have spent the rest of his life as a celebrated explorer and scientist. Instead, after the First World War, his stature took him into international politics. In 1920 the new League of Nations asked him to help bring home hundreds of thousands of prisoners of war still held in Russia and elsewhere. He then turned to a terrible famine in Russia, and to the millions of refugees who had lost their homes, and often their nationality, in wars and revolutions. Many had no papers at all, which meant that no country would let them in.

His solution was a simple identity document, which soon became known as the Nansen passport. It allowed people without a state to travel and to look for work across borders, and more than fifty governments eventually recognised it. Among those who are said to have held one were the composer Igor Stravinsky and the painter Marc Chagall. In 1922 Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize for his humanitarian work.

He died in 1930 at his home near Oslo. In hindsight, his two careers seem less different than they first appear. In both, he looked at a problem that others thought impossible, studied it patiently and with relentless energy, and found a solution that worked with reality instead of against it.

questions.q: Why was the Fram given a rounded hull?
options: So that it could sail faster in open water.
So that it could carry more dogs and sledges.
So that it could break through the ice like an icebreaker.
So that the pressure of the ice would push it up rather than crush it.
questions.explain: Metinde geminin yuvarlak gövdesi sayesinde buz iki yandan sıkıştırınca kırılmak yerine yukarı itileceği anlatılıyor; doğru cevap “So that the pressure of the ice would push it up rather than crush it.”

questions.q: What problem did the Nansen passport solve?
options: Refugees without papers could not legally cross borders or find work.
Explorers needed permission to enter the frozen north.
Prisoners of war could not afford the journey home.
Artists were not allowed to perform in other countries.
questions.explain: Metne göre pek çok mültecinin hiçbir belgesi yoktu ve hiçbir ülke onları kabul etmiyordu; Nansen pasaportu bu insanların sınır geçip iş aramasını sağladı. Doğru cevap “Refugees without papers could not legally cross borders or find work.”

title: The Man Who Made the Leaves Talk
text:
In the early nineteenth century, the Cherokee people of the south-eastern United States watched white settlers do something that seemed almost magical. The newcomers made marks on paper, and other people, far away, could look at the marks and know exactly what had been said. Some Cherokee called these papers 'talking leaves'. Most believed that this power belonged to the whites alone. One man, a silversmith named Sequoyah, decided to find out whether that was really true.

Little about his early life is certain. He was probably born around 1770 in a Cherokee town in what is now Tennessee, and he was raised by his mother. He never went to school and could not read or write in any language, but he was a skilled craftsman who made objects of silver, and an injury left him with a permanent limp. Some accounts say he fought alongside American troops in the war of 1812 to 1814 and noticed that, unlike the white soldiers, he and his Cherokee companions could not write letters home or read orders. Whether or not that story is exact, the idea took root in his mind: his people needed a way to write their own language.

He began, it seems, by trying to create a separate picture for every word. This quickly proved impossible; there were far too many words, and the symbols became endless. Then came the crucial insight. Spoken Cherokee, he noticed, was built from a limited number of sounds, syllables such as 'ga', 'lo' or 'tsi', which combined again and again to make words. If he gave each syllable its own symbol, a small set of signs could write anything. It would not be an alphabet in the usual sense, but something simpler for a speaker to learn. After years of work he ended up with eighty-five or eighty-six characters. Some resemble English letters, which he had seen in books he could not read, but they stand for completely different sounds.

The work cost him a great deal. Neighbours, and according to some accounts even his wife, thought he had lost his mind or was practising witchcraft. In one story, his cabin was burned along with all his notes, and he had to start again. His closest ally was his young daughter, Ayoka, who learned the system from him. Around 1821 the two of them demonstrated it to Cherokee leaders. Father and daughter were placed out of sight of each other; the leaders spoke a message to one, who wrote it down, and the paper was carried to the other, who read the words aloud. The doubters were convinced.

What happened next is perhaps the most remarkable part of the story. Because each symbol matched a sound the learner already knew, a Cherokee speaker could become literate in a matter of days or weeks rather than years. The system spread from person to person, without schools or teachers paid by any government. Within a few years, according to many historians, a large share of the Cherokee nation could read and write in its own language, possibly a higher share than among the white settlers around them. In 1828 the Cherokee began publishing a newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, with columns in both English and Cherokee.

Sequoyah's achievement is often described as unique. Writing has been invented from nothing only a few times in human history, in places like ancient Iraq, China and Central America, and over very long periods. Sequoyah, an illiterate man, created a complete and practical writing system largely on his own, within his own lifetime. Linguists still discuss how much he borrowed and how much he invented, but few doubt that his work was groundbreaking or question the scale of his ingenuity.

Sadly, the story does not end happily for his people. In the 1830s the American government forced most Cherokee to leave their homeland and move west, a journey on which thousands died and which is remembered as the Trail of Tears. It was a time of bitter persecution. Sequoyah himself had already moved west some years before. In his last years he travelled towards Mexico, possibly searching for a group of Cherokee who had settled there, and he died around 1843.

Yet the writing he created has stood the test of time. Cherokee symbols still appear on road signs in parts of Oklahoma and North Carolina, and they have been included in computer keyboards and phone software. The giant sequoia trees of California are widely believed to have been named after him, though even this is debated. For a man who could not read a single line of English, it is an extraordinary legacy.

questions.q: Why did Sequoyah give up his first method?
options: His daughter could not learn it.
A separate symbol for every word would have needed far too many signs.
The Cherokee leaders refused to accept pictures.
He did not know enough English letters.
questions.explain: Metne göre her kelime için ayrı bir resim yapmak imkânsızdı, çünkü kelime sayısı çok fazlaydı ve semboller sonsuza dek çoğalıyordu; doğru cevap “A separate symbol for every word would have needed far too many signs.”

questions.q: Why could Cherokee speakers learn the new system so quickly?
options: Because it was taught in government schools.
Because it used the same sounds as English letters.
Because each symbol stood for a sound they already used when speaking.
Because the newspaper printed lessons every week.
questions.explain: Metinde her sembolün öğrencinin zaten bildiği bir sese karşılık geldiği, bu yüzden okumanın günler ya da haftalar içinde öğrenilebildiği söyleniyor; doğru cevap “Because each symbol stood for a sound they already used when speaking.”

title: A Quaker in Newgate
text:
In January 1813, a well-dressed Quaker woman walked through the gates of Newgate, London's most notorious prison, and asked to see the women's section. The governor warned her not to go in. The women there, he said, were wild; they would tear her clothes and steal her watch. She went in anyway.

What Elizabeth Fry found stayed with her for the rest of her life. About three hundred women and their children were packed into a few overcrowded rooms. They slept on the floor on dirty straw, cooked, washed and fought in the same space, and sanitation hardly existed. Some had been convicted of serious crimes, others were simply waiting for a trial, and a few were waiting to be hanged. Children who had committed no crime grew up inside, learning nothing but the life of the prison. Strong drink was sold openly, and the noise, the smell and the despair were overwhelming.

Fry was not a typical reformer. Born Elizabeth Gurney in Norwich in 1780, she came from a wealthy Quaker banking family, and as a girl she was said to enjoy music, dancing and fine clothes more than religion. At seventeen, moved by a travelling preacher, she became a more serious Quaker and began helping the poor near her home. She married Joseph Fry, a London merchant, and had eleven children. Running such a household would have filled most people's lives. Yet after that first visit she could not forget what she had seen.

Her first response was practical: she came back with clothes for the babies. For the next few years family matters kept her away, but by 1816 she was back with a plan. She proposed a school for the children inside the prison and asked the women themselves to choose a teacher from among them. To the officials' surprise, they chose a young prisoner who had been convicted of stealing a watch. Fry then formed a group of Quaker women who visited daily, organised sewing and knitting work so that prisoners could earn a little money, and agreed a set of rules with the women themselves: no swearing, no gambling, no fighting. The prisoners voted to accept them.

The change was startling. Visitors who came expecting chaos found women quietly working and listening as Fry read aloud from the Bible. Officials, writers and even members of the royal family came to watch. In 1818 she was invited to explain her methods to a committee of the House of Commons, becoming one of the first women ever to give evidence to Parliament. She argued that imprisonment should reform people rather than merely punish them, and that female prisoners should be guarded by women rather than men, to protect them from abuse.

She also turned her attention to the ships that carried convicted women to Australia. Before they sailed, prisoners were often chained and driven through the streets in open carts while crowds shouted insults. Fry persuaded the authorities to use closed carriages instead, and she and her helpers visited the ships before departure, giving every woman a bag of sewing materials, so that she could make something to sell when she arrived. According to some estimates, she visited more than a hundred such ships over the years.

Not everyone admired her. Some critics ridiculed the idea of a mother of eleven spending her days among criminals, and accused her of neglecting her family. Others argued that her compassionate approach made prison too comfortable and weakened its value as a deterrence against crime. Her husband's bank failed in 1828, which damaged both her reputation and her finances. Later in the century, too, the government moved towards a harsher system of silence and lonely cells that was almost the opposite of what she had hoped for.

Yet her ideas did not disappear. She travelled through Europe, meeting kings and queens and inspecting their prisons, and her example encouraged reform groups in many countries. She also founded a training school for nurses, one of the earliest of its kind in England. She died in 1845, still a staunch believer in the power of kindness. From 2002 to 2016 her portrait appeared on the Bank of England's five-pound note, showing her reading to prisoners at Newgate: a fitting picture of a woman who insisted that even people society had given up on deserved humane treatment and a second chance.

questions.q: Who chose the teacher for the prison school?
options: The prison governor.
Fry’s Quaker friends.
A committee of the House of Commons.
The women prisoners themselves.
questions.explain: Metne göre Fry, okul için öğretmeni kadın mahkûmların kendi aralarından seçmesini istedi; doğru cevap “The women prisoners themselves.”

questions.q: What was one criticism made against Fry?
options: That her methods made prison too soft to stop people committing crimes.
That she refused to visit the convict ships.
That she wanted men to guard female prisoners.
That she spent her bank’s money on the prison.
questions.explain: Bazı eleştirmenler onun şefkatli yaklaşımının hapishaneyi fazla rahat hale getirdiğini ve suçtan caydırma işlevini zayıflattığını savundu; doğru cevap “That her methods made prison too soft to stop people committing crimes.”

title: A City Built of Words
text:
Around the year 1390, a young widow in Paris faced a problem that many women of her time knew well. Her husband had died suddenly, and she was left with three small children, her mother and a niece to support, with debts she had not known about and lawsuits she did not know how to fight. Most women in her position would have remarried or entered a convent. Christine de Pizan did something almost unheard of: she began to earn her living with her pen.

She had been born in Venice around 1364. When she was a small child, her father, Tommaso da Pizzano, a respected physician and astrologer, was invited to the court of King Charles V of France, and the family moved to Paris. Christine grew up close to one of the finest royal libraries in Europe, and her father, unusually for the period, encouraged her to study. Her mother reportedly would have preferred an upbringing centred on spinning and other household skills. At fifteen Christine married Étienne de Castel, a young royal secretary, and by all accounts the marriage was a happy one. Then her father died, and in 1390 Étienne died too, probably of an infectious illness, when Christine was about twenty-five.

She later wrote that grief made her feel as if she had been turned into a man, forced to steer the ship of her family through a storm. She taught herself enough law to fight for the money owed to her husband, a struggle that went on for years. At the same time, she began writing poems of love and loss, and her short poems about widowhood are still moving today. She presented them to wealthy patrons, who paid for copies. It was an uncertain way to live, but it worked, and writing gradually became her true vocation. Over the next three decades she produced dozens of works: poetry, a life of Charles V, books on politics and on the art of war, and advice for princes.

What makes her especially interesting today is her defence of women. At the time, one of the most popular books in France was the Romance of the Rose, a long poem whose second part contained bitter attacks on women as dishonest and foolish. Christine publicly criticised its misogyny in a series of letters with some of the leading scholars of Paris, around 1401 and 1402. They sent condescending replies, suggesting that a woman could not really understand such learned matters. She did not back down. The debate made her famous, and it is sometimes described as the first public literary quarrel in French history.

Her best-known answer came in 1405 with The Book of the City of Ladies. In it, Christine describes herself sitting in her study, depressed after reading yet another book that insulted women. Three crowned ladies, named Reason, Rectitude and Justice, appear and invite her to build an imaginary city in which worthy women of the past can live safely. Each stone of the city is a story: of queens who ruled wisely, women who invented crafts, scholars, warriors and saints. In eloquent and patient prose, the book argues that women's apparent weakness comes not from their nature but from a lack of education.

Christine was also a careful businesswoman. She supervised the copying and decoration of her manuscripts, choosing illustrators and checking the texts, and many beautiful copies of her work survive. Some of them show her at her desk in a blue dress and white headdress, writing, or presenting a book to a queen.

In 1418, as civil war and English invasion tore France apart, she retired to a convent, probably the one at Poissy, where her daughter was a nun. For years she wrote almost nothing. Then, in 1429, news reached her that a peasant girl, Joan of Arc, had led French troops to victory. Christine, now in her sixties, wrote a joyful poem in her honour, the only such poem known to have been written while Joan was still alive and winning. It is the last work we have from her, and she probably died a few years later.

For centuries she was largely forgotten, remembered only by specialists. In the twentieth century, however, scholars rediscovered her, and she is now widely seen as one of the first women in Europe to make writing her profession. Some modern readers call her an early feminist, although the word did not exist in her day. Her city of ladies, built entirely of words, has proved surprisingly strong.

questions.q: Why did Christine de Pizan begin writing for money?
options: Her father wanted her to become a court poet.
After her husband’s death she had to support her family.
The king ordered her to write his life story.
She had lost a lawsuit against a group of scholars.
questions.explain: Metne göre kocası ölünce üç çocuğunu, annesini ve yeğenini geçindirmek zorunda kaldı ve geçimini kalemiyle kazanmaya başladı; doğru cevap “After her husband’s death she had to support her family.”

questions.q: According to The Book of the City of Ladies, why did women seem weaker?
options: Because they were naturally less intelligent.
Because they were not allowed to fight in wars.
Because they had not been given an education.
Because they spent too much time in convents.
questions.explain: Kitap, kadınların görünürdeki zayıflığının doğalarından değil, eğitim eksikliğinden kaynaklandığını savunur; doğru cevap “Because they had not been given an education.”

title: The Man in the Round Tower
text:
On his thirty-eighth birthday, in 1571, a French nobleman named Michel de Montaigne did something that his neighbours found puzzling. He gave up his position as a judge in Bordeaux, withdrew to his family estate, and shut himself up in a round stone tower with about a thousand books. He painted the wooden beams of the ceiling with favourite sayings from ancient writers, and in a Latin inscription on the wall he announced that he intended to spend his remaining days in freedom, calm and leisure.

He did not quite manage the calm. Instead, he invented a new kind of writing.

Montaigne's upbringing had been extraordinary. He was born in 1533 to a wealthy family near Bordeaux. His father, full of new ideas about education, sent the baby to live with a poor family in a nearby village for his first years, so that he would feel close to ordinary people. Then he arranged for the boy to learn Latin before French: a German tutor who spoke no French was hired, and everyone in the household, including the servants, had to speak to the child only in Latin. To spare him any sudden shock, he was even woken each morning by the gentle sound of music. The result was a boy who spoke Latin with complete fluency at six and found school, when he finally went, rather dull.

As an adult he trained in law and worked as a judge. In Bordeaux he met Étienne de La Boétie, a young writer and fellow judge, and the two formed one of the most famous friendships in literature. When asked later why they had loved each other so much, Montaigne could only answer: because it was he, because it was I. La Boétie died of an illness in 1563, and many readers believe that Montaigne's writing was partly an attempt to replace the conversation he had lost.

In his tower he began to write short pieces on whatever subject came to mind: sadness, laziness, liars, cannibals, thumbs, smells, sleep, the education of children. He called them 'essais', a French word meaning attempts or trials, because each was an experiment in thinking rather than a finished argument. He would start with a question, wander off into anecdotes from ancient history, compare them with his own experience, and often end somewhere quite unexpected. When he played with his cat, he once asked, how could he know that she was not playing with him?

What was new was not only the form but the subject. Earlier writers had written about God, kings or great events. Montaigne wrote, above all, about himself: his kidney stones, his bad memory, his dislike of doctors, his changing moods. He insisted that this was not vanity. Every person, he believed, carries within them the whole human condition, so by studying one ordinary man honestly he hoped to understand people in general. This reflective habit was summed up in his motto, a simple question: 'What do I know?'

That question was more than a pose. Montaigne lived through the French Wars of Religion, decades of brutal fighting between Catholics and Protestants in which neighbours killed each other in the name of certainty. Against this background, his doubt was a kind of moral position. He distrusted anyone who was sure enough of the truth to burn others for it, and he argued that the customs of distant peoples, which Europeans called barbaric, were often no more cruel than their own. Such ideas were brave at a time of fierce religious persecution.

His retreat did not last. He travelled through Germany, Switzerland and Italy, partly in search of a cure for his illness, and while abroad he learned that he had been elected mayor of Bordeaux, a post he then held for two terms. He also acted as a go-between in talks between rival leaders. Through all this he kept adding to his essays, writing new thoughts in the margins of earlier editions rather than removing old ones, so that the book grew like a living thing. The first edition appeared in 1580; he was still revising it when he died in 1592.

More than four centuries later, the essays have stood the test of time remarkably well. Writers from Shakespeare to modern bloggers have borrowed from them, and the form he invented is now practised by students everywhere. Few authors have managed to be so frank, so funny and so humble at the same time.

questions.q: Why did Montaigne call his writings ‘essais’?
options: Because they were written for students.
Because each one was an attempt to think something through, not a final answer.
Because they were short summaries of ancient books.
Because his father had chosen the name.
questions.explain: Metne göre “essais” kelimesi deneme ya da girişim anlamına gelir ve her yazı bitmiş bir argüman değil, bir düşünme denemesiydi; doğru cevap “Because each one was an attempt to think something through, not a final answer.”

questions.q: How did Montaigne’s doubt connect to the times he lived in?
options: It was a reaction against people who killed others because they were certain they were right.
It made him refuse to take any public job.
It led him to support one side in the religious wars.
It was caused by his poor memory and illness.
questions.explain: Yazar, din savaşları döneminde insanların kesinlik adına birbirini öldürdüğünü, Montaigne’in şüphesinin de buna karşı ahlaki bir duruş olduğunu söylüyor; doğru cevap “It was a reaction against people who killed others because they were certain they were right.”

title: Nine Years and Forty Thousand Words
titleTr: Dokuz Yıl ve Kırk Bin Kelime
text:
In 1746 a group of London booksellers made a bold business decision. England, unlike France and Italy, had no great dictionary of its own language, and they believed that one would sell well. They chose as its author a large, clumsy, half-blind man of thirty-seven who had little money and no university degree. His name was Samuel Johnson, and he promised to finish the job in three years.

Johnson was born in 1709 in Lichfield, the son of a struggling bookseller. As a baby he caught a disease that damaged his sight and hearing and left scars on his face, and throughout his life he suffered from strange nervous movements and noises that made strangers stare at him. He was, however, a brilliant reader with an astonishing memory. He went to Oxford but had to leave after about a year because his family could not pay the fees. In his twenties he married a widow much older than himself, tried and failed to run a school, and in 1737 walked to London with one of his former pupils, the future actor David Garrick, to try his luck as a writer. For years he lived on poorly paid work for magazines, mostly published in anonymity.

For the dictionary he rented a house in Gough Square, near Fleet Street, and turned the top floor into a workshop. Six assistants sat at a long desk copying out quotations. His method was groundbreaking. Instead of simply inventing definitions, he read through the best English writers of the previous two centuries, including Shakespeare, Milton and many scientific and religious authors, and marked passages that showed how words were actually used. The assistants copied each passage onto slips of paper, which were then sorted by word. In this way he collected well over a hundred thousand illustrative quotations, although only some of them made it into the final work. He also tried, not always successfully, to explain the etymology of each word.

Three years was a wildly hopeful estimate. The work took about nine. Johnson liked to compare his achievement with that of the French Academy, whose forty members had taken several decades to produce their dictionary. In one conversation he reportedly joked that, since forty times forty is sixteen hundred, and three is to sixteen hundred as an Englishman is to a Frenchman, the result was exactly what one should expect.

When A Dictionary of the English Language finally appeared in 1755, it contained around forty-two thousand entries in two enormous volumes. It was not the first English dictionary, but it was by far the most thorough, and it shaped how the English lexicon was defined and spelled for over a century, until the great Oxford dictionary began to appear. It is also, unusually for such a work, enjoyable to read. Johnson allowed himself a few personal jokes. He defined a lexicographer, that is a writer of dictionaries, as 'a harmless drudge'. Oats, he wrote, were a grain given to horses in England but which in Scotland supported the people, a definition that his Scottish friends never quite forgave.

There was also a famous quarrel. When Johnson began, he had asked the wealthy Lord Chesterfield to act as his patron, but received almost no help. Shortly before publication, Chesterfield wrote two flattering articles praising the coming dictionary, perhaps hoping that it would be dedicated to him. Johnson replied with a letter that is still quoted as a model of polite contempt. Is a patron, he asked, someone who watches a man struggling in the water and then, when he has reached the shore, offers to help him? The help had come too late to be useful.

The dictionary did not make Johnson rich; most of the money had been spent on the work itself. But it brought him eminence, and in 1762 the government gave him a yearly pension that freed him from debt. He went on to edit Shakespeare, write a celebrated series of lives of English poets, and talk, above all, to talk. His friend James Boswell recorded so many of his witty remarks that Boswell's Life of Johnson, published after Johnson's death in 1784, became one of the most famous biographies ever written.

Today his dictionary has long been replaced, yet it remains a monument to what one tenacious, troubled man could achieve with books, paper, a few helpers and an enormous appetite for words.

questions.q: How did Johnson find out how words were really used?
options: He asked his assistants to invent definitions.
He copied the French Academy’s dictionary.
He collected passages from respected English writers that showed each word in use.
He interviewed booksellers and their customers.
questions.explain: Metne göre Johnson önceki iki yüzyılın iyi yazarlarını okuyup kelimelerin gerçekte nasıl kullanıldığını gösteren pasajları işaretledi; doğru cevap “He collected passages from respected English writers that showed each word in use.”

questions.q: Why was Johnson angry with Lord Chesterfield?
options: Chesterfield had criticised the definition of oats.
Chesterfield offered praise only when the hard work was almost finished.
Chesterfield refused to pay the assistants.
Chesterfield wanted the dictionary to be written in French.
questions.explain: Chesterfield başta neredeyse hiç yardım etmemiş, sözlük yayımlanmak üzereyken övgü dolu yazılar yazmıştı; Johnson bu geç gelen ilgiye kızdı. Doğru cevap “Chesterfield offered praise only when the hard work was almost finished.”

title: The Widow Who Went Round the World
text:
In 1842 a respectable Viennese woman of forty-four told her family that she was going on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Her relatives were horrified. Women of her class did not travel alone, and certainly not to distant lands where there were no proper hotels, roads or doctors. Ida Pfeiffer quietly made her will, packed a small bag and left. Over the next fifteen years she would travel around the world twice and become one of the best-known travel writers of her time.

She had been born Ida Reyer in Vienna in 1797, the only daughter in a family of boys. Her father, a wealthy merchant, gave her an upbringing much like her brothers'; she wore boys' clothes, played their games and dreamed of adventure. After his death, her mother tried hard to turn her into a proper young lady, and she later described this period as deeply unhappy. At twenty-two she was married to a lawyer more than twenty years older than her, and the couple soon lost most of their money. For years she struggled to raise their two sons, giving piano and drawing lessons to pay for their education. Only when her sons were grown up did she feel free to follow her old dream.

Her first journey took her through Constantinople to the Holy Land and Egypt. She kept a diary, which she had no intention of publishing, but friends persuaded her, and the book appeared without her name in 1844. It sold well, and it gave her something she had never had: a little money of her own. She used it for another trip, this time to Iceland and Scandinavia, and then, in 1846, she set off on the first of her journeys around the world.

Pfeiffer travelled in a way that astonished her readers. She had very little money, so she went cheaply, often on cargo ships and sailing boats rather than comfortable steamers, and she slept in local homes, in tents or in the open air.
