On her first great journey she crossed parts of Brazil, Chile, Tahiti, China, India, Persia and Russia; on her second, between 1851 and 1855, she visited Borneo, Sumatra and other islands of what is now Indonesia, and then the Americas. She ate whatever she was offered, walked for days through the jungle, and was attacked by robbers at least once. On Sumatra she visited communities that were said to be hostile to strangers, and reportedly calmed a tense situation by joking, with gestures and a few local words, that she was far too old and tough to eat.

She was not a trained scientist, but she had a sharp eye and a methodical habit of collecting. She brought back insects, shells, minerals and botanical specimens, and sold many of them to museums in Vienna, London and Berlin, which helped to pay for further travels. Several species were named after her. Her books, written in a plain, direct style, were translated into many languages, and she was made an honorary member of geographical societies in Berlin and Paris, though the famous society in London did not yet accept women.

Modern readers may find parts of her writing uncomfortable. Like most Europeans of her time, she sometimes judged other peoples by narrow standards and fell back on stereotypical descriptions that now seem prejudiced. Yet she was also curious and frank, and often critical of European colonialism and of the way her fellow Europeans behaved abroad, noticing things that some of her male contemporaries preferred to ignore.

Her last journey ended badly. In 1857 she travelled to Madagascar, where she became caught up, apparently without meaning to, in a failed plot by some Europeans against the island's queen. The consequences were unforeseen and harsh. She was expelled, and during the long, forced march to the coast she caught a severe fever, probably malaria. She never fully recovered and died in Vienna in 1858, at the age of sixty-one.

In hindsight, Ida Pfeiffer's greatest achievement may not have been the distances she covered, impressive as they were, but the example she set. She showed that a middle-aged woman of modest means, with no official support, could see the world on her own terms and write about it well enough that thousands of readers wanted to follow her.

questions.q: How did Pfeiffer pay for some of her later journeys?
options: By selling the things she collected to museums.
By working as a piano teacher on board ships.
With money from her wealthy husband.
With a pension from the government in Vienna.
questions.explain: Metne göre topladığı böcekleri, kabukları ve bitkileri Viyana, Londra ve Berlin’deki müzelere sattı ve bu, yeni yolculuklarının masrafını karşılamaya yardımcı oldu; doğru cevap “By selling the things she collected to museums.”

questions.q: What does the writer consider her greatest achievement?
options: Discovering new species on Sumatra.
Being the first woman to visit Madagascar.
Showing that an ordinary middle-aged woman could travel the world alone and write about it.
Becoming a member of the London geographical society.
questions.explain: Son paragrafta yazar en büyük başarısının, mütevazı imkânlara sahip orta yaşlı bir kadının dünyayı kendi başına gezip bunu iyi yazabileceğini göstermesi olduğunu söylüyor; doğru cevap “Showing that an ordinary middle-aged woman could travel the world alone and write about it.”

title: The Man in the Small Print
text:
On 6 April 1909, a small group of men and dogs stopped on the frozen surface of the Arctic Ocean, and their leader, the American naval officer Robert Peary, announced that they had reached the North Pole. Standing beside him was a man whose name, for decades, appeared only in the small print of the story: Matthew Henson, the team's most experienced member and, by his own account, the first to arrive at the spot.

Henson was born in Maryland in 1866, the year after the end of the American Civil War, to a free Black family who worked as farmers. Both his parents died while he was a child, and at about twelve he walked to the port of Baltimore and signed on as a cabin boy on a merchant ship. It was the best luck of his early life. The ship's captain, a man named Childs, took an interest in the boy and taught him to read and write, along with mathematics and navigational skills. Over several years Henson sailed to China, Japan, Africa and Russia, and he learned to handle ropes, sails, tools and people.

When the captain died, Henson returned to land and took whatever work he could find. In 1887 he was working in a hat shop in Washington when Peary came in to buy a hat. Peary was about to leave for a survey in Central America and needed a servant, and the owner of the shop recommended Henson. It was the start of a partnership that would last more than twenty years and include seven journeys to the far north.

In the Arctic, Henson soon proved essential. He was the best carpenter and mechanic in the group, able to build and repair the wooden sledges they depended on. More importantly, he spent a great deal of time with the Inuit, the people of northern Greenland, whose help made the journeys possible. He learned to speak their language fluently, to drive dog teams, to hunt and to build snow houses, and many Inuit came to like and trust him. Some explorers of the period treated local people as servants; Henson treated them as teachers. Peary himself reportedly admitted that he could not do without him.

The final push came in the spring of 1909. A large group of men and dogs left the coast of Ellesmere Island and moved north across the sea ice, in relentless cold, with support teams turning back one after another. For the last stage, Peary chose only Henson and four Inuit men: Ootah, Egingwah, Seegloo and Ooqueah. Peary, whose feet had been badly damaged by frostbite years before, often rode on a sledge, while Henson broke the trail ahead. By Henson's account, he arrived at what they took to be the Pole about forty-five minutes before Peary, which may have caused tension between the two men.

Whether they really reached the exact Pole is still debated. Their speed over the final days seemed remarkably fast, and Peary's records were incomplete; some historians believe they may have stopped many kilometres short. At the time, a rival American, Frederick Cook, also claimed to have got there first, and the public argument was bitter. But the doubts about Peary do not change the formidable skill and courage of Henson and the four Inuit, without whom the journey would have been impossible.

What happened next was a lesson in the discriminatory attitudes of the age. Peary received honours, promotion and public acclaim. Henson, who was Black, received very little. He worked for years as a clerk in a government office in New York, and when he published a book about his experiences in 1912, it attracted limited attention. Only slowly did his stature grow. In 1937 he was admitted to the Explorers Club in New York, and in 1944 Congress awarded him and other members of the team a medal. He died in New York in 1955 and was buried in a modest grave.

In 1988, thanks partly to the efforts of a researcher who had spent years on his story, his body was moved to Arlington National Cemetery and buried next to Peary's. Today ships, schools and a part of the Arctic bear his name. His story is no longer in the small print, and that change came largely because a few people refused to let it be forgotten.

questions.q: How did Henson first meet Peary?
options: They sailed together on a merchant ship.
Peary came into the hat shop where Henson worked.
Henson answered an advertisement in a newspaper.
They met at the Explorers Club in New York.
questions.explain: Metne göre 1887’de Henson Washington’daki bir şapka dükkânında çalışırken Peary şapka almak için dükkâna geldi; doğru cevap “Peary came into the hat shop where Henson worked.”

questions.q: What was one reason Henson was so valuable on the journeys?
options: He was the only one who could read Peary’s maps.
He paid for the dogs and the equipment.
He was a trained naval officer.
He had learned the language and skills of the Inuit.
questions.explain: Metinde Henson’ın İnuitlerin dilini akıcı konuştuğu, köpek kızağı sürmeyi, avlanmayı ve kar evi yapmayı öğrendiği anlatılıyor; doğru cevap “He had learned the language and skills of the Inuit.”

title: A Name on the Cover
text:
In 1892 a novel appeared in Istanbul with an unusual name on its cover. It was called Muhâdarât, and its author was Fatma Aliye, the daughter of one of the most respected statesmen of the Ottoman Empire. A few years earlier, a book translated by her had been published with no name at all, only the words 'a woman'. Now she signed her own. She is widely regarded as the first woman novelist in Turkish literature, and since 2009 her portrait has appeared on the fifty-lira banknote.

Fatma Aliye was born in Istanbul in 1862. Her father, Ahmed Cevdet Pasha, was a historian, legal scholar and minister, best known for leading the group of scholars that prepared the Mecelle, the Ottoman civil code. The family lived for periods in different provinces as her father's work moved him around the empire, and the house was always full of books and educated guests. Even so, the schooling of girls was limited, and her upbringing followed the customs of her class. According to her own memories, she learned much of what she knew by listening to her brother's lessons, and she taught herself French, reading whatever she could find. Her father, impressed by her intelligence, gradually began to support her studies.

At seventeen she married Faik Bey, a young army officer chosen by the family. The early years were not easy for her intellectual life. Her husband apparently disapproved of women reading novels, especially French ones, and for some years she read little and wrote nothing. But attitudes changed, and with time he came to accept and even take pride in her work. Their household, with its four daughters, became a place where the education of women was taken seriously.

Her literary career began with a translation. Around 1890 she translated a French novel by Georges Ohnet into Turkish, and it was published under the words 'Bir Kadın', meaning 'a woman'. At the time it was unusual for a woman's work to be printed at all, and this modest pseudonym protected her reputation behind a kind of anonymity. The translation caught the attention of Ahmet Mithat Efendi, one of the most popular writers and publishers of the day, who encouraged her and became her guide. Together they wrote a novel, Hayal ve Hakikat, published in 1891, with Fatma Aliye writing the chapters told from the point of view of the heroine. A year later came Muhâdarât, which she wrote alone.

Over the following years she published several more novels, including Udî, about a woman musician. Her stories focused on the lives of educated Ottoman women: their marriages, their families, their struggles with tradition and their search for dignity. She was not a revolutionary. Her heroines generally remain within the moral framework of their society, and she often defended traditional values. Yet within that framework she argued again and again that women deserved education, respect and a voice in their own lives, gently questioning the patriarchal habits of her time.

She also worked in journalism and wrote many essays. In newspapers aimed at women, she wrote about girls' schooling and about the position of women in Islam, arguing that the faith itself did not justify keeping women ignorant. In one well-known exchange she politely but firmly challenged a male writer who had defended a man's right to several wives. She also helped to found one of the first charitable organisations run by Ottoman women, which supported soldiers' families during the war of 1897. Her books were even sent to the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago, where they were displayed in a library of works by women writers from around the world.

Her later life was sadder. One of her daughters changed religion and moved to France, which caused Fatma Aliye great pain and some public embarrassment. Literary tastes changed, and her style came to seem old-fashioned to a new generation of writers. She died in Istanbul in 1936, and for decades she was largely forgotten, remembered more as Ahmed Cevdet Pasha's daughter than as an author.

The rediscovery came late. Researchers in the 1990s began to study her life and works, and some described her as an early feminist voice. The choice of her portrait for the banknote brought her name to millions of people who had never heard of her. In hindsight, her achievement looks remarkable. Writing at a time when a woman's name on a book was itself a small act of courage, she set a precedent and opened a door through which many later Turkish women writers would walk.

questions.q: How did Fatma Aliye’s husband feel about her reading at first?
options: He encouraged her to write novels in French.
He asked Ahmet Mithat to teach her.
He did not approve of women reading novels.
He wanted her to translate books for money.
questions.explain: Metne göre kocası Faik Bey başlangıçta kadınların roman, özellikle de Fransızca roman okumasını onaylamıyordu; doğru cevap “He did not approve of women reading novels.”

questions.q: Which statement best describes her ideas about women?
options: She wanted women to reject all traditional values.
She argued, within the values of her society, that women deserved education and respect.
She believed women should only write anonymously.
She thought religion required women to stay ignorant.
questions.explain: Yazar onun devrimci olmadığını, toplumunun ahlaki çerçevesi içinde kalarak kadınların eğitimi, saygıyı ve söz hakkını hak ettiğini savunduğunu belirtiyor; doğru cevap “She argued, within the values of her society, that women deserved education and respect.”

title: The Engineer Who Made Towers Hollow
titleTr: Kuleleri içi boş bir tüpe çeviren mühendis
text:
In the early 1960s, anyone who wanted to build a very tall office tower faced a simple and expensive problem. The higher a building rose, the more steel it needed to stand up against the wind, and beyond a certain height the cost became almost absurd. A quiet engineer from what is now Bangladesh looked at the problem from a different angle, and in doing so he changed the skyline of cities around the world.

Fazlur Rahman Khan was born in 1929 in Dhaka, which was then part of British India. His father was a teacher who, by most accounts, encouraged his children to think for themselves rather than learn things by heart. Khan studied civil engineering in Calcutta and Dhaka, and in 1952 he won a scholarship to the University of Illinois in the United States. Within a few years he had collected two master's degrees and a doctorate, a pace that his professors apparently found remarkable.

In 1955 he joined Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, a large architecture firm in Chicago, and there he met the problem of height. Traditional towers were built like a tall cage: a grid of columns and beams spread evenly through the floors, with the inner structure doing most of the work. Khan's insight was to move the strength to the outside. If the outer walls were made of closely spaced columns tied firmly together, the whole building would behave like a hollow tube standing on its end, much as a drinking straw resists bending far better than a loose bundle of sticks.

The idea sounds simple in hindsight, but it took careful calculation to prove it. Khan relied on early computers, which were still slow and rare, to model how the forces would travel through the frame. The first building to use his “framed tube” was a 43-storey apartment block in Chicago, finished in the mid-1960s. It used noticeably less steel than a conventional design of the same height, and developers quickly took note.

Over the next decade Khan kept refining the concept, improving each version in an iterative way. For the John Hancock Center, completed in 1969, he added huge diagonal braces that crossed the face of the building in giant X shapes. Rather than hiding the structure, the architects made it the building's most striking feature. Then came the Sears Tower, now known as the Willis Tower, finished in 1973. Here Khan grouped nine square tubes together, like pencils held in a fist, and let some of them stop at lower levels so that the tower stepped back as it rose. Remarkably, it remained the tallest building in the world for about a quarter of a century.

Colleagues described Khan as modest, curious and fond of long conversations that had little to do with steel. He insisted that engineers and architects should work in tandem with each other rather than in separate offices, and he often said that a structure should be honest about how it stands. He also cared deeply about his homeland. During the 1971 war in which Bangladesh won its independence, he went to great lengths to raise money and political support in the United States, often working through the night after his normal office hours.

Not all of his projects were towers. One of his last was the Hajj Terminal at Jeddah airport in Saudi Arabia, a vast field of white fabric roofs designed to shelter huge numbers of pilgrims from the desert sun. The tent-like roofs looked light and almost fleeting, yet they were calculated with the same rigour as his skyscrapers. In 1982, while visiting Jeddah, Khan died of a heart attack. He was only 52.

His influence, however, has stood the test of time. Many of the super-tall towers built since then, from East Asia to the Gulf, depend on versions of the tube idea that he developed. A sculpture of him stands in the lobby of the Willis Tower, and engineering students still study his groundbreaking calculations. Perhaps the most fitting tribute is invisible: every time a tall building sways gently in a storm and then settles, it is doing exactly what Khan said it would do.

questions.q: What was the main idea behind Khan's “framed tube”?
options: Using fabric roofs instead of steel frames
Placing columns evenly through every floor
Putting most of the building's strength in its outer walls
Making towers shorter but much wider
questions.explain: Metinde Khan'ın fikrinin dayanımı dışarıya taşımak olduğu söyleniyor: sık aralıklı dış kolonlar binayı içi boş bir tüp gibi çalıştırır. Bu yüzden doğru cevap “Putting most of the building's strength in its outer walls”.

questions.q: What did Khan do during the war of 1971?
options: He raised money and political support for Bangladesh in the United States
He returned to Dhaka to design new buildings
He stopped working for his Chicago firm
He wrote a book about the tube idea
questions.explain: Metne göre 1971 savaşında Khan, ABD'de Bangladeş için para ve siyasi destek toplamak için büyük çaba gösterdi. Doğru cevap “He raised money and political support for Bangladesh in the United States”.

title: A Village Built from Earth
text:
In the 1940s the Egyptian government faced an awkward situation on the west bank of the Nile, opposite the city of Luxor. A village called Gourna had grown up on top of ancient tombs, and some villagers were said to be quietly selling objects dug out from beneath their homes. The authorities decided to move the whole community to a new site nearby. The architect they chose for the job, Hassan Fathy, saw the project as far more than a simple move. He believed it could become a showcase, proving to the world that poor people could build beautiful homes with their own hands.

Fathy was born in 1900 into a wealthy family and grew up mostly in Cairo, far from village life. He trained as an architect at a time when Egyptian cities were filling with concrete buildings copied from European models. Concrete and steel were expensive and had to be imported, and they made houses unbearably hot in the Egyptian summer. Fathy began to wonder whether the answer lay not in imported materials but in the oldest building material of all: earth.

Mud brick had been used along the Nile for thousands of years. The difficulty was the roof. Wood was scarce and costly, so an earth house usually ended with a flat roof made of whatever beams could be found. Fathy's breakthrough came when he travelled south to Nubia and watched local builders at work. These masons could raise curved vaults and domes from mud bricks alone, without any wooden support underneath while the roof was going up. They laid the bricks in sloping rows, each layer leaning gently on the one before. Fathy was fascinated by their ingenuity, and he invited Nubian masons to come north and teach their technique.

At New Gourna, building began in the mid-1940s. Fathy designed courtyards that trapped cool air, thick walls that kept the heat out during the day and released it slowly at night, and wooden screens that let in breezes while protecting privacy. He built a mosque, a market, a theatre and a school, and he tried to design each family's house around the way that particular family actually lived. In his view, architecture should grow out of the local culture rather than be forced on people from above.

The project, however, did not go as planned. Many villagers did not want to leave their old homes, partly because the tombs beneath them provided an income and partly because the upheaval of moving had been decided for them rather than with them. Fathy later came under fire from critics who argued that, for all his good intentions, he had shown the same top-down attitude that he criticised in others. Funding dried up, the work stalled, and only part of the village was ever finished. For years the half-empty buildings seemed to suggest that his ideas had failed.

Fathy did not give up. He spent the following decades teaching, writing and building houses for private clients, most of them in Egypt but some abroad, including a small community in New Mexico in the United States. In 1969 he published a book telling the story of Gourna, later translated into English as Architecture for the Poor. The book struck a chord with a new generation of architects who were growing disillusioned with glass towers and worried about the cost of energy. In 1980 he received the Right Livelihood Award, sometimes called the alternative Nobel Prize, and the Aga Khan Award for Architecture honoured him in the same year.

Fathy died in Cairo in 1989. In hindsight, the story of New Gourna carries a double lesson. On the one hand, it shows that traditional materials and skills can produce homes that are cheap, comfortable and lovely to look at. On the other, it reminds planners that a good design cannot simply be handed to people; it has to be shared with them. Today, as architects search for ways to cool buildings without air conditioning, Fathy's thick walls and shaded courtyards no longer look antiquated. They look surprisingly modern.

questions.q: What did Fathy learn from the builders of Nubia?
options: How to import cheap steel from Europe
How to build curved mud-brick roofs without wooden support
How to sell objects found in old tombs
How to design glass towers for hot climates
questions.explain: Fathy, Nubyalı ustaların tonoz ve kubbeleri altta ahşap destek olmadan sadece kerpiçle yükselttiğini gördü. Doğru cevap “How to build curved mud-brick roofs without wooden support”.

questions.q: According to the text, why was New Gourna only partly finished?
options: The Nubian masons refused to work there
The houses were too hot to live in
An earthquake destroyed the new buildings
Many villagers did not want to move, and the money ran out
questions.explain: Metne göre köylülerin çoğu eski evlerini bırakmak istemedi, para kaynağı kurudu ve iş durdu. Doğru cevap “Many villagers did not want to move, and the money ran out”.

title: The Surgeon Who Brought a Microscope to the Brain
text:
For most of the twentieth century, operating on the human brain was a little like repairing a watch while wearing thick gloves in a dim room. Surgeons worked with their naked eyes, sometimes with simple magnifying glasses, and the tiny blood vessels and nerves they needed to protect were often impossible to see clearly. Many patients survived the operation only to be left with serious damage. One of the people who changed this was a doctor born in a small town in south-eastern Turkey.

Mahmut Gazi Yaşargil was born in 1925 in Lice, in the province of Diyarbakır. He began studying medicine in Ankara, then moved to Germany and later to Switzerland, completing his medical degree in Basel. In the early 1950s he joined the neurosurgery department of the University Hospital of Zurich, which was run by the respected surgeon Hugo Krayenbühl. Yaşargil would remain connected to Zurich for most of his working life.

The turning point came in the mid-1960s. Yaşargil spent around a year at a laboratory in Burlington, in the American state of Vermont, where researchers were using operating microscopes to sew together blood vessels in animals. The vessels were often only a millimetre or two wide, and the work demanded extraordinary precision. Yaşargil practised for hundreds of hours, by most accounts working late into the night until his hands could perform the movements almost automatically.

Back in Zurich he began to bring the microscope into the operating room for brain surgery. In 1967 he and his colleagues are reported to have performed one of the first bypass operations on a human brain, connecting an artery outside the skull to one inside it in order to improve blood flow. Over the following years he used the microscope to treat aneurysms, which are weak, swollen spots in the walls of arteries, as well as tumours and tangled vessels deep inside the brain that surgeons had previously considered impossible to reach.

A microscope alone was not enough, however. Existing instruments were too large and clumsy for such delicate work, so Yaşargil designed his own: fine forceps, tiny clips to close off aneurysms, and special scissors. He also worked with engineers on a new kind of operating microscope that was balanced by counterweights, so that the surgeon could move it smoothly with a light touch, or even with his mouth, while both hands stayed busy. Many of these tools, refined in small, incremental steps over the years, are still used in operating rooms today in modern forms.

His groundbreaking methods did not win acceptance overnight. Some older surgeons were sceptical, arguing that the microscope narrowed their view and slowed operations down. Yaşargil answered with results. He kept detailed records of thousands of cases, and his outcomes, especially for aneurysms, were far better than what had been considered normal. He also trained a large number of young surgeons from around the world, who carried his techniques back to their own countries. Over time microneurosurgery gained momentum and became the rule rather than the exception.

In 1999 the journal Neurosurgery named him “Neurosurgery's Man of the Century” for the years 1950 to 1999, a remarkable accolade from the profession he had helped to reshape. After retiring from Zurich in the early 1990s, he moved to the United States and continued to operate and teach at the University of Arkansas in Little Rock for many years. Throughout this period his wife, Dianne, a nurse, worked alongside him and helped to organise his vast collection of case records.

Colleagues often describe Yaşargil as demanding, patient and almost obsessed with detail. He reportedly believed that a surgeon's hands should be trained as carefully as a musician's, through daily practice that never really ends. His story is a case in point for an idea that runs through the history of medicine: sometimes the greatest advance does not come from a new drug or a new theory, but from finally being able to see clearly what is in front of you.

questions.q: Why did Yaşargil go to Burlington in the 1960s?
options: To finish his medical degree
To meet Hugo Krayenbühl
To teach at the University of Arkansas
To practise joining tiny blood vessels under a microscope
questions.explain: Burlington'daki laboratuvarda araştırmacılar hayvanlarda mikroskop altında kan damarlarını dikiyordu; Yaşargil bu çok hassas işi yüzlerce saat çalıştı. Doğru cevap “To practise joining tiny blood vessels under a microscope”.

questions.q: How did Yaşargil respond to surgeons who doubted the microscope?
options: He stopped using it for aneurysms
He showed them his results from thousands of cases
He moved to another country to avoid them
He wrote angry letters to the journal
questions.explain: Metinde Yaşargil'in şüphecilere sonuçlarla cevap verdiği, binlerce vakanın ayrıntılı kaydını tuttuğu söyleniyor. Doğru cevap “He showed them his results from thousands of cases”.

title: The Princess Who Painted Giant Canvases
text:
In 2017, visitors to Tate Modern in London stood in front of a painting more than five metres wide, its surface broken into thousands of bright fragments of colour that seemed to spin and shatter like glass. Many of them had never heard of the artist. Yet in the 1950s Fahrelnissa Zeid had been one of the most talked-about painters in Paris and London, and her life story was almost as colourful as her canvases.

She was born in 1901 on Büyükada, one of the Princes' Islands off Istanbul, into an Ottoman family of officials and intellectuals. Her family was large, talented and often stormy; one of her brothers, Cevat Şakir, later became famous as the writer known as the Fisherman of Halicarnassus. As a young woman she enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts for women in Istanbul, at a time when few women anywhere were encouraged to treat painting as a career, and she later studied for a while in Paris.

Her first marriage, to the writer İzzet Melih Devrim, gave her three children, two of whom also became artists. In 1934 she married again, this time to Prince Zeid bin Hussein, a member of the Iraqi royal family. When he was appointed Iraq's ambassador, first in Berlin and later in London, she found herself at the centre of diplomatic life, hosting formal dinners and receptions. By her own account she was often unhappy in that role, and painting became her refuge and her true vocation.

In the early 1940s, back in Istanbul, she joined a circle of young Turkish artists known as the D Group, who wanted to bring modern European styles into Turkish art. Her early works showed scenes of everyday life, but her style was changing rapidly. After the Second World War she settled in London and began to work in a completely abstract way. She painted with tremendous energy, sometimes for many hours without stopping, and her canvases grew larger and larger. Critics compared the effect to stained glass, to Byzantine mosaics and to the patterns of the Islamic tiles that she had known since childhood.

The 1950s were the culmination of her career. She held exhibitions in London, Paris and New York, won considerable acclaim, and some critics placed her among the leading abstract painters of her day. Ironically, her title was also a slight problem: a princess and an ambassador's wife was not what many people imagined a serious modern painter to be, and a few reviewers seemed unable to look past it.

Then, in 1958, came an upheaval that changed everything. A revolution in Baghdad overthrew the Iraqi monarchy, and many members of her husband's family were killed. The couple lost their official position and much of their income. Fahrelnissa had to come to terms with a far more modest life, first in London and then in a small flat in Paris. Her painting changed too. She began to paint portraits of family and friends with large, staring eyes, and she experimented with an unusual material: she painted on small bones left over from meals and set them in clear resin, creating glowing little objects.

In 1975 she moved to Amman, Jordan, where her son Prince Ra'ad lived. There, already in her seventies, she opened her home as an art school and taught a generation of young Jordanian women to paint. The institute that grew out of her lessons is said to have influenced many women artists in the region. She died in Amman in 1991.

For decades after her death, Fahrelnissa Zeid was largely forgotten outside Turkey and Jordan, partly because she did not fit neatly into any single national story. She was Ottoman and Turkish, Iraqi by marriage, and part of the art world of Paris and London. The Tate exhibition helped to change that, and she has risen to new prominence as her enormous canvases find a fresh audience. Standing in front of them, it is easy to understand why painting meant so much to her.

questions.q: What happened to Fahrelnissa Zeid's life after the revolution of 1958?
options: She and her husband lost their position and lived far more modestly
She became Iraq's ambassador in London
She stopped painting completely
She returned to Büyükada for good
questions.explain: 1958 devriminden sonra çift resmi konumunu ve gelirinin çoğunu kaybetti; Fahrelnissa çok daha mütevazı bir hayata alışmak zorunda kaldı. Doğru cevap “She and her husband lost their position and lived far more modestly”.

questions.q: What did she do in Amman?
options: She worked as a diplomat for Jordan
She painted only giant abstract canvases
She opened her home as an art school for young women
She wrote a book about the D Group
questions.explain: Metne göre Amman'da evini sanat okulu olarak açtı ve genç Ürdünlü kadınlara resim öğretti. Doğru cevap “She opened her home as an art school for young women”.

title: The Doctor Who Learned to Store Blood
text:
In the summer of 1940, German bombs were falling on British cities, and hospitals in London were running short of blood for wounded patients. Across the Atlantic, American doctors wanted to help, but there was a practical difficulty. Whole blood does not keep for long, and it could not easily survive a long journey by ship. The man chosen to solve this problem was a young African American surgeon named Charles Richard Drew.

Drew was born in 1904 in Washington, D.C., the eldest of five children. As a student he was better known for sport than for science. At Amherst College in Massachusetts he was a star of the football and athletics teams, and he reportedly became interested in medicine after his younger sister died of illness. Medical schools in the United States admitted very few Black students at the time, so he went to McGill University in Montreal, Canada, where he graduated in 1933 near the top of his class.

He later moved to Columbia University in New York to continue his training, and there he threw himself into research on how blood could be stored. His doctoral thesis, completed in 1940, carried the plain title Banked Blood, but it gathered almost everything then known about the subject and added careful experiments of his own. He became the first African American to earn a doctorate in medical science from Columbia, a fact that says as much about the barriers of the time as about his own ability. The work placed him at the forefront of a young field.

One of the key ideas Drew worked with was the use of plasma, the yellowish liquid part of blood that remains when the red cells are removed. Plasma lasts far longer than whole blood, it can be given to patients without worrying about blood types, and it is very useful for treating shock after serious injuries. When the “Blood for Britain” programme was launched in 1940, Drew was appointed its medical director. He set strict standards for collecting, testing and processing blood so that every bottle shipped across the ocean would be safe, and he applied them with great rigour. Under his supervision, large quantities of plasma reached British hospitals for transfusion.

The programme was so successful that in 1941 the American Red Cross asked him to help set up a national blood bank. Drew introduced refrigerated trucks, later known as “bloodmobiles”, which could travel to donors rather than waiting for donors to come to a hospital. The idea was simple and practical, and versions of it are still in use around the world. In many ways, his work laid the groundwork for modern blood donation.

Yet the same system soon adopted a rule that Drew found unacceptable. At first, the military did not want blood from Black donors at all; later it accepted their blood but insisted that it be kept separate from the blood of white donors. Drew publicly denounced the rule, pointing out again and again that it was baseless: human blood does not differ according to race. When his objections were ignored, he resigned. The policy, which most people now regard as a blatant injustice, was not fully abandoned until years later.

Drew returned to Washington to head the department of surgery at Howard University, one of the country's leading Black universities. He devoted the rest of his career to training young African American surgeons, many of whom went on to become leaders in their own field. He was demanding but loyal, and he wanted his students to be not just good but exemplary, so that nobody could question their right to be there.

In 1950, while driving to a medical conference in Alabama with colleagues, Drew fell asleep at the wheel and the car crashed in North Carolina. He died of his injuries at the age of 45. A story later spread that he had died because a white hospital refused to treat him. The colleagues who were in the car said this was untrue and that the doctors did their best to save him. The myth probably survived because it seemed to fit the injustices he had fought against. The real story is sad enough: a man who had helped to save countless lives lost his own far too early.

questions.q: Why was plasma especially useful for the “Blood for Britain” programme?
options: It could only be given to soldiers
It was cheaper to collect than whole blood
It lasts much longer than whole blood and does not depend on blood types
It could be produced without donors
questions.explain: Metne göre plazma tam kandan çok daha uzun dayanır ve kan grubuna bakılmadan verilebilir; bu da uzun deniz yolculuğu için idealdi. Doğru cevap “It lasts much longer than whole blood and does not depend on blood types”.

questions.q: What does the text say about the story that a white hospital refused to treat Drew?
options: It is confirmed by hospital records
The colleagues in the car said it was not true
Drew himself told it before he died
It explains why the policy on blood ended
questions.explain: Arabadaki meslektaşları bu hikâyenin doğru olmadığını, doktorların onu kurtarmak için ellerinden geleni yaptığını söyledi. Doğru cevap “The colleagues in the car said it was not true”.

title: From the Fencing Hall to the Stone Lions
text:
In August 1936, two young Turkish women stepped onto the fencing floor at the Olympic Games in Berlin. One of them was a twenty-year-old named Halet Çambel. Neither of them won a medal, but they are widely described as the first Muslim women ever to compete at the Olympics. For most athletes, such a moment would be the high point of a lifetime. For Çambel, it turned out to be only the first chapter of a long and remarkable life that would be devoted mostly to the distant past.

Çambel was born in Berlin in 1916, where her father, Hasan Cemil Çambel, was serving as a military officer attached to the Ottoman embassy. She grew up between languages and countries, studied at the American College for Girls in Istanbul, and became a keen fencer. According to a story she told in later interviews, the team was invited to meet Adolf Hitler during the Berlin Games, and she refused to go. Whether or not every detail is accurate, the story says something about the strong will that would mark her whole career.

After the Games she went to Paris to study archaeology at the Sorbonne, then returned to Turkey and joined Istanbul University. The great event of her academic life came in the late 1940s, when she began working with the German archaeologist Helmuth Theodor Bossert in the foothills of the Taurus Mountains, in the region of the modern town of Osmaniye. There, on a hill called Karatepe, the team uncovered the remains of a fortress from around the eighth century BC, with gates guarded by stone lions and sphinxes and walls lined with carved scenes.

The most seminal find was a long inscription written in two languages: Phoenician, which scholars could already read, and a form of Luwian written in hieroglyphs, which was only partly understood. Because the two texts said roughly the same thing, this double inscription worked like a key, allowing experts to check and correct their reading of the hieroglyphs. It became one of the foundations of the modern study of the ancient languages of Anatolia.

Çambel could have moved on to the next exciting site, as many archaeologists do. Instead, she stayed at Karatepe for decades, and her name became inextricably linked with the site. She believed the carvings should remain where they had been found, rather than being taken away to a museum in a distant city. So she set out to create an open-air museum on the hill itself, with protective roofs over the stones and paths for visitors. The work on the hill was slow and often frustrating, and she frequently had to argue with officials who did not share her priorities.

Her greatest battle came when plans were made for a dam on the Ceyhan River below Karatepe. The rising water threatened to flood part of the ancient site. Aware of what was at stake, Çambel campaigned relentlessly, writing letters, meeting ministers and refusing to be ignored. In the end the plans were modified, and the main monuments were protected. The episode showed a side of her that friends knew well: she was polite, but tenacious and absolutely unwilling to accept what she considered wrong.

She also cared about the people who lived near the site. She trained local villagers to work on the excavations and on the care of the stones, and some of them stayed with her for many years. In her private life she was married to Nail Çakırhan, a poet and journalist who later became a self-taught architect; his house in Akyaka, built in a traditional local style, won an international architecture award in the 1980s.

Çambel kept working into very old age, a staunch defender of cultural heritage to the end. In 2004 she received the Prince Claus Award from the Netherlands for her work. She died in Istanbul in 2014, at the age of 97. Few people manage to leave a mark in two such different worlds as sport and archaeology. Halet Çambel did both, and the stone lions of Karatepe, still standing where she insisted they should stay, are perhaps her finest monument.

questions.q: Why was the Karatepe inscription so important?
options: It was the oldest text ever found in Turkey
It described the first Olympic Games
It was written by Halet Çambel's family
It gave the same text in a known and a partly understood language
questions.explain: Yazıt aynı metni okunabilen Fenikçe ve kısmen anlaşılan hiyeroglif Luvicesiyle veriyordu, bu yüzden bir anahtar gibi işledi. Doğru cevap “It gave the same text in a known and a partly understood language”.

questions.q: What did Çambel want to do with the carvings at Karatepe?
options: Keep them on the hill in an open-air museum
Send them to a museum in Istanbul
Sell them to pay for new excavations
Move them before the dam was built
questions.explain: Çambel oymaların bulundukları yerde kalması gerektiğine inanıyordu ve tepede bir açık hava müzesi kurdu. Doğru cevap “Keep them on the hill in an open-air museum”.

title: The Runner Who Raced Against Time
text:
Photographs of Paavo Nurmi from the 1920s often show the same strange detail. As he runs around the track, lean and serious, he is holding a stopwatch in his hand. Other runners raced against the people beside them. Nurmi, it seemed, was racing against time itself, checking his pace lap after lap as if the race were a scientific experiment.

Nurmi was born in 1897 in Turku, in south-western Finland, which was then part of the Russian Empire. His family was poor, and when his father died, the boy, then about twelve, had to leave school and work, pushing heavy carts of goods up the steep streets of the town. He later suggested that this hard physical labour had strengthened his legs. He was inspired to take up running by the success of an earlier Finnish runner, Hannes Kolehmainen, at the 1912 Olympics, and he trained alone for hours in the forests near his home.

What made Nurmi different was not only talent but method. At a time when many athletes trained by feel, he approached running in a systematic, almost methodical way. He kept records of his training, experimented with different distances and speeds, and paid careful attention to his diet, although some of his ideas about food were rather unusual. Above all, he learned to run at an even pace, which he checked with his stopwatch. He understood that a runner who wastes energy early in a race pays for it later.

His first Olympics came in Antwerp in 1920, where he won three gold medals. But it was the Paris Games of 1924 that propelled him to legendary status. There he won five gold medals in a few days. On one afternoon he won the 1,500 metres and then, reportedly less than an hour later, the 5,000 metres. A few days afterwards he won the cross-country race, held in such terrible heat that many runners collapsed and some were carried away on stretchers. Nurmi crossed the line looking, as some observers noted, almost untroubled.

By the end of his stellar career he had collected nine Olympic gold medals and three silver medals, and he had set numerous world records at distances from 1,500 metres to 20 kilometres. Newspapers called him “the Flying Finn”, and he made a famous tour of the United States, racing indoors in crowded halls against formidable local rivals. For a small, young country that had only become independent in 1917, he was a source of enormous pride. People said that he had put Finland on the world map.

His relationship with the public, however, was complicated. Nurmi was famously reserved. He rarely smiled for photographers, gave few interviews and seemed indifferent to fame. Some people found him cold or even arrogant; others saw a shy man who simply preferred to let his running speak for him. His career also ended in controversy. Shortly before the 1932 Olympics in Los Angeles, he was banned from international competition, accused of breaking the strict amateur rules of the time by accepting too much money for travel expenses. Many Finns felt the decision was unwarranted, and some suspected that rivalries between sports officials had played a part.

Away from the track, Nurmi became a successful businessman, building and selling apartment blocks in Helsinki. But his most moving public moment came in 1952, when Helsinki hosted the Olympic Games. During the opening ceremony the crowd saw a familiar figure running into the stadium with the Olympic torch. It was Nurmi, then fifty-five years old, and his surprise appearance brought the crowd to its feet. He ran a lap of the track with the same smooth stride and lit the flame.

Nurmi died in 1973. A bronze statue of him in full stride, made by the sculptor Wäinö Aaltonen, stands near the Olympic Stadium in Helsinki. Modern runners use heart-rate monitors and satellite watches rather than a stopwatch held in the hand, yet the basic lesson of his relentless training has stood the test of time: train with purpose, measure what you do, and learn how to spend your energy wisely.

questions.q: Why did Nurmi carry a stopwatch while running?
options: To time the other runners in the race
To keep an even pace throughout the race
To show the crowd how fast he was
Because the officials asked him to
questions.explain: Metne göre Nurmi eşit bir tempoyla koşmayı öğrenmişti ve bu tempoyu kronometresiyle kontrol ediyordu. Doğru cevap “To keep an even pace throughout the race”.

questions.q: Why was Nurmi banned before the 1932 Olympics?
options: He refused to meet the officials
He had been injured in the United States
He was accused of breaking the amateur rules by accepting too much money
He had decided to become a businessman
questions.explain: Metinde Nurmi'nin seyahat masrafları için fazla para alarak o dönemin katı amatörlük kurallarını çiğnemekle suçlandığı belirtiliyor. Doğru cevap “He was accused of breaking the amateur rules by accepting too much money”.

title: A Museum Lifted into the Air
text:
On Avenida Paulista, one of the busiest streets in São Paulo, there is a building that seems to float. A long box of glass and concrete hangs above the ground, held up by two enormous red frames at its ends, and beneath it lies a wide, open square where people meet, protest, sell things and listen to music. This is the São Paulo Museum of Art, known as MASP, and it was designed by a woman who had arrived in Brazil as a newcomer after the Second World War. Her name was Lina Bo Bardi.

She was born Achillina Bo in Rome in 1914. She studied architecture there, in a school dominated by older and rather conservative professors, and then moved to Milan, where she worked with the designer Gio Ponti and wrote and edited articles for design magazines. During the war her office was destroyed in a bombing raid, an experience that, by her own account, showed her how fragile everything people build really is. In 1946 she married the art dealer and critic Pietro Maria Bardi, and the couple sailed to Brazil.

They intended to stay only for a short time, but Brazil changed their plans. Pietro was invited by the media owner Assis Chateaubriand to create a new art museum in São Paulo, and Lina was soon involved in designing its spaces. She fell in love with her new country, became a Brazilian citizen in 1951, and in the same year finished her own home on the edge of the city, the Glass House, which stands on thin columns among the trees as if it were a lookout point in the forest.

The museum's permanent home on the avenue opened in 1968 after years of work. The city required that the view from the avenue towards the old centre be kept open, so Bo Bardi lifted the entire gallery into the air, leaving a span of more than seventy metres beneath it with no columns at all. It was a groundbreaking piece of engineering, and it gave the city a covered public square. She insisted that this space belonged to everyone, not only to museum visitors, and it soon became a showcase for the life of the city.

Inside, she made an even more unusual decision. Instead of hanging the paintings on walls, she placed them on sheets of glass held upright by concrete blocks, so that the works seemed to float in a single large room. Visitors could walk freely among them, seeing a Renaissance portrait next to a modern painting, with the information about each work placed on the back. Some critics praised the idea as a brave attempt to free art from the formal order of traditional museums; others decried it as confusing. The glass stands were removed in the 1990s, but after years of debate they were reinstated in 2015.

Bo Bardi also spent several years in the north-east of Brazil, in the city of Salvador, where she directed a museum and became fascinated by the objects ordinary people made from whatever they could find: makeshift lamps from old tins and toys from scraps of wood. She admired the ingenuity behind these objects and believed that such popular creativity was as valuable as any fine art. A military coup in 1964 brought this work to an abrupt end, and she returned to São Paulo.

Her other masterpiece, the SESC Pompéia leisure centre, was built between the late 1970s and the mid-1980s in the shell of an old factory. Instead of knocking the factory down, she kept its brick halls for reading, eating and playing, and added a pair of rough concrete towers for sports, linked by bridges and pierced by irregular windows that look as if they had been punched out by hand. At weekends the centre is full of families, and many visitors find it one of the most joyful public buildings anywhere.

Bo Bardi died in São Paulo in 1992. For a long time she was better known in Brazil than abroad, but in recent decades her reputation has grown steadily, and in 2021 she was honoured with a special Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at the Venice Architecture Biennale, almost thirty years after her death. Her buildings remain a reminder that architecture is not only about shapes and materials but about the life that happens in and around them.

questions.q: Why did Bo Bardi lift the MASP gallery into the air?
options: Because the city required the view from the avenue to stay open
Because the land was too wet to build on
To protect the paintings from street noise
To make room for a car park
questions.explain: Metne göre şehir, caddeden eski merkeze doğru manzaranın açık kalmasını şart koşmuştu; bu yüzden galeri havaya kaldırıldı. Doğru cevap “Because the city required the view from the avenue to stay open”.

questions.q: What did Bo Bardi do at SESC Pompéia?
options: She knocked down an old factory to build a museum
She designed a glass house among the trees
She organised an exhibition of objects from Salvador
She kept an old factory's halls and added new concrete towers
questions.explain: Bo Bardi eski fabrikayı yıkmak yerine tuğla salonlarını korudu ve spor için iki beton kule ekledi. Doğru cevap “She kept an old factory's halls and added new concrete towers”.

title: A Sign on a Door in Cağaloğlu
text:
In 1923 a small sign appeared on a building in Cağaloğlu, in the old heart of Istanbul. It announced the clinic of Dr. Safiye Ali, and it attracted a good deal of curiosity. Women doctors had practised in the city before, but they had usually been foreigners. Safiye Ali was a Turkish woman, and she is generally regarded as the first in her country to work as a fully qualified doctor.

She was born in Istanbul in 1891. Her father, by most accounts, was an educated man who believed his daughter should receive the best schooling available, and she attended the American College for Girls in the city. At that time, however, there was no medical school in the Ottoman Empire that admitted women. If she wanted to become a doctor, she would have to go abroad.

In the years around the First World War she travelled to Germany and enrolled at the medical faculty of the University of Würzburg. The war years were hard for students far from home: food was scarce, letters were slow and news from Istanbul was often alarming. Yet she kept going, and in the early 1920s she completed her studies and earned her doctorate. She then returned to an Istanbul that was still under Allied occupation and full of refugees, poverty and disease.

She soon proved that her training was badly needed. She specialised in the illnesses of women and children, two areas in which the need was enormous. Infant mortality was high, many mothers had little information about nutrition or hygiene, and some women were unwilling to be examined by male doctors. For them, the presence of a woman doctor made a real difference. According to accounts from the period, her clinic was often crowded, and she is said to have treated many poor patients without charging them.

Her work extended beyond the clinic. She is reported to have taught at a nursing school and to have worked with the Süt Damlası, or “Drop of Milk”, an organisation that provided clean milk and regular health screening for babies from poor families. Programmes like this were part of a wider effort across Europe at that time to reduce infant deaths, and in Istanbul they gave practical help to families who could not afford a doctor. She also encouraged girls to continue their education, arguing that the health of women was a matter of public health for the whole nation.

Not everyone welcomed her. Some people found it difficult to accept a woman in such a position, and she reportedly faced open doubts about whether a woman could really be trusted with serious medical decisions. There was also a certain stigma attached to women who worked outside the home in a profession dominated by men. She responded, it seems, mainly through her work, building a loyal circle of patients one family at a time. By doing so, she helped to lay the groundwork for the many women who would follow her into paediatric and maternity care.

Then her life unexpectedly took a new direction. She married a German doctor, Max Krüger, and in the late 1920s the couple moved to Germany, where she continued to practise medicine. Little is publicly known about her later years. She died in Dortmund in 1952, reportedly after a long illness, and for many decades her name was almost forgotten in Turkey.

In recent years, however, interest in her story has grown. Historians have searched old records for traces of her life, streets and health centres have been named after her, and she now appears regularly in lists of pioneering Turkish women. Many details of her life are still uncertain, and some of the stories told about her may be exaggerated. But the main facts are clear enough: at a time when it was extremely difficult for a woman to do so, she studied medicine, came home and used her skills to help the people who needed them most. In doing so she opened a door that thousands of Turkish women doctors have walked through since.

questions.q: Why did Safiye Ali study medicine in Germany?
options: Her father was working there as a diplomat
German universities offered free food to students
No medical school in the Ottoman Empire admitted women
She wanted to marry a German doctor
questions.explain: Metne göre o dönemde Osmanlı'da kadınları kabul eden bir tıp okulu yoktu; doktor olmak için yurt dışına gitmesi gerekiyordu. Doğru cevap “No medical school in the Ottoman Empire admitted women”.

questions.q: According to the text, why did her presence matter to many women patients?
options: She charged lower prices than foreign doctors
Some women did not want to be examined by male doctors
She was the only doctor in Cağaloğlu
She gave them free milk for themselves
questions.explain: Metinde bazı kadınların erkek doktorlarca muayene edilmek istemediği, bu yüzden bir kadın doktorun varlığının fark yarattığı söyleniyor. Doğru cevap “Some women did not want to be examined by male doctors”.

title: The Engineer Behind India's Engineers' Day
text:
Every year on 15 September, schools, universities and companies across India celebrate Engineers' Day. Students give talks, professional bodies hand out awards, and newspapers publish articles about the country's great builders. The date was not chosen at random. It is the birthday of Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya, a venerable engineer and administrator who was born in 1861 and lived to be a hundred, and whose career stretched from the age of horse-drawn carts to the age of jet planes.

Visvesvaraya was born in a village in what is now the state of Karnataka, in southern India. His father, a scholar of Sanskrit and a practitioner of traditional medicine, died when the boy was still young, and the family had little money. With the help of relatives and scholarships, he studied in Bangalore and then at the College of Science in Pune, where he graduated in civil engineering in 1883. He joined the Public Works Department of the Bombay government, which was then part of British India, and was sent to work on irrigation and water supply in what was still a largely agrarian society.

Water was the great problem of his age. Much of India depends on the monsoon, which brings huge amounts of rain in a few months and very little for the rest of the year. Storing that water safely in reservoirs was essential, but floods could damage dams, and too much water released at the wrong moment could ruin the fields downstream. Visvesvaraya's best-known invention addressed this. He designed a system of automatic gates that opened when the water in a reservoir rose above a certain level and closed again when it fell. The gates were first installed, by most accounts, at the Khadakwasla reservoir near Pune in 1903, and later at other dams. They allowed engineers to keep reservoirs fuller without endangering the dam itself.

His reputation grew quickly. After a devastating flood struck the city of Hyderabad in 1908, he was invited to design a flood protection system for the city, along with improvements to its drainage and sanitation. He then moved to the princely state of Mysore, where he became chief engineer and played a central role in planning the Krishna Raja Sagara dam on the Kaveri River. The dam, completed in stages over many years, provided water for farming across a large area and for the famous gardens laid out below it.

In 1912 the ruler of Mysore appointed him Diwan, a position similar to that of a chief minister. For an engineer this was an unusual step, but Visvesvaraya believed that the same habits of careful planning could be applied to an entire state. During his six years in office he encouraged the creation of new industries, a bank, technical schools and a university, and he urged people to see education and industry as the path out of poverty. Some critics felt that he moved too fast or relied too heavily on large projects, but supporters argued that he laid the groundwork for the region's later prosperity.

Stories about his personal habits are almost as famous as his dams. He was said to be extremely punctual and conscientious, always neatly dressed, and he reportedly prepared his speeches with great precision, even in old age. One popular story claims that, while travelling on a train, he noticed from the sound and vibration that something was wrong with the track and pulled the emergency chain just in time to prevent an accident. Like many such stories it is impossible to check, but it shows the kind of reputation he had: an engineer who paid attention to everything.

India honoured him with its highest civilian award, the Bharat Ratna, in 1955. He continued to write and give advice on planning well into his nineties, and he died in 1962, at the age of 100. Many of the institutions he helped to found still exist today, and the gates and dams he designed remain part of the landscape of southern India.

In a country that now produces huge numbers of engineering graduates every year, Visvesvaraya has become something more than a historical figure. He is a symbol of the idea that technical skill should serve the public good. When students celebrate his birthday each September, they are honouring not just a set of clever gates, but a lifetime spent turning water, money and knowledge into something useful for ordinary people.

questions.q: What did Visvesvaraya's automatic gates do?
options: They pumped water up to farms on high ground
They measured how much rain fell during the monsoon
They cleaned the water before it reached the city
They opened and closed by themselves depending on the water level
questions.explain: Kapılar haznede su belli bir seviyenin üstüne çıkınca açılıyor, düşünce yeniden kapanıyordu. Doğru cevap “They opened and closed by themselves depending on the water level”.

questions.q: What does the text say about the story of the train?
options: It cannot be checked, but it reflects his reputation for attention to detail
It is confirmed by railway records from the time
It explains why he became Diwan of Mysore
It shows that he disliked travelling by train
questions.explain: Metne göre tren hikâyesinin doğruluğu kontrol edilemez, ama her şeye dikkat eden bir mühendis olarak ününü gösterir. Doğru cevap “It cannot be checked, but it reflects his reputation for attention to detail”.

title: The Suitcase Full of Jam
text:
Selin had been travelling for nineteen hours when she finally reached the baggage hall at İzmir airport. Her flight from Toronto had been delayed twice, her connection in Istanbul had been a race through endless corridors, and all she wanted now was her own bed. So when a dark blue suitcase with a red ribbon on the handle came round on the belt, she grabbed it hastily, pulled it into a taxi and gave the driver her mother's address without a second thought.

It was only at midnight, after a bowl of her mother's lentil soup, that she opened the suitcase to find her pyjamas. There were no pyjamas. Instead, wrapped carefully in towels and old newspapers, there were jars. She counted them in disbelief: forty-two jars of jam, each with a handwritten label. Quince, sour cherry, fig, rose petal, and one mysterious jar that said only “For Emre, do not share.”

“You took somebody's suitcase,” her mother said from the doorway, sounding more amused than surprised. “And that somebody has a grandmother who loves him very much.”

Selin sat on the floor, baffled. Her own suitcase was also dark blue. It also had a red ribbon, because a friend in Toronto had told her it would make the bag easy to recognise. Apparently half the world had received the same advice. Somewhere, a stranger was probably opening her bag at this very moment and finding three novels, a broken hair dryer and a large box of maple sweets she had bought for her nephews.

The label on the handle was no help. The ink had run in the rain, and all she could read was “Emre” and part of a phone number. She tried every possible combination of the missing digits for almost an hour, apologising to a sleepy baker, an irritable taxi driver and a woman who simply laughed and hung up. It was all to no avail.

In the morning she called the airport. A tired man at the lost luggage desk listened to her story and sighed. A young man had indeed reported a missing blue suitcase with a red ribbon, but he had already left the country. He had been flying on to Hamburg, where he was starting a new job, and the bag he had collected in İzmir, her bag, Selin realised, had gone with him.

“So my maple sweets are in Germany,” she said.

“And his grandmother's jam is in Karşıyaka,” the man replied, and for a moment they both laughed at the ludicrous predicament.

The airline promised to sort it out swiftly, but it would take at least ten days. Selin looked at the jars lined up on her mother's kitchen table and felt strangely guilty, and a little nostalgic for her own grandmother's kitchen. Every label had been written in the same careful, slightly shaky hand. Someone had spent a whole summer stirring pots of fruit for a grandson who was moving far away, and now the jars were sitting with the wrong person.

On the third day her mother had an idea. One of the jars carried a second, smaller label: “Bornova, Gül Street, the house with the lemon tree.” It was probably the grandmother's own address, added out of habit. That afternoon, Selin and her mother took a minibus to Bornova, carrying the suitcase between them like a heavy secret.

The house with the lemon tree was not hard to find. A small, apprehensive woman in a flowered headscarf opened the door, looked at the suitcase, and put both hands over her mouth. Her name was Nermin Hanım, and she had hardly slept since Emre's call from Hamburg. He had opened the bag, she explained, and found novels in English and a box of sweets shaped like leaves. He had been so disappointed that he had not even tasted the sweets.

The old woman insisted they come in. Within minutes there was tea on the table, a plate of pastries, and a long phone call with a very relieved young man in Germany. Unsurprisingly, Emre promised to send the bag back by courier at once. Selin promised to send the jam the same way, carefully packed this time.

Before they left, Nermin Hanım opened the special jar marked “do not share” and spread a spoonful on a piece of bread for each of them. It was bitter orange, thick and dark and wonderful.

“He will never know,” she whispered, with a wink.

Two weeks later, Selin's suitcase arrived, complete with novels, hair dryer and an unexpected extra: a small jar of German honey with a note in clumsy Turkish. “Thank you for looking after my grandmother's jam. The red ribbon was a terrible idea.”

She agreed completely. The next time she travelled, she tied a bright yellow sock to her handle. Nobody else in the world, she was sure, would ever do that.

questions.q: How did Selin finally find the owner of the jam?
options: The airport gave her his address in Hamburg.
She guessed the missing digits of his phone number.
An address written on one of the jars led her to his grandmother.
Emre saw her advertisement and called her.
questions.explain: Kavanozlardan birinin üzerinde Bornova’daki limon ağaçlı evin adresi yazıyordu; Selin bu sayede büyükanneyi buldu. Doğru cevap: "An address written on one of the jars led her to his grandmother." Telefon numarası denemeleri ise sonuç vermemişti.

questions.q: Why did both suitcases have a red ribbon?
options: Their owners had followed the same common advice.
The airline ties ribbons to delayed bags.
Nermin had tied one to each bag.
Selin and Emre had bought the same suitcase together.
questions.explain: Selin, kurdeleyi bir arkadaşının tavsiyesiyle takmıştı ve "dünyanın yarısı aynı tavsiyeyi almış" diye düşünüyor. Doğru cevap: "Their owners had followed the same common advice."

title: The Parrot Who Knew a Number
text:
When Deniz moved into a small flat above a grocery shop in Ayvalık, the landlord mentioned, almost as an afterthought, that the previous tenant had left something behind. “Nothing big,” he said, handing her the keys. “Just a bird.”

The bird turned out to be an elderly grey parrot called Kaptan, who lived in a large cage by the kitchen window and looked at Deniz with deep suspicion. He had belonged to a retired sailor, the landlord explained, who had gone to live with his daughter and had left in a hurry. Nobody seemed to know exactly where. The grocer downstairs had been feeding Kaptan for a week, and he was clearly glad to hand over the job.

Deniz had never owned anything more demanding than a cactus, but she could not bring herself to give the parrot away. She bought a book about birds, learned that he liked walnuts and hated the vacuum cleaner, and slowly they became, if not friends, then respectful neighbours.

Kaptan talked, of course. He said “Good morning” at all hours of the day, he copied the creak of the door perfectly, and he whistled the first few notes of an old sea song whenever it rained, which sounded oddly nostalgic. But there was one thing he said more than anything else, usually at six in the evening, in a voice that was strangely gentle. It was a string of numbers: zero, five, three, two, and then seven more digits, always in the same order, always with the same little pause in the middle.

For a month Deniz paid no attention. Then one evening, as Kaptan recited his numbers for the third time, she realised with a jolt that it was a mobile phone number. Eleven digits, starting with zero five. She wrote it down on the back of an envelope, stared at it for a long time, and put it away. Calling a stranger because a parrot told her to felt preposterous.

But the idea would not leave her. What if the old sailor had taught the bird his daughter's number? What if somebody was missing Kaptan as much as Kaptan, in his quiet evening voice, seemed to be missing someone? After three days of hesitation, she dialled.

A woman answered, sounding wary. Deniz explained, in a rush of apologetic sentences, that she lived in a flat in Ayvalık, that there was a parrot, and that the parrot seemed to know this number. There was a long silence on the line. Then the woman began to cry.

Her name was Ayten. Her father, the sailor, had fallen ill in the winter, and she had brought him to her home in Bursa to look after him. In the confusion of the move, she had arranged for a friend to collect the parrot, but the friend had broken a leg and the plan had collapsed. Her father had been asking about Kaptan every day since. He had lost his appetite. He sat by the window at six o'clock, the time he used to feed the bird, and said nothing.

“He taught him my number years ago,” Ayten said, laughing through her tears. “As a joke. In case the bird ever got lost.”

The next Saturday, Deniz put Kaptan's cage on the back seat of a borrowed car, covered it with a blanket and drove to Bursa. The parrot complained loudly for the first hour and then fell asleep. She was uneasy the whole way. What if the old man did not remember? What if the bird did not remember him?

She need not have worried. The moment she carried the cage into the small living room, Kaptan lifted his head, looked at the thin man in the armchair, and said, very clearly, “Good morning, Captain.” The old man laughed so hard that he had to take off his glasses and wipe his eyes.

Deniz stayed for dinner. The sailor, a born storyteller, told stories about storms off the coast of Africa and about the day Kaptan had escaped in an Italian port and been found sitting on the head of a statue. His daughter kept filling her plate, and the parrot kept stealing the walnuts from the salad.

When Deniz got home that night, the flat felt enormously quiet. There was no one to say good morning at midnight, no one to whistle when it rained. She missed the bird far more than she had expected.

A week later, a parcel arrived from Bursa. Inside was a bag of walnuts, a photograph of an old man and a grey parrot, and a short note in Ayten's handwriting. “Kaptan has learned a new number,” it said. “He says it every evening at six. It is yours. Please come and visit.”

questions.q: Why did Deniz finally decide to call the number?
options: The landlord asked her to find the sailor.
She thought someone might be missing the parrot.
The grocer recognised the number.
She wanted to sell the parrot.
questions.explain: Deniz, yaşlı denizcinin papağana kızının numarasını öğretmiş olabileceğini ve birinin Kaptan’ı özlüyor olabileceğini düşündü. Doğru cevap: "She thought someone might be missing the parrot."

questions.q: What does the note at the end suggest?
options: The sailor wants his walnuts back.
Ayten wants Deniz to adopt another bird.
Kaptan has forgotten every number he knew.
The parrot now remembers Deniz as part of his family.
questions.explain: Notta Kaptan’ın her akşam altıda yeni bir numara söylediği ve bu numaranın Deniz’in numarası olduğu yazıyor; yani papağan artık Deniz’i de kendi yakınlarından sayıyor. Doğru cevap: "The parrot now remembers Deniz as part of his family."

title: The Quiz in the Dark
text:
Every Thursday evening for twenty-two years, the Anchor Inn in a small fishing village on the west coast of Scotland had held a quiz. It was run by Mrs Fiona MacLeod, a retired schoolteacher with a loud voice and a famously strict attitude to cheating. Phones had to be placed in a basket by the door. Anyone caught whispering to the next table lost five points. The prize was modest, a bottle of whisky and a voucher for the fish shop, but the honour was enormous.

That particular Thursday, the competition was fierce. The Fishermen, who had won three weeks in a row, sat by the fire looking smug. The Librarians, two sisters and their cousin, had brought a new member, a quiet young man who was rumoured to have read an entire encyclopaedia. The Knitting Circle had taken the table nearest the bar, which they claimed was lucky. Outside, the wind was rising, and rain was hitting the windows like handfuls of gravel.

Mrs MacLeod had just read the question “What is the capital of Mongolia?” when the lights went out. There was a groan, then a flurry of laughter, then the sound of the landlord, Duncan, swearing quietly as he walked into a chair. The whole village had lost power. Somewhere a dog barked.

Most quizmasters would have given up. Mrs MacLeod did not even pause. “Candles, Duncan,” she said, and within a few minutes there were candles on every table and two old storm lamps on the bar. In the soft yellow light, the pub looked like a painting from another century. Mrs MacLeod held her question cards close to a flame and carried on, her voice as calm and relentless as ever.

The final round was the hardest of the night. When it was over, the teams handed in their papers, and Mrs MacLeod reached for her answer sheet to mark them. It was not there. She lifted her handbag, her cards, the candle. She looked under the table. The sheet, with the correct answers to all sixty questions, had vanished.

The room went silent. Then, inevitably, people began to cast suspicious looks at the Fishermen. They had been sitting closest to her table, and everyone knew how badly they wanted a fourth victory. “Don't be daft,” said their captain, a large man named Angus, turning red. “Why would we steal it after the quiz is finished?”

“To change your own answers before she marks them,” said one of the Librarians sharply, and for a moment it looked as if the friendly evening would end in a real argument.

Mrs MacLeod raised her hand. “Nobody leaves,” she said, and suddenly everyone was back in her classroom. She asked who had come near her table in the dark. Angus had, to borrow a candle. One of the knitters had, to return a pencil. Duncan had brought her a glass of water. And Hamish, the landlord's elderly spaniel, had been lying under her chair for most of the evening, as he always did.

She bent down with a candle and gave Hamish the kind of scrutiny she had once given to homework. Hamish looked back at her with an expression of pure innocence. Then he burped. Beside his nose lay a small, wet piece of paper on which the word “Ulaanbaatar” was still clearly visible. The culprit had been found.

The laughter lasted for several minutes. The landlord, deeply apologetic, explained that the dog had a long history of eating paper napkins, beer mats and on one occasion a fisherman's betting slip. Angus demanded a written apology from the Librarians, and got a hug instead.

But there was still a problem: how could the papers be marked without the answers? Mrs MacLeod simply closed her eyes, and in the candlelight she recited all sixty answers from memory, one after another, without a single hesitation. Unsurprisingly, every answer was correct. She had written every question herself.

At the end of the marking, the Fishermen and the Librarians had exactly the same score. A tie-breaker was needed. Mrs MacLeod thought for a moment and smiled. “How many times,” she asked, “has the power gone off during this quiz since it began twenty-two years ago?”

The teams argued in whispers. The Librarians guessed three. The Fishermen guessed seven. The answer, according to Mrs MacLeod's own notebook, was six, so the triumphant Fishermen won their fourth week in a row by one candle.

When the lights came back on just before midnight, people were almost disappointed. Duncan has since suggested holding one quiz a year in the dark on purpose. Ironically, the only member of the pub who actually swallowed the answers is no longer allowed under the quizmaster's chair.

questions.q: Why did people first suspect the Fishermen?
options: They had been seen eating paper.
They were sitting nearest to the quizmaster and wanted to win badly.
Angus had refused to put his phone in the basket.
They had arrived late and missed the first round.
questions.explain: Balıkçılar, yarışmacının masasına en yakın oturuyordu ve dördüncü galibiyeti çok istedikleri biliniyordu. Doğru cevap: "They were sitting nearest to the quizmaster and wanted to win badly."

questions.q: How was the problem of the missing answer sheet solved?
options: Duncan found a copy in the office.
The teams marked each other's papers.
Mrs MacLeod remembered all the answers herself.
The quiz was cancelled until the next week.
