questions.explain: Bayan MacLeod soruların hepsini kendisi yazdığı için altmış cevabın tamamını ezberden okudu. Doğru cevap: "Mrs MacLeod remembered all the answers herself."

title: The Driving Test and the Goat
text:
Murat was thirty-four years old and had failed his driving test twice. The first time, he had forgotten to release the handbrake and driven the whole course with a strange burning smell following the car. The second time, he had been so nervous that he had greeted the examiner, shaken his hand and then climbed into the back seat. His sister still told that story at every family dinner.

So on the morning of his third attempt, in a small town outside Kayseri, he had prepared like an athlete. He had slept eight hours. He had avoided caffeine. He had practised every manoeuvre in his uncle's old car until his neighbours knew the sound of his engine better than their own doorbells. And he had repeated to himself, over and over, the only advice his instructor had given him: “Stay calm. Whatever happens, stay calm.”

Then he saw who his examiner was, and his calm disappeared. Mr Hikmet was a formidable figure in the region, and not in a good way. He was said to have failed a candidate for using the indicator too enthusiastically. He never smiled, he wrote constantly on a clipboard, and he had a habit of sighing deeply, as if each mistake caused him physical pain.

The test began well. Murat checked his mirrors, adjusted his seat and pulled out into the street so smoothly that he almost surprised himself. He stopped at the right places, signalled at the right moments, and parked between two cars without touching either of them. His parking was impeccable. Mr Hikmet wrote something on his clipboard and said nothing at all, which Murat, still apprehensive, chose to interpret as a positive sign.

For the last part of the test, they left the town and drove along a narrow road between fields of sunflowers. The sky was a perfect blue. Murat began, very cautiously, to relax.

That was when they came round a bend and found the road completely blocked by goats. There were perhaps two hundred of them, brown and black and white, walking in no particular direction and in no particular hurry. Somewhere in the middle of them, a boy of about twelve was waving a stick and shouting, with little effect.

Murat stopped the car. The goats flowed around it like a river around a rock. One of them, a large white animal with a beard and an air of great self-importance, stopped beside the bonnet, looked through the glass at Murat and then, with surprising ease, jumped up onto the bonnet itself.

There was a long, uneasy silence inside the car. It was, Murat thought, a ludicrous predicament. Murat could hear his own heart. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Mr Hikmet's pen hovering above the clipboard.

Every instinct told Murat to do something: to sound the horn, to reverse, to get out and push the animal away. Instead, he remembered his instructor's words. He switched off the engine, put on the hazard lights and sat with his hands resting on the wheel. Then he wound down the window and asked the boy, very politely, whether the goat had a name.

“Paşa,” the boy said, embarrassed. “He likes cars.”

They waited. Paşa inspected the car, chewed thoughtfully on the rubber around the mirror and stared at Mr Hikmet for a long time. Eventually, bored, he jumped down and followed the rest of the herd into a field. The whole episode had lasted perhaps eleven minutes. Murat started the engine again, checked his mirrors twice and drove carefully back to the test centre.

In the car park, Mr Hikmet finally spoke. “Do you know why most people fail this test?” he asked. Murat shook his head. “Not because they cannot drive. Because they cannot wait. Something unforeseen happens, and they panic. They hit the horn, they hit the goat, they hit the wall.” He signed the form. “You waited. Congratulations.”

Murat was so baffled that he forgot to say thank you. It was only when he was standing in the street, holding the piece of paper that said he had passed, that he noticed a small wet hole in one corner of the form. Paşa, it seemed, had tried to eat that as well.

He framed it. It still hangs in his hallway, next to a photograph of a white goat with a beard, which his sister took the following summer on a special trip to find the animal and thank it in person.

questions.q: What did Murat do when the goat jumped onto the car?
options: He sounded the horn to frighten it away.
He got out and pushed it off the bonnet.
He reversed slowly back towards the town.
He turned off the engine and waited patiently.
questions.explain: Murat eğitmeninin "sakin kal" tavsiyesini hatırladı, motoru kapattı, dörtlüleri yaktı ve bekledi. Doğru cevap: "He turned off the engine and waited patiently."

questions.q: According to Mr Hikmet, why do most people fail the test?
options: They panic when something unexpected happens.
They drive too slowly in the town.
They do not check their mirrors.
They are too nervous to park properly.
questions.explain: Hikmet Bey’e göre çoğu kişi araba kullanamadığı için değil, beklenmedik bir şey olduğunda paniğe kapılıp bekleyemediği için kalır. Doğru cevap: "They panic when something unexpected happens."

title: The Great Pickle Contest
text:
For eleven years in a row, Hatice Hanım had won the pickle contest at the autumn festival in her small town near Tokat. Her jars of green tomatoes, cabbage and peppers were famous across the region. People said her pickles were so crisp that you could hear someone eating one from the other side of the market. Her trophies stood in a long line on the sideboard, between photographs of her grandchildren.

This year, two weeks before she was due to start, she slipped on a wet step and broke her right wrist. The doctor put it in plaster and told her firmly that she must not lift anything heavier than a teacup for six weeks. The old woman listened politely, went home, and telephoned her granddaughter in Ankara.

Elif was twenty-nine, worked as an accountant and had never made a pickle in her life. She tried to explain this to her grandmother. Her grandmother did not seem to hear. “You have hands,” she said. “I have a head. Together we have one cook. Come on Friday.”

So Elif took a week of holiday, packed her laptop and arrived in the town with a notebook and feeling deeply doubtful. Her grandmother sat in a chair in the middle of the kitchen like a general, and Elif did the work. She washed vegetables, boiled water, measured salt and sterilised jars. Being an accountant, she was methodical and wrote everything down. By the second evening she had built a spreadsheet with the weight of every vegetable, the exact amount of salt and the temperature of the room.

Her grandmother was rather dismissive of the spreadsheet. “Pickles are not numbers,” she said. “Pickles are patience.” She would not, however, explain what that meant. When Elif asked for the secret ingredient that the whole town talked about, her grandmother gave a wry smile and changed the subject.

The competition was fierce. Their main rival was Şükran Hanım from across the street, who had come second for eleven years and was determined that this would finally be her year. She visited twice that week, bringing pastries and asking innocent questions about salt. Each time, Hatice Hanım covered the jars with a cloth and talked about the weather.

What followed was a long process of trial and error. The first batch was a disaster. Elif, impatient, opened a jar after four days to see how it was going, and the cabbage was soft and sad. The second batch was too salty. With only nine days left before the festival, she began to panic. She stayed up late comparing her spreadsheet with recipes on the internet, looking for the mysterious secret.

On the fifth night, unable to sleep, she came downstairs and found her grandmother in the kitchen in the dark, sitting beside the new jars with her good hand resting on one of them. She was not doing anything. She was just sitting there.

“What are you doing?” Elif asked.

“Waiting,” said her grandmother. “Every year, everyone asks me for the secret. There is a little chickpea in the jar, a little vinegar, a little grape leaf. Everybody knows that. But fermentation cannot be hurried. The secret is that I do not touch them. I do not open them to look. I do not taste them too early. I sit with them and I wait.” She laughed. “It is the hardest thing in the world.”

Elif sat down beside her. For the next eight days, she did not open a single jar. It was, as promised, extremely hard.

On the day of the festival, the judges walked along the long table, tasting and making notes. Elif's pickles were good: crisp, sour and bright. But this year, at last, Şükran Hanım's were better. A triumphant Şükran Hanım won first prize and burst into tears, and Elif's grandmother was the first person to hug her. Elif came third, which for a beginner was considered something close to a miracle.

On the drive back to Ankara, she thought about her spreadsheet. She had recorded everything except the one thing that mattered. She added a new column at the end, with a single heading: “Days without opening the jar.”

Next autumn, she has promised, she will come back for two weeks instead of one. Her grandmother's wrist has healed, but they have agreed to enter the contest together, as a team. Their old rival has already been seen asking questions about salt.

questions.q: What was the real "secret" of Hatice Hanım's pickles?
options: A special kind of salt from Tokat.
Elif's careful spreadsheet.
Waiting patiently without opening the jars.
A recipe she had copied from Şükran Hanım.
questions.explain: Hatice Hanım’a göre nohut, sirke, asma yaprağını herkes biliyor; asıl sır kavanozlara dokunmadan, açmadan sabırla beklemek. Doğru cevap: "Waiting patiently without opening the jars."

questions.q: How did Hatice Hanım react when Şükran Hanım won?
options: She hugged her first.
She complained to the judges.
She refused to speak to her.
She left the festival early.
questions.explain: Şükran Hanım birinci olup ağladığında ona ilk sarılan kişi Hatice Hanım oldu. Doğru cevap: "She hugged her first."

title: Where Is Pastel?
text:
Tomás lived alone on the third floor of an old yellow building in Lisbon, in one of those steep neighbourhoods where the trams groan as they climb. He worked from home as a translator, and his only regular company was a small orange cat called Pastel, named after the custard tarts that Tomás ate far too many of.

One Tuesday in March, Pastel disappeared. Tomás had opened the kitchen window to let out the smell of burnt toast, and when he turned round, the cat was gone. He searched the flat, the stairs, the tiny courtyard and the street. He called her name until the woman in the bakery opposite came out to ask if he was all right.

That night he made a poster. It had a large photograph of Pastel looking unimpressed, his phone number and the word “REWARD” in big letters. The next morning he put up forty copies on every lamp post, café window and tram stop within half a kilometre.

The phone began ringing almost immediately, and the calls were incessant. Over the next three days, Tomás received calls about fourteen different cats. There was a ginger cat on a balcony in the next street, which turned out to be enormous and male. There was an orange cat in a park, which ran away and climbed a tree. There was a cat seen sleeping in a shop window, which was in fact a woollen scarf. One elderly man called simply to describe, in great detail, a cat he had owned in the nineteen sixties, sounding deeply nostalgic. Each time, Tomás went out full of hope and came back alone.

By Friday he had sunk into melancholy and stopped working. He could not concentrate on his translations. He kept hearing a faint sound in the building, a thin, sad cry that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere. He pressed his ear against the walls. He knocked on the pipes. He began to wonder if it was a delusion.

The building had five flats. On the second floor, directly below him, lived Dona Amália, who was eighty-three and had once been a piano teacher. Every evening at seven, she played for exactly one hour, always the same pieces: some Chopin, some old Portuguese songs, and a waltz that Tomás had heard so many times he could hum it in his sleep.

On Friday evening, the music sounded wrong. The high notes were the same as always, but every time Dona Amália played in the lower part of the keyboard, something strange happened. Instead of a deep, rich note, there was a dull thud, and once, unmistakably, a small and indignant meow.

Tomás ran down the stairs and knocked on her door so hard that she opened it holding a walking stick, ready to defend herself. He tried to explain, but he was speaking too fast, and she was rather deaf and thoroughly baffled. In the end he simply pointed at the piano.

It was a tall, dark upright piano, older than both of them, standing against the wall beneath an open window. Together, they lifted the heavy lid at the top and looked inside. There, lying on the thick felt hammers among years of dust, was Pastel, thinner and dirtier but entirely alive. She looked at Tomás with an expression that seemed to say that the whole situation was his fault.

It took them half an hour, a ladder, a tin of sardines and a great deal of patience to get her out. In hindsight, it was easy to reconstruct what had happened. She had jumped from Tomás's kitchen window onto the window ledge below, climbed into Dona Amália's flat, and found the open top of the piano the perfect place to hide. When the lid was closed, she had been trapped. For four days she had survived on a plant pot of water on the windowsill, which she must have reached during the night, and had protested loudly every time the hammers hit the strings beneath her.

“I thought I was going deaf in only one hand,” Dona Amália said, laughing until she had to sit down.

Tomás offered her the reward. She refused it. Instead, she suggested that he might like to come down on Friday evenings and listen to the music properly, now that it sounded right again. He has been going every week since. Pastel usually comes too, and sleeps on the piano stool, as far from the keys as possible.

The posters stayed on the lamp posts for months. Tomás forgot to take them down, and every so often somebody still calls to tell him about an orange cat.

questions.q: What made Tomás realise where Pastel was?
options: The woman in the bakery saw her.
A strange sound came from the low notes of the piano.
Someone called him after seeing a poster.
He found her footprints on the stairs.
questions.explain: Dona Amália piyanonun alt notalarına bastığında boğuk bir ses ve bir miyavlama duyuldu; Tomás böylece kediyi buldu. Doğru cevap: "A strange sound came from the low notes of the piano."

questions.q: What did Dona Amália ask for instead of the reward?
options: Help with cleaning her piano.
A box of custard tarts.
That Tomás take down his posters.
That Tomás come and listen to her play.
questions.explain: Ödülü reddeden Dona Amália, Tomás’ın cuma akşamları gelip müziği dinlemesini önerdi. Doğru cevap: "That Tomás come and listen to her play."

title: The Runaway Vacuum Cleaner
text:
Kemal Bey had taught mathematics in Antalya for thirty-eight years, and he did not trust any machine that claimed to be cleverer than he was. So when his son gave him a robot vacuum cleaner for his seventy-first birthday, he thanked him politely and left it in its box, as if it might stay there indefinitely.

It was the dust that defeated him. Since his wife had died, the flat had grown slowly untidy, and his knees no longer liked bending down to clean under the sofa. One rainy afternoon, he opened the box, read the instructions twice with a pencil in his hand, and switched the gadget on.

He had expected to hate it. Instead, he found it oddly charming. The little autonomous machine moved around the living room with great seriousness, bumping gently into chair legs, turning, trying again. When it got stuck under the radiator, it played a small sad tune until he rescued it. Within a week, he had given it a name, Bulut, and had started talking to it while he drank his morning tea. It was, he admitted to his son on the phone, rather good company.

The trouble began on a Thursday. A delivery man rang the bell with a parcel, and Kemal Bey opened the front door and stood in the corridor signing for it. He was perhaps a minute. When he turned round, the door was still wide open, and Bulut was nowhere in the flat.

At first he assumed it was a glitch and the machine was hiding under a bed. Then he noticed a line of clean floor running out of the door and along the dusty corridor towards the lift. And the lift, which had been standing open when the delivery man left, was now going down.

Kemal Bey had not run anywhere for fifteen years, but he ran now, down six floors of stairs, holding the handrail and breathing heavily. He arrived in the lobby just in time to see the lift doors open on an empty space. Bulut had already left. The doorman, Hasan, was watching a football match on his phone and had seen nothing.

The search that followed involved almost the whole building. Hasan checked the car park. The twins from the fourth floor checked the garden, enthusiastic but hardly methodical. Mrs Sevim from the ninth floor, the building's main source of gossip, suggested that the machine had probably been stolen by the man in flat twelve, who she had never liked. Somebody called the café next door, where a waiter reported that something round and grey had indeed passed under the tables about ten minutes earlier and then gone back out through the side door.

Then Kemal Bey remembered something from the instructions. The vacuum had an app on his phone, which his son had installed and which he had never once opened. With trembling fingers, and with help from the twins, he found it. On the screen was a map, drawn by Bulut itself, of every room it had cleaned. The newest room was not in his flat at all. It was on the second floor, flat four.

Flat four belonged to Leyla Hanım, a retired nurse who lived alone and whom Kemal Bey had greeted in the lift for years without ever learning her name. He knocked, feeling apprehensive and rather foolish. She opened the door holding Bulut in her arms like a lost puppy.

“It came in while I was carrying in the shopping,” she said. “It cleaned my whole kitchen. I didn't know who it belonged to, so I made it a cup of tea.” She paused. “That was a joke. But I did make tea. Would you like some?”

He stayed for two hours. They grew nostalgic about Antalya in the nineteen seventies, and talked about the hospital and the school, about their children who lived far away and called too rarely. When he finally left, carrying Bulut under his arm, it was dark outside, and he realised he had not felt so cheerful in a very long time.

The next week, Kemal Bey left his front door open on purpose while Bulut was cleaning. Ironically, the machine did not go anywhere. Kemal Bey went downstairs anyway, to return a cake tin.

His son, when he heard the whole story, asked whether he wanted the machine fixed so that it would not escape again. Kemal Bey said no. In his opinion, the machine was working perfectly.

questions.q: How did Kemal Bey find out where the vacuum cleaner had gone?
options: The doorman had followed it.
A waiter brought it back to him.
The map in the phone app showed a new room on the second floor.
Mrs Sevim saw the man in flat twelve take it.
questions.explain: Kemal Bey ikizlerin yardımıyla telefondaki uygulamayı açtı; harita, süpürgenin en son ikinci kattaki dört numaralı daireyi temizlediğini gösteriyordu. Doğru cevap: "The map in the phone app showed a new room on the second floor."

questions.q: Why did Kemal Bey not want the machine fixed?
options: Its escape had brought him a new friendship.
He wanted to buy a new one.
He thought repairs were too expensive.
He had stopped using it.
questions.explain: Süpürgenin kaçması sayesinde Leyla Hanım’la tanıştı ve uzun zamandır olmadığı kadar neşelendi; bu yüzden makinenin "kusursuz çalıştığını" söylüyor. Doğru cevap: "Its escape had brought him a new friendship."

title: The Best Man's Shopping List
text:
Jamal had been working on his best man's speech for six weeks. His older brother Kareem was getting married in a hotel in Manchester, and Jamal had decided early on that this would be a flawless speech, the greatest in the history of the family. He had written eleven drafts. He had practised in front of the bathroom mirror, in front of his flatmates and, on one memorable occasion, in front of a confused postman. The final version fitted onto five small white cards, which he kept in the inside pocket of his suit.

On the morning of the wedding, everything went wrong in small ways. His tie would not sit straight. He spilled coffee on his shoe. His grandmother, who was staying with him, needed to be driven to the hotel early and spent the journey reminding him that she had been to forty-seven weddings and that most of the speeches had been far too long and full of tedious anecdotes.

The ceremony itself was beautiful. Kareem cried, the bride laughed at him, and the photographer climbed onto a chair to take a picture of the whole family. By the time the meal was over and the plates had been cleared, Jamal was almost upbeat. Then the master of ceremonies tapped a glass, announced the best man, and two hundred faces turned towards him.

He stood up, smiled, took the cards from his pocket and looked down at the first one. It said, in his grandmother's careful handwriting: “Eggs, two dozen.”

He turned it over. Nothing. He looked at the second card. “Lemons. Olive oil, the good one. Bread for Sunday.” The third card said “Washing powder” and was underlined twice.

He understood at once. His grandmother had borrowed his cards that morning to write her shopping list, and somewhere in his flat, probably next to the kettle, were five white cards covered in his finest jokes. There was a long pause. Somebody gave a hesitant cough. The bride's mother looked at her watch.

Jamal could have panicked. Instead, he cleared his throat and held up the first card. “Eggs,” he said seriously. “Two dozen.” A few people laughed uncertainly. “When Kareem was fourteen,” he continued, “he decided to make breakfast for our mother on her birthday. He used two dozen eggs. We still don't know how. The kitchen ceiling was never the same.”

The room laughed, properly this time. Jamal looked at the next card. “Lemons,” he said. “Kareem's first car was a lemon. In every sense. It was yellow, it was sour, and it broke down on the way to his first date with Laila.” The bride was laughing so hard she had to put down her glass.

He went through the whole list. Olive oil led to the time Kareem had tried to impress Laila's father with his cooking and set off the fire alarm. Bread for Sunday led to the long Sunday lunches at their grandmother's house, where Kareem had always protected his younger sibling from the teasing of older cousins. Washing powder, underlined twice, led to a story about a white shirt, a red sock and a job interview that the family still did not discuss in public.

Then he reached the last card. It contained only one word: “Flowers.” Jamal looked at it for a moment, and his voice became quiet and sincere. He said that their father, who had died when they were young, had bought their mother flowers every Friday, and that Kareem had quietly continued the tradition ever since, without ever telling anyone. He said that Laila was marrying the kindest man he knew. Then he raised his glass, and two hundred people raised theirs.

The applause went on for a long time. Afterwards, at least six guests told him it was the best wedding speech they had ever heard, and an aunt called him a natural storyteller. Kareem hugged him and asked how long it had taken to write. Jamal said, with a wry smile, about three minutes.

His grandmother, who had been sitting at the front table throughout, waited until the noise had died down. Then she leaned over and said, loudly enough for the whole room to hear: “Very nice. But now how am I going to do my shopping?”

The next day, Jamal went to the supermarket and bought everything on the list. He kept the cards. They are in a frame in his brother's kitchen now, next to the wedding photograph. In hindsight, everyone agrees, it was the best mistake his grandmother ever made.

questions.q: Why did Jamal have a shopping list instead of his speech?
options: His brother had played a joke on him.
His grandmother had used his speech cards for her list.
He had forgotten to write the speech.
The bride had swapped the cards.
questions.explain: Büyükannesi sabah alışveriş listesini yazmak için Jamal’ın kartlarını ödünç almıştı; konuşma kartları evde kalmıştı. Doğru cevap: "His grandmother had used his speech cards for her list."

questions.q: What did the word "Flowers" lead Jamal to talk about?
options: A funny accident at a flower shop.
His grandmother's garden.
The flowers at the wedding ceremony.
A quiet family tradition that Kareem had continued.
questions.explain: "Flowers" kelimesi Jamal’a, babalarının her cuma annelerine çiçek aldığını ve Kareem’in bu geleneği kimseye söylemeden sürdürdüğünü anlattırdı. Doğru cevap: "A quiet family tradition that Kareem had continued."

title: The Ring in the Bread
text:
Hacer had run the small bakery at the bottom of her street in Trabzon for nineteen years, and in all that time she had never once forgotten to take off her wedding ring before she started kneading. She always put it in the same place: a little blue saucer next to the scales. On the morning of the first snow, however, the saucer was empty.

She noticed at about eight o'clock, when the first rush of customers was over and the shelves were almost bare. She looked at the saucer, then at her hand, then at the saucer again. Her stomach dropped. It was a dreadful predicament. The ring had belonged to her husband's grandmother, and it was old, thin and slightly too large for her finger.

She searched the bakery from top to bottom. She emptied the flour sacks, looked under the ovens and went through the rubbish with a torch. Nothing. There was only one explanation, and it was a terrible one. At four that morning, half asleep, she must have forgotten to take the ring off. It had slipped from her finger into the dough. And the dough had become forty round loaves, and the loaves had been sold.

Her apprentice, a lanky seventeen-year-old called Oğuz, took the news remarkably well. He found a piece of paper and, together, they began to reconstruct the morning. Who had come in? Who had bought what? Hacer knew most of her customers by name, and Oğuz had an excellent memory for faces. Within half an hour they had a list of twenty-six people, with a small tally mark beside each name for every loaf.

They divided the list and set off through the snow.

It was the strangest morning of Oğuz's life. He knocked on doors and asked people, as politely as he could, whether they had found a ring in their bread. Some laughed. Some were incredulous, and some were openly suspicious. One woman thought it was a new kind of advertising campaign and asked whether there was a prize. A retired fisherman insisted on cutting his loaf into thin slices in front of Oğuz, examining each one like a detective, and then made him stay for tea. A student admitted she had already eaten her whole loaf on the way to the bus stop, and looked so worried that Oğuz had to reassure her that she would have noticed.

Hacer, meanwhile, was having a similar experience on the other side of the hill. The imam's wife searched three loaves with a fork. A young couple with a baby offered to help her look in other houses. By noon, they had checked twenty-four of the twenty-six names. No ring.

The last two were the hardest. One was a tourist from Istanbul who had bought a loaf for the ferry and was probably halfway to Rize by now. The other was Nazmi Bey, a retired judge who lived alone at the top of the hill, who was famous for being the most bad-tempered man in the neighbourhood, and who had once complained to the council because Hacer's bakery smelled too good in the mornings.

Neither of them wanted to go; both were deeply apprehensive. In the end, they went together. They climbed the icy hill, knocked on Nazmi Bey's door and waited. Nobody answered. They knocked again. Nothing. Feeling gloomy, they walked back down to the bakery, already composing in their heads what Hacer would tell her husband.

There, sitting on the bench outside the bakery door, covered in a thin layer of snow, was Nazmi Bey. He had been waiting for more than an hour. In his gloved hand he held a small paper bag, and in the paper bag was half a loaf, and in the half a loaf, shining slightly, was the ring.

“I almost broke a tooth,” he said, without any greeting. “I came to return it. The bakery was closed. I have been sitting here like a fool.”

Hacer burst into tears and hugged him, which clearly shocked him far more than the ring had. Oğuz made tea. For the first time in anyone's memory, Nazmi Bey came inside the bakery, sat by the warm oven and stayed for an hour, telling them stories about strange things people had tried to hide during his years in court.

Ironically, the man who once complained about the smell of her bread has come in every morning at seven since that day. He buys one loaf, which he breaks open in front of the counter and examines carefully before he leaves. Hacer has never charged him for it. And she now keeps her ring on a chain around her neck, under her apron, where the dough cannot reach it.

questions.q: How did Hacer and Oğuz try to find the ring?
options: They made a list of the morning's customers and visited each one.
They put a notice in the local newspaper.
They asked the police to search the houses.
They baked new loaves to replace the old ones.
questions.explain: Sabahki müşterilerin listesini çıkarıp karda kapı kapı dolaştılar. Doğru cevap: "They made a list of the morning's customers and visited each one."

questions.q: Why did nobody answer at Nazmi Bey's house?
options: He had gone on the ferry to Rize.
He did not want to talk to Hacer.
He was waiting outside the bakery to return the ring.
He was asleep after eating his bread.
questions.explain: Nazmi Bey yüzüğü geri vermek için bir saattir fırının önündeki bankta bekliyordu. Doğru cevap: "He was waiting outside the bakery to return the ring."

title: Who Is Eating My Lunch?
text:
Ji-woo had been working at a small design company in Seoul for three months when her lunch began to disappear. It was always the same lunch: rolls of kimbap that her mother made for her on Sunday evenings, packed in a green plastic box with her name written on the lid in black marker. She left the box in the office fridge every morning. On Monday, at lunchtime, it was half empty. On Tuesday, it was completely empty, and someone had politely washed the box and put it back.

At first she was too shy to say anything. She was the youngest designer in the office, and she did not want to cause trouble. She bought lunch from the convenience store downstairs and told herself it had been a mistake. But on Wednesday, it happened again, and on Thursday, and by Friday Ji-woo was no longer shy. She was outraged.

She approached the problem the way she approached a difficult design: methodically. That weekend she drew a plan of the office and made a spreadsheet of everyone who used the kitchen. There were eleven people. She noted who arrived early, who stayed late, who often skipped lunch and who had been seen near the fridge. By Sunday night, she had narrowed it down to four suspects, each of whom deserved careful scrutiny.

The first was Min-jun, a programmer who ate constantly and was always complaining that he was hungry. The second was the office manager, Mrs Choi, who had a key to everything. The third was a quiet intern called Seo-yeon, who had started at the same time as Ji-woo and sometimes looked as if she had not slept. The fourth suspect she hardly dared to write down. It was the director himself, Mr Park, who was usually the first to arrive in the morning.

She needed conclusive proof. On Sunday evening, she asked her mother to make one extra roll of kimbap, and to fill it, very carefully, with the hottest chilli paste in the house. Her mother, who had heard the whole story and was even angrier than Ji-woo, added a generous spoonful of crushed dried chillies as well. They placed the special roll in the middle of the box, where it looked exactly like the others.

On Monday, Ji-woo sat at her desk and pretended to work. At ten past eleven, she heard the fridge door open in the kitchen. A minute later there was a strange choking sound, followed by the sound of running water, followed by a long, desperate silence.

She walked calmly into the kitchen. Standing at the sink, red in the face, with tears streaming down his cheeks and a carton of milk in his hand, was Mr Park. She had found the culprit.

For a moment neither of them spoke. Then the director, still unable to breathe properly, waved his hand towards the green box and tried to explain. He had thought, he said between gasps, that the kimbap was for everyone. At his previous company, people often brought food from home to share. He had found the box every morning, eaten a few pieces, and even washed it, because he did not want to be rude. He had assumed it was a kind gesture from someone who knew he never ate breakfast.

“It has my name on it,” said Ji-woo.

Mr Park put on his glasses, which he had not been wearing for three weeks because he had broken one arm of them, and read the lid. He went even redder, which Ji-woo would not have thought possible.

He was deeply apologetic, and said sorry so many times that she eventually began to feel sorry for him. He told her, a little sadly, that his wife had moved to Busan for a year to look after her elderly mother, and that he had more or less stopped cooking. The kimbap, he said, had tasted like home.

Unsurprisingly, the story spread through the office within an hour. Min-jun, baffled at first, laughed so hard he had to leave the room. Mrs Choi made a new rule that all food in the fridge must be labelled in letters at least two centimetres high.

But something else changed, too. The following Monday, Ji-woo's green box contained twice as many rolls as usual, with a small note from her mother: “For the director. Not spicy.” Ji-woo and Mr Park ate them together at the kitchen table. Soon Seo-yeon joined them, and then Min-jun, and before long the whole office was sharing lunch on Mondays, each person bringing something from home.

Mr Park now brings the dessert. He has also bought new glasses.

questions.q: How did Ji-woo catch the person eating her lunch?
options: She hid a camera in the kitchen.
She asked Mrs Choi to lock the fridge.
She followed each suspect at lunchtime.
She put an extremely spicy roll in her box.
questions.explain: Annesiyle birlikte kutunun ortasına çok acı bir kimbap koydu; Mr Park bunu yiyince yakalandı. Doğru cevap: "She put an extremely spicy roll in her box."

questions.q: Why had Mr Park been eating the kimbap?
options: He wanted to test the new designer.
He believed the food had been left for everyone to share.
He knew it was Ji-woo's and thought it was funny.
Mrs Choi had told him to clean the fridge.
questions.explain: Mr Park, eski şirketindeki alışkanlıkla yemeğin herkes için bırakıldığını sanmıştı; gözlüğü kırık olduğu için kapaktaki ismi de okuyamamıştı. Doğru cevap: "He believed the food had been left for everyone to share."

title: The Joy of Being a Beginner
text:
Last spring, at the age of thirty-four, I bought a cheap sketchbook and a box of pencils and decided to learn to draw. I had no talent and no plan. I simply wanted to do something I was bad at, and to do it without anyone giving me a grade. For most of my adult life I had chosen activities that I was already good at, because being good at things feels safe. Being a beginner, by contrast, feels a little like standing in the street in your pyjamas.

My first drawings were, to put it kindly, mediocre. A cup looked like a bucket. My neighbour's cat, who sat very patiently for me one afternoon, came out looking like a small, worried potato. I laughed so hard that the cat left. In the past, a result like that would have dampened my enthusiasm for weeks. This time, strangely, it did the opposite. Because I expected nothing, every tiny improvement felt like a gift.

There is a particular pleasure in the early stage of learning that experts rarely enjoy. When you know almost nothing, progress is fast and easy to see. On Monday you cannot draw a shadow; by Friday you can draw one that looks roughly as if it belongs to the object. Nobody at the top of a field gets that kind of weekly reward. A concert pianist may practise for a year to play one passage slightly better. A beginner improves by trial and error almost every evening.

Being a beginner also changed how I behaved with other people. At work I am usually the one who explains things. In the drawing class I joined at the community centre, I was the one asking naive questions. Why does my circle look flat? How do you know where the light is coming from? The teacher, a retired architect with a wry sense of humour, never made me feel foolish. She once told me that the most dangerous student is not the one who knows nothing, but the one who has stopped asking. I have thought about that sentence many times since.

Of course, there were evenings when I wanted to give up. Learning anything new has a way of exposing your shortcomings, and some nights the gap between what I could see and what I could draw felt enormous. On those nights I followed a simple rule of thumb: draw one thing, however small, and then stop. A spoon. A key. My own left hand. Often that single drawing turned into five, because the hardest part was simply starting. Small, regular effort paid dividends that big, rare bursts of energy never did.

I think many of us lose sight of this as we grow older. School teaches us to collect correct answers, and exams teach us to fear mistakes. Both are useful, but they can leave us with the idea that being wrong is something shameful. Drawing reminded me that mistakes are simply information. A line in the wrong place shows you where the right place is. In hindsight, I wish I had understood this when I was a student, sitting in front of practice tests and feeling that each wrong answer was a small judgement on my worth.

I am still not a good artist, and I may never be one. But my sketchbook is nearly full, and when I turn its pages I can watch myself learning, line by line. The worried potato is still there on page three. I would not remove it for anything. It is the clearest proof I have that every skill begins somewhere awkward, and that the awkward beginning is nothing to hide. If you have spent a long year learning one difficult thing, perhaps the best reward is to start learning another, just for fun, and to let yourself be terrible at it for a while.

questions.q: Why did the writer's poor first drawings not discourage her this time?
options: Her teacher had told her to ignore them.
Because she expected nothing, every small improvement felt like a gift.
She compared them with her neighbour's drawings and felt better.
She had drawn a lot as a child and knew she would improve.
questions.explain: Yazar hiçbir beklentisi olmadığı için her küçük ilerlemenin bir armağan gibi geldiğini söylüyor; doğru yanıt 'Because she expected nothing, every small improvement felt like a gift.'

questions.q: What does the writer say about mistakes?
options: They should be hidden from other people.
They prove that a person has no talent.
They are information that shows where the right answer is.
They only matter in exams.
questions.explain: Yazar hataların yalnızca bilgi olduğunu, yanlış yerdeki bir çizginin doğru yeri gösterdiğini anlatıyor: 'They are information that shows where the right answer is.'

title: In Praise of the Wrong Turn
text:
A few summers ago my phone died on the second afternoon of a holiday, and I discovered that I had almost forgotten how to be lost. I was in a small coastal town whose name I will keep to myself, partly because I am not sure I could find it again. My map, my tickets and my hotel address were all inside a black screen. For about ten minutes I felt a rising panic. Then, because there was nothing else to do, I started walking.

Modern travel is built to prevent wrong turns. Our phones tell us where to eat, which way to walk and how long it will take, and they swiftly find a new route the moment we drift off the path. This is enormously useful, and I would not want to return to the days of folding paper maps in the wind. Yet something is lost when every step is planned beforehand. The trip becomes a list to complete rather than a place to discover.

Without my phone, the town unfolded slowly, the way towns used to. I followed a narrow street simply because it smelled of fresh bread, and found a bakery so small that the baker had to step outside so that I could step in. I climbed a staircase that seemed to lead nowhere and arrived at a tiny square where old men were playing cards under a fig tree. One of them, noticing my confused face, asked where I was going. When I admitted that I had no idea, he laughed and said that this was the best way to arrive anywhere.

I spent the rest of the afternoon in a pleasant lull, with no schedule and no reviews to read. I ate whatever the café had left, which turned out to be a stellar plate of grilled sardines. I watched a wedding party pass with a band playing slightly out of tune. I got properly lost twice more and, each time, asked a stranger for help. Every conversation was short and clumsy, a mixture of gestures, smiles and the four words I knew in the local language, but each one left me feeling more welcome than any guidebook could.

That evening, in a reflective mood, I wondered why the day felt so vivid. Psychologists sometimes say that we remember new experiences more clearly than routine ones, because the brain pays closer attention when it cannot predict what comes next. I cannot judge the science, but it matches my experience. I remember almost nothing about the famous church I had planned to visit that day. I remember the baker's flour-covered hands, the card players' arguments and the exact blue of a door I passed three times without meaning to.

I am not suggesting that anyone should throw away their phone or wander into danger. Getting lost works best in safe places, in daylight, with enough time and a little money in your pocket. But I still feel a little nostalgic for that town, and I have started to leave room for unforeseen moments when I travel. I plan the first day and leave the second one empty. I walk in one direction until something interesting appears, and I let small surprises steer the route.

There is a lesson here that reaches beyond holidays. Much of life, especially the life of a student, is about following the most efficient route from one goal to the next. That discipline is valuable, and it is often what gets us through a hard year. But when the goal has been reached, it is worth remembering that a wrong turn can be a gift. Sometimes the street you never meant to take leads to the bread you will still be thinking about years later.

questions.q: What did the old man say when the writer admitted she had no idea where she was going?
options: He told her the town was dangerous at night.
He offered to lend her his phone.
He gave her directions back to her hotel.
He laughed and said it was the best way to arrive anywhere.
questions.explain: Yaşlı adam gülüp bunun herhangi bir yere varmanın en iyi yolu olduğunu söylüyor: 'He laughed and said it was the best way to arrive anywhere.'

questions.q: What does the writer do now when she travels?
options: She plans the first day and leaves the second one empty.
She plans every hour of the trip carefully.
She never asks strangers for help.
She always travels without a phone.
questions.explain: Yazar artık ilk günü planlayıp ikinci günü boş bıraktığını söylüyor: 'She plans the first day and leaves the second one empty.' Telefonu tamamen bırakmayı ise önermiyor.

title: Friends Who Pick Up Where They Left Off
text:
I have a friend called Deniz whom I see perhaps once every two years. We met at university, shared a terrible flat with a leaking roof, and then life sent us in different directions: she to a hospital in another country, I to an office in Ankara. She is the closest thing I have to a sibling, yet we are both bad at keeping in touch. Weeks go by without a message, and sometimes months. Still, whenever we meet, the old rapport returns at once, and the conversation starts in the middle, as if we had paused it the day before.

For a long time I felt guilty about this. I assumed that real friendship required constant contact, and that a friend who did not call every week was somehow failing. Social media did not help. It showed me other people's friendships as an incessant stream of shared dinners, birthday photos and long affectionate comments. Compared with that bright display, my own friendships looked thin and neglected.

It took me years to see that there are different kinds of friendship, and that each kind has its own rhythm. Some friends are part of our daily lives: the colleague we have lunch with, the neighbour who waters our plants. These friendships are built on frequency. Others are built on depth. They may be quiet for long stretches, but the bond underneath them does not weaken. When Deniz and I meet, we do not need to recap everything that has happened. We share the gist in five minutes and then talk about what really matters.

I think the secret lies partly in shared history. Two people who have been naive together, made the same blunders and laughed at the same disasters carry a kind of private language. A single word can bring back a whole evening. When Deniz says 'the soup', we both start laughing, because we remember the night we tried to cook for twenty guests with one pot and no recipe. Nobody else would find it funny, which is exactly the point. Memories like these form a quiet foundation that years of silence cannot remove.

Even so, I have learned that deep friendships need a little care. Silence is not the same as neglect, but it can become neglect if we allow it to continue indefinitely. A short message saying 'I saw this and thought of you' costs almost nothing, and it keeps the connection alive. I have started to send such messages without worrying whether they are interesting enough. Usually they are not interesting at all. They simply say: you are still in my life.

There is also a lesson here about being kind to ourselves. During a long and demanding year, many of us become the friend who disappears. We cancel plans, forget birthdays and reply to messages days late. It is easy to feel ashamed of this and to assume that the damage is permanent. In my experience, good friends understand. They have had demanding years too. The friendships worth keeping are usually strong enough to survive a period of silence, and they often blossom anew once the pressure is over.

Last month Deniz visited for a weekend. We walked for hours, ate too much and stayed up far later than people our age should. On Sunday evening, as she left for the airport, she said, 'See you in two years, then.' We both laughed, because we knew it was probably true and that it did not matter. Some friendships are like a well-kept room in a house you rarely visit. The door may stay closed for a long time, but when you open it, everything is still exactly where you left it, and the light comes in just the same.

questions.q: Why did the writer once feel guilty about her friendship with Deniz?
options: She had forgotten Deniz's birthday several times.
Deniz had complained about her long silences.
She believed that real friendship required constant contact.
They had argued about their shared flat.
questions.explain: Yazar uzun süre gerçek dostluğun sürekli iletişim gerektirdiğini düşündüğü için suçluluk duyduğunu söylüyor: 'She believed that real friendship required constant contact.'

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about friendships during a demanding year?
options: Strong friendships can survive a period of silence and grow again later.
Friends who disappear during hard times should be forgotten.
People should never cancel plans with friends.
Social media is the best way to keep friendships alive.
questions.explain: Yazar değerli dostlukların bir sessizlik dönemini atlatacak kadar güçlü olduğunu ve baskı bitince yeniden canlandığını söylüyor: 'Strong friendships can survive a period of silence and grow again later.'

title: The Table with One Short Leg
text:
The most important piece of furniture in my childhood was not a bed or a sofa but a wooden kitchen table with one short leg. My father kept a folded piece of cardboard under that leg for nearly twenty years, and he replaced it every time it wore out, as seriously as if he were repairing a bridge. Nobody ever suggested buying a new table. It would have felt like replacing a member of the family.

That table was where everything happened. In the morning it held bread, olives, cheese and the sound of the radio. In the afternoon it became my desk, covered with textbooks, erasers and the remains of a biscuit. In the evening it was where we ate, argued, made up and argued again, usually about football, which was a perennial subject in our house. My mother paid the bills at one end while my brother built model aeroplanes at the other, and the smell of glue mixed with the smell of onions in a way that I still connect with home.

It is strange how ordinary objects become containers for memory. If you asked me to describe a single conversation from my childhood, I might struggle. But if I picture the table, with its scratches, its burn mark from a hot pan and the small initials my brother cut into it when he was seven, whole evenings come back. I can hear my grandmother telling the same anecdote about her wedding for the hundredth time, and I can see everyone pretending, out of kindness, that it was the first.

In hindsight, the table also taught me things I only understood later. It was at that table that I learned to do homework with noise around me, a skill that served me well in crowded libraries. It was where I learned that people can disagree loudly and still love each other, and that a quarrel at dinner does not have to spoil dessert. It was where my parents, who had little money and spent it sparingly, showed me that a meal does not need to be impressive to be generous. Lentil soup and bread, shared with whoever happened to visit, felt like a feast.

When my parents moved to a smaller flat a few years ago, the table finally had to go. Understandably, there was simply no space for it. We held a kind of farewell dinner, half joking and half serious, and my brother made a short speech. Then the table went to a young couple who had just moved into the building, cardboard and all. I felt a momentary sadness watching it leave, but also an odd pleasure. Someone else's children would now do their homework on it, scratch it and spill tea on it.

Since then I have paid more attention to the ordinary objects in my own life. I am not nostalgic by nature, but I notice them now: the chipped mug I drink from every morning, the lamp by which I read late at night, the worn armchair where I fall asleep over novels. None of these things are valuable, and some of them are, frankly, a little shabby. But they quietly hold the shape of my days. They are the background against which everything important takes place.

We tend to remember life through its momentous events: graduations, weddings, departures. Those moments matter, but they are rare, and most of life happens in between. It happens at kitchen tables, over tea and toast, in conversations nobody records. A modest upbringing taught me that long before I could put it into words. If you are tired after a long year, it may be worth taking a moment to notice the ordinary things that have carried you through it: the desk, the mug, the chair. They have been doing their quiet work all along, without asking for anything in return.

questions.q: Why did the family never buy a new kitchen table?
options: A new table was too expensive for them.
The father was planning to repair the old one properly.
Their flat was too small for a bigger table.
Replacing it would have felt like replacing a member of the family.
questions.explain: Yazar masayı değiştirmenin bir aile üyesini değiştirmek gibi geleceğini söylüyor: 'Replacing it would have felt like replacing a member of the family.'

questions.q: What happened to the table when the writer's parents moved?
options: It went to a young couple who had just moved into the building.
The writer took it to her own flat.
The brother sold it to a furniture shop.
It was broken up because of its short leg.
questions.explain: Masa, binaya yeni taşınan genç bir çifte verildi: 'It went to a young couple who had just moved into the building.'

title: Lessons from a Shoe Shop
text:
The summer I turned seventeen, I worked in a shoe shop on a busy street in my hometown. I had imagined the job would involve standing around, looking bored and occasionally taking a box down from a shelf. Instead, it turned out to be one of the most useful lessons of my life, though I did not realise it at the time. Most of what I know about patience, I learned on my knees, helping strangers with their laces.

The owner, Mr Selim, was a short, tidy man in his sixties who had sold shoes for forty years. He was conscientious about everything, from the order of the boxes to the shine on the window. He also had an almost magical ability to judge a customer's size from across the room, and he rarely made a mistake. On my first morning he gave me one instruction: 'Never tell a customer their feet are big. Tell them the shoe is small.' I thought it was a joke. It was, in fact, the whole philosophy of the shop.

I was not a natural salesman. In the first week I made blunder after blunder. I brought the wrong colours, mixed up shoes from different pairs and once, unforgettably, tried to sell a pair of winter boots to a woman who had come in for sandals. Mr Selim never shouted. He would simply appear beside me, solve the problem in a few seconds and then explain, quietly and later, what I should have noticed. His corrections were brief, specific and never cruel, which is probably why I remember them so clearly.

The most important thing he taught me was to listen. Customers rarely said exactly what they wanted. A man asking for 'something comfortable' might really want something that would impress his new colleagues. A grandmother looking for school shoes for her grandson might mostly want someone to talk to. Mr Selim was astute and observant, and he could hear the question behind the question. He let people talk, asked one or two gentle questions and only then went to the shelves. Ironically, the less he tried to sell, the more he sold, and many customers returned year after year because of the rapport he built with them.

I also learned that work has a rhythm of its own. There were mornings so quiet that we dusted the same shelves three times, and Saturday afternoons so busy that the floor disappeared under open boxes. At first the busy hours exhausted me and the quiet hours bored me. By August I had come to appreciate both. The rush brought a kind of shared energy, and the lull afterwards was a respite in which Mr Selim told stories about the street as it had been when he was young.

When the summer ended, he paid me my last wages in an envelope and gave me, as a gift, a pair of black leather shoes. 'For your university interviews,' he said. They were half a size too big, which made us both laugh, because it was the first time I had ever seen him get a size wrong. I wore them anyway, with an extra pair of socks, for years.

I have had several jobs since then, most of them in offices, and some of them more impressive on paper. Yet I often find myself using lessons from that shop. When a colleague asks for one thing but seems to need another, I think of the grandmother and her grandson. When I have to point out someone's mistake, I try to say 'the shoe is small' rather than 'your feet are big'. No job is too small to teach you something, provided you pay attention. In hindsight, that summer gave me far more than wages. It gave me a way of working with people that has served me ever since.

questions.q: What was the real meaning of Mr Selim's instruction about feet and shoes?
options: Customers should always buy a bigger size.
Shoes must be measured carefully before they are sold.
A customer should never be made to feel at fault.
The shop only sold small sizes.
questions.explain: Talimatın amacı müşteriyi hiçbir zaman kusurlu hissettirmemekti; yazar bugün de birinin hatasını söylerken bu ilkeyi kullanıyor: 'A customer should never be made to feel at fault.'

questions.q: Why did the writer and Mr Selim laugh when he gave her the leather shoes?
options: The shoes were for winter, not for summer.
They were too big, and she had never seen him get a size wrong before.
The envelope with her wages was empty.
She had already bought the same pair herself.
questions.explain: Ayakkabılar yarım numara büyüktü ve yazar onun ilk kez numarada yanıldığını görüyordu: 'They were too big, and she had never seen him get a size wrong before.'

title: One Page a Night
text:
For years I believed that changing my life required a dramatic decision. Every January I made ambitious plans: I would run five kilometres every morning, read fifty books, learn Spanish and stop eating sugar. My January energy always proved fleeting, and by the middle of February, predictably, I had abandoned all of these plans. They were too big, and when I failed at one part I felt I had failed at everything. Then a friend gave me a piece of advice so modest that I almost ignored it.

'Choose one tiny thing,' she said, 'so small that you cannot say no to it. Do it every day. Don't add anything else until it feels automatic.' She had started, she told me, by doing two push-ups each morning. Two. Not twenty. I laughed at her, but she was the fittest person I knew, so I decided to try. My tiny thing was to read one page of a book every night before sleep. Not a chapter, not an hour. One page.

The first week felt almost silly. I would read my single page, close the book and turn off the light. But something interesting happened in the second week. Often, after one page, I wanted to read another, and then another. Some nights I read for an hour. Other nights, when I was exhausted, I read exactly one page and stopped, with no guilt at all. The rule was easy to keep precisely because it asked so little. And because I never broke it, the habit began to take root.

I have since read a little about why this approach works. Researchers who study behaviour suggest that the hardest part of any action is often the start, and that once we begin, continuing is much easier. A small habit also avoids a common trap: the feeling that if we cannot do something perfectly, there is no point doing it at all. That kind of thinking is counterproductive. It turns every missed day into a disaster, every small step into a disappointment, and every evening into an occasion for relentless criticism of ourselves.

Of course, tiny habits are not magic. One page a day will not turn anyone into a great scholar overnight, and some goals do require long, hard effort. But small habits have a ripple effect. Reading every night changed the way my evenings felt. I spent less time habitually scrolling through my phone, slept a little better and had more to talk about with friends. One small change gently nudged several others in the same direction, without any of the struggle my grand January plans had involved.

There is another quiet benefit that I did not expect. Keeping a small promise to yourself, day after day, slowly builds trust. After months of reading a page every night, I began to believe that I was someone who could follow through. That belief made other changes feel possible. I added a short walk after lunch. Later, I started writing three sentences in a notebook each evening. None of these steps was impressive on its own, but together they reshaped my days.

If you have spent a year following a demanding study plan, the idea of building new habits may sound exhausting. You may simply want to rest, and that is reasonable. But when you are ready, consider starting smaller than seems sensible. Pick one tiny thing you enjoy, and protect it. It does not need to be useful or ambitious. It only needs to be yours. Over time, a single page can grow into a library, and a single step into a long and pleasant walk.

questions.q: What was the friend's advice?
options: Make one big plan each January and follow it strictly.
Do two hundred push-ups every morning.
Read at least one chapter every night.
Choose one tiny daily action and add nothing else until it feels automatic.
questions.explain: Arkadaşı, hayır diyemeyeceği kadar küçük bir şey seçip otomatikleşene kadar başka bir şey eklememesini öneriyor: 'Choose one tiny daily action and add nothing else until it feels automatic.'

questions.q: According to the writer, what did keeping a small promise to herself bring?
options: It made her believe she could follow through, so other changes felt possible.
It helped her learn Spanish within a year.
It allowed her to stop eating sugar completely.
It made her friends want to copy her.
questions.explain: Kendine verdiği küçük sözü tutmak yavaş yavaş güven inşa etti ve başka değişiklikleri mümkün kıldı: 'It made her believe she could follow through, so other changes felt possible.'

title: In Praise of Waiting
text:
I used to hate waiting. Queues at the post office, delayed trains, the long minutes in a doctor's surgery with a magazine from three years ago: all of it felt like time stolen from my life. Like most people, I developed a habit of filling every gap with my phone and its incessant stream of news. Thirty seconds at a traffic light was enough to check my messages. Two minutes in a lift was enough to read the headlines. I was never bored, and I was rarely at rest.

Then, one winter, I broke my phone screen and had to wait a week for a repair. During that week I rediscovered something I had almost forgotten: the strange, slow texture of waiting with nothing to do. At first it was uncomfortable. At the bus stop my hand kept reaching for my empty pocket. Unexpectedly, after a few days the discomfort faded, and something else took its place.

I began to notice things. The woman at the bus stop who fed the pigeons from a paper bag every morning at exactly the same time. The way the light changed on the buildings opposite as the sun rose. The conversations of strangers, which were often funnier than anything I might have read online. Once, an elderly man next to me told me, without being asked and with a wistful smile, the entire history of the street, one anecdote after another, including which shop had once been a cinema and which bakery had sold the best bread in 1974.

I also noticed what my own mind did when it was left alone. It wandered. It returned to old memories, made odd connections and occasionally came up with ideas I would never have reached by trying hard. Some researchers have suggested that these idle moments matter, and that a mind allowed to drift may help us sort our memories and find new solutions. I cannot say how strong that evidence is, but I know that several of my best ideas that week arrived at bus stops.

There is a long tradition of praising idleness, and it is easy to sound pretentious about it. I do not believe that waiting is always pleasant, or that boredom is always productive. A long delay at an airport when you are trying to reach a funeral is no gift. But much of our waiting is neither urgent nor painful. It is simply empty, and we have become oddly afraid of emptiness. We rush to fill it, as if a quiet minute were a problem to be solved.

When my phone came back, I kept a small rule: at least once a day, I wait without it. At the bus stop, in the queue, in the corridor before a meeting, I simply look around. Some days I see nothing worth mentioning. Other days I watch a child explain the rules of an invented game to her grandfather, or a pair of sparrows quarrel over a crumb. These are tiny scenes, fleeting and ordinary, but they make me feel more present in my own life.

If you have spent months studying, your mind has probably been working without a pause. Every free moment may have been filled with vocabulary lists and practice questions. That effort deserves respect. But now and then, give your mind a respite. Enjoy the lull between one task and the next. Sit on a bench and wait for nothing in particular. Let your thoughts go where they want. You may find, as I did, that a few empty minutes are not wasted at all. They are where the mind quietly puts its house in order.

questions.q: What happened while the writer was waiting for her phone to be repaired?
options: She began to notice people and small scenes around her.
She became more impatient with strangers.
She started reading old magazines in waiting rooms.
She stopped taking the bus to work.
questions.explain: Telefon tamirdeyken yazar çevresindeki insanları ve küçük sahneleri fark etmeye başladı: 'She began to notice people and small scenes around her.'

questions.q: What rule did the writer keep after her phone came back?
options: She never uses her phone outdoors.
She talks to at least one stranger every day.
She waits without her phone at least once a day.
She turns her phone off every evening.
questions.explain: Yazar telefonu geri gelince günde en az bir kez telefonsuz bekleme kuralı koydu: 'She waits without her phone at least once a day.'

title: Very Embarrassed in Spain
text:
On my second day as an exchange student in Spain, I wanted to tell my host family that I was embarrassed about arriving late for dinner. I had studied Spanish for three years, and I was rather proud of my grammar. So I said, confidently, 'Estoy muy embarazada.' The table went silent. Then my host mother put down her spoon and asked, very gently, whether I needed to see a doctor. I had just announced that I was very pregnant.

It is one of the oldest jokes among language learners, and I had walked straight into it. The Spanish word looks as if it should mean 'embarrassed', but it does not. Such words are often called false friends, and every pair of languages has dozens of them. It was a classic blunder. At that moment, however, I was not thinking about linguistics. I was thinking about how quickly I could disappear under the table.

What happened next changed the way I learned the language. After the first shock, my host family laughed so hard that the father had to wipe his eyes. Then they began, one by one, to tell me their own stories of language disasters: the grandfather's attempt to order fish in Paris, and the daughter's English exam, in which she had described her teacher as 'very sensible' when she meant 'very sensitive'. By the end of dinner I was no longer an awkward guest. I was part of a shared joke, and the laughter built a rapport that perfect grammar could never have built.

Until then I had been a cautious speaker. I would build a sentence in my head, check every ending and only then say it, by which time the conversation had usually moved on. I was so afraid of mistakes that I hardly spoke at all. My Spanish was correct, but it was also nearly silent. The pregnancy incident, oddly, took that fear away. I had already made the most embarrassing mistake I could imagine, and nothing terrible had happened. What else was there to be afraid of?

After that, I spoke more, and my fluency grew quickly. I still made mistakes, of course, dozens every day. I confused verbs, forgot genders and occasionally invented words that did not exist. When words failed me, gestures and body language filled the gaps. People corrected me kindly, and my pronunciation slowly improved. Each correction stuck in my memory because it was attached to a real conversation, a face and often a laugh. I learned more Spanish in those four months of clumsy talking than in three years of careful study.

I now think that the fear of looking foolish is one of the biggest impediments to learning a language, perhaps bigger than any difficulty with grammar or vocabulary. Exams, for good reasons, reward accuracy. But real communication rewards courage. A native speaker will almost always prefer a friendly sentence with three mistakes to a perfect silence. Most people are touched, not annoyed, when a foreigner tries to speak their mother tongue, and they are usually happy to help.

If you have spent a year preparing for an exam, you have built something valuable: a solid knowledge of how the language works. The next step is to let that knowledge out into the world, imperfectly and without too much worry. Speak to tourists, join a conversation club, write to someone in English. You will make mistakes, some of them funny. Collect them. In hindsight, you may find, as I did, that your favourite memories of a language are not the sentences you got right, but the ones you got gloriously, unforgettably wrong.

options: That she was very hungry.
That she was angry about dinner.
That she needed to see a doctor.
That she was very pregnant.
questions.explain: İspanyolca 'embarazada' kelimesi 'hamile' anlamına geldiği için yazar farkında olmadan çok hamile olduğunu söylemiş oldu: 'That she was very pregnant.'

options: She stopped speaking Spanish at home.
She lost her fear of mistakes and began to speak much more.
She decided to study only from grammar books.
She asked her host family to speak English with her.

title: A Suitcase Full of Worries
text:
The first time I travelled abroad alone, I took a suitcase so heavy that the airline charged me extra and a kind stranger had to help me lift it onto a train. I had packed hastily the night before. Inside were three pairs of shoes, two thick jumpers for a summer trip, a hairdryer the hotel already provided, four novels and a first-aid kit large enough for a football team. I used perhaps a third of it. For two weeks I dragged the rest up stairs, across bridges and over stone streets, cursing my own caution.

Packing, I have come to believe, is a kind of portrait of our fears. Every unnecessary item is meant to stave off an imagined disaster. What if it rains every day? What if there are no shops? What if I am invited to a wedding? Each possibility seems reasonable on its own, and for someone with my propensity to worry, each item goes into the case. The result is a suitcase full of worries, carried at great effort across half a continent.

On my third or fourth trip I tried a different approach, partly out of necessity, because I was flying with a small airline that allowed only a cabin bag. I packed for one week and planned to wash clothes on the way. I took one book instead of four, one pair of comfortable shoes and a light jacket. Standing at the door with my small bag, I felt apprehensive and, at the same time, oddly free. Surely I had forgotten something important.

I had not. Or rather, the few things I had forgotten turned out not to matter. Learning by trial and error, I solved each problem as it came. When I needed a toothbrush, I bought one at a pharmacy and practised my bad Italian with a patient shop assistant. When it rained, I bought a cheap umbrella that later became a souvenir. When I ran out of things to read, I swapped my book with another traveller at a hostel, and we spent the evening discussing the endings. Each small lack turned into a small adventure.

Travelling light changed the trip itself. Without a heavy case, I could walk from the station instead of looking for a taxi. I could change plans swiftly, take a later bus or follow a recommendation from a stranger. I spent less time guarding my belongings and more time looking around. The lightness was physical, but it also seemed to spread into my mood. I was more upbeat, more curious and more willing to say yes.

It is tempting to turn this into a grand lesson about life, and I will try not to push it too far. Some people genuinely need more things when they travel, and there is no prize for suffering in the name of travelling light. Still, I think the suitcase teaches something useful. Many of the things we carry, in bags and in our heads, are there because of problems that may never materialize. Preparing for every unforeseen event can become a burden that weighs down the very experience it is meant to protect.

Exams encourage a similar habit. We collect notes, summaries, word lists and practice tests, afraid that something important will be missing. That careful preparation has its place, and it is often what gets us through. But once the exam is over, it may be worth emptying the suitcase a little. Keep what was truly useful, let go of the rest and leave some space for whatever comes next. You never know what you might want to bring home.

questions.q: According to the writer, what does the way we pack show?
options: How much money we have.
How experienced we are as travellers.
Our taste in clothes.
Our fears about imagined disasters.
questions.explain: Yazara göre bavul hazırlamak korkularımızın bir portresidir; her gereksiz eşya hayali bir felaketi önlemek içindir: 'Our fears about imagined disasters.'

questions.q: What did the writer do when she ran out of things to read?
options: She bought four more novels.
She swapped her book with another traveller at a hostel.
She read the magazines in her hotel.
She downloaded books onto her phone.
questions.explain: Okuyacak bir şeyi kalmayınca kitabını bir hostelde başka bir gezginle değiş tokuş etti: 'She swapped her book with another traveller at a hostel.'

title: After the Last Page
text:
There is a peculiar feeling that comes at the end of something long. I first noticed it after I finished writing my thesis at university. It was the culmination of eighteen months that had shaped every day: what I read, when I slept, even what I talked about at dinner. Then one afternoon I handed it in, walked out of the building and stood on the steps in the sunshine, waiting to feel happy. Instead, I felt strangely empty, like a runner who has crossed the finish line and does not know where to go next.

I have since learned that this feeling is common. Athletes describe it after major competitions, actors after the last night of a long show, and students after the final exam. When a goal has organised our lives for months, its sudden disappearance can leave a gap. The routine, the relentless pressure and even the anxiety had given each day a shape. Without them, the days can feel oddly loose, and we may not know what to do with ourselves.

My first instinct was to fill the gap immediately with a new project. I hastily made lists of courses to take, books to read and skills to learn. Within a week I was nearly as busy as before, twice as tired and close to burnout. A wiser friend, who had finished her own degree a year earlier, told me to stop. 'You have been running for a year and a half,' she said. 'Walk for a while. You do not need to know what is next yet.'

Her advice felt almost uncomfortable, but I followed it and took a short hiatus from all serious plans. I slept late without setting an alarm. I cooked slow meals and invited people to eat them. I read novels that had nothing to do with my subject and walked through parts of the city I had never had time to visit. At first I felt guilty, as if I were wasting time. Gradually the guilt faded, and I began to understand that rest is not the opposite of work. It is the part of work that makes the next effort possible.

It also helps, I think, to take stock of what the long effort has given you, whatever the final result. A year of study changes you in ways that a score cannot measure. You have learned to keep going on difficult days. You have discovered how your mind works, when you concentrate best and what helps you recover from a bad week. You have read hundreds of texts and thousands of words that are now part of you. These things remain, quietly, long after the exam paper has been forgotten.

Celebration matters too, and it is often neglected. We are quick to criticise ourselves for what went wrong and slow to recognise what went right. After my thesis, my family insisted on a small dinner. I almost refused, because the work did not feel finished or perfect. I am glad I went. Hearing the people I loved say they were proud of me helped me see the effort as an achievement, not merely a duty completed. There is no need to be unduly hard on yourself at the end of a long road.

So, if you are reaching the end of a long year, here is some advice from someone who has stood on those sunny steps. Allow yourself to feel a little lost; it will pass. Rest without apology, and enjoy the respite. Celebrate, even if the result is not what you hoped. And when you are ready, which may be sooner or later than you expect, begin anew, choosing your next adventure slowly and with curiosity. The end of one long road is also the beginning of an open field, and there is no hurry to cross it.

questions.q: How did the writer feel just after handing in her thesis?
options: Proud and full of energy.
Strangely empty.
Angry with her teachers.
Ready to start a new degree at once.
questions.explain: Tezini teslim edip basamaklarda dururken mutlu olmayı beklerken tuhaf bir boşluk hissetti: 'Strangely empty.'

questions.q: What did the writer come to understand about rest?
options: It is a waste of valuable time.
It should come only after a new project has started.
It is the part of work that makes the next effort possible.
It is mainly important for athletes and actors.
questions.explain: Yazar dinlenmenin çalışmanın karşıtı olmadığını, bir sonraki çabayı mümkün kılan kısmı olduğunu anladı: 'It is the part of work that makes the next effort possible.'
